1007265304937350|d4c3.headline: Develop with 5...Nf6; grabbing 5...dxc3 opens lines to your king
1007265304937350|d4c3.why: 5...dxc3 grabs a second pawn but opens lines for White's queen: 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 7.Qd5+ forks the king and the bishop on c5, and after 7...Kf8 8.Qxc5+ Black's king has lost the right to castle. 5...Nf6 develops and counterattacks the pawn on e4 instead. After 6.e5 d5 Black hits the bishop on c4, and the knight lands on e4 after 7.Bb5 Ne4.
1007265304937350|d4c3.principle: Take gambit pawns only if you can consolidate: with f7 exposed and the bishop on c5 loose, develop with a counter-threat instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d4

1012847495954800|d7d6.headline: Hit the queen with 3...Nf6 and develop with tempo.
1012847495954800|d7d6.why: 3...d6 is too slow: White plays 4.Bc4, threatening mate on f7, and Black has to spend the next moves defending. 3.Nf3 did nothing for the queen on h5, so 3...Nf6 develops while attacking both the queen and the pawn on e4, and White must move the queen again with 4.Qh4.
1012847495954800|d7d6.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop the piece that attacks it, so each of your developing moves costs them a queen move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

1012847495954800|g7g6.headline: Kick the queen with a developing move: 3...Nf6
1012847495954800|g7g6.why: 3...g6 chases the queen with a pawn move that develops nothing and weakens the kingside, and after 4.Qg5 White simply offers a queen trade, so the error 3.Nf3 goes unpunished. 3...Nf6 develops a knight while attacking both the queen on h5 and the pawn on e4, so White must move the queen again. After 4.Qh4 Black is ahead in development and free to play in the centre.
1012847495954800|g7g6.principle: Against an early queen, attack it with a piece that develops, not with a pawn move that only weakens your position.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

1017365272404305|b1c3.headline: Take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5: e5 has no defender
1017365272404305|b1c3.why: 2...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and not defended at all, and 3.Nc3 gives Black time to fix that: in the engine line 3...d6 holds the pawn and the game is level. 3.Nxe5 just takes it. The theory calls this Busch-Gass gambit unsound; Black can transpose to a Stafford gambit with 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6, but stays a pawn down.
1017365272404305|b1c3.principle: Check what is loose after every opponent move: an undefended centre pawn is worth taking when the replies are under control.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

1017365272404305|d2d3.headline: Take the free e5 pawn
1017365272404305|d2d3.why: 2...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and not defended at all, and 3.d3 fails to capitalise: Black gets time to defend it with 3...d6. 3.Nxe5 simply takes the pawn; the gambit is considered unsound, and if Black hits back with 3...Qh4, either 4.Qe2 or the sharper 4.d4 deals with the threat to f2.
1017365272404305|d2d3.principle: Before a quiet move, check what the opponent left undefended: a central pawn is worth taking when the piece that takes it is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

1017365272404305|d2d4.headline: Take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5; 3.d4 lets Black swap it
1017365272404305|d2d4.why: 2...Bc5 leaves the e5 pawn with no defender. 3.d4 lets Black trade it off with 3...exd4, and after 4.Bc4 d6 5.Nxd4 material is level and so is the game. 3.Nxe5 takes it: the theory calls this gambit unsound, because if 3...Qh4, threatening mate on f2 and hitting the knight, 4.Qe2 meets both threats. In the engine line 3...Nc6 4.Nxc6 dxc6 turns it into a Stafford gambit and you stay a pawn up with a clear advantage.
1017365272404305|d2d4.principle: Start with captures, then check your opponent's forcing replies: here the e5 pawn is free, and the only scary answer, ...Qh4, is met by Qe2.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

1017365272404305|f1c4.headline: Take the free e5 pawn: the Busch-Gass gambit is unsound
1017365272404305|f1c4.why: 2...Bc5 leaves the e5 pawn with no defender, which hands White a clear advantage. 3.Bc4 throws that away by giving Black time for 3...Nc6 or 3...d6, and the game is level again. Take it with 3.Nxe5: Black's idea is 3...Qh4, hitting f2 and the knight, but 4.Qe2 meets both threats, and theory rates the gambit unsound as long as you stay calm.
1017365272404305|f1c4.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when you can meet the threats behind it; declining for safety gives back the advantage the gambit handed you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Bc5/3. Nxe5

105834763665320|d4d3.headline: Develop and guard the pawn instead of pushing it
105834763665320|d4d3.why: 3...d3 gives the pawn back for nothing: after 4.Qxd3 White's queen is developed and Black has spent another move on a pawn. 3...Bc5 develops the bishop to a square where it guards d4, and if White recaptures with 4.Nxd4, Black gets normal Scotch play, here hitting e4 with 4...Nf6.
105834763665320|d4d3.principle: When you can keep material by developing, develop; a pawn push that hands the pawn back develops your opponent's queen instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Nf3

105834763665320|f7f5.headline: Develop with 3...Bc5; 3...f5 drops d4 and weakens your king
105834763665320|f7f5.why: 3...f5 does nothing for the pawn on d4: 4.Nxd4 wins it back with the knight centralised, and the pawn move has weakened Black's king while developing nothing. 3...Bc5 develops the bishop toward the centre with an eye on d4. After 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black attacks e4 and is ahead in development, and 4...Nc6 would transpose to the Classical Scotch.
105834763665320|f7f5.principle: When pawns are traded in the centre, develop a piece toward the contested square instead of making a pawn move away from it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Nf3

1062777786489002|c1b2.headline: The queen on f6 is a target: 8.e5 kicks it
1062777786489002|c1b2.why: 7...Qf6 puts the queen where your e-pawn can hit it. 8.Bb2 is too slow: Black answers 8...d3, and after 9.e5 Qh6 the queen has found a good square and your advantage is gone. 8.e5 claims the centre and attacks the queen at once; after 8...Qd8 she is back home, and 9.Re1 Be7 10.cxd4 wins back a pawn and builds your centre, with a large advantage.
1062777786489002|c1b2.principle: When an enemy piece, especially the queen, stands where one of your pawns can attack it, push the pawn: you gain space and your opponent loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

1086376395792345|d8f6.headline: Don't copy 2.Qf3; develop the knight with 2...Nf6
1086376395792345|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 copies White's mistake: it brings the queen out with four minor pieces at home and takes f6 from Black's own knight, which is exactly what is wrong with 2.Qf3. White just develops with 3.Nc3 and 4.Bc4 and gains time. 2...Nf6 puts the knight on its best square and blocks the queen on f3 from f7.
1086376395792345|d8f6.principle: Answer an early queen by developing, not by bringing out your own; a knight on f6 shuts the queen out of f7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1086376395792345|f7f6.headline: Against 2.Qf3, develop 2...Nf6 instead of pushing the f-pawn
1086376395792345|f7f6.why: 2...f6 develops nothing, takes the best square from Black's king's knight and weakens the diagonal toward Black's king that White's bishop uses after 3.Bc4. 2...Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square and blocks the queen on f3 from f7, so Black can develop freely while White's queen sits in the knight's way.
1086376395792345|f7f6.principle: Answer an early queen with a developing move; a pawn move that weakens your king gives the queen and bishop the target they want.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1086376395792345|g8h6.headline: Answer the early queen with normal development
1086376395792345|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 puts the knight on the rim, where it plays no part in the centre, and White develops calmly with 3.Bc4 and 4.Ne2. 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre and blocks the queen's line to f7; after 3.Bc4 Black can gain space with 3...c6 and ...d5, and the early queen becomes a target.
1086376395792345|g8h6.principle: An early queen on f3 blocks White's own knight and can be attacked; develop normally and gain time against it with pawn moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1095756382312296|d1e2.headline: Punish ...g6 with ...e6: 8.Nb5 jumps at the d6 hole
1095756382312296|d1e2.why: With ...g6 and ...e6 both played, no black pawn can ever guard d6, and your bishop on f4 already eyes d6 and c7. 8.Qe2 is too slow: Black closes the hole with 8...a6 and 9...d6, and the chance is gone. 8.Nb5 jumps straight at those squares: after 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Black's king is stuck on f8, Black's pieces are tied up, and White is close to winning. The theory warns that ...g6 combined with ...e6 weakens the dark squares around Black's king and gives the same 8.Nb5 jump as the punishment.
1095756382312296|d1e2.principle: A square the enemy pawns can no longer cover is an outpost: once ...e6 is played, aim your knight and bishop at d6 before Black can plug it with a piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1095756382312296|e1h1.headline: Strike at d6 with 8.Nb5 before Black castles
1095756382312296|e1h1.why: 8.O-O gives Black time for 8...a6 9.Bb3 Nge7 and castling, and almost all of your huge advantage disappears. Theory warns that combining ...g6 with ...e6 badly weakens the dark squares around Black's king, and with your bishop already on f4 the d6 square is a target. 8.Nb5 aims the knight at d6 and c7 together: after 8...Qa5+ 9.Kf1 Kf8 Black has given up castling, and 10.Bc7 b6 11.Bd6+ Nge7 keeps Black's pieces tied up.
1095756382312296|e1h1.principle: With more pieces out and the enemy king uncastled, open lines and strike at once; give Black one quiet move and Black castles to safety.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1102494195291015|f3g5.headline: Recapture on c3 with a new piece, not a lone f7 raid
1102494195291015|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and 8...Ne5 covers f7: after 9.Nxf7 Nxf7 10.Bxf7+ Kxf7 you have given a knight for a pawn and Black is better. Black's 7...dxc3 grabbed another pawn instead of developing, and the pawn on c3 is attacked once and not defended at all. 8.Nxc3 wins it back while developing toward the centre, and Black is so far behind that the engine's line has 8...Kf8, giving up castling, while you keep a big advantage.
1102494195291015|f3g5.principle: In a gambit you have paid pawns for a lead in development, so each move should bring another piece into the game, not send an already developed knight on a raid that can be parried.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bd6

1110098787406126|c1e3.headline: 6.f3 starts a pawn chase against the bishop and the e6 queen
1110098787406126|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 develops, but it lets Black trade bishops with 6...Bxe2 7.Qxe2 and settle with ...Nf6, ...c6 and ...Nd5; your edge shrinks. As the theory notes say, the early queen checks achieve little and Black's queen blocks the e-pawn. 6.f3 attacks the bishop on g4, and after 6...Bf5 7.g4 Bg6 8.f4 your pawns gain space with tempo, since a pawn on f5 would hit both the queen on e6 and the bishop on g6; Black has to stop it with 8...f5, and White keeps a large advantage.
1110098787406126|c1e3.principle: When the opponent's bishop and early queen stand where your pawns can reach them, advance the pawns with tempo: you gain space and they lose time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

1132065952318888|g5f3.headline: 6...f6 opens the king: check with 7.Qh5+
1132065952318888|g5f3.why: 6...f6 attacks the knight but opens the diagonal from h5 to Black's king. 7.Nf3 just retreats, a second knight move, and Black consolidates with 7...Nf7. 7.Qh5+ uses the diagonal: after 7...Ke7 Black can no longer castle, and 8.Nf7 attacks the queen on d8 and the rook on h8. Following 8...Qe8 9.Bxh6 gxh6 10.Qf3 Rf8 11.Nxh6 White is a pawn up with Black's king stuck in the centre.
1132065952318888|g5f3.principle: When your piece is attacked, look at checks first: a check against a weakened king can answer the threat and win more.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

1189776554630624|c6d4.headline: Against the Scotch, take with the pawn: 3...exd4.
1189776554630624|c6d4.why: 3...Nxd4 trades Black's only developed piece. After 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.Qxd4 White's queen sits in the centre and Black has nothing out. 3...exd4 is played almost every time: it releases the tension and keeps the knight. After 4.Nxd4 Black develops with tempo against White's centre, as with 4...Nf6.
1189776554630624|c6d4.principle: When the centre opens, capture with a pawn and keep your developed pieces rather than trading them off for nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4

1189776554630624|d7d5.headline: Take back on d4; don't open a second front with ...d5
1189776554630624|d7d5.why: 3...d5 leaves e5 to White's knight: 4.Nxe5 dxe4 5.Bb5 pins the knight on c6, and White is well ahead in development while Black has only one piece out. 3...exd4 is played in 99.6% of master games: it releases the central tension and removes White's d-pawn. After 4.Nxd4 Black can develop with tempo by hitting the centre with 4...Bc5 or 4...Nf6.
1189776554630624|d7d5.principle: When White's d-pawn attacks your e5 pawn, trade it off so White is left with one centre pawn, instead of leaving your own pawn hanging.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4

1189776554630624|d7d6.headline: In the Scotch, take with 3...exd4 and free your game
1189776554630624|d7d6.why: 3...d6 keeps the tension but lets White gain space with tempo: 4.d5 kicks the knight to e7, and after 5.c4 g6 6.Nc3 Bg7 7.c5 White is attacking on the queenside while Black is cramped. 3...exd4 is played in 99.6% of master games: it releases the tension and opens the game. After 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops with an attack on e4.
1189776554630624|d7d6.principle: A knight on c6 standing in front of White's d-pawn is a target; trade the pawn off before it can kick the knight and gain space.

1189776554630624|f7f5.headline: Take on d4; don't open your king with f5
1189776554630624|f7f5.why: 3...f5 ignores the attack on e5 and opens the diagonal to your king: after 4.Nxe5 fxe4 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.Qh5+ Black has to walk the king out with 6...Ke7. 3...exd4 releases the tension, removes White's threat of 4.d5 and leads to an open, balanced game; after 4.Nxd4 Black can develop with tempo by 4...Nf6 or 4...Bc5 against the centralised knight.
1189776554630624|f7f5.principle: With the king still in the centre, resolve the central tension first and keep the f-pawn home, since moving it opens lines toward your own king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4

1189776554630624|f7f6.headline: Don't prop up e5 with the f-pawn; take on d4
1189776554630624|f7f6.why: 3...f6 holds e5 but takes f6 from Black's knight and opens the diagonal from c4 to Black's king: in the line 4.Bc4 d6 5.O-O Nge7 6.c3 Bd7 7.Qb3 the bishop and queen line up on f7, and 8.Bf7+ lands. 3...exd4 releases the tension and opens the game with plenty of space for both sides, and after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops normally. Masters choose it in 99.6% of games.
1189776554630624|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with pieces or trade it, not with the f-pawn, which blocks your knight and weakens the squares around your king.

1189776554630624|f8d6.headline: Take 3...exd4; 3...Bd6 blocks your own d-pawn for nothing.
1189776554630624|f8d6.why: White threatens 4.d5, kicking the knight and winning e5, and 3...Bd6 shuts in Black's d-pawn and queen's bishop. After 4.c3 exd4 5.cxd4 White has a full pawn centre and the bishop has to move again with 5...Bb4+. 3...exd4 releases the tension and is played in 99.6% of master games: after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo against the e4 pawn.
1189776554630624|f8d6.principle: When White strikes at e5 with a pawn, capture to release the tension; a bishop standing in front of your d-pawn can't help hold the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4

1189776554630624|g7g6.headline: Release the tension with 3...exd4; 3...g6 drops e5
1189776554630624|g7g6.why: 3...g6 ignores the attack on e5: 4.dxe5 wins the pawn, and after 4...d6 5.exd6 Qxd6 6.Qxd6 Bxd6 the queens are off with Black simply a pawn down. 3...exd4 is played in 99.6% of master games: it releases the tension, and after 4.Nxd4 Black develops with tempo, 4...Nf6 against e4 or 4...Bc5 against the knight.
1189776554630624|g7g6.principle: When a pawn attacks your centre pawn, capture so the trade happens on your terms and your pieces get open lines.

1189776554630624|g8f6.headline: In the Scotch, take on d4 before d5 kicks your knight
1189776554630624|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 ignores the threat to e5: 4.d5 drives the knight on c6 back with 4...Nb8, and 5.Nxe5 wins the pawn. 3...exd4 is played almost every time: it removes the pawn that was attacking, and after 4.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo against e4. Masters choose it in 99.6% of games.
1189776554630624|g8f6.principle: e5 is attacked twice and only the knight on c6 defends it, so trade on d4 before that defender can be driven away.

1206106476480095|d5e6.headline: Keep queens on: 9.Bxc6 wins another pawn against an exposed king
1206106476480095|d5e6.why: 9.Bxe6+ Kxe6 10.Qh3+ Qf5 11.Qxf5+ Kxf5 trades queens, and without them Black's wandering king is no longer in danger, so a good part of your advantage evaporates. 9.Bxc6 removes the knight instead: after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 you win a pawn, your queen hits the bishop on e6 and the rook in the corner, and Black's queenside pawns are broken. With queens still on the board and Black's king on f7, you keep a big attacking advantage.
1206106476480095|d5e6.principle: When you have the attack against an exposed king, keep the queens on and win material with threats; a queen trade lets the advantage fade.

1206106476480095|f3f6.headline: Keep the queens on against the exposed king: 9.Bxc6
1206106476480095|f3f6.why: 9.Qxf6+ trades queens, and after 9...gxf6 10.Bxe6+ Kxe6 Black's king is perfectly safe in an endgame, so most of your advantage evaporates. 9.Bxc6 removes the knight on c6 instead, and after 9...bxc6 10.Qxc6 your queen takes a second pawn with the queens still on the board, against a king that can no longer castle.
1206106476480095|f3f6.principle: Play to your imbalances: your trump is Black's exposed king, so keep the queens on and win material with the minor pieces rather than trading into an endgame.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nxd5/6. Nxf7/6...Kxf7

1251051945717105|a5c7.headline: Develop with 7...Nf6; the queen can move later
1251051945717105|a5c7.why: 7...Qc7 moves the queen again while all four of your minor pieces are still at home. White uses the time: after 8.d5 Bd7 9.Rc1 your queen faces the rook on c1 with only the c3 knight in between, and after 9...Nf6 10.Nf3 Qd8 she has gone back home while White is clearly better. 7...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre; in the line 8.Bc4 Nc6 9.Nf3 Be7 10.O-O O-O the queen does go to c7, with 11...Qc7, but only once your pieces are out and your king is safe.
1251051945717105|a5c7.principle: In the opening, every move should develop a piece or fight for the centre; a queen move that does neither must have a concrete reason, and fear of a future attack is not enough.

1261108510304489|e1h1.headline: Two pawns down, aim at f7 with 7.Qb3
1261108510304489|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is too slow when you are two pawns down: 7...Nf6 8.e5 Ne4 9.cxd4 d5 hits your bishop and Black comes out better. 7.Qb3 lines the queen up behind the bishop on c4 against f7, which only the king defends, so Black has to deal with 8.Bxf7+ at once. In the main line 7...Na5 8.Bxf7+ Kf8 9.Qa4 Kxf7 10.Qxa5 you win back a pawn and the game is level.
1261108510304489|e1h1.principle: When f7 is guarded only by the king, a queen and bishop aimed at it make a threat the opponent must answer before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Be7

1273971384127904|g8h6.headline: Block f7 with 3...Nf6, not with a knight on the rim
1273971384127904|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 stops the mate but puts the knight on the edge, where 4.d4 opens the bishop on c1 onto it; after 4...Qe7 the queen blocks the bishop on f8, and White builds a big centre with 5.Nc3 and 6.d5. 3...Nf6 blocks the queen's line to f7, develops toward the centre and attacks e4. White's queen on f3 has also taken the knight's best square, so after 4.Ne2 Be7 Black castles in comfort.
1273971384127904|g8h6.principle: Parry the threat with a developing move that fights for the centre: from f6 the knight blocks the queen and also attacks e4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qf3

1314504257002276|f1d3.headline: Close the centre with 3.e5 instead of defending with Bd3
1314504257002276|f1d3.why: The theory notes call 3.Bd3 irregular: after 3...dxe4 4.Bxe4 Nf6 Black develops with tempo on the bishop, which must move again, or be swapped for a knight with 5.Nc3 Nxe4 6.Nxe4, giving up the bishop pair. In the line 5.Bf3 Bf5 Black has easy development and is slightly better. 3.e5, the advance variation and the masters' top choice (39.9%), closes the centre and gains space; after 3...Bf5 4.Nf3 e6 5.Be2 White keeps a small edge. 3.Nc3, 3.Nd2 and 3.exd5 are also good.
1314504257002276|f1d3.principle: Don't put a piece where the opponent can make it move again with tempo; every extra move of the same piece is development your opponent gets for free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Bd3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5

1317312578379376|f3c6.headline: The f6 queen guards c6: keep your queen with 10.Qh5+
1317312578379376|f3c6.why: After the Fried Liver sacrifice you are clearly winning, but 10.Qxc6+ grabs a pawn the queen on f6 defends along the sixth rank: 10...Qxc6 wins your queen and turns the game around. 10.Qh5+ keeps the attack instead: 10...g6 loosens Black's kingside, and 11.Qe2 keeps your queen and the pressure on a king stuck in the centre.
1317312578379376|f3c6.principle: Before any capture, and especially a capture with check, count the defenders of the square, including a queen guarding it from along a rank.

132233271809428|a7a6.headline: Break the pin on c6 with 5...Bd7
132233271809428|a7a6.why: 5.Bb5 pins your knight on c6, and White threatens Bxc6+, which 5...a6 does not prevent: after 6.Bxc6+ bxc6 your c-pawns are doubled, and in the line 7.d3 c4 8.dxc4 you end up a pawn down. 5...Bd7 develops and blocks the pin, so if 6.Bxc6 you recapture with the bishop (6...Bxc6) and keep a sound pawn structure. Then the king's knight comes into play with 7...Nh6 and 8...Nf5, and Black is better.
132233271809428|a7a6.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the king, block the pin with a developing move so that the exchange on c6 no longer wrecks your pawns.

1336500176424022|e7e5.headline: Castle before you open the centre in the Modern
1336500176424022|e7e5.why: 4...e5 lets White open the centre with 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8: the queens come off, Black loses the right to castle, and White develops with gain of time through 7.Be3 and 8.O-O-O+ along the open d-file. 4...Nf6 develops the last kingside piece and prepares to castle with 5.Be3 O-O, and only then does Black strike at the centre with 6...c5.
1336500176424022|e7e5.principle: Before you open the centre with a pawn break, castle; a queen trade with your king still on e8 can leave it stranded in the middle.

1364829931449246|c1e3.headline: Keep the queens on with 7.Qd3; your space needs them
1364829931449246|c1e3.why: Black threatens 7...Qxd4, and 7.Be3 only meets it by allowing the queen trade: after 7...Qxd4 8.Bxd4 Ne7 9.Be3 Be6 10.Bxe6 fxe6 the queens and light-squared bishops are gone and your advantage has evaporated. Theory notes that in the Paris Defence Black's kingside bishop is shut in behind the pawn chain while White has more space. 7.Qd3 keeps the queens on so that space counts: after 7...Be7 8.O-O c6 9.Re1 Nh6 10.h3 you are castled, your rook is on the e-file and Black is still untangling.
1364829931449246|c1e3.principle: Your trumps here are space and development; avoid trades that relieve the cramped side and keep the queens on.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

1436063243700465|f6d5.headline: Recapture with the pawn, 4...cxd5, so e4 can't chase your knight
1436063243700465|f6d5.why: 4...Nxd5 puts the knight where a pawn can hit it: 5.e4 Nb6 builds White a full pawn centre with tempo, and after 6.h3 g6 7.Nc3 Bg7 White is clearly better. The pawn on d5 is attacked three times and not defended at all, so you can choose how to take it back. 4...cxd5, played in 99.7% of master games, recaptures toward the centre and keeps a pawn on d5, so White has no e4 with tempo; after 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nc3 a6 the game is level.
1436063243700465|f6d5.principle: A knight in the centre that an enemy pawn can attack loses time when it is chased; recapture with a pawn when you can.

1436639890177008|e4e5.headline: When ...d5 hits the bishop on c4, answer it with 4.Bb5+.
1436639890177008|e4e5.why: 3...d5 attacks the bishop on c4, and 4.e5 pushes past the threat instead of answering it, so 4...dxc4 simply wins the bishop. The theory notes that playing ...d5 before ...Nc6 leaves Black's king open to a check from White's light-squared bishop, and 4.Bb5+ uses exactly that: the bishop escapes with check. After 4...Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.exd5 Qxd5 the pieces come off and the game is level.
1436639890177008|e4e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, look at your opponent's captures; here ...dxc4 was on the board, and only a move that answers it with a check or a capture keeps the material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

144526251450061|g1f3.headline: After 2...Bf5, take on d5 before Black can support it
144526251450061|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 gives Black time to support d5 with 3...e6, reaching a solid Queen's Gambit Declined with the bishop already outside the pawn chain. 2...Bf5 left d5 without pawn support, and 3.cxd5 punishes that: Black has no pawn ready to recapture. To win the pawn back Black plays 3...Bxb1 4.Rxb1 Qxd5, giving White the bishop pair and an easy game.
144526251450061|g1f3.principle: Strike at a centre pawn as soon as it has lost its pawn support, before your opponent can add ...e6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...Bf5

1453935289757629|c1f4.headline: Against the Marshall Defence, take on d5 and gain time
1453935289757629|c1f4.why: 3.Bf4 leaves c4 hanging: 3...dxc4 takes the pawn and 4...b5 holds on to it. 3.cxd5 takes a pawn Black can only win back with a piece, and that piece becomes a target. If 3...Nxd5, then 4.e4 gains a tempo and the centre; if 3...Qxd5, then 4.Nc3 hits the queen.
1453935289757629|c1f4.principle: Trade on d5 when Black can only recapture with a piece, then gain time by attacking that piece with pawns and knights.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...Nf6/3. cxd5

1454642951891787|f6d7.headline: Trade queens first, then put the knight on d5
1454642951891787|f6d7.why: Both queens face each other on the open d-file and the pawn on e5 attacks the knight on f6. 5...Nfd7 saves the knight by moving it a second time and keeps the queens on, and after 6.f4 White builds a big centre with quick development and a clear edge. 5...Qxd1+ trades queens first, 6.Nxd1 recaptures, and only then 6...Nd5 puts the knight on a strong central square; without queens, White's extra space matters much less.
1454642951891787|f6d7.principle: When your knight is attacked and the queens face each other, look at the forcing trade first: it settles the position before you spend a tempo retreating.

1454642951891787|f6g4.headline: Make the queen trade yourself so your king keeps castling
1454642951891787|f6g4.why: 5...Ng4 leaves the queens on, so 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 strands Black's king in the centre without castling rights. After 7.Nf3 Bg7 8.Bf4 the e5 pawn is firmly defended, the knight on g4 has moved twice for nothing, and 9.Rd1+ and 10.Bb5 keep harassing the king. 5...Qxd1+ makes the trade on Black's terms: White recaptures with 6.Nxd1, Black's king keeps its castling rights, and the knight escapes the e5 pawn's attack with 6...Nd5.
1454642951891787|f6g4.principle: With the queens facing each other down an open file, make the capture yourself, so your opponent's piece recaptures and your king stays home.

1455931362502230|c8f5.headline: After 4.Bf4, c4 is undefended: take it with 4...dxc4
1455931362502230|c8f5.why: 4.Bf4 develops a bishop but leaves c4 attacked once and defended not at all. 4...Bf5 lets that go, and 5.Qb3 attacks b7, which the bishop stopped guarding when it left c8, so White takes over the initiative. Take the pawn with 4...dxc4: the theory says that after 4.Bf4 Black keeps it without White getting compensation, which is why 4.e3, ruling out 4...dxc4, is the normal move.
1455931362502230|c8f5.principle: After each opponent move, check what has become loose: a developing move that leaves the c4 pawn unguarded is a free pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6

1479849493158304|d2d3.headline: Against 3...Qa5, take the centre with 4.d4.
1479849493158304|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too modest: it shuts in the bishop on f1 and gives up the centre, so Black develops comfortably with ...g6, ...Bg7 and ...c5. 4.d4 is the main line, played 78% of the time. It pins White's own knight for now, but it claims the centre and frees d2 for the bishop. The knight can then move with tempo against the black queen.
1479849493158304|d2d3.principle: When the opponent spends time on queen moves, use it to build a full pawn centre with both centre pawns.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

1479849493158304|f1b5.headline: Against 3...Qa5, build the centre with 4.d4
1479849493158304|f1b5.why: 4.Bb5+ achieves nothing: 4...Bd7 blocks with a developing move, and White soon retreats with 5.Be2, having spent two moves on the bishop. 4.d4 is the main line, chosen in 77.6% of master games: it takes the centre and frees d2 for the bishop, so White can later move the knight with tempo on the queen.
1479849493158304|f1b5.principle: With the opponent's queen out early, take the centre and develop; the queen becomes a target later, a pointless check only wastes time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

1483132126480579|c1d2.headline: Use your lead: 7.e5 keeps the g8 knight off f6
1483132126480579|c1d2.why: 7.Bd2 is a passive square for the bishop, and Black catches up calmly with 7...d6 8.h3 Nf6 9.O-O O-O: your gambit compensation is gone and Black is slightly better. The theory notes recommend 7.e5 (48.5% of masters games): the pawn takes f6 away from Black's knight, and it is not really hanging, because after 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+ Kg7 11.Qxe5+ White wins the piece back. If Black challenges it with 7...d6 8.exd6, the recapture 8...exd6 runs into 9.Nb5.
1483132126480579|c1d2.principle: In a gambit your pawn buys time, so use it: keep the opponent's pieces out of play and open lines before they finish developing, instead of making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1483132126480579|c1g5.headline: 7.e5 takes f6 from Black's knight; the pawn is tactically defended
1483132126480579|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 lets Black develop normally with 7...Nf6, and after 8.h3 d6 9.O-O O-O Black has castled and keeps the gambit pawn with a slightly better game. Theory recommends 7.e5: while the pawn stands there, Black's knight cannot develop to f6, and in the engine line it goes to h6 instead. The pawn only looks loose: theory shows 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 Bxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qd5+ Kg7 11.Qxe5+ wins the piece back with the better game for White.
1483132126480579|c1g5.principle: Ask where your opponent's next developing move wants to go and take that square away, especially when a tactic covers the pawn that does it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

1513949415486855|e4d5.headline: Gain space with 4.e5 instead of releasing the tension
1513949415486855|e4d5.why: 4.exd5 exd5 releases the tension and gives Black an open, symmetrical position with free development, so most of your edge disappears. Black's threat was 4...dxe4, and 4.e5, the main move in 84.2% of master games, meets it by taking space with tempo on the knight on f6, which the theory describes as the main answer to ...Nf6. After 4...Nfd7 Black has to attack your centre with ...c5 and ...Nc6, and you support it with 6.c3 and castle, keeping the extra space.
1513949415486855|e4d5.principle: When you can choose between a space advantage and a symmetrical exchange, keep the imbalance that favours you: the e5 pawn cramps Black, while exd5 leaves nothing to play for.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...Nf6

1557996217562153|c2c3.headline: 2...Nc6 lets you gain space with 3.d5
1557996217562153|c2c3.why: Against 2.d4 Black should take with 2...cxd4. 2...Nc6 instead attacks d4 and threatens 3...cxd4, winning a pawn, but it puts the knight where your d-pawn can hit it. 3.c3 defends passively, and after 3...d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 Black is comfortable. 3.d5 attacks the knight and takes space: after 3...Na5 4.Nf3 g6 5.h4 the knight on a5 is offside.
1557996217562153|c2c3.principle: When a knight on c6 attacks your d4 pawn, pushing d5 saves the pawn, gains space and drives the knight to a worse square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

1557996217562153|g1f3.headline: Punish 2...Nc6 with 3.d5, kicking the knight
1557996217562153|g1f3.why: The theory says Black should play 2...cxd4; after 2...Nc6, 3.Nf3 lets Black take on d4 anyway, and 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 is an ordinary open Sicilian in which your big advantage is gone. 3.d5 punishes the move: the pawn steps out of the c5 pawn's reach, gains space and attacks the knight on c6. After 3...Na5 the knight is stuck on the rim, and White keeps a big space advantage and a clear edge.
1557996217562153|g1f3.principle: When a knight lands in front of your centre pawns and a pawn advance can hit it, push: you gain space and the knight loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

15856967415293|c1g5.headline: Castle first with 7.O-O; 7.Bg5 just gets chased around
15856967415293|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 hits the queen, but 7...Nge7 blocks with a developing move, and then ...h6, ...Ne5 and ...N5g6 chase your bishops while Black castles, leaving Black clearly better. 7.O-O is the main move (58.7% of master games; 7.Qb3 is the other): your king is safe before the centre opens. In the main line 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 9.d5 gains space with tempo on the knight, and 10.Qd4 and 11.Bg5 bring your pieces in with a roughly balanced game.
15856967415293|c1g5.principle: In open gambit positions castle before starting operations; a piece sortie that the opponent meets with gain of time leaves your king in the centre for nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

15856967415293|f3g5.headline: Castle to break the pin on c3, then retake with 8.cxd4

ideas.title: Unpin, then rebuild the centre
ideas.text: The a5-bishop pins your c3 pawn; once your king leaves e1, 8.cxd4 restores your pawns on e4 and d4.

ideas.title: Development is your compensation
ideas.text: You're two pawns down for time and open lines; moving pieces that are already out wastes that pay.

ideas.title: Hit f7 with tempo
ideas.text: Queen on b3 and bishop on c4 aim at f7. A knight jump to g5 only works once Black can no longer cover f7 from h6.

ideas.title: Greed needs a spare tempo
ideas.text: Taking a third pawn on c3 right after you castle is dangerous for Black; after a wasted move it is safe.

habit.why: 7.Ng5 moves the same knight again while your queenside pieces sleep, and 7...Nh6 covers f7 with a developing move. You castle a move late and Black safely takes a third pawn: 8.O-O dxc3 9.Qb3 O-O 10.Nxc3 d6 leaves you two pawns down with no centre.

strays.text: The pin on c3 stays, giving Black time to guard f7 and grab c3.

taught.why: Castling ends the pin, so 8.cxd4 is threatened at once. After 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 you gain time with every move, 9.d5 hitting the c6-knight and 10.Qd4 forking the loose e4-knight and g7, and the game stays roughly level despite the pawns.

enforces.text: With your king off e1, 8.cxd4 puts a pawn back beside e4.

15856967415293|f3g5.principle: Your c3 pawn is pinned to your king, so deal with the pin first: 7.O-O makes 8.cxd4 possible at once, while 7.Ng5 gives Black time for 7...Nh6 and 8...dxc3.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: Your queen joins the c4-bishop against f7, so Black must spend the reply defending it, as with 7...Qf6. Masters play it in 41% of games.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O is just as good and more popular (59%): it breaks the pin first and keeps your queen free for 10.Qd4, while 7.Qb3 makes Black defend f7 first and castles a move later.

alternatives.label: mistake
alternatives.before: 7.Nxd4 wins one pawn back and nothing more: after 7...Nge7 Black develops calmly, stays a pawn up, and your e4 pawn stands alone.
alternatives.after: 7.O-O keeps the recapture for the c-pawn: after 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 you have pawns on e4 and d4 again. GM Mihail Marin calls 7.Nxd4 illogical for giving that up.

After 7...Nf6 8.cxd4 Nxe4 you gain time with every move, 9.d5 hitting the c6-knight and 10.Qd4 forking the loose e4-knight and g7, and the game stays roughly level despite the pawns.

1607436244732164|c6d4.headline: 4...Nd4 leaves e5 hanging; develop with 4...Nf6.
1607436244732164|c6d4.why: Moving the knight a second time removes e5's only defender, so 5.Nxe5 wins a pawn and then strikes at f7 with 6.Nxf7. 4...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4, leading to the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo after 5.d3; it is the choice in 89.6% of master games.
1607436244732164|c6d4.principle: A second knight move before the kingside knight is out must win something concrete; here it only abandons the e5 pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. O-O

1642112043242450|f6d5.headline: After 5.exd5, play 5...Na5 and take the bishop off f7
1642112043242450|f6d5.why: 5...Nxd5 opens the door to the Fried Liver: 6.Nxf7 Kxf7 7.Qf3+ drags the black king into the centre, and White brings more pieces with 8.Nc3 while it is stuck there. 5...Na5, the Polerio variation, moves the attacked knight out of the pawn's reach and hits the bishop on c4, ending its pressure on f7. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 Black is a pawn down but has the more active pieces, and is considered equal.
1642112043242450|f6d5.principle: With White's knight on g5 and bishop on c4 both aimed at f7, drive the bishop off that diagonal before you open lines near your king.

1642112043242450|f6e4.headline: Save the c6 knight with 5...Na5, hitting the bishop
1642112043242450|f6e4.why: White threatens 6.dxc6, and 5...Ne4 doesn't address it: it moves the f6 knight onto a square where the g5 knight takes it with 6.Nxe4, and the c6 knight is still attacked. 5...Na5, the Polerio variation, is the theory's best move: it gets the knight out of the pawn's way and attacks the c4 bishop. After 6.Bb5+ c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 White is a pawn up, but Black has more active pieces and is considered equal.
1642112043242450|f6e4.principle: First check which of your pieces are attacked; when a pawn hits a knight, move that knight, ideally to a square where it attacks something.
