1652894211754070|g1f3.headline: 4...Bg6 is unusual: strike with 5.e6 before Black plays ...e6
1652894211754070|g1f3.why: Theory calls 4...Bg6 a highly unusual reply to 4.Bd3: Black avoids the bishop trade but hasn't played ...e6, so the e6 square is still open to your pawn. 5.Nf3 lets Black fix that with 5...e6 and reach a normal Advance structure. 5.e6 strikes first: after 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 Black's king is loosened, and 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 hits the bishop on f7, with a clear advantage.
1652894211754070|g1f3.principle: When your opponent spends moves shuffling a bishop, open lines with a pawn break before they finish developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Bd3/4...Bg6

1652894211754070|h2h4.headline: Break with 5.e6 while Black's kingside is undeveloped
1652894211754070|h2h4.why: 5.h4, the usual pawn chase against the g6 bishop, gives Black time to trade it with 5...Bxd3 6.cxd3, leaving you with doubled d-pawns and much of your edge gone. 5.e6 strikes before Black has developed a kingside piece: the pawn hits f7, and after 5...Qc8 6.exf7+ Bxf7 7.Nf3 Nf6 8.Ne5 e6 9.Nxf7 Kxf7 you have the bishop pair, Black's king has lost the right to castle, and you keep a clear advantage.
1652894211754070|h2h4.principle: 4...Bg6 handed you a real advantage, and an advantage has to be used at once: open lines against the uncastled king before Black untangles, instead of a slow wing plan.

1657768441002862|g7g6.headline: Knight first: 3...Nf6, then decide on the fianchetto
1657768441002862|g7g6.why: 3...g6 empties g7 before your knight or bishop can cover the long diagonal: after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Qxd4 the queen hits the rook on h8, and after 5...Nf6 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.e5 dxe5 8.Qxd8+ you lose the right to castle. 3...Nf6, the most common master move (62.4%), develops and hits e4, so after 4.d4 cxd4 White recaptures with 5.Nxd4 and you reach a normal Open Sicilian, such as the Najdorf with 5...a6.
1657768441002862|g7g6.principle: The knight's best square, f6, is clear right away, while the bishop's depends on how the pawns settle; bring the knight out first and keep the fianchetto for later.

1694081511794223|g5e6.headline: Win e6 with the queen; Nxe6 allows Bxf2+
1694081511794223|g5e6.why: 7.Nxe6 grabs the pawn but walks into 7...Bxf2+: the bishop on c5 was aimed at f2, and after 8.Kf1 Qd7 9.Nxc7+ Qxc7 10.Kxf2 White's king has lost the right to castle and most of the advantage is gone. 7.Qg4 attacks the pawn on e6 a second time while the knight stays on g5, so after 7...Qf6 8.Qxe6+ White wins the pawn with check and can trade queens with 9.Qxf6.
1694081511794223|g5e6.principle: Before grabbing material, look at your opponent's checks and captures first; here the bishop check on f2 answers the knight capture.

17066305934542|f3e5.headline: Save the attacked bishop by taking on f7 with check
17066305934542|f3e5.why: 6...Na5 attacks the bishop on c4, and 7.Nxe5 doesn't save it: after 7...Nxc4 8.Nxc4 d5 Black has traded off the strong bishop and White's advantage is gone. 7.Bxf7+ moves the attacked bishop with a capture and a check: it wins the pawn on f7, after 7...Kf8 Black can no longer castle, and 8.Nxe5 follows with threats like 10.Ng6+.
17066305934542|f3e5.principle: With f7 defended only by the king, an attacked bishop on c4 should go there: it escapes and strips the king of castling at the same time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

1706874451895020|c8g4.headline: A pawn up in the Roscher Gambit, consolidate with 4...g6.
1706874451895020|c8g4.why: 4...Bg4 leaves the knight on e4 and the pawn on b7 both loose, and 5.Bd5 attacks them at once; after 5...Nf6 6.Bxb7 White regains the pawn and then takes the rook in the corner with 7.Bxa8. Black has already won the e4 pawn, and the theory calls the gambit unsound as long as Black keeps it. 4...g6 prepares ...Bg7 and castling, and the knight drops back with 6...Nf6 once White plays 6.Re1.
1706874451895020|c8g4.principle: After accepting a gambit pawn, spend your next moves on development and king safety and keep your pieces defended, rather than starting adventures.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

1711540021875497|b8c6.headline: Stop e4 with 3...Nf6; the knight on c6 lets White expand
1711540021875497|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 doesn't control e4, so White plays 4.e4 and gains space with 5.e5, kicking your knight; after 5...Ne4 6.Ne2 f6 Black has to push pawns to free the position. 3...Nf6 develops and guards e4, so White's knight on c3 is left blocking its own c-pawn with no central break. After 4.Qd3 Bb4 Black pins that knight and jumps in with 5...Ne4.
1711540021875497|b8c6.principle: In closed 1.d4 openings, keep control of e4 so White can't add a second centre pawn; the knight on f6 does that while developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Nc3

1743288401012634|e1h1.headline: Black ignored f7: take it now
1743288401012634|e1h1.why: 5.O-O lets Black off the hook: 4...Bc5 ignored the attack on f7, and after 5...O-O 6.d3 d5 Black is castled with free development while the knight on g5 does nothing. f7 is attacked twice and defended only by the king, so 5.Nxf7 forks the queen and the rook on h8 and wins the rook: after 5...Bxf2+ 6.Kf1 Qe7 7.Nxh8 White must still weather Black's attack. Masters more often take with the bishop, Bxf7+, which is also good.
1743288401012634|e1h1.principle: When the opponent ignores your knight and bishop aimed at f7, take on f7 at once: the point is defended only by the king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7

1783814385093536|d7d5.headline: Behind in development, keep it closed: 5...a6, not 5...d5
1783814385093536|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the centre while White has the lead in development: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.exd5 exd5 8.Ne5 Bd7 9.Qxd5 Nxe5 10.Qxe5+ wins back the gambit pawn with check to your king, and White is clearly better. Theory notes that after 4.Nxc3 White's development is simple while Black still needs pawn moves to catch up. 5...a6 is the useful one: it takes b5 away from White's bishop and knight, and after 6.Bf4 Nc6 7.Be2 d6 8.O-O Be7 you develop behind a compact pawn wall; masters choose it 42.2% of the time.
1783814385093536|d7d5.principle: When your opponent leads in development, keep the centre closed and finish developing before you open lines with a pawn break.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

1783814385093536|f8b4.headline: Consolidate with 5...a6; 5...Bb4 gets hit by 6.Qd4
1783814385093536|f8b4.why: 5...Bb4 puts the bishop where nothing defends it: 6.Qd4 hits it and the g7 pawn at once, and after 6...Bf8 you have spent two moves to bring the bishop home, handing White the initiative. 5...a6, the most common master move (42.2%), keeps White's knight and bishop off b5, and you then develop calmly with ...Nc6, ...d6 and ...Be7, keeping the extra pawn in a level game. 5...Nc6, leading to the usual Smith-Morra main line, is just as good.
1783814385093536|f8b4.principle: You accepted the gambit, so consolidate: White leads in development and will hit any loose piece with tempo, so use modest, protected moves until your king is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4

1790000171764366|f3g5.headline: Ng5 hangs the knight to the queen; strike with 5.d4
1790000171764366|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 drops the knight: with Black's e-pawn on e5 and the f-pawn gone to e6, the diagonal from d8 to g5 is open and 5...Qxg5 just takes it. Black has spent the opening on pawn moves and the trade on e6, so 5.d4, played in 71% of master games, opens the centre while Black's kingside pieces are still at home. After 5...exd4 6.Nxd4 the knight is centralised and eyes the weak e6 pawn.
1790000171764366|f3g5.principle: Before a knight jump, check every enemy piece that can reach the landing square: the queen on d8 covered g5 along the open diagonal.

1890995340270663|d1d5.headline: Save the bishop with 9.Bb3, then develop by taking on c3
1890995340270663|d1d5.why: 8...Kf8 means Black can never castle, but the king now attacks your bishop on f7. 9.Qd5 holds it with the queen, but after 9...d6 10.Bxg8 Rxg8 11.Ng5 Qe8 12.Nxh7+ Ke7 the king walks out of danger and your edge shrinks. 9.Bb3 keeps the bishop on the same diagonal, and after 9...d6 10.Nxc3 you win the pawn back while developing a piece, keeping a large advantage. 9.Nxc3 is also good.
1890995340270663|d1d5.principle: With the enemy king already stuck in the centre, you don't need a queen raid; bring the rest of your pieces into play, ideally with moves that also win material.

1891225405277048|f1c4.headline: After 2...b6, take the centre with 3.d4
1891225405277048|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 points the bishop at a pawn wall on e6, and 3...d5 hits it: after 4.exd5 exd5 it has to retreat with 5.Be2 and White has lost time. 2...b6 did nothing for the centre, so 3.d4 builds a two-pawn centre for free; the masters play it 92.9% of the time. The bishop then develops with 4.Bd3, where it guards e4 against the bishop on b7.
1891225405277048|f1c4.principle: When your opponent spends a move on the wing, occupy the centre with pawns before developing a bishop into a pawn's reach.

1895778820316678|d1b3.headline: 8.Ba3 keeps Black's king from castling
1895778820316678|d1b3.why: 8.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and Black simply castles with 8...O-O, taking the king away from f7; after 9.cxd4 Nxe4 Black has also taken your e4 pawn and is clearly better. 8.Ba3, the masters' choice 60% of the time, develops the bishop onto the open a3-f8 diagonal, where it covers f8 and stops Black from castling short. Black has to spend 8...d6 blocking it, and after 9.e5 Ne4 10.exd6 cxd6 11.Qe2 the e-file opens toward the king and the game stays close to level.
1895778820316678|d1b3.principle: When you have gambited for development, use it to keep the enemy king in the centre: a bishop that covers the castling squares is worth more than an early queen raid.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

1905410911939124|e1h1.headline: Stop ...f4 with 6.f4 before castling
1905410911939124|e1h1.why: 6.O-O ignores Black's threat of 6...f4, which shuts the bishop on c1 out of g5 and leaves the knight on g5 exposed to the queen on d8; White has to spend moves holding it with 7.h4, and Black takes over. 6.f4 occupies that square first, so the pawn on f4 now guards the knight on g5 itself and also hits e5. After 6...fxe4 7.Nc3 White keeps developing with the advantage.
1905410911939124|e1h1.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move prepares: here ...f4 was coming, so take the square before tucking your king away.

1922438896562435|f1c4.headline: After 2...Nc6, take the whole centre with 3.d4
1922438896562435|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 runs into 3...d5, which attacks the bishop and frees Black's game; after 4.exd5 exd5 the bishop has to move again with 5.Bb5, and Black's centre is fine. 2...Nc6 put the knight in front of Black's c-pawn, so Black has no quick pawn strike against d4: 3.d4 sets up two central pawns, and after 3...d5 4.e5 White has a clear space advantage. Masters choose it 91% of the time.
1922438896562435|f1c4.principle: When the opponent's piece blocks the pawn that would challenge your centre, put a second pawn in the middle at once.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3

1931050112551786|e6e5.headline: Just recapture with 4...exd5
1931050112551786|e6e5.why: 4...e5 leaves the d5 pawn alone and puts a second pawn where your opponent can take it: 5.fxe5 Qxd5 6.Nc3 leaves Black a pawn down with the queen already being chased, and White is close to winning. The d5 pawn is attacked twice and defended by nothing, so take it back with 4...exd5, keeping a pawn in the centre and a good game. After 5.Bb5+ Nc6 Black develops normally with ...Nf6 and ...Be7.
1931050112551786|e6e5.principle: When the opponent has just captured in the centre, look at the recapture first; a counter-push that ignores it usually loses material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. f4

1957522496653461|f8c5.headline: After 3.d3, develop 3...Nf6 first; 3...Bc5 allows the fork trick.
1957522496653461|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 lets White play 4.Nxe5, because after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 the pawn forks bishop and knight and White wins the piece back. 3...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and adds pressure on e4, and the bishop can still come to c5 later, as in 3...Nf6 4.g3 Bc5.
1957522496653461|f8c5.principle: Bring the king's knight out before the bishop: f6 is clearly its best square, while a bishop on c5 can be hit by a d4 fork.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6

1976310622037328|c7c5.headline: Prepare ...e5 with 5...c6; don't open lines with the king uncastled
1976310622037328|c7c5.why: 5...c5 gives White 6.dxc5, and after 6...Qa5 7.Bb5+ Bd7 Black's king is checked and Black only wins the pawn back with 9...dxc5 once White has developed and castled. 5...c6 is the calm, flexible move: after 6.h3 O-O 7.Bd3 Nbd7 8.a4 e5 Black gets the classic central strike with the king already safe. It is the masters' top choice here.
1976310622037328|c7c5.principle: With the king still on e8, avoid pawn breaks that open lines toward it; castle and prepare the central break with ...c6 and ...Nbd7 instead.

1976310622037328|e7e5.headline: Against 5.Bg5, prepare ...e5 with 5...c6 and castling first.
1976310622037328|e7e5.why: 5...e5 opens the centre too soon: after 6.dxe5 dxe5 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the king has lost castling, and 8.Nd5 adds a second attacker to the knight on f6, already hit by the bishop on g5, so after 9.Bxf6+ Bxf6 10.Nxf6 White wins a piece. 5...c6 keeps the centre closed and makes useful moves: Black castles and brings the knight to d7, and only then plays 8...e5, when 9.dxe5 Nxe5 recaptures with a piece instead of trading queens.
1976310622037328|e7e5.principle: Delay ...e5 until you have castled and can recapture with a piece, so a queen trade on d8 doesn't strand your king in the centre.

2036399053007590|b8c6.headline: In the French, follow 1...e6 with ...d5 straight away
2036399053007590|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White build the full centre with 3.d4, and after 3...d5 4.e5 the knight on c6 blocks Black's c-pawn, the usual lever against White's pawn chain. 2...d5 is played in 92.3% of master games: it claims the centre and attacks the pawn on e4 at once, in the spirit of the French defence.
2036399053007590|b8c6.principle: The e6 pawn is there to support the d-pawn, so push it to d5 and challenge e4 before White can add a second centre pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5

2067858163173673|d4c6.headline: Answer the threat on d4 with 6.Nb5, hitting c7
2067858163173673|d4c6.why: Black threatens 6...Qxd4, winning your knight, so it has to move. 6.Nxc6 dxc6 solves that, but it also helps Black: the c8 bishop is free, and after 7.O-O Be6 8.Bb3 Bc5 your edge is small. 5...Qf6 took the queen away from c7, so 6.Nb5 saves the knight with a threat of its own: a jump into c7 with check that would also hit the rook on a8. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Kd8 Black guards c7 with the king and can no longer castle, and you keep a clear edge.
2067858163173673|d4c6.principle: When one of your pieces is attacked, look for the retreat that creates a threat of its own; it saves the piece and gains time instead of trading it for nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2067858163173673|d4f3.headline: Save the d4 knight with a threat: 6.Nb5 hits c7
2067858163173673|d4f3.why: Black threatens 6...Qxd4, winning the knight, and 6.Nf3 saves it by moving it a second time with two minor pieces still at home; after 6...Bb4+ 7.Nbd2 Nge7 8.O-O O-O Black has caught up and the game is level. Theory notes that 3...h6 loses time, which 4.d4 exploits, so keep gaining time: 6.Nb5 saves the knight and attacks the pawn on c7. After 6...Bb4+ 7.Bd2 Bxd2+ 8.Nxd2 Black has to cover c7 with 8...Kd8, giving up castling, and you keep a clear advantage.
2067858163173673|d4f3.principle: If a piece has to move again, move it to a square where it wins something concrete or makes a threat, so the extra move costs your opponent time instead of you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2094672111620588|d4e5.headline: Answer 3...f6 with 4.Bc4, aiming at the weakened light squares
2094672111620588|d4e5.why: 3...f6 holds e5 but costs a developing move and opens the a2-g8 diagonal toward Black's king. 4.dxe5 releases the tension: after 4...dxe5 the e5 pawn is firmly protected by the f6 pawn, and White's edge is small. 4.Bc4 develops onto that open diagonal, aiming through f7 at g8, where Black's king wants to castle; after 4...Nc6 5.h3 Nge7 6.O-O exd4 7.Nxd4 you have the extra development the theory says 3...f6 hands White, and a clear advantage.
2094672111620588|d4e5.principle: Black's ...f6 cost them development and weakened their king, so keep building your lead with developing moves and castling, and open the centre once your pieces are ready.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

2107090482514507|c1e3.headline: Castle with 7.O-O to break the pin on c3
2107090482514507|c1e3.why: 6...Bb4 pins your knight on c3 to the king. 7.Be3 leaves the pin in place, and after 7...O-O 8.Qe2 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Black takes the knight with check and most of your edge is gone. 7.O-O breaks the pin by taking the king off the diagonal. Black can still swap on c3 later, as in 7...O-O 8.Qe2 b6 9.Bg5 Bxc3 10.bxc3, but by then your bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 and you keep a clear edge; the theory notes that 3...Qd8 gives White a free hand to develop.
2107090482514507|c1e3.principle: Break a pin before the pinned piece is attacked again: castling takes your king off the b4-e1 diagonal and turns the knight on c3 back into a normal piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

2118572924932318|g7g6.headline: 4...g6 ignores 5.Ng5; develop the bishop with 4...Bc5.
2118572924932318|g7g6.why: White threatens 5.Ng5, attacking f7 together with the bishop on c4, and 4...g6 does nothing about it: after 5.Ng5 d5 6.exd5 Black loses a pawn. 4...Bc5 develops the bishop toward the centre and readies castling, transposing into the Giuoco Pianissimo.
2118572924932318|g7g6.principle: When a knight and the bishop on c4 can combine against f7, develop the pieces that let you castle instead of spending time on a pawn move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. d3

2122895618389281|c8f5.headline: Undermine the d5 pawn with 3...c6 before White consolidates
2122895618389281|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 develops but leaves White's extra pawn alone: after 4.d4 e6 5.dxe6 fxe6 you are a pawn down with an isolated pawn on e6, and White is clearly better. Theory explains that White's 3.c4 is an attempt to hold the d5 pawn, and that Black's two main answers chip away at the pawn chain with 3...c6 or 3...e6. After 3...c6 4.d4 cxd5 you have the pawn back and the game has transposed into a Panov-Botvinnik Caro-Kann, which theory now rates as even; masters choose 3...c6 52.8% of the time.
2122895618389281|c8f5.principle: If you delay recapturing a gambit pawn, use your next move to win it back before your opponent can consolidate it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. c4

2162412998029713|f1c4.headline: 3...e6 prepares ...d5: put the bishop on d3, not c4
2162412998029713|f1c4.why: After 3...e6 Black is ready for ...d5, which hits a bishop on c4. In the line 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bd3 your bishop has to move again and Black has a free, equal centre, and most of your edge is gone. 4.Bd3 is the masters' top choice (28.9%): it develops the bishop toward the centre and defends e4 in advance, so after 4...Nc6 5.e5 White keeps space. 4.Nc3, 4.c3 and 4.Be2 also avoid the problem.
2162412998029713|f1c4.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move prepares; when ...e6 readies ...d5, develop your bishop to a square that the pawn push will not hit.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

2173517444444160|b2b3.headline: Against the Pirc fianchetto, take the centre with 4.d4.
2173517444444160|b2b3.why: 4.b3 prepares a slow fianchetto and leaves the centre alone: after 4...Bg7 5.d4 O-O White plays the central move anyway, a move later, and Black hits back with 6...c5. 4.d4 sets up the two-pawn centre on e4 and d4 straight away and keeps the initiative, with 5.Be3 and 6.Qd2 to follow. Masters play 4.d4 in 87.5% of games.
2173517444444160|b2b3.principle: When the opponent fianchettoes and leaves the centre empty, occupy it with a second pawn before anything slower.

2179133986956493|f1c4.headline: e4 has no defender: develop with 5.Bd3, not 5.Bc4
2179133986956493|f1c4.why: Black threatens 5...Nxe4, and 5.Bc4 does nothing about it: the e4 pawn has no defender, so 5...Nxe4 wins it and Black is better. 5.Bd3, the masters' choice 84.3% of the time, develops the bishop toward the centre and guards e4 in the same move. After 5...O-O 6.O-O Nbd7 7.Re1 e5 8.h3 your centre of pawns on e4, d4 and c3 stands firm.
2179133986956493|f1c4.principle: Before picking a square for a developing piece, check what is loose: put the piece where it develops and also guards the undefended pawn.

2185074222383401|d2d3.headline: 4...Qe7 doesn't hold f7: take it with 5.Bxf7+
2185074222383401|d2d3.why: 5.d3 is too slow: Black kicks the knight with 5...h6, and after 6.Nf3 Nxe4 the e4 pawn is gone. 4...Qe7 does not really defend f7, which the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5 both attack. 5.Bxf7+ takes the pawn with check; after 5...Kd8 the knight on g5 protects the bishop, and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
2185074222383401|d2d3.principle: f7 is guarded mainly by the king, which cannot take a protected piece, so with bishop and knight both on it, the capture wins a pawn and castling rights.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5

2185074222383401|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop, with check: 5.Bxf7+
2185074222383401|g5f7.why: 5.Nxf7 grabs the pawn and hits the rook, but lets Black open the game with 5...d5; after 6.Bxd5 Nxd5 7.exd5 Qxf7 the trades leave Black with active pieces and a safe king after 9...O-O. 4...Qe7 looks like it guards f7, but 5.Bxf7+ wins the pawn with check: the bishop is protected by the knight on g5, so neither the king nor the queen can take it. After 5...Kd8 Black's king is stuck in the centre and can no longer castle, and 6.Bb3 keeps the bishop safe.
2185074222383401|g5f7.principle: f7 is guarded only by the king and queen while the bishop on c4 and the knight on g5 both hit it; capture with the piece that gives check and stays protected.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5

2185447105552102|e1h1.headline: ...dxe4 forks d3 and f3: push 6.e5 before castling
2185447105552102|e1h1.why: 5...d5 threatens 6...dxe4, and that pawn would attack the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 at once. 6.O-O ignores it: after 6...dxe4 7.Bxe4 Nxe4 you have lost a bishop, because once the d-pawn has gone the bishop on b7 also guards e4. 6.e5 (87.9% of masters games) takes the pawn out of the exchange, gains space by attacking the knight on f6 and leaves the b7 bishop blocked by Black's own pawn on d5; you keep a clear edge.
2185447105552102|e1h1.principle: Before a quiet move like castling, look at your opponent's captures; when a pawn capture would hit two of your pieces, resolve the central tension first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3/3...Nf6

221633201643279|d2d4.headline: 1...b5 hangs a pawn: take it with 2.Bxb5
221633201643279|d2d4.why: 2.d4 declines the free pawn, and after 2...Bb7 Black gets the queenside fianchetto at no cost, which gives back part of your advantage. The b5 pawn is attacked by your bishop and defended by nothing: 2.Bxb5 wins it and develops at the same time. The theory lists Black's ideas afterwards, ...Bb7 against your centre and ...a6 to kick the bishop (2...a6 3.Bc4), and they gain Black only a little time.
221633201643279|d2d4.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can consolidate easily; here the capture is also a developing move, so there is nothing to consolidate.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b5/2. Bxb5

2219393363100507|f8d6.headline: Hit the centralised queen with 3...Nc6
2219393363100507|f8d6.why: 3...Bd6 leaves the pawn on g7 unprotected against the queen on d4, so 4.Qxg7 wins it, and the bishop also blocks Black's d-pawn. 3...Nc6 is the usual answer to the Centre Game: it develops with an attack on the queen, so White has to move it again and Black gains time.
2219393363100507|f8d6.principle: When the opponent's queen sits in the centre, develop a piece that attacks it and make it move again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4/3...Nc6

2227650220427205|d7d5.headline: Don't push ...d5 into three attackers; 5...h6 is the quiet move
2227650220427205|d7d5.why: 5...d5 drops a pawn: d5 is hit by the pawn on e4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4, and after 6.Nxd5 Nxd5 7.Bxd5 White has won it. 5...h6 is a useful waiting move that takes g5 away from White's knight and bishop, so Black can castle with 6.O-O O-O without worrying about a pin or a hit on f7.
2227650220427205|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a central pawn, count the attackers on its square: here three white pieces cover d5 and Black has fewer defenders.

2264630549471820|a2a3.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; 5.a3 wastes time and loosens e4
2264630549471820|a2a3.why: 5.a3 spends a tempo inviting 5...Bxc3, and after 6.dxc3 Nxe4 the e4 pawn is gone; White wins the knight back with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7 8.Qd5+ Ke8 9.Qxe4, but has traded off the attacking bishop and Black has the easier game. 5.O-O gets the king safe and keeps the tempo: after 5...Bxc3 6.bxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.Nxe5 White has the pawn back with active pieces. It is the most common master move here.
2264630549471820|a2a3.principle: A pawn move like 5.a3 that neither develops nor fights for the centre needs a concrete reason; castling finishes White's kingside development instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

2264630549471820|c3b5.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; the c3 knight is e4's only guard
2264630549471820|c3b5.why: 5.Nb5 moves a developed knight again and abandons the e4 pawn, so 5...Nxe4 wins it for nothing. 5.O-O is the most common master move: it tucks the king away first. After 5...Bxc3 6.bxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd5 Nf6 8.Bxc6 dxc6 9.Nxe5 White wins the pawn back.
2264630549471820|c3b5.principle: Before moving a piece, count what it defends: if it is the only guard of a centre pawn, leave it and improve another piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

2326611116094961|c1e3.headline: Answer the threat on d4 with 6.Bxf7+ check first
2326611116094961|c1e3.why: 5...Bc5 attacks your knight on d4 (6...Bxd4 is the threat), and 6.Be3 defends it but throws away a winning advantage and leaves the game roughly level. 6.Bxf7+ comes first: it takes the f7 pawn with check, and after 6...Kf8 Black can no longer castle. Then 7.Nxc6 moves the attacked knight with a capture that hits the queen, and you come out a pawn up against a stranded king.
2326611116094961|c1e3.principle: When the opponent makes a threat, check your own checks and captures before defending: a forcing move can solve the threat and gain material at the same time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2326611116094961|d4c6.headline: Check on f7 first: 6.Bxf7+ before trading knights
2326611116094961|d4c6.why: 3...h6 cost Black a tempo, and 5...Bc5 now attacks your knight on d4 twice, threatening 6...Bxd4. 6.Nxc6 answers the threat but lets the queen join with 6...Qf6, threatening mate on f2, and after 7.O-O dxc6 most of White's advantage is gone. 6.Bxf7+ first wins a pawn and drags the king to f8, where it can no longer castle; only then 7.Nxc6.
2326611116094961|d4c6.principle: Before answering a threat, check your own forcing moves: a check that wins something can come first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

2385998627357413|b2b4.headline: 7.b4 drops a pawn; gain queenside space with 7.a4
2385998627357413|b2b4.why: 7.b4 tries to chase the bishop on c5, but the knight on c6 already covers b4, and in the engine line 7...Nxb4 simply wins the pawn. After 8.a4 d5 9.exd5 Nxd5 Black also frees the centre. 7.a4 gains queenside space without leaving a pawn to be taken, and White castles later with 10.O-O.
2385998627357413|b2b4.principle: Before pushing a pawn next to enemy pieces, count who attacks and who defends the square it lands on.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

2446703153094283|b8c6.headline: Against 1.Nf3, keep your options open with 1...Nf6
2446703153094283|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, and after 2.d4 d5 3.c4 White gets a Queen's Gambit in which Black cannot use the c-pawn to support d5 or to strike back with ...c5. 1...Nf6 is the most flexible reply and the most popular among masters at 46%: it develops, stops White from playing e4, and keeps every pawn free, so Black can choose a setup such as 1...Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.g3 g6.
2446703153094283|b8c6.principle: The knight on f6 controls e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, while a knight on c6 in front of the c-pawn takes away Black's usual way to fight for d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

2446703153094283|e7e5.headline: After 1.Nf3, e5 just hangs; play 1...Nf6
2446703153094283|e7e5.why: 1...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 attacks it and nothing defends it, so 2.Nxe5 wins it; theory calls it the dubious Ross Gambit. 1...Nf6 is the most flexible reply: it keeps the position symmetrical and leaves Black free to choose a setup later. Masters choose it in 46.4% of games.
2446703153094283|e7e5.principle: Before putting a pawn on a square, count: e5 is attacked by the knight and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

2463215796795915|f1e2.headline: Take the undefended c5 pawn before Black trades it off: 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 lets Black release the tension with 6...cxd4 7.cxd4, which is what the theory says Black wants here, and your edge is gone. The c5 pawn is attacked once and defended by nothing, and the theory points out that 5...Bg4 does not stop you taking it: 6.dxc5. In the main line Black wins back the e5 pawn with 7...Nxe5, but 10.b4 then supports your pawn on c5 and gains space on the queenside, and you keep a small edge.
2463215796795915|f1e2.principle: Ask what your opponent wants: here Black wants ...cxd4 to free the position, so take on c5 first, which stops it and wins the undefended pawn.

2463215796795915|h2h3.headline: Don't spend a move on h3: take on c5 with 6.dxc5
2463215796795915|h2h3.why: 6.h3 invites 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3, and once the f3 knight is gone d4 has lost a defender: 7...cxd4 wins a pawn and Black is better. The pin on your knight does not need an answer yet; the theory points out that 5...Bg4 does not stop you taking on c5. The c5 pawn is attacked once and defended by nothing, so 6.dxc5 grabs it, and in the main line 10.b4 later supports it and gains queenside space.
2463215796795915|h2h3.principle: In the Advance, Black's play is aimed at the base of your chain, d4; don't help by inviting the exchange of its defender, and remove Black's c5 lever instead.

2465468553870240|c8f5.headline: Knight first: 5...Nc6, because ...Bf5 leaves b7 and d5 short
2465468553870240|c8f5.why: 5...Bf5 takes the bishop away from b7, and 6.Qb3 hits b7 and d5 at once: 6...Qb6 saves b7 but stops guarding d5, and 7.Nxd5 Nxd5 8.Qxd5 wins a pawn. 5...Nc6 is the main move (93% of master games): it develops toward the centre, adds pressure on d4, and keeps the bishop home until it can come out safely. The theory's line 5...Nc6 6.Bf4 Bf5 7.e3 e6 shows the bishop still reaches f5 a move later, and the game stays equal.
2465468553870240|c8f5.principle: In symmetrical positions the knight's square is obvious and the bishop's depends on the pawns, so develop the knight first and keep the bishop guarding b7 until its square is safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. cxd5/3...cxd5/4. Nc3/4...Nf6

2466581236058373|c8d7.headline: Block the check with 5...Nc6, keeping the queen guarding d5
2466581236058373|c8d7.why: After 5...Bd7, 6.Qe2+ forces 6...Qe7, and the queen on e7 no longer guards d5: 7.Bxd7+ Nxd7 8.Nxd5 Qxe2+ 9.Kxe2 leaves you a pawn down and White clearly better. 5...Nc6 (88% of masters games) blocks the check with the piece that wanted to go to c6 anyway, develops toward the centre and leaves the queen on d8 behind the d5 pawn. After 6.O-O Nf6 7.d4 Bd6 Black has a normal game, with only a small edge for White.
2466581236058373|c8d7.principle: Bring the knight to its natural square before committing a bishop; when you must block a check, block with the knight that was heading there anyway.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...e6

2471617853961957|e8e7.headline: Take the bishop on f7 with your king; nothing defends it
2471617853961957|e8e7.why: 7...Ke7 leaves White's bishop alive: after 8.Bxg8 Qxg8 White has traded it for a knight, kept the pawn it took on f7, and Black's king has lost the right to castle. The bishop on f7 is attacked by the king and defended by nothing, so 7...Kxf7 wins it. White's trick 8.Nxe5+ is a check that opens the queen's path to g4, but after 8...dxe5 9.Qxg4 Black has still won a knight for a pawn.
2471617853961957|e8e7.principle: When a piece lands on f7 with check, count its defenders before stepping aside: with none, take it and then meet the follow-up.

2480011064030415|f3g5.headline: Ng5 hits nothing once Black castles; build with 5.c3
2480011064030415|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight a second time while two minor pieces are still at home, and its target disappears after 5...O-O, because the rook now guards f7. In the engine line the knight has to go back with 7.Nf3, so Black has simply gained time. 5.c3, the masters' top choice at 42%, is the Giuoco Pianissimo plan: a slow buildup that prepares d4, while 7.O-O, 8.Re1 and 9.Nbd2 finish development.
2480011064030415|f3g5.principle: Finish developing before going after f7: with pieces still at home, a knight raid that castling parries only hands your opponent moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3/4...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

2566699904980904|f8g7.headline: Play 3...d6 so e5 never kicks your knight
2566699904980904|f8g7.why: After 3...Bg7, 4.e5 kicks the knight on f6 and it has to go all the way back with 4...Ng8, leaving White with lots of space and Black undeveloped. 3...d6 covers e5, so the knight stays on f6 and the game transposes into the Pirc defence, the choice in about three quarters of master games. Black then follows with ...Bg7 and castles.
2566699904980904|f8g7.principle: A knight on f6 is a target for White's e-pawn; control e5 with a pawn first so the pawn can't chase the knight and gain space.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3

2583228623150903|d7d5.headline: Knight on c3 and bishop on c4 hit d5: develop first
2583228623150903|d7d5.why: 2...e6 prepares ...d5, but with the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4 both aiming at d5, the push comes too early. After 3...d5 4.exd5 exd5 the d5 pawn has two attackers and only the queen defends it, so 5.Qe2+ Be7 6.Nxd5 wins it and White is clearly better. 3...Nc6 is the main move (48.3% of masters games): it develops toward the centre, and after 4.Nf3 Nf6 the game stays level.
2583228623150903|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a contested square, count who attacks it and who defends it; here d5 is covered by the c3 knight and the c4 bishop, so it needs more support first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nc3/2...e6

2615425569294719|c8f5.headline: ...Bf5 leaves b7 loose to Qb3: develop with 4...Nf6 first
2615425569294719|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 takes the bishop off c8, where it was the only guard of b7, and 5.Qb3 attacks b7 and d5 together: after 5...Nc6 6.Nf3 Nf6 7.Qxb7 the b-pawn falls. 4...Nf6 is the main move (75.9% of master games): it develops toward the centre and adds a defender to d5. The bishop can still come to f5 later, as in 4...Nf6 5.Bf4 Nc6 6.Nf3 Bf5, once the knights are out.
2615425569294719|c8f5.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it stops guarding: the c8 bishop is b7's only defender, so it stays home until Qb3 no longer wins a pawn.

2615583540108407|b8c6.headline: Answer 2.f3 with 2...d5 so that e4 costs White a pawn.
2615583540108407|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White carry out the plan: 3.e4 builds a big centre and after 4.e5 Ng8 Black's knight is pushed back home. 2.f3 weakens White's kingside and takes the knight's natural square just to prepare e4, and 2...d5 makes that push fail: if 3.e4 dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4, Black is a pawn up.
2615583540108407|b8c6.principle: When White prepares e4 with a weakening pawn move, add a second guard of e4 with your d-pawn so the advance costs material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. f3

2615583540108407|g7g6.headline: Answer 2.f3 with 2...d5 so e4 never comes
2615583540108407|g7g6.why: 2.f3 prepares 3.e4, and 2...g6 lets it happen: after 3.e4 d5 4.e5 the knight is kicked to d7 and White has a big pawn centre. 2...d5 adds a second guard to e4, so White cannot push the e-pawn without losing it: if 3.e4 anyway, 3...dxe4 4.fxe4 Nxe4 leaves Black a pawn up. Masters play it in 83% of games, and White's f-pawn move is left looking weakening.
2615583540108407|g7g6.principle: When White prepares a central pawn advance, add a pawn guard to that square at once so the advance loses material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. f3

2671625836318681|b8c6.headline: Release the d5 tension with 5...dxe4 before it becomes a weak pawn
2671625836318681|b8c6.why: White threatens to win your d5 pawn with exd5, and 5...Nc6 doesn't stop it: after 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.Nxd5 the isolated d5 pawn falls and White is clearly better. With the d5 pawn under fire from the e4 pawn and the c3 knight, take first: 5...dxe4 claims the centre and leaves you with no weak pawn to defend. After 6.Nxe4 a6 7.Bd3 Be7 8.O-O Nf6 you develop smoothly and White's edge is small.
2671625836318681|b8c6.principle: When a centre pawn of yours is attacked and you cannot keep enough defenders on it, count the attackers and release the tension before it becomes an isolated target.

2692473875865858|c8f5.headline: In the Slav, 3...Nf6 first: an early ...Bf5 drops a pawn
2692473875865858|c8f5.why: Once the bishop leaves c8, b7 is undefended and a queen on b3 hits b7 and d5 together. Theory calls 3...Bf5 a grave mistake here: 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 wins a pawn, and the engine's 4.Qb3 Qb6 5.Qxb6 axb6 6.cxd5 does the same. 3...Nf6, Black's most common reply by far, defends d5 and keeps the balance; the bishop can come out once ...e6 and the knight make it safe.
2692473875865858|c8f5.principle: Before developing a piece, check what it was guarding; in the Slav the c8 bishop holds b7, and Qb3 punishes it for leaving early.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6

269926073920586|c1e3.headline: Question the pinning bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 lets Black keep the pin on your knight on f3 and finish developing with 6...e6 and 7...c6, and most of your advantage disappears. 6.h3, the choice in 89.9% of master games, asks the bishop on g4 to decide now: after 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and an active queen, then 8.Bd2 unpins the knight on c3 before 9.O-O-O, with a clear edge. If Black retreats instead, the theory shows the bishop being chased by g4 to g6.
269926073920586|c1e3.principle: A pin ties your knight to the queen; break it while it costs Black something, here by hitting the pinning bishop with the h-pawn before Black can support it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

269926073920586|f1e2.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once with 6.h3
269926073920586|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 is not a blunder, but it lets Black finish ...Nbd7 and ...c6 before deciding about the bishop: after 6.Be2 Nbd7 7.a3 c6 8.h3 Bxf3 9.Bxf3 your edge shrinks to a small one. 6.h3 (89.9% of masters games) puts the question immediately. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you keep both bishops, your queen is already in play, and the plan 8.Bd2 and 9.O-O-O keeps a clear edge.
269926073920586|f1e2.principle: When an enemy bishop pins or eyes your knight from a square a pawn can attack, chase it with the pawn right away, while the trade still costs your opponent time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

2731765578959899|c4b3.headline: 6.Bf1 guards g2 and hits b5: the refutation of 5...b5
2731765578959899|c4b3.why: 5...b5 deflects your bishop so Black can recapture on d5 with the queen, hitting g2. 6.Bb3 leaves g2 unguarded and lets the knight jump to d4 with tempo, 6...Nd4; after 7.d3 Bc5 Black is fully active and slightly better. 6.Bf1, played in 83.5% of master games, looks backward but guards g2 and attacks the b5 pawn: the theory shows that 6...Qxd5 then runs into 7.Nc3 with tempo, and after 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 you have picked up the pawn and keep a small edge.
2731765578959899|c4b3.principle: Ask what your opponent's move is for and stop it: Black's pawn offer aims at ...Qxd5 with an attack on g2, so put the bishop where it guards g2.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...b5

2731765578959899|c4b5.headline: Refute the Ulvestad with 6.Bf1: guard g2 and keep b5 in sight
2731765578959899|c4b5.why: 6.Bxb5 takes the bait: 6...Qxd5 attacks both your bishop and the g2 pawn, and after 7.Be2 Bb7 Black's pieces come out with tempo and the game is level. Theory explains that 5...b5 is offered to deflect your bishop from d5 and f7 so that Black can recapture with the queen. 6.Bf1 is the refutation: the bishop guards g2 and still eyes b5, your d5 pawn attacks the knight on c6, and if 6...Qxd5 then 7.Nc3 hits the queen with tempo. In the engine line 6...Nxd5 7.Bxb5 wins the pawn back anyway; masters choose 6.Bf1 83.5% of the time.
2731765578959899|c4b5.principle: Before grabbing a gambit pawn, check your opponent's forcing replies: a queen recapture that attacks two things at once is the whole point of the offer.

27382415154004|d3d4.headline: Count the guards on d4 before you push
27382415154004|d3d4.why: 6.d4 pushes onto a square Black hits three times, with the pawn on e5, the knight on c6 and the bishop on c5, while White covers it only twice, so 6...exd4 simply wins a pawn. 6.Na4 goes after the bishop on c5 first: after 6...Bb6 7.O-O Nge7 8.Nxb6 axb6 one of d4's attackers is gone, and 9.d4 comes once it can be supported.
27382415154004|d3d4.principle: In the quiet Italian, push d4 only when you guard it as often as Black attacks it; otherwise trade off one of the attackers first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

275585188789254|f3d4.headline: 5.e5 kicks the f6 knight before you collect d4
275585188789254|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 recaptures, but your e4 pawn has no defender and 5...Nxe4 takes it; after 6.Nxc6 bxc6 7.Qe2 Qe7 8.O-O Nd6 Black trades queens and is slightly better. Theory points out that Black is a pawn up here but has weaknesses: the e5 square, the knight on f6 and the f7 square. 5.e5, the masters' choice 70% of the time, uses them: it attacks the knight, and after 5...d5 6.Bb5 Ne4 7.Nxd4 you have won the pawn back with more space in the centre.
275585188789254|f3d4.principle: When your opponent's extra pawn comes with weaknesses, play on the weaknesses first; the pawn can usually be won back afterwards.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d4/4...exd4

2781218480891122|g1f3.headline: Kick the e5 knight with 4.f4 and take the centre
2781218480891122|g1f3.why: After 3.d5 Ne5 the black knight sits in the centre with no pawn to support it. 4.Nf3 offers to trade it, and after 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3 Black is relieved and White's big advantage shrinks. 4.f4 attacks it with a pawn instead: the knight retreats with 4...Ng6, and after 5.Nf3 d6 6.Nc3 you have a broad centre and a big space advantage.
2781218480891122|g1f3.principle: A knight in the centre without pawn support is a target: chase it with a pawn and gain space as it retreats.

2782228191759896|g1f3.headline: ...dxe4 is threatened: settle the centre with 5.e5 first
2782228191759896|g1f3.why: The pawn on d5 attacks e4, and nothing defends it, so 5.Nf3 simply loses it: 5...dxe4 6.Ne5 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 Ne7 and Black is a pawn up. 5.e5 (66.3% of masters games) takes the pawn out of the capture and claims space: backed by d4, it takes the f6 square from Black's knight, which has to go the long way with 6...Nge7 and 7...Nf5, and White keeps a small edge. 5.exd5 also keeps the material level.
2782228191759896|g1f3.principle: Before developing, check your opponent's captures: when a pawn attacks one of your central pawns, resolve the tension by advancing, exchanging or defending.

2790758909279175|d1e2.headline: ...g6 plus ...e6 leaves d6 weak: jump in with 8.Nb5
2790758909279175|d1e2.why: Theory flags 7...e6 as a mistake: combined with ...g6 it leaves the dark squares around Black's king, d6 above all, without a pawn to guard them. 8.Nb5 heads straight for d6: in the engine line 8...a6 9.Nd6+ Kf8 costs Black the right to castle, and theory's 8...Nf6 9.Qd6 threatens Nc7+. 8.Qe2 is a normal developing move but lets Black cover the hole with 8...a6 9.a4 Qc7, and most of White's advantage is gone.
2790758909279175|d1e2.principle: A square the opponent's pawns can no longer cover is an outpost; when ...e6 and ...g6 leave d6 unguarded, a knight landing there dominates.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...g6

2797760506254471|d2d3.headline: Refute the Latvian with 3.Nxe5: take the undefended pawn
2797760506254471|d2d3.why: 3.d3 defends e4 but lets Black keep the initiative in the centre: after 3...Nc6 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Nf6 Black has the e4 pawn and easy development, and the game is level. Theory calls the Latvian utterly unsound: 2...f5 leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and not defended at all and opens the e8-h5 diagonal to Black's king. 3.Nxe5, played by masters 76.4% of the time, takes it, and Black dare not answer 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+; after the main 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 Black has spent moves on the queen and pawns while you develop, and White is clearly better.
2797760506254471|d2d3.principle: Meet an unsound gambit by taking the material when your opponent's counterattack fails tactically, here because Black's king is exposed on the e8-h5 diagonal.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5

2797760506254471|f1c4.headline: Refute the Latvian by taking e5 at once with 3.Nxe5
2797760506254471|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 declines the gambit and lets Black carry out the idea behind 2...f5: after 3...fxe4 4.Nxe5 Qg5 the queen hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once, and 5.d4 Qxg2 wins the pawn with a level game. 3.Nxe5 (76.4% of masters games) takes the undefended e-pawn right away. Black dare not reply 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+, winning an exchange or more, so the main line is 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3, and you keep a clear edge.
2797760506254471|f1c4.principle: Check captures first: when a gambit leaves a central pawn undefended and the capture also opens a check on the weakened e8-h5 diagonal, take it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f5/3. Nxe5

2816849754100076|g8f6.headline: Hit the bishop that aims at f7
2816849754100076|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 attacks the queen but leaves f7 guarded only by the king: 4.Qxf7# is mate. 3...d5 breaks the attack at its source by hitting the bishop on c4 with a pawn and opening the way for the c8-bishop; after 4.Bb3 Be6 that bishop covers f7 and Black has the better centre.
2816849754100076|g8f6.principle: Answer a threat with a move that also gains time: attacking the piece that aims at f7 removes the danger and frees your own development.

2823299714850307|b8c6.headline: Hit the base of White's pawn chain with 3...c5
2823299714850307|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks Black's own c-pawn, the one lever against White's chain, and the theory says it gives White an easy game; after 4.Nf3 f6 5.Bb5 White piles on the knight. 3...c5 attacks the base of the chain on d4 and is played in 95.8% of master games. Black follows up with ...Nc6 and ...Qb6 to add pressure on d4, and once the chain is gone the kingside pieces find good squares.
2823299714850307|b8c6.principle: When White's pawns lock the centre on d4 and e5, strike the base of the chain with your c-pawn and keep that pawn free to move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5

283181713049681|g7g5.headline: 2...g5 hangs a pawn; mirror White with 2...g6
283181713049681|g7g5.why: 2...g5 simply loses a pawn: the knight on f3 takes it with 3.Nxg5 and Black gets nothing for it. 2...g6 mirrors White's setup: Black prepares ...Bg7 and castling, and after 3.c4 Bg7 4.Bg2 the game is balanced. It is the masters' most common reply, at 42%.
283181713049681|g7g5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, count who attacks its new square: g5 is hit by the knight on f3 and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6/2. g3

2861143771416580|e7e6.headline: 4.Bg5 leaves c4 hanging: take it with 4...dxc4
2861143771416580|e7e6.why: 4...e6 lets White keep a comfortable position: after 5.e3 h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6 White's centre stands and White is slightly better. 4.Bg5 develops the bishop but leaves c4 attacked once and defended by nothing, so 4...dxc4, the most common master move (43.4%), wins a pawn. After 5.e3 b5 the pawn is backed by your queenside pawns, and 6...Qb6 and 7...a6 keep it supported, so Black is better.
2861143771416580|e7e6.principle: Accept a pawn when you can consolidate: here ...b5, ...a6 and ...Qb6 hold c4, and you finish developing afterwards.

2885293173565302|d2d3.headline: 4.c3 prepares d4 and opens b3 for the queen
2885293173565302|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too modest: Black develops comfortably with 4...Be7 and 5...Nc6, and White's edge fades. 4.c3 prepares d4 and opens the way to b3 for the queen. After 4...Nf6 5.Qb3 the queen hits b7 and backs up the bishop on c4 against f7, so Black spends a move on 5...Qc7 to cover both, and 6.d4 strikes at the centre.
2885293173565302|d2d3.principle: While Black's king is uncastled, aim the queen and bishop at f7, using a pawn move that also prepares d4.

2927847296126403|e7e6.headline: Take on f3 with 4...exf3 and keep the gambit pawn
2927847296126403|e7e6.why: White's f3 pawn attacks your e4 pawn, and 4.fxe4 would win back the gambit pawn. 4...e6 does nothing about it: after 5.fxe4 material is level, White has a broad pawn centre, and White is better. 4...exf3, the master choice in 78.7% of games, keeps the extra pawn; after 5.Nxf3 White has development for it, but you fianchetto with ...g6 and ...Bg7, castle, and stay a pawn up with the better game. 4...Bf5 and 4...e3 are also playable.
2927847296126403|e7e6.principle: Accept a gambit only if you can hold on to the pawn: here capturing on f3 keeps it, and a quick fianchetto and castling consolidate.

2927859860869340|f3g5.headline: After 3...d6, the queen covers g5; strike with 4.d4 instead.
2927859860869340|f3g5.why: With Black's e-pawn gone from e7, the queen on d8 sees g5, so 4.Ng5 just loses the knight to 4...Qxg5. 3...d6 is a passive move that blocks Black's own bishop and concedes space, and 4.d4 takes that space: after 4...exd4 5.Nxd4 White has a centralised knight, open lines and an easy lead in development.
2927859860869340|f3g5.principle: When the opponent shuts in a bishop with a passive pawn move, claim the centre with your d-pawn instead of launching a lone piece attack.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

2939336997955700|b8c6.headline: Win back the c5-pawn with 3...e6 and the bishop
2939336997955700|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 lets White keep the extra pawn: 4.a3 and then 6.b4 support the c5-pawn with pawns, and Black has no easy way to regain it. 3...e6 opens the diagonal for the king's bishop so it can recapture: after 4.c4 Bxc5 Black has the pawn back with an active bishop.
2939336997955700|b8c6.principle: When a pawn of yours has been taken, prefer the developing move that also wins it back: here the e-pawn frees the bishop to recapture on c5.

2949088022019168|g7g6.headline: When 3.Bc4 leaves e4 undefended, take it with 3...Nxe4.
2949088022019168|g7g6.why: 3...g6 ignores the loose pawn and lets White use it: 4.e5 dxe5 5.Nxe5 threatens a bishop mate on f7, and Black spends the next moves defending instead of developing. White's 3.Bc4 left e4 attacked once and not defended at all, so 3...Nxe4 wins a clean pawn. After 4.d4 g6 Black still gets the usual fianchetto, just a pawn up.
2949088022019168|g7g6.principle: Your knight on f6 hits e4 from move two, so every time White develops without covering that pawn, count its defenders and take it if there are none.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

2973368771887475|f3e5.headline: Don't grab e5: 5.c3 kicks the knight and prepares d4
2973368771887475|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 takes the knight off the f-file, and 5...Qf6 at once threatens mate on f2 and hits the knight; after 6.O-O Qxe5 you have lost a knight for a pawn. Theory explains that the point of 4.b4 is to achieve c3 and d4 with tempo. 5.c3 does exactly that: it attacks the knight on b4, and after 5...Nc6 6.d4 exd4 7.cxd4 Bb6 you have the full pawn centre in return for the gambit pawn.
2973368771887475|f3e5.principle: Answer a capture of your gambit pawn with a pawn move that attacks the capturing piece and builds your centre, so you gain time while your opponent retreats.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4

2977407816810866|a7a6.headline: After White castles, Bxc6 and Nxe5 is a real threat
2977407816810866|a7a6.why: With White castled, 4...a6 no longer holds e5: 5.Bxc6 removes its defender and 6.Nxe5 wins the pawn, because the old ...Qd4 counter fails now that the rook on f1 guards f2. 4...Nd4 attacks the bishop on b5 and takes the knight out of the exchange; after 5.Nxd4 Bxd4 Black recaptures with the bishop. Masters choose it in 43.4% of games.
2977407816810866|a7a6.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move threatens: castling made Bxc6 and Nxe5 work, so move the knight with a counterattack instead of a slow pawn move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5/4. O-O

3001047939008470|e7e5.headline: e5 has no defender here: play the solid 5...e6
3001047939008470|e7e5.why: 5...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn and the f3 knight both attack it and nothing defends it: 6.dxe5 wins it and also kicks the knight on f6 back to d7. White then follows with 7.Nd4 against the bishop on f5 and 8.f4, and Black is close to lost. 5...e6 is the main move (58.1% of master games): your light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain on f5, so ...e6 supports d5 and opens the way for ...Be7, keeping the game level.
3001047939008470|e7e5.principle: Before a pawn break, count who attacks and who defends the square it lands on; a break that is attacked twice and defended zero times just loses the pawn.

3021266198007975|d8f6.headline: Develop the knight to f6, not the queen
3021266198007975|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and 6.Nd5 hits it at once. After 6...Qd8 Black has spent two queen moves for nothing while White builds the centre with 7.c3 and 8.d4. 5...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre, puts pressure on e4 and prepares to castle, as in the line with 6...O-O.
3021266198007975|d8f6.principle: Bring the knights out before the queen: a queen on f6 takes the knight's natural square and gives White's pieces a target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

3024364401435985|g8h6.headline: Grab the centre with d5 against the early queen
3024364401435985|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 does nothing for the centre or for the pawn on e5, and after 3.d4 d5 4.dxe5 White has won it. 2...d5 takes the centre with a second pawn while White's queen sits in front of its own knight; after 3.Qg3 the queen has moved twice, and 3...Nc6 develops while guarding e5.
3024364401435985|g8h6.principle: An early queen blocks its own pieces and wastes time; answer it by taking the centre with pawns and developing, not with a knight on the rim.

3047838571696673|d7d5.headline: Develop with 2...Bc5 and aim at the d4 hole
3047838571696673|d7d5.why: 2...d5 is the Bavarian gambit, and the theory marks it as a mistake: 3.cxd5 wins a pawn. 2.c4 is slow and leaves White with a permanent hole on d4. 2...Bc5, the most common master reply, develops the bishop to a square that aims at d4 and f2.
3047838571696673|d7d5.principle: When your opponent's pawn moves leave a square that no pawn can cover, point your pieces at it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. c4

3047838571696673|d8g5.headline: Develop with 2...Bc5; an early queen just gets chased
3047838571696673|d8g5.why: 2...Qg5 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White develops by attacking it: 3.Nf3 sends it back to e7, and Black has lost time. 2.c4 left a permanent hole on d4 and blocked White's own king's bishop, and 2...Bc5 exploits that: the bishop takes an active diagonal aimed at d4 and f2.
3047838571696673|d8g5.principle: An early queen sortie invites knights and bishops to come out with tempo; develop a minor piece toward the squares your opponent has weakened instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. c4

3078274341826662|f3e5.headline: The d6 pawn guards e5: recapture on d4 instead
3078274341826662|f3e5.why: 6.Ne5 puts the knight where the pawn on d6 takes it: 6...dxe5, and 7.Qh5+ Kd7 8.Qxe5 does not win it back, leaving you a knight down. The Qh5+ trick that wins the rook on h8 in the 3...f5 line does not work here: Black answers 7.Qh5+ with 7...Kd7. Meanwhile d4 is attacked twice and not defended at all, so 6.Nxd4 (95.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and centralises the knight, with a small edge for White.
3078274341826662|f3e5.principle: Moving a developed piece again is only worth it when it wins something concrete: here the knight's second move should collect the free pawn on d4, not walk into a pawn capture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3087437353600707|d1e2.headline: Open lines with 7.e5 before Black finishes developing
3087437353600707|d1e2.why: 6...Nf6 develops without first playing ...e6, which the theory says Black uses to blunt your bishop and prepare ...Be7 and castling. 7.Qe2 is too slow: 7...Bg4 pins your knight on f3 to the queen, Black swaps it with 9...Bxf3, and Black is slightly better. 7.e5, the top master choice (56.7%), hits the knight on f6; after 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 Black's d6 pawn is isolated and the e-file opens for 11.Re1, which gives you full compensation for the pawn.
3087437353600707|d1e2.principle: You are a pawn down but ahead in development, so open lines while Black's king is still in the centre; a slow queen move gives Black time to catch up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...d6/6. Bc4

3087437353600707|f3g5.headline: No Ng5 raid: 7.e5 hits the f6 knight instead
3087437353600707|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 eyes f7, but one quiet move shuts the bishop on c4 out: after 7...e6 8.O-O Be7 9.Qe2 O-O 10.Nf3 the knight has gone back where it came from, two tempi wasted in a gambit, and Black is better. 7.e5 (56.7% of masters games) claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6. It also sets the trap from the theory notes: 7...Nxe5 8.Nxe5 dxe5 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Qxd8 wins Black's queen. After the main line 7...Ng4 8.exd6 exd6 9.O-O the game is balanced.
3087437353600707|f3g5.principle: Moving a developed piece again only pays when it wins something concrete; a knight sortie that one pawn move can parry just loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3105714547729451|c8g4.headline: Develop 2...Nf6 and hit e4 before pinning with the bishop
3105714547729451|c8g4.why: 2...Bg4 develops the bishop before the knights and lets White strike with 3.d4: after 3...e5 4.dxe5 Black loses a pawn. 2...Nf6 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4 right away, so White answers 3.Nc3 to defend it. It is the choice of 62.4% of masters.
3105714547729451|c8g4.principle: Bring the knights out before the bishops: the knight's square on f6 is clear and hits e4 now, while the bishop's best square isn't clear yet.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

3119368342174684|e7e6.headline: Strike at e5 with d6 before it gets support
3119368342174684|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is slow: it lets White shore up the advanced pawn with 4.Nc3 and 5.f4, leaving Black cramped behind it. 3...d6 attacks e5 together with the bishop on g7 before it can be supported; after 4.exd6 Qxd6 the queen and bishop both bear on d4, and 5...c5 attacks White's centre again.
3119368342174684|e7e6.principle: When White pushes a centre pawn to the fifth rank early, hit it with a pawn at once, before other pawns arrive to support it.

3179485995949204|c1f4.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 6.e5 once ...Be7 blocks its retreat
3179485995949204|c1f4.why: 6.Bf4 lets Black strike back with 6...c5, and after 7.Nc3 cxd4 8.Nxd4 your d4 pawn is traded off and much of your advantage goes with it. 5...Be7 was slow, and with the bishop on e7 the knight on f6 can no longer drop back to e7. 6.e5 gains space with tempo on the knight, which goes all the way back to g8 in the engine line, and after 7.O-O you are far ahead in development with a big advantage.
3179485995949204|c1f4.principle: A knight on f6 in front of an advanced e-pawn is a target: push the pawn when the knight has no good square, and you gain space and time together.

3179485995949204|e1h1.headline: Use your lead: 6.e5 sends the f6 knight back home
3179485995949204|e1h1.why: Black's 5...Be7 is passive and does nothing about the e4-e5 advance. 6.O-O is the most common move (83.3% of masters games), but it gives Black time for 6...O-O 7.c4 d5, and your large edge is cut in half. 6.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6; after 6...Ng8 the knight has to undo its development, and you keep a large advantage.
3179485995949204|e1h1.principle: When your opponent's quiet move hands you a clear advantage, act on it at once with a forcing advance; a routine move gives them the time to catch up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3

3191630614517678|f2f3.headline: Punish 2...Nh6 by developing 3.Nc3, not with f3
3191630614517678|f2f3.why: 3.f3 props up e4 but takes f3 from White's knight and doesn't hold: after 3...c6 4.d4 d5 5.Bb3 dxe4 Black wins a pawn. 2...Nh6 put Black's knight on the rim, away from the centre; 3.Nc3 simply develops, defends e4 and controls d5, and White keeps the lead in development.
3191630614517678|f2f3.principle: When your opponent puts a knight on the rim, just develop toward the centre; a pawn move like f3 needs a concrete reason and takes your knight's best square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4

3244175099892819|f7f6.headline: Against 1.g4, take the centre and hit g4 with 1...d5.
3244175099892819|f7f6.why: 1...f6 weakens Black's own king and does nothing against the g4 pawn, so White settles in comfortably with 2.d4 d5 3.h3. The theory calls 1.g4 one of the worst first moves because it loosens White's kingside and leaves the pawn on g4 hard to defend. 1...d5 takes central space and attacks g4 at once with the bishop on c8, and masters play it in 66.9% of games.
3244175099892819|f7f6.principle: Answer a flank opening by occupying the centre, ideally with a move that also hits the flank pawn, as ...d5 does to g4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4
Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5

3244175099892819|g8f6.headline: Against the Grob, take the centre with 1...d5
3244175099892819|g8f6.why: 1...Nf6 eyes the g4 pawn, but 2.g5 kicks the knight, which has no good square besides h5 and its starting square; after 2...Nh5 it sits on the rim while White builds a centre with 3.e4 and 5.d4. 1...d5, played in 66.9% of master games, takes central space and opens the line of the bishop on c8 to g4, so the pawn is attacked at once. After 2.c4 d4 Black gains even more space.
3244175099892819|g8f6.principle: A knight on f6 is exactly what White's g-pawn wants to chase, so take the centre with a pawn first and make the advanced pawn the target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4
Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5

3249639623522672|c7c6.headline: Use the fork trick: 6...Nxe4 and 7...d5
3249639623522672|c7c6.why: 6...c6 is slow, and 7.e5 kicks the knight back to 7...Ne8, leaving White with a big centre and Black cramped. 6...Nxe4, the masters' most common move at 36.1%, uses a fork: after 7.Nxe4 d5 the pawn attacks both the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4, and 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4 wins the piece back. The trade removes White's e-pawn and frees Black's game.
3249639623522672|c7c6.principle: When White's centre pawn is guarded only by a piece that a pawn fork can hit, trade it off before it advances and cramps you.

3253136195144505|f7f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...f6 weakens your king and wastes time
3253136195144505|f7f6.why: 3...f6 is a third pawn move that takes the f6 square from your own knight and opens the diagonal from the bishop on c4 toward g8, so castling kingside becomes risky. After 4.d4 Nc6 5.Be3 White has a strong centre and a lead in development. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4, which gains time; after 4.Nc3 Be7 Black is ready to castle.
3253136195144505|f7f6.principle: With two pawn moves already played and the bishop on c4 eyeing your king, every extra pawn move costs time and loosens the king; develop a piece instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3294566395905444|f1c4.headline: Punish 3...Bd6 with 4.Nxe5 and a pawn fork
3294566395905444|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 lets Black off the hook: after 4...Nc6 e5 is defended and the game is normal. 3...Bd6 puts the bishop beside the knight where White's centre pawns can reach them both, and 4.Nxe5 exploits it: after 4...Bxe5 5.d4 Bd6 6.e5 the pawn hits bishop and knight together, and after 6...Bb4 7.exf6 Qxf6 White has won back the piece and is a pawn up.
3294566395905444|f1c4.principle: When an enemy bishop and knight stand side by side within reach of your centre pawns, check the capture that clears the way for a pawn fork.

3294907482050607|f3g5.headline: Develop a new piece with 4.Nc3, don't jump to g5
3294907482050607|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight a second time, and Black calmly answers 4...e6: the bishop on c4 is shut off from f7, the knight on g5 has no target, and White still has two minor pieces at home. 4.Nc3 develops a new piece and defends the pawn on e4, and after 4...e6 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 White reaches an Open Sicilian with the bishop already on c4.
3294907482050607|f3g5.principle: Answer an attack on your e-pawn with a developing move that defends it, rather than moving an already developed piece again.

3297019676720294|d8e7.headline: 5...Qg5 hits the knight on e5 and the g2 pawn at once
3297019676720294|d8e7.why: 5...Qe7 does attack the knight, but it lets White play 6.d4 with gain of time against the bishop on c5, which the theory warns can be kicked by d4. Black only wins the pawn back after 8.O-O Bxe5 9.dxe5 Qxe5, having traded the bishop for the knight while White has castled and kept developing. 5...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 together, and after 6.Ng4 d5 7.d4 Qxg4 8.Qxg4 Bxg4 9.dxc5 dxe4 Black has the pawn back with the queens off.
3297019676720294|d8e7.principle: When you need to win back a pawn, do it with a move that makes two threats, so the opponent spends the move answering instead of developing with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

3303598185152393|d1d5.headline: Develop with 4.Nc3; the early 4.Qd5 just gets chased
3303598185152393|d1d5.why: 4.Qd5 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and Black develops by attacking it: 4...Nc6, then 5...Be6 hits the queen again, and after 6.Qd2 dxe5 Black has won back the pawn. 4.Nc3 develops and, as the theory notes, adds a defender to the queen on d1, which takes the sting out of the Derek Wu trap that 3...d6 sets up. In the line White keeps the extra pawn: 6.exd6 cxd6 only swaps the e-pawn for Black's d-pawn.
3303598185152393|d1d5.principle: Keep the queen at home while the minor pieces are undeveloped; in the centre it only gives Black's knights and bishops targets to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5/2...Bc5

3324621583464853|c6e5.headline: Develop with 5...Bb4 instead of moving the c6 knight again
3324621583464853|c6e5.why: 5...Ne5 moves the knight a second time and puts it where White's pawns can chase it: 6.f4 kicks it back to c6 and 7.e5 sends the other knight home to g8, so White gains a lot of time. 5...Bb4 develops a bishop, pins the knight on c3 and prepares to castle. After 6.Bd2 O-O 7.Bd3 d5 Black strikes in the centre, the break that White's queen retreat 4.Qd1 allows.
3324621583464853|c6e5.principle: With both bishops still at home, a second knight move needs a concrete gain; this one has none and only gives White's pawns a target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4/3. Qxd4/3...Nc6

3337365835027440|d2d3.headline: Punish the early 3...Qf6 by opening the centre with 4.d4.
3337365835027440|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too modest: after 4...Be6 Black trades off the bishop on c4, and the queen goes home with 6...Qd8 having lost little. Black's 3...Qf6 brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the king's knight, so White should open the centre while Black is behind. 4.d4 attacks the pawn on e5 at once, and after 4...Nc6 5.d5 Nb8 the knight is driven home; by 6...Qd8 the queen has gone back too, and White is well ahead in development.
3337365835027440|d2d3.principle: When your opponent brings the queen out early, open the centre and gain time against it rather than making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

3350501418691275|a7a6.headline: Cover e5 with 5...d6 so your f6 knight can't be kicked
3350501418691275|a7a6.why: 5...a6 does nothing about e5, so 6.e5 drives your knight all the way back to g8, and after 7.Bf4 Ne7 8.Bd3 Ng6 9.Bg3 White has a big lead in development and is clearly better. Theory stresses finding out how White deals with the e4 pawn before moving more pawns, and once White has played Nc3 the push e5 is the danger. 5...d6, the masters' choice 54.9% of the time, takes e5 under control, so the knight stays on f6 and keeps pressing e4; after 6.g4 h6 7.Rg1 Nc6 8.Be3 Bd7 you later strike back with 9...d5.
3350501418691275|a7a6.principle: Before a useful-looking pawn move, ask what your opponent wants next; here it is e5 to kick your knight, so control that square first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

3383188774541308|d8f6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qg5 forks the knight and g2.
3383188774541308|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 attacks only the knight, and 6.Ng4 hits the queen while White keeps the pawn. 5...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 together, and after 6.Ng4 h5 7.Ne3 Nxb5 8.Nxb5 Bxe3 Black wins a knight for a pawn.
3383188774541308|d8f6.principle: When a knight grabs a pawn, look for the queen move that attacks it and a second target at once; a double attack beats a single one.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

3400735200665154|g5e4.headline: Check on f7 first; the knight on e4 can wait
3400735200665154|g5e4.why: 5.Nxe4 walks into the fork trick: 5...d5 hits the knight and the bishop at once, and after 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 Black has the piece back and the better game. 4...Nxe4 left f7 attacked twice and defended only by the king, so 5.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check and drags the king out; after 5...Ke7 Black can no longer castle. Then 6.d4 means Black cannot yet take on g5 without losing the queen.
3400735200665154|g5e4.principle: With the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4 both aimed at f7, which only the king defends, look at the capture on f7 before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Nxe4

3400735200665154|g5f7.headline: Take on f7 with the bishop, with check: 5.Bxf7+
3400735200665154|g5f7.why: 4...Nxe4 grabs a pawn but leaves f7 defended only by the king. 5.Nxf7 looks tempting because it forks the queen and rook, but 5...Qh4 threatens mate on f2, and after 6.Qe2 Nd4 7.g3 Nxe2 8.gxh4 Nd4 9.Nxh8 Black's knight forks on c2 and your edge is gone. 5.Bxf7+ takes with check instead: after 5...Ke7 Black can no longer castle, and 6.d4 means Black can't yet take on g5 without losing the queen.
3400735200665154|g5f7.principle: f7 is defended only by the king at the start; when your opponent neglects it, take there with the piece that gives check and keep your attackers.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Nxe4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Nxe4/5. Nxf7

3408833361615716|e2e3.headline: A pawn up, develop with 3.Nc3 and keep the e5 pawn
3408833361615716|e2e3.why: 3.e3 blocks the bishop's pressure on f2 but is slow, and Black wins the e5 pawn back: after 3...Nc6 4.Nf3 Qe7 5.Bd2 d6 6.exd6 Bxd6 material is level. 2...Bc5 did nothing to attack e5, so White can keep the extra pawn by developing quickly. 3.Nc3 develops a piece and, as the theory notes, adds another defender to the queen to defuse Black's tricks; later 5.Ne4 hits the bishop on c5.
3408833361615716|e2e3.principle: When you are a pawn up, develop quickly and with threats so your opponent never gets the time to win it back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5/2...Bc5

3415269394174453|b2b4.headline: No Evans here: 5.d3 develops, 5.b4 just drops a pawn
3415269394174453|b2b4.why: 5.b4 offers an Evans-style pawn, but the follow-up of hitting the bishop with c3 is impossible with your knight already on c3: 5...Bxb4 simply wins a pawn, and after 6.Nd5 O-O 7.Nxb4 Nxb4 Black stays a pawn up and is better. 5.d3, the masters' choice 88.4% of the time, guards e4 and opens the diagonal for your c1 bishop. After 5...a6 6.O-O d6 7.a4 you have a solid position with the game level.
3415269394174453|b2b4.principle: In the opening, play the pawn moves that free your pieces and support the centre; a flank pawn push that neither develops nor gains time just costs material.

3415269394174453|f3e5.headline: The fork trick fails here; play the quiet 5.d3.
3415269394174453|f3e5.why: 5.Nxe5 Nxe5 6.d4 hopes to fork the knight and the bishop on c5, but the knight answers 6...Nxc4 by taking White's own bishop. After 7.dxc5 White has given a knight for a pawn. 5.d3 is the hallmark of the Giuoco Pianissimo: it defends e4, opens a line for the dark-squared bishop, and prepares a slow build-up.
3415269394174453|f3e5.principle: Before a capture that relies on a follow-up fork, check what your own loose pieces can be taken in reply.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

3415269394174453|f3g5.headline: Support e4 with 5.d3 and develop; Ng5 gets nowhere
3415269394174453|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, and 5...O-O puts a rook behind f7, so the attack has no target; after 6.d3 Nd4 the knight goes back with 7.Nf3, and Black takes over the centre with ...c6 and ...d5. 5.d3, played in 88.4% of master games, shores up e4, which the theory names as the weak point of this Italian variation because of ...Nxe4 tricks, and opens the bishop on c1 before 6.O-O.
3415269394174453|f3g5.principle: A knight that jumps to g5 must win something at once; once Black castles and covers f7, the trip only gives Black time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Nc6

3420590449456095|c1e3.headline: Pin the c6 knight with 6.Bb5 before ...e5 arrives
3420590449456095|c1e3.why: 5...Nc6 adds pressure on d4 and prepares ...e5, which the theory says the queen on a5 supports. 6.Be3 lets Black carry it out: after 6...Bg4 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 O-O-O 9.O-O-O e5 10.d5 Nd4 Black's knight lands in the centre and Black has active play. 6.Bb5, the most popular master move (48%), pins the knight on c6 to the king so it cannot join the fight for d4, and if Black lets you take it, 8.Bxc6+ bxc6 leaves Black with doubled c-pawns.
3420590449456095|c1e3.principle: A pin ties down two pieces at once: pin the knight that is doing Black's work against d4, and Black's central break loses its support.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

3420590449456095|f1d3.headline: Black is eyeing d4: pin the c6 knight with 6.Bb5
3420590449456095|f1d3.why: Your d4 pawn is defended by the queen and the knight on f3, and 6.Bd3 cuts the queen off. Black goes straight for the other defender: 6...Bg4 7.Bd2 O-O-O 8.Nb5 Qb6 9.a4 Bxf3 10.Qxf3 Nxd4, and Black has won the pawn and is slightly better. 6.Bb5, the masters' top choice (48%), develops the bishop and pins the knight on c6 to the king, so it cannot join an attack on d4. 6.Bd2 is also good.
3420590449456095|f1d3.principle: Ask what your opponent is preparing: here ...Nc6, ...Bg4 and ...O-O-O all aim at d4, so develop with a move that takes one of those attackers out of the game.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

3428826784804820|d7d5.headline: Against the Bishop's Opening, attack e4 with 2...Nf6.
3428826784804820|d7d5.why: The bishop on c4 already watches d5, so 2...d5 just gives up a pawn after 3.exd5. Black gets some activity, but not enough for the pawn. 2...Nf6 develops and attacks the pawn on e4, and it also covers h5, ruling out the early 3.Qh5 aimed at f7.
3428826784804820|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a central square, count how many enemy pieces and pawns already attack it.
