3428826784804820|d7d6.headline: Answer the Bishop's Opening with 2...Nf6, developing with a threat
3428826784804820|d7d6.why: 2...d6 overprotects a pawn that isn't attacked, since White has not played Nf3, and it shuts in Black's own king's bishop. 2...Nf6 develops with a threat to the pawn on e4, and it also controls h5, so White can't aim the queen at f7 with 3.Qh5. It is the choice in 83.2% of master games.
3428826784804820|d7d6.principle: When the e4-pawn is unprotected, develop the knight to f6 so your developing move also gains time by attacking it.

3428826784804820|d8e7.headline: Against 2.Bc4, develop 2...Nf6 instead of the queen
3428826784804820|d8e7.why: 2...Qe7 guards e5 and f7 with the queen and blocks the bishop on f8 while all four minor pieces are still at home; White just develops with 3.Nf3 and 4.O-O and then strikes with 5.d4. 2...Nf6 develops the king's knight with an attack on e4 and takes h5 away from White's queen, ruling out 3.Qh5. Masters choose it in 83.2% of games.
3428826784804820|d8e7.principle: Meet early pressure with a developing move that attacks, not with the queen, which only blocks your own pieces and becomes a target.

3428826784804820|d8f6.headline: Develop with 2...Nf6, which attacks e4 and guards h5
3428826784804820|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home and takes the knight's natural square. White develops calmly, and in the engine line the knight jumps to d5 with 7.Nd5, gaining time on your queen. 2...Nf6, played in 83% of master games, develops while attacking the e4 pawn and controls h5, so the scholar's-mate idea 3.Qh5 is off the table.
3428826784804820|d8f6.principle: Bring the knights out first and let them do the defending; the queen on f6 blocks the knight and becomes a target.

3428826784804820|d8h4.headline: Answer 2.Bc4 with 2...Nf6, not an early queen raid
3428826784804820|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home; after 3.Nc3 Bc5 4.Qe2 d6 5.Nf3 the knight hits the queen and it goes back with 5...Qd8, so Black has spent two moves for nothing. 2...Nf6 develops, attacks the pawn on e4 and controls h5, which rules out White's own queen raid. It is the master choice in 83% of games.
3428826784804820|d8h4.principle: An early queen only gives White targets to develop against with gain of time; bring out the knight that attacks e4 instead.

3428826784804820|f7f5.headline: Answer 2.Bc4 with 2...Nf6, not a risky f-pawn push
3428826784804820|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is the Calabrese Countergambit, a risky system that loosens Black's king before any piece is out, while the bishop on c4 already aims at f7. White opens lines with 3.d4 exd4 and gets active pieces, as in 4.Nh3 Nc6 5.Ng5. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on e4 and covers h5, which rules out 3.Qh5; masters choose it in 83.2% of games.
3428826784804820|f7f5.principle: With White's bishop on c4 aiming at f7, keep the f-pawn home and develop the knight to f6, which also covers h5.

3428826784804820|f7f6.headline: Put the knight on f6, not the pawn
3428826784804820|f7f6.why: 2...f6 takes the g8-knight's best square and opens the diagonal from c4 to your king, while White calmly builds the centre with 3.d4 and develops with 4.Nf3 and 5.O-O. 2...Nf6 develops with an attack on the pawn on e4 and covers h5, so it fights for the centre and keeps White's queen out at the same time.
3428826784804820|f7f6.principle: The bishop on c4 already aims at f7 and g8, so never loosen that diagonal further; meet it with pieces, not pawn moves around your king.

3428826784804820|g8h6.headline: Knight to f6, not the rim: hit e4 and cover h5
3428826784804820|g8h6.why: 2...Nh6 puts the knight on the rim, where it neither attacks e4 nor contests d5, and White gets a free hand in the centre with 3.Nf3 and 4.d4. 2...Nf6 develops the same knight to its natural square, attacks the pawn on e4 and covers h5, so the scholar's-mate idea 3.Qh5 is off the table.
3428826784804820|g8h6.principle: A knight on f6 controls central squares and hits e4, while on h6 it controls nothing central; pick the square that fights for the middle.

3450965353871567|d8f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6, which also stops 4.Qg4
3450965353871567|d8f6.why: 3...Qf6 guards g7 against 4.Qg4, but it brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home and takes the best square from your knight. In the engine line the knight has to settle for 4...Ne7, and White's knight jumps to b5 with 6.Nb5 to go after c7. 3...Nf6 is the most popular move in master games: it develops toward the centre and covers g4, so the queen can't come there to attack g7.
3450965353871567|d8f6.principle: Meet a threat with a developing move when you can; the queen should stay home while the minor pieces are still undeveloped.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3450965353871567|f7f6.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...f6 opens the king to checks.
3450965353871567|f7f6.why: 3...f6 weakens the squares around Black's king. After 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qh4 Black has a loose kingside, and the bishop on c4 eyes g8, so castling is uncomfortable. White was also threatening 4.Qg4 to win a pawn. 3...Nf6 develops the knight to its natural square, covers g4 and h5, and prepares to castle.
3450965353871567|f7f6.principle: When the bishop on c4 aims at your king's side, protect it by developing pieces, not by moving the f-pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3451177064254537|d8b6.headline: Strike with 6...d5 instead of an early queen move
3451177064254537|d8b6.why: White threatens to push d5 and win a pawn, and 6...Qb6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home instead; after 7.O-O Nf6 8.Nc3 Be7 9.d5 exd5 10.exd5 Ne5 11.Nxe5 the centre opens with your king still uncastled and White is clearly better. 6...d5 claims the centre and attacks both the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4, so White has to react. After 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 10.O-O you develop with tempo and the game is level.
3451177064254537|d8b6.principle: Don't spend a move on the queen while your minor pieces are at home; a central pawn break that attacks something does more and keeps the queen safe.

3451177064254537|g8f6.headline: Hit White's two-pawn centre at once with 6...d5
3451177064254537|g8f6.why: After 6.cxd4 White has pawns on e4 and d4, and the push d4-d5 against your knight on c6 is a real threat. 6...Nf6 lets the centre roll: 7.Qe2 Be7 8.e5 Nd5 drives your knight away and White gains space and a comfortable edge. 6...d5 claims the centre and attacks both the bishop on c4 and the pawn on e4; after 7.exd5 exd5 8.Bb3 Bb4+ 9.Nc3 Nf6 your pieces come out freely and the game is level.
3451177064254537|g8f6.principle: When your opponent builds a two-pawn centre, strike at it with a pawn before it advances and gains space with tempo.

3453954165498770|g7g6.headline: Hit the queen and e4 at once with 3...Nf6.
3453954165498770|g7g6.why: 3...g6 does chase the queen, but it develops nothing and ignores e4. After 4.Qd1 White has lost nothing, and Black has weakened the kingside. 3.Bb5 left the pawn on e4 without a defender, and 3...Nf6 attacks the queen on h5 and that pawn at the same time. After 4.Qd1 Nd4 5.a4 Nxe4 Black wins the pawn while developing.
3453954165498770|g7g6.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, chase it with a developing piece that also attacks something else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

3462820906204562|d7d6.headline: 4...Nd4 counterattacks; 4...d6 leaves Black cramped and passive.
3462820906204562|d7d6.why: 4...d6 shuts in the bishop on f8 and lets White open the centre with 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4, leaving Black cramped and a step behind. 4...Nd4 is the Rubinstein variation: the knight jumps to the centre, where it attacks the bishop on b5 and the knight on f3, and after 5.Nxd4 exd4 6.e5 dxc3 7.exf6 Qxf6 Black's pieces come alive.
3462820906204562|d7d6.principle: Answer a developing move with a centralising move that attacks something, rather than a pawn move that only defends.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6/4. Nc3

3464521704326894|e1h1.headline: Defend e4 with 4.d3 before castling
3464521704326894|e1h1.why: 4.O-O leaves e4 hanging, and after 4...Nxe4 White has to spend time getting the pawn back: 5.Bd5 Nf6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.Nxe5 Bc5 gives up the strong bishop and leaves Black with free, active development. 4.d3 simply defends e4 and opens the diagonal for the dark-squared bishop, leading to the calm Giuoco Pianissimo structure that masters choose in 74.6% of games.
3464521704326894|e1h1.principle: Before castling, check whether your e4-pawn is attacked and defended; protect it first, since castling can wait a move.

3472532178632675|f1b5.headline: Put the bishop on c4: 5...e5 left f7 weak
3472532178632675|f1b5.why: 5...e5 does nothing for f7, unlike the main move ...e6, which the theory says relieves the bishop's pressure there. 6.Bb5 aims at the knight on c6 instead: after 6...Be7 7.Qa4 Nf6 8.O-O d6 Black simply develops, and even when 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qxc6+ Bd7 wins the pawn back, Black has the bishop pair and the better game. 6.Bc4 puts the bishop on its best diagonal, the move the theory's plan for White calls for; if 6...Nf6, then 7.Ng5 d5 8.exd5 wins the pawn back with a strong initiative, and White is clearly better.
3472532178632675|f1b5.principle: Develop each piece to the square where it does the most: in the Morra the bishop belongs on c4, especially once ...e5 has left f7 without help.

347661827882589|b8a6.headline: Play 3...e6 first; 3...Na6 lets White double your pawns.
347661827882589|b8a6.why: 3...Na6 guards c7 before it is threatened, and after 4.e3 Bf5 5.Bxa6 bxa6 White trades the bishop for the knight and leaves Black with doubled, isolated a-pawns. 3...e6 reinforces the centre and opens the dark-squared bishop; only after 4.Nb5 threatens the fork on c7 does Black play 4...Na6, and then ...c6 kicks the knight back so Black's knight can reroute via c7.
347661827882589|b8a6.principle: Make the useful developing move first and meet the c7 threat only once it exists, so your knight's placement answers White's actual choice.

3481634403483951|f7f6.headline: Trade on c4 so the knight has nothing to win on e6
3481634403483951|f7f6.why: White threatens 6.Nxe6 fxe6 7.Bxe6, trading on e6 and then taking the pawn. 5...f6 makes it worse: the f-pawn no longer guards e6, so 6.Nxe6 wins the bishop outright. 5...Bxc4 removes the bishop on c4 that backs up the attack, and after 6.dxc4 h6 7.Nf3 the knight has to retreat and Black is fine.
3481634403483951|f7f6.principle: The bishop on e6 is attacked twice, by the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4, and defended once, by the f7 pawn; remove an attacker rather than weaken the defender.

3516647903289485|f8d6.headline: Knight to f6 first: 6...Bd6 gets hit by e4 and d4
3516647903289485|f8d6.why: After 6...Bd6 7.e4 the pawn hits your bishop and d5 together, and 8.d4 opens the centre while your pieces are still loose; after 9.exd5 cxd5 10.Nb5 Bb8 11.dxe5 your centre has broken up and White is clearly better. 6...Ngf6 develops the knight toward the centre and adds a guard against e4. After 7.e4 dxe4 8.Nxe4 Nxe4 9.dxe4 Be6 pieces come off and the game stays level.
3516647903289485|f8d6.principle: Bring out the knight whose square is obvious before committing a bishop that can become a target for the opponent's central pawns.

3520598348324233|d2d3.headline: Punish the early queen: 3.Nc3 heads for d5 with tempo
3520598348324233|d2d3.why: 2...Qf6 brought the queen out early and took f6 away from Black's knight, and 3.d3 lets Black off with a pawn move instead of attacking it. 3.Nc3 develops and threatens 4.Nd5, centralising the knight with tempo on the queen. After 3...Nc6 4.Nd5 Qd8 the queen has gone back home and White is clearly ahead in development, with Bc4 and castling to follow.
3520598348324233|d2d3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop your pieces to squares where they attack it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

3540159667319526|b7b6.headline: Develop with 5...Nc6 instead of spending a tempo on ...b6
3540159667319526|b7b6.why: 5...b6 is a pawn move that neither develops nor holds anything, and White uses the time: 6.dxc5 Bxc5 7.b4 drives the bishop back, and after 7...Be7 8.Bb5+ Kf8 your king has lost the right to castle, and White is clearly better. 5...Nc6 is the main move (70.2% of masters games): it develops a piece and adds pressure on d4. 5...Nf6 and 5...Bd6 are fine developing alternatives.
3540159667319526|b7b6.principle: In an open position, only move the pawns that free your pieces or fight for the centre; a flank pawn move costs a tempo your opponent can turn into threats against your king.

3541436241248924|c4f7.headline: Bxf7+ with no follow-up is just a lost bishop
3541436241248924|c4f7.why: 5.Bxf7+ gives up a bishop for one pawn: after 5...Kxf7 no other white piece can join in, because the knight on f3 is pinned against the queen by the bishop on g4. Black's 3...Bg4 delayed castling and knight development, so White should keep building instead: 5.c3 prepares 6.b4 and castling, and White keeps the easier position.
3541436241248924|c4f7.principle: f7 is attacked only by the bishop and defended by the king, so the capture just trades a bishop for a pawn; take on f7 only when a second piece also hits it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

3557627017946811|b7b5.headline: In the Pirc, play 3...g6 and fianchetto; 3...b5 just drops a pawn.
3557627017946811|b7b5.why: 3...b5 puts a pawn where the bishop on f1 can take it with check, and after 4.Bxb5+ c6 5.Be2 Black is simply a pawn down. 3...g6 is the main move: it prepares ...Bg7 to press on White's centre from the long diagonal, followed by castling kingside, in the hypermodern style. Masters play it in 49.1% of games.
3557627017946811|b7b5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check which enemy pieces see its new square; b5 is covered by White's bishop on f1.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

3562880418201798|b8c6.headline: Control d4 with a pawn: 1...c5 stops White's two-pawn centre
3562880418201798|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 eyes d4 but doesn't stop White's two-pawn centre: after 2.d4 the queen also guards d4, and 2...d5 3.e5 gains White space. 1...c5, the Sicilian, controls d4 with a pawn and is the most popular reply among masters (45.9%). When White plays d4, Black trades the c-pawn for White's d-pawn and is left with two central pawns to one.
3562880418201798|b8c6.principle: Against 1.e4, put a pawn where it controls d4, so White can't keep two pawns side by side in the centre.

3562880418201798|g8f6.headline: Fight for d4 with 1...c5 instead of inviting e5
3562880418201798|g8f6.why: 1...Nf6 invites 2.e5, and after 2...Nd5 3.d4 d6 4.c4 Nb6 5.f4 White's pawns chase the knight around and take over the centre with gain of time. 1...c5, the Sicilian and the masters' most common reply at 45.9%, controls d4 with a pawn so White can't keep a two-pawn centre. After 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has traded a flank pawn for a centre pawn and keeps two central pawns to White's one.
3562880418201798|g8f6.principle: Contest d4 with a pawn from move one, so White can never set up pawns on both e4 and d4 and kick your pieces.

3563738946985954|d1f3.headline: The knight on h6 guards f7; retreat 6.Nf3 instead of 6.Qf3
3563738946985954|d1f3.why: 6.Qf3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and 6...Nd4 attacks her at once, so 7.Qd1 sends her home while Black develops with 7...Qf6 and 8...Qg6. The knight on h6 already covers f7, so the attack from g5 has no target. 6.Nf3 admits it and returns the knight to the centre, then 7.O-O and 8.c3 continue the slow build-up of the Giuoco Pianissimo.
3563738946985954|d1f3.principle: Bring out the minor pieces before the queen: on f3 she is exposed to ...Nd4, which develops Black with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

3586492073419954|g7g6.headline: Develop 6...Be7; ...g6 after ...e6 weakens your dark squares
3586492073419954|g7g6.why: With ...e6 and ...d6 already played, 6...g6 leaves the dark squares around your king with no pawn cover: 7.Bg5 at once pins the knight on f6 to your queen, and after 7...Nbd7 8.Qe2 h6 9.Be3 e5 you have spent several pawn moves and White is clearly better. 6...Be7, the main master move (55.3%), develops, covers the dark squares and breaks any pin in advance, so you can castle next; after 7.Be3 a6 8.Bb3 b5 9.f3 O-O you have a normal Sicilian and a roughly level game.
3586492073419954|g7g6.principle: Only make the pawn moves you need: once ...e6 is played, ...g6 leaves holes on the dark squares, so develop the bishop to e7 and castle instead.

3598575371397628|b1c3.headline: Kick the knight with 3.e5; 3.Nc3 lets Black equalise
3598575371397628|b1c3.why: 3.Nc3 lets Black transpose into a comfortable open game with 3...e5, where Black's pieces develop freely, as in 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 Bb4. 2...Nf6 put the knight where White's e-pawn can kick it, and 3.e5 exploits that: it gains space with tempo and drives the knight back to g8, then White takes the centre with 4.d4. Masters choose 3.e5 in 84.6% of games.
3598575371397628|b1c3.principle: When an enemy knight on f6 can be hit by your e-pawn, the push gains space and costs the knight time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3598575371397628|d2d3.headline: Push e5 and kick the knight
3598575371397628|d2d3.why: 3.d3 is passive: it holds e4 but gives Black an easy game, and after 3...e5 4.g3 Black has a free hand in the centre. 3.e5 attacks the knight on f6 and takes the pawn out of danger in one move; after 3...Ng8 4.d4 Black's pieces are back home while White owns the centre.
3598575371397628|d2d3.principle: A knight on f6 that your e-pawn can reach with one push is a target: kick it to gain space and time.

3598575371397628|d2d4.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 3.e5; 3.d4 drops the e4 pawn
3598575371397628|d2d4.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, and 3.d4 ignores it: 3...Nxe4 wins the pawn, and after 4.d5 Nb8 White has little for it. 3.e5, the master choice in 85% of games, gains space with tempo, and the knight retreats with 3...Ng8. After 4.d4 d6 White has a big centre and a lead in development.
3598575371397628|d2d4.principle: A knight on f6 that your e-pawn can reach is a target: push to gain space and time instead of leaving e4 to be taken.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3598575371397628|f1c4.headline: Kick the knight with 3.e5 instead of leaving e4 hanging
3598575371397628|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 leaves e4 undefended, and 3...Nxe4 simply takes it; after 4.d4 d5 Black keeps the extra pawn and blocks the bishop. 3.e5 punishes the knight's arrival on f6: the pawn gains space with tempo and drives the knight back to g8, after which White builds the centre with 4.d4. Masters play 3.e5 in 84.6% of games here.
3598575371397628|f1c4.principle: When a knight on f6 attacks your e-pawn and your pawn can advance with tempo, push it: you gain space and the knight loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3601332546328408|f3g5.headline: Castle and play d4; Ng5 only gets kicked back
3601332546328408|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again, but 5...O-O puts the rook on f8 behind f7 and the attack has no target. After 6.d4 h6 7.Nf3 the knight has gone back, and 7...Nxe4 8.Nxe4 d5 strikes at White's centre, forking bishop and knight to win back the piece. 5.O-O, the most common master move (55%), tucks the king away and prepares 6.d4, building the centre the Pirc lets White have.
3601332546328408|f3g5.principle: A knight that jumps to g5 must win something at once; once Black castles and covers f7, the trip only gives Black time.

3610881811711296|d7d5.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not the Elephant Gambit
3610881811711296|d7d5.why: 2...d5 is the Elephant Gambit, and it is unsound: after 3.exd5 e4 4.Qe2 Black is a pawn down without enough to show for it, and in the game line 6.Nxe4 picks off the advanced pawn as well. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4, which is why it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|d7d5.principle: When the knight on f3 attacks e5, defend it with a developing move instead of giving up a pawn for activity you don't have yet.

3610881811711296|d8f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not the queen.
3610881811711296|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home and takes f6 away from the king's knight. White develops with gain of time, for example 3.Nc3 with the idea Nd5 hitting the queen, and Black falls behind. 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing and also controls d4, which is why it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|d8f6.principle: Defend attacked pawns with developing pieces; a queen used as a defender becomes a target for White's next knight move.

3610881811711296|f7f5.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; the Latvian gambit 2...f5 is unsound
3610881811711296|f7f5.why: 2...f5 leaves e5 hanging and opens the diagonal from h5 to your king: after 3.Nxe5 you can't grab e4 with 3...fxe4 because of 4.Qh5+, and in the engine line 3...Qf6 4.d4 d6 5.Nc4 fxe4 6.Nc3 White is simply better developed. The theory calls the gambit utterly unsound. 2...Nc6 is the main line, chosen in 86% of master games: it develops a piece, defends e5 and also controls d4.
3610881811711296|f7f5.principle: Answer an attack on e5 with a developing move that defends it, not with a pawn move that leaves the pawn loose and weakens your king.

3610881811711296|f7f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...f6 only seems to defend it
3610881811711296|f7f6.why: 2...f6 only seems to defend e5: 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn anyway, because 3...fxe5 runs into 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+, forking the king and the rook on h8. It also takes f6 away from the knight and opens the diagonal to Black's king. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4, and is played in 86% of master games.
3610881811711296|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with a developing piece, not with a pawn move that weakens your king.

3610881811711296|f8c5.headline: 2.Nf3 attacks e5: defend it with 2...Nc6 before developing elsewhere
3610881811711296|f8c5.why: 2...Bc5 develops but ignores the attack on e5, so 3.Nxe5 just wins a pawn. The theory calls this Busch-Gass gambit unsound: Black hopes for play with 3...Qh4, but gets no real compensation if White keeps their head. 2...Nc6, the main line and 86% of master games, develops the knight while defending e5 and controlling d4.
3610881811711296|f8c5.principle: Before choosing a developing move, check what your opponent's last move attacks: 2.Nf3 hit e5, so the developing move should also defend it.

3610881811711296|f8d6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6, not a bishop that blocks your d-pawn
3610881811711296|f8d6.why: 2...Bd6 defends e5 but blocks Black's d-pawn, so the queen's bishop stays shut in, and White can open the centre with 3.d4 exd4 4.Bc4, aiming at f7 before Black is organised. 2...Nc6 develops a piece while defending e5 and controlling d4; it is about five times more popular than everything else combined.
3610881811711296|f8d6.principle: Defend attacked pawns with pieces developing toward the centre, without blocking the pawns that free your other pieces.

3610922251931051|c1d2.headline: The c3 knight is pinned: guard e4 with 4.Bd3
3610922251931051|c1d2.why: Black threatens 4...Qxe4+, and the c3 knight can't really defend e4 because the b4 bishop pins it. 4.Bd2 doesn't help: 4...Bxc3 5.Bxc3 Qxe4+ removes the defender and takes the pawn with check. 4.Bd3 develops a bishop that defends e4 directly, and in the engine line Black's queen has to go back with 5...Qd8 while White castles.
3610922251931051|c1d2.principle: A pinned piece is not a real defender; protect what it guards with a piece that is free to recapture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4

3610922251931051|c1e3.headline: Defend e4 with a piece the pin can't remove
3610922251931051|c1e3.why: Black's queen attacks e4 and the bishop on b4 pins its only defender, the knight on c3: after 4.Be3 Bxc3+ 5.bxc3 Qxe4 the knight is gone and so is the pawn. 4.Bd3 develops a bishop that guards e4 directly, and after 4...d5 5.Nf3 White develops with an attack on the queen, which has to retreat with 5...Qd8.
3610922251931051|c1e3.principle: When a pinned piece is the only guard of a pawn, give the pawn a second defender that the pin can't take away.

3610922251931051|g2g3.headline: Guard e4 first: 4.Bd3 develops and defends the pawn
3610922251931051|g2g3.why: 4.g3 attacks the queen but leaves e4 hanging: Black's 3...Bb4 pins the knight on c3, so after 4.g3 Qxe4+ the queen checks and hits the rook on h1 as well, and 5.Qe2 Qxh1 costs White a whole rook. 4.Bd3 develops a piece and protects e4, and after 4...d5 5.Nf3 Qd8 Black's queen has to retreat while White keeps a clear lead in development.
3610922251931051|g2g3.principle: Before kicking the queen, check what your move leaves loose: with the knight pinned, e4 has no real defender.

361821916697346|f3g5.headline: In the slow Italian, gain queenside space with 7.a4
361821916697346|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with the queenside pieces still at home, and after 7...O-O f7 is safe, so the knight has nothing to hit and goes back with 11.Nf3. 7.a4 builds on the pawns already on b4 and c3: after 7...a5 8.b5 the knight on c6 is pushed away and White gains queenside space before castling. Masters choose it in 69% of games.
361821916697346|f3g5.principle: A knight jump at f7 only pays if f7 can't be defended; once Black can castle, spend the move gaining space instead of moving the knight again.

362391570447215|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 drops e4: take it with 4...dxe4
362391570447215|c5d4.why: 4...cxd4 releases the tension in White's favour: after 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.Nxd4 you are left with an isolated pawn on d5, White develops with checks like 8.Qe2+, and the edge passes to White. 4.d4 abandoned the e4 pawn, which is attacked once and not defended at all. 4...dxe4 wins it and kicks the knight, and after 5.Ne5 Nf6 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 Nbxd7 you have developed smoothly and kept the extra pawn.
362391570447215|c5d4.principle: Every time your opponent changes the pawn structure, check what is newly undefended; a loose centre pawn is worth taking before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6

3649736493107135|b7b6.headline: Castle before queenside moves; e5 is coming
3649736493107135|b7b6.why: 5...b6 is a slow wing move with the king still in the centre: 6.e5 hits the knight on f6, and after 6...dxe5 7.dxe5 Nfd7 8.e6 the pawn breaks into Black's position. 5...O-O completes the Pirc plan from the theory: fianchetto the bishop to pressure White's centre, then castle kingside, and after 6.O-O Nc6 Black starts working on the centre. Masters castle here in 85% of games.
3649736493107135|b7b6.principle: With White's pawn ready to advance to e5 and open lines, castle before spending moves on the queenside.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

3678353102233444|g8f6.headline: Recapture at once with 3...exd5 in the Exchange QGD
3678353102233444|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 lets White capture again: after 4.dxe6 Bxe6 White has taken two pawns for one. d5 is attacked twice and not defended, so 3...exd5 recaptures at once, keeps a pawn on d5 and opens the diagonal for the light-squared bishop that 2...e6 had blocked.
3678353102233444|g8f6.principle: Recapture toward the centre straight away: the pawn on d5 holds your share of the centre and frees the bishop on c8.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6

3692429315258999|c4e2.headline: Challenge the pinning bishop with 6.h3 instead of retreating
3692429315258999|c4e2.why: Black threatens 6...dxe5 to win the pawn back, and 6.Be2 doesn't stop it; it also moves the bishop a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and after 6...dxe5 the game is level. 5...Bg4 pins your f3 knight to the queen, so ask the bishop at once: 6.h3 attacks it, and in the engine line Black gives it up with 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3. After 7...Nxe5 8.Qe2 Nxc4 9.Qxc4 c6 10.Nc3 your queen is active, Black's light-squared bishop is gone and you keep the lead in development.
3692429315258999|c4e2.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, question it with h3 before it does damage, rather than spending a move on a passive interposition.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

3699514865674152|d1e2.headline: 7.Ng5 hits f7 twice and wins the gambit pawn back
3699514865674152|d1e2.why: The theory explains that Black usually plays ...e6 to relieve your bishop's pressure on f7; ...e5 and ...Nf6 leave f7 guarded only by the king. 7.Qe2 is too slow: Black plays 7...Be7 and castles, f7 is safe, and with the gambit pawn in hand Black is slightly better. 7.Ng5 hits f7 a second time, so Black answers 7...d5 to block the bishop, but 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 wins the pawn back and your d5 pawn hits the knight on c6, leaving White clearly better.
3699514865674152|d1e2.principle: Moving the knight a second time is justified when it wins something concrete: here it doubles the attack on f7 and forces Black to give the pawn back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3699514865674152|e1h1.headline: ...e5 leaves f7 exposed: 7.Ng5 before castling
3699514865674152|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is natural but slow: Black gets 7...Be7 and castles, your gambit compensation is gone and Black keeps the extra pawn. Black chose ...e5 rather than ...e6, which the theory notes would have relieved the bishop's pressure on f7, so 7.Ng5 hits f7 a second time while only the king defends it. In the main line Black blocks with 7...d5, and 8.Bxd5 Nxd5 9.exd5 wins a pawn back with the better game.
3699514865674152|e1h1.principle: When the opponent leaves the bishop on c4 staring at f7, add a second attacker before you castle; f7 is defended only by the king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3/4...Nc6/5. Nf3

3708088433535320|f1b5.headline: Take the whole centre with d4 against 1...b6
3708088433535320|f1b5.why: 2.Bb5 develops the bishop to a square with no target: Black hits e4 with 2...Bb7 and chases the bishop with 3...a6 and 4...b5. 1...b6 lets White take the centre for free, and 2.d4 does so: both centre pawns stand side by side and both bishops are ready to come out.
3708088433535320|f1b5.principle: When the opponent's first move ignores the centre, occupy it with a second pawn before sending pieces to squares without a purpose.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4

3725666597101221|c2c3.headline: Develop with 3.Bb5; 3.c3 leaves e4 loose
3725666597101221|c2c3.why: 3.c3 prepares d4 but takes the c3 square from White's own knight, so the pawn on e4 is loose and Black can hit it at once with 3...d5 or 3...Nf6. 3.Bb5, the Ruy Lopez, is the master choice (65%): it develops, gets White ready to castle, and pressures the knight on c6 that defends e5.
3725666597101221|c2c3.principle: Develop a piece with pressure before spending a move on pawn preparation like c3.

3725666597101221|d2d3.headline: Develop with 3.Bb5 rather than the passive 3.d3
3725666597101221|d2d3.why: 3.d3 defends e4 before it is attacked and shuts in the bishop on f1, so Black takes free play in the centre, as in 3...Nf6 4.g3 d5. 3.Bb5, the Ruy Lopez, develops the bishop instead, gets White ready to castle, and puts pressure on the knight on c6, the defender of e5. Masters choose it in 65% of games.
3725666597101221|d2d3.principle: When nothing of yours is attacked, develop a piece that pressures the opponent rather than a pawn move that guards what is already safe.

3726374757153429|f1c4.headline: 5.Bg5 pins the e7 knight and stops 5...Nec6
3726374757153429|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black untangle at once with 5...Nec6, and after 6.Nc3 Be7 7.Nd5 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 O-O the knights are traded and Black is comfortable, so half your edge is gone. 4...Ne7 blocks the f8 bishop, and 5.Bg5 pins that knight to the queen on d8, so it cannot move without losing the queen. Black spends 5...h6 chasing the bishop, and after 6.Be3 Nec6 7.Nc3 Be7 8.Nd5 O-O 9.Nb5 your knights take over d5 and b5 while Black's knight ends up on a6.
3726374757153429|f1c4.principle: Develop your bishop to a square where it pins or attacks, so the opponent has to spend a move answering it instead of carrying out their plan.

3729547871689507|f1c4.headline: Answer 1...Nc6 with 2.Nf3; a c4 bishop runs into ...d5
3729547871689507|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 puts the bishop where Black's centre pawns can hit it: after 2...e6 3.d4 d5 4.exd5 exd5 it has to move again with 5.Bb3, and 6...Na5 chases it once more. 2.Nf3 develops the knight to its best square and is the most popular master move at 60%. If Black answers 2...e5 the game is a normal Open Game, and other replies leave Black's knight awkwardly placed.
3729547871689507|f1c4.principle: The knight's best square, f3, is clear already, while the bishop's depends on how Black's pawns settle; Black can still choose ...e6 and ...d5, which would hit a bishop on c4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

3729547871689507|f2f4.headline: Develop the king's knight; save pawn moves for the centre
3729547871689507|f2f4.why: 2.f4 develops nothing, and after 2...d5 3.e5 d4 Black gains space and White's edge is gone. 2.Nf3 develops the knight to its most active square and invites 2...e5, a normal Open Game; if Black avoids it, the knight on c6 gets in the way of Black's usual pawn breaks.
3729547871689507|f2f4.principle: With no reason yet to commit pawns, bring the king's knight out first; its best square is already clear.

3747843569338814|d2d4.headline: After 3...Bc5, use the fork trick: 4.Nxe5 and 5.d4
3747843569338814|d2d4.why: 4.d4 loses a pawn after 4...exd4, and 5.Nd5 does not win it back. 4.Nxe5 takes the e5 pawn because the knight on c6 is not really defending it: after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 the pawn forks the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5, and White wins the piece back. Material stays level, but White gets the freer game and the centre.
3747843569338814|d2d4.principle: Look at captures first: e5 looks defended, but after the capture 5.d4 forks two pieces, so the defence is an illusion.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

3772385141189769|d2d4.headline: Prepare d4 with 2.Nf3 so a knight, not the queen, recaptures.
3772385141189769|d2d4.why: 2.d4 cxd4 leaves an awkward choice: 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen, and 3.Nf3 allows 3...e5, keeping the extra pawn. Playing 2.Nf3 first means that after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 White recaptures with the knight and keeps the tempo, and Black has no time to defend the d4 pawn.
3772385141189769|d2d4.principle: Prepare the central break so a knight recaptures on d4; a queen there is chased by ...Nc6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5

3772385141189769|f1c4.headline: Play 2.Nf3 against the Sicilian; 2.Bc4 runs into ...e6 and ...d5.
3772385141189769|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 aims at f7, but Black answers 2...e6 and later ...d5, blunting the bishop and gaining time on it with an easy central position. 2.Nf3 adds control of d4 and prepares 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4, opening the position while Black, whose 1...c5 did nothing for development, is still catching up.
3772385141189769|f1c4.principle: Against the Sicilian, put your pieces where they support the d4 break, not on squares Black can hit with a central pawn.

3772385141189769|f2f4.headline: Against the Sicilian, develop with 2.Nf3 and prepare d4
3772385141189769|f2f4.why: 2.f4 starts a kingside attack before White has developed, and Black answers by striking in the centre: after 2...e6 3.Nf3 d5 White has to commit with 4.Bb5+ Nd7 5.e5, and Black's position is fine. 2.Nf3 develops and prepares 3.d4; after the pawn trade White recaptures with the knight and gets open lines for both bishops and the queen. It is the choice in 83% of master games.
3772385141189769|f2f4.principle: 1...c5 does nothing for Black's development, so develop and open the centre with d4 rather than spend a move on a flank pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5

3800718395256466|c6d5.headline: Recapture 7...Nxd5 and keep c6 guarding b5
3800718395256466|c6d5.why: 7...cxd5 removes the pawn that kept White's knight out of b5: 8.Nb5 threatens a fork on c7, Black has to answer 8...Kd8, and after 9.Ne5 Bg6 10.Nxa7 White's rook on a1 helps win the a7 pawn, leaving White clearly better. 7...Nxd5 takes back the pawn, which was attacked twice and defended only by the knight on c3, and leaves the c6 pawn in place. After 8.e4 Nxc3 9.exf5 Nd5 material is level and White's edge is small.
3800718395256466|c6d5.principle: In a queenless position judge the differences: 7.axb3 gave White a half-open a-file against a7, so keep the c6 pawn covering b5 and recapture with a piece.

3815488023003540|b8c6.headline: Resolve the tension with 5...cxd4 before d5 kicks your knight
3815488023003540|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 leaves the c5 and d4 pawns facing each other, and White pushes past with 6.d5: the knight is hit and goes to the rim with 6...Na5, and the pawn on d5 cramps Black, giving White a clear advantage. 5...cxd4 trades your flank pawn for White's centre pawn and claims the centre. After 6.a4 b4 7.Nxd4 Black has the half-open c-file and develops comfortably with 7...Qc7 and 8...Nf6, with a level game.
3815488023003540|b8c6.principle: Before putting a knight in front of the opponent's centre pawns, check whether a pawn advance can hit it; trading that pawn off first removes the threat.

3815955546086349|d8f6.headline: Take the centre with 2...d5; a queen on f6 is a target.
3815955546086349|d8f6.why: 2...Qf6 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White gains time on it: after 3.c4 c6 4.Bg2 the queen has to move again with 4...Qe6. 2.g3 is slow, and 2...d5 punishes it by building a full pawn centre, as in 3.d4 Nc6 4.Nf3 e4, where Black gains space with tempo on the knight.
3815955546086349|d8f6.principle: Against a slow flank setup like e3 and g3, occupy the centre with both pawns; that is worth more than an early queen sortie.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5

3842365322435851|b8c6.headline: Take the free pawn: 3...Nxe4 punishes 3.Nf3
3842365322435851|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 is a decent move, but it gives White time to cover e4 with 4.d3, and the game becomes a quiet Italian where Black's chance is gone. White's 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. After 3...Nxe4 4.Nxe5 d5 Black's pawn attacks the bishop on c4 and takes the centre; the bishop retreats with 5.Be2 and Black develops with 5...Bd6.
3842365322435851|b8c6.principle: Every time your opponent moves, check what they left undefended: here the e4 pawn was hanging to the f6 knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|d7d5.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|d7d5.why: 3...d5 gives up a pawn for nothing: 4.exd5 takes it, and after 4...e4 5.Ne5 White's knight is active while Black is a pawn down. 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by the knight and defended by nothing, so 3...Nxe4 simply takes it. After 4.Nxe5 d5 Black hits the bishop on c4 and shuts it off from f7.
3842365322435851|d7d5.principle: Before each move, check what is loose: White's e4 pawn has no defender, so take it before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|d7d6.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 undefended: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends e5 but passes up a free central pawn, and after 4.Nc3 White has covered e4 and the chance is gone. White's 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by your knight and defended by nothing. 3...Nxe4 takes it; White can only win back e5 with 4.Nxe5, and then 4...d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and builds a strong centre, with 5...Bd6 hitting the knight on e5 next.
3842365322435851|d7d6.principle: Check what is loose after every opponent move: White's third move developed a piece but left the e4 pawn hanging.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3842365322435851|f6h5.headline: 3.Nf3 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
3842365322435851|f6h5.why: 3...Nh5 moves the knight a second time to the rim and leaves e5 unprotected: 4.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and after 4...Qg5 5.Bxf7+ Kd8 6.Qxh5 the knight on h5 falls too. 3.Nf3 left e4 attacked and not defended at all, so 3...Nxe4 simply takes it, and after 4.Nxe5 d5 Black has a solid centre and easy development.
3842365322435851|f6h5.principle: Check what is loose on both sides before moving: White's e4 pawn was free, and taking it also gets your knight out of trouble.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

3881559155902992|d7d5.headline: Guard e5 with 4...d6; 4...d5 just drops a pawn.
3881559155902992|d7d5.why: White threatens 5.Nxe5, and 4...d5 doesn't help: d5 is attacked by the e4 pawn, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4, more times than Black can defend it, so 5.Nxd5 wins it. 4...d6 calmly defends e5 and opens the c8 bishop, and Black castles next, as in 5.O-O O-O.
3881559155902992|d7d5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count: d5 is hit three times by White and covered only twice by Black.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Bc5

3903276797068408|a2a3.headline: Take on c5 now: 7.dxc5 wins a pawn
3903276797068408|a2a3.why: 7.a3 is too slow: after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 Qb6 Black's queen hits b2 and backs up the attack on d4, and the position tips slightly in Black's favour. The theory notes explain that White threatens to take on c5 and that ...Bg4 does not stop it, so Black should have released the tension with ...cxd4. 7.dxc5 takes the pawn while it is there, and after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you are a pawn up with a small edge.
3903276797068408|a2a3.principle: In the Advance structure Black aims every break at the base of your chain on d4; when the pawn attacking it can be captured for free, take it instead of letting the pressure build.

3903276797068408|h2h3.headline: Take on c5 with 7.dxc5 before Black liquidates
3903276797068408|h2h3.why: 7.h3 invites 7...Bxf3, and after 8.gxf3 Qb6 your kingside pawns are doubled, Black's queen hits b2 and Black is better. Theory notes that in this line White keeps threatening to take on c5, which is why Black should liquidate the tension with ...cxd4. 6...e6 didn't, so take now: 7.dxc5 wins a pawn, and after 7...Bxf3 8.Qxf3 you recapture with the queen and keep your pawn structure intact.
3903276797068408|h2h3.principle: Look at captures before quiet moves: when your opponent leaves the central tension in place, the capture may simply win a pawn.

3931450314873962|d2d3.headline: Black's light-squared bishop is gone: hit b7 with Qb3
3931450314873962|d2d3.why: 6.d3 is solid but slow: it leaves the queen on f3 with nothing to do and lets Black catch up in development. Black's 3...Bg4 traded off the bishop that guarded b7, so 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 and lines up behind the bishop on c4 against f7. After 6...d5 7.Qxb7 White wins a pawn.
3931450314873962|d2d3.principle: When the opponent gives up the bishop that guards a pawn, check whether your queen can reach that loose pawn while keeping pressure elsewhere.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

3931450314873962|g2g4.headline: Black's light-squared bishop is gone: hit b7 with Qb3
3931450314873962|g2g4.why: 6.g4 weakens White's own kingside and achieves nothing: Black just develops with 6...Nc6 and later castles long. Black's 3...Bg4 traded off the bishop that guarded b7, so 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 straight away; after 6...d5 7.Qxb7 White is a pawn up and ahead in development.
3931450314873962|g2g4.principle: Once the opponent gives up the bishop that guarded b7, check whether your queen can reach that pawn before starting a pawn storm.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

3941407114211180|a2a3.headline: Castle first, so e5 later hits the queen with tempo
3941407114211180|a2a3.why: 5.a3 is a slow pawn move: after 5...d6 6.d4 Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 the pawn on d4 attacks the knight on c3, and White ends up a pawn down. 5.O-O tucks the king away first, so in the same sequence 8.e5 attacks the queen on f6 with gain of time and White stays ahead in development. Black's early queen and 4...c6 have cost time, and castling keeps that lead alive.
3941407114211180|a2a3.principle: Black's queen came out on move two; keep developing and castle, so that central pawn moves gain time by attacking it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6/3. Bc4

397857285398425|d5d4.headline: Keep the tension with 4...Nc6; 4...d4 hands White e4
397857285398425|d5d4.why: 4...d4 kicks the knight, but your pawn no longer covers e4, so the knight jumps straight there with 5.Ne4, and after 5...Nc6 6.d3 f5 7.exf6 Nxf6 8.g3 the game is level. 4.e5 has given you a French-type structure, and 4...Nc6, the main master move (77.3%), develops and aims at d4; in the line 5.Nf3 Bd7 6.d4 Nh6 7.Ne2 Qb6 8.c3 f6 Black piles up on d4, then hits e5 with ...f6, and is slightly better.
397857285398425|d5d4.principle: Against a pawn chain, keep your own pawns where they are and aim your pieces at its base: here the knight on c6 and queen on b6 work against d4.

3987932696906099|d1f3.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; a queen on f3 only becomes a target.
3987932696906099|d1f3.why: 5.Qf3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and Black meets it with 5...Qf6, offering a trade, so White's queen has to retreat with 6.Qe2 having achieved nothing. 5.O-O tucks the king away first and prepares Re1 behind the e4 pawn, as in 5...Nf6 6.d3 c6 7.Re1, keeping the lead in development the trade on d4 gave White.
3987932696906099|d1f3.principle: With the knights traded, finish development and castle before bringing the queen out, so Black gets nothing to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

399137672893272|f1b5.headline: Take the pawn with 4.exd5; 4.Bb5+ lets Black push ...d4.
399137672893272|f1b5.why: 4.Bb5+ c6 5.Be2 wastes time, and 5...d4 drives the knight back to b1, after which Black takes on e4 with 6...Nxe4 and has the active game. 3...d5 is a loose pawn break, and 4.exd5 wins the pawn and claims the centre. After 4...Bd6 Black spends a move defending e5, and White can still give the check 5.Bb5+ once it gains something.
399137672893272|f1b5.principle: Among forcing moves, look at captures before checks: a check that wins nothing only helps the opponent improve.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

399137672893272|f1c4.headline: Take the offered pawn with 4.exd5; c4 is covered by d5
399137672893272|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 puts the bishop where the d5 pawn takes it: 4...dxc4 wins a piece, and 5.Nxe5 gets back only a pawn. 3...d5 was a loose pawn push, and 4.exd5 simply takes it while claiming the centre. After 4...Bd6 5.Bb5+ c6 6.dxc6 Nxc6 White still has the extra pawn.
399137672893272|f1c4.principle: Before developing a piece, check which squares enemy pawns attack: the d5 pawn covers c4, and it is itself the loose target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

3996150506658750|f3g5.headline: Castle with 6.O-O; here 6.Ng5 has no target and gets chased.
3996150506658750|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and the knight on d5 blocks the bishop's line to f7, so there is nothing to attack. 6...f6 sends it on another trip after 7.Nc3 Bb4 8.Ne4, while Black's pawns take over the centre. 6.O-O tucks the king away and prepares 7.Re1, lining up the rook against the e5 pawn. Masters castle in 87.8% of games.
3996150506658750|f3g5.principle: Before moving a developed piece again, ask what it attacks; with nothing to hit on f7, finish development and castle instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d3

4040334401902569|c4e2.headline: Hit the pinning bishop with 5.h3, then kick the knight with d5
4040334401902569|c4e2.why: 4...Bg4 threatens to remove the defender of d4: after 5.Be2 Bxf3 6.Bxf3 Nxd4 you are a pawn down and your bishop has moved twice for nothing. 5.h3 questions the bishop at once. After 5...Bh5, 6.d5 takes the pawn out of the attack with tempo on the knight, which goes back to 6...Nb8, and you keep a big space advantage and develop easily with 7.Be3.
4040334401902569|c4e2.principle: When the opponent's pieces sit where your pawns can hit them, push with tempo: h3 and d5 gain space while the bishop and knight lose time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

4040334401902569|d4e5.headline: Break the pin with 5.h3 instead of releasing the centre
4040334401902569|d4e5.why: In the Paris Defence White has the extra space, and 4...Bg4 pins your f3 knight to the queen, so d4 is only defended in name and Black threatens 5...Nxd4. 5.dxe5 solves that by trading your space away: after 5...dxe5 most of White's advantage is gone. 5.h3 questions the bishop at once, and after 5...Bh5 6.d5 you gain even more space with tempo on the knight.
4040334401902569|d4e5.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, everything that knight guards is loose; break the pin, usually with h3, before your opponent cashes in.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

4084843176360845|f8e8.headline: Use the fork trick: 6...Nxe4, then ...d5 hits two pieces
4084843176360845|f8e8.why: 6...Re8 is slow: 7.e5 kicks the knight on f6, and after 7...d5 8.Bd3 Nh5 it sits on the edge while White has more space. 6...Nxe4 is the fork trick: after 7.Nxe4 d5 the pawn attacks both the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4, so Black regains the piece with 8.Bd3 dxe4 9.Bxe4. Then 9...c5 strikes at d4, and White's centre is broken up.
4084843176360845|f8e8.principle: Look at captures first: ...Nxe4 works whenever ...d5 can then fork a bishop on c4 and a knight on e4.

4111926581298046|d6e5.headline: Against 5.e5, retreat 5...Nfd7 and hit d4 with ...c5
4111926581298046|d6e5.why: 5...dxe5 opens the d-file with the queens facing each other, and after 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 Ng4 the e5 pawn is still held by the f4 pawn, so Black wins nothing. 9.Nd5 then hits c7, and Black's king has to step to 9...Kd8. 5...Nfd7, the masters' choice 59.2% of the time, keeps the tension and prepares to attack the centre from the side: after 6.Nf3 c5 Black hits d4.
4111926581298046|d6e5.principle: White's pawns on d4 and e5 form a chain; aim your pawn break at its base on d4 rather than swapping at the head.

4120112958252679|f6d7.headline: Trade queens with check first, then move the knight
4120112958252679|f6d7.why: 6...Nfd7 dodges 7.exf6 but walks into 7.e6: after 7...fxe6 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qxd8+ Kxd8 10.f4 the knight on e5 is chased and lost to 11.fxe5. 6...Qxd1+ trades queens with check, so after 7.Nxd1 Black has a free move to rescue the knight, and 7...Ng4 puts it where it attacks the e5 pawn. Black wins that pawn back by 10...fxe6 and ends up a pawn ahead.
4120112958252679|f6d7.principle: When a pawn attacks your knight, look at checks and captures first: a capture with check buys the tempo to move the knight to an active square.

4120112958252679|f6g4.headline: Trade queens with check first, then hunt e5 with the knights
4120112958252679|f6g4.why: 6...Ng4 moves the knight a second time and lets White trade first: 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 costs Black the right to castle, and after 8.Bf4 and 9.Rd1+ White's pieces swarm around the exposed king. 6...Qxd1+ captures first with check, so 7.Nxd1 pulls White's knight back, and then 7...Ng4 and 8...Nc6 both attack the pawn on e5. The line ends with Black a pawn up after 10.e6 fxe6.
4120112958252679|f6g4.principle: When queens face each other on an open file, capture first with check so your king keeps its shelter and the opponent's pieces are pulled back.

4138915868453329|b7b5.headline: Develop the light-squared bishop before starting queenside play
4138915868453329|b7b5.why: 4...b5 is a flank pawn move while White already has a full centre and two knights out; after 5.Bd3 b4 6.Ne2 the pawns run forward, but Black's kingside is still at home and White simply castles. 4...Bg4 develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the knight on f3, which defends d4. After 5.h3 Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 Black has a solid pawn chain and can still expand with ...b5 later, as in the line; masters choose it in 77% of games.
4138915868453329|b7b5.principle: Before starting play on the wing, bring out the pieces still at home; the light-squared bishop belongs outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6

4140088474015032|e7e5.headline: Finish the fianchetto with 2...Bg7; 2...e5 abandons the plan.
4140088474015032|e7e5.why: 2...e5 mixes two setups: after 3.d4 exd4 4.Qxd4 White's queen sits in the centre, and the dark squares on Black's kingside, weakened by 1...g6, have no bishop to guard them. 2...Bg7 completes the fianchetto that 1...g6 prepared: Black lets White build a centre and undermines it later with ...d6 and ...Nf6, as in 2...Bg7 3.d4 d6 4.Nc3 Nf6.
4140088474015032|e7e5.principle: Complete the setup your first move committed to: after 1...g6, the bishop on g7 is the piece that makes that pawn move worthwhile.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

4141510809291242|d7d5.headline: 1.c4 targets d5: develop with 1...Nf6 instead
4141510809291242|d7d5.why: 1.c4 discourages 1...d5, and the theory notes say that capturing the pawn gives White a small advantage: after 2.cxd5 Nf6 3.d4 c6 4.dxc6 Nxc6 White has traded the c-pawn for your centre pawn and is a pawn up. 1...Nf6 is the most popular reply (27.7% of masters games): it develops toward the centre, controls d5 and e4 with a piece, and keeps your options open; after 2.d4 the game can turn into an Indian defence. 1...e5, 1...e6 and 1...c5 are also good.
4141510809291242|d7d5.principle: Your king's knight's best square is clear from move one, while the right pawn setup depends on what White does next; so develop the knight first and choose the pawn moves later.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. c4
Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. c4/1...Nf6

4149741967394205|c1f4.headline: Knight first: 4.Nc3 before deciding where the bishop goes
4149741967394205|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 lets Black take on c4: after 4...dxc4 5.Qa4+ Nbd7 White spends queen moves regaining the pawn, and 6...Nd5 7.Bxc4 Nxf4 8.exf4 swaps off the early bishop and doubles White's f-pawns. 4.Nc3 develops the knight toward the centre and adds pressure on d5. It is one of White's main moves here and the choice of 61.7% of masters.
4149741967394205|c1f4.principle: The knight's best square on c3 is clear now, while the queen's bishop's best square depends on how Black's pawns settle, so bring the knight out first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nf3/3...Nf6

4149982820903367|e8h8.headline: Release the tension with 7...dxc4 before White strips d5's defenders
4149982820903367|e8h8.why: White threatens to win a pawn on d5, and 7...O-O doesn't stop it: after 8.Bxf6 Bxf6 9.Bxf5 exf5 10.cxd5 White's two bishop trades remove the knight and pawn that guarded d5, and you are a pawn down. 7...dxc4 takes the target away first and makes the d3 bishop move a second time with 8.Bxc4. Then 8...h6 9.Bh4 Ne4 forces trades that free your position, and after 10.Nxe4 Bxe4 11.Bxe7 Qxe7 the game is level.
4149982820903367|e8h8.principle: Count the defenders of a centre pawn under pressure, including pieces your opponent can exchange off, and release the tension before a routine move like castling.

4150297190773573|e7e5.headline: In the Pirc, finish the fianchetto with 4...Bg7 before playing ...e5.
4150297190773573|e7e5.why: 4...e5 opens the d-file with Black's king still in the centre: after 5.dxe5 dxe5 6.Qxd8+ Kxd8 Black has lost the right to castle, 7.Bg5 pins the knight on f6 to the king, and after 7...Be7 8.Nxe5 the e5 pawn falls. 4...Bg7 is the Pirc plan: the bishop presses on the centre from the long diagonal and Black castles next, as in 5.Be2 O-O 6.O-O. Masters choose it in 97.5% of games.
4150297190773573|e7e5.principle: Don't open the centre while your king is still on e8: castle first, then challenge White's pawns.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

4164085910631465|c1g5.headline: Rebuild the Evans centre: take back with 8.cxd4
4164085910631465|c1g5.why: You are two pawns down here, and the Evans Gambit pays for them with the centre. 8.Bg5 leaves the d4 pawn alone, and after 8...dxc3 9.Nxc3 you are still two pawns down with only the e4 pawn left in the middle, and Black is better. The pawn on d4 is attacked three times and defended twice, so 8.cxd4 wins one pawn back and puts pawns on e4 and d4, the centre 6.d4 was aiming for; White keeps a small edge.
4164085910631465|c1g5.principle: In a gambit, the material you gave is paid for by the centre and development; whenever a pawn capture lets you rebuild the centre, take it before developing further.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4164085910631465|c4f7.headline: Win d4 back with 8.cxd4 instead of sacrificing on f7
4164085910631465|c4f7.why: 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.cxd4 gives a bishop for two pawns, and Black is better. 7...Nge7 left the d4 pawn attacked three times and defended only twice, so you can simply take it back: 8.cxd4 rebuilds the e4-d4 centre the gambit was played for and hits the bishop on c5, which retreats with 8...Bb6. Then 9.Ng5 adds a second attacker to f7 while Black's king is still on e8, and you keep the advantage.
4164085910631465|c4f7.principle: The Evans Gambit gives a pawn for a big centre and fast development, so when you can win the centre pawn back cleanly, do that before any sacrifice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4175344914430296|e7e5.headline: Nothing defends e5: play the solid 4...e6
4175344914430296|e7e5.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 attacks it and nothing of yours defends it, so 5.Nxe5 simply wins it, and after 5...Bd6 6.Nf3 Nf6 White is clearly better. 4...e6, the masters' top choice (43.2%), backs up d5, opens the way for the f8 bishop and keeps the game level. 4...Nf6 and 4...h6 are also fine.
4175344914430296|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count who attacks the square and who defends it; a pawn on e5 facing a knight with no defender is just lost.

4211428648959227|c5d4.headline: Recapture 4...exd5 at once; 4...cxd4 leaves White's d5 pawn alive
4211428648959227|c5d4.why: The white pawn on d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, so take it back now. 4...cxd4 lets it live: after 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.dxe6 fxe6 7.cxd4 your e6 pawn is isolated, the c3 square is free for White's knight again, and White is clearly better. 4...exd5, played in 89.8% of master games, recaptures and opens a diagonal for your c8 bishop, and the game stays level; the theory notes that Black is in no hurry to play ...cxd4, because that frees c3 for White's knight.
4211428648959227|c5d4.principle: Recapture toward the centre: taking on d5 with the e-pawn restores your central pawn and frees a bishop, while ...cxd4 hands White's pieces the c3 square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. c3

4215612887472399|b8c6.headline: Meet the Vienna Gambit with 3...d5, hitting back in the centre
4215612887472399|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 lets White play 4.fxe5, and after 4...Nxe5 5.d4 Ng6 6.e5 the white pawns chase both black knights, sending the one on f6 back to g8. 3...d5 is the correct counterstrike: it hits e4 at once, so after 4.fxe5 Nxe4 Black's knight lands on a strong central square and Black has active play.
4215612887472399|b8c6.principle: When White pushes the f-pawn against your e-pawn, counter in the centre against e4 rather than defending e5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. f4

4215612887472399|d7d6.headline: Meet the Vienna Gambit with 3...d5, striking back in the centre
4215612887472399|d7d6.why: 3...d6 is too slow: after 4.Nf3 Be7 5.fxe5 dxe5 6.Nxe5 White has won the e5 pawn, and 6...Nxe4 7.Nxe4 costs Black a knight. The theory says the correct move is 3...d5. It counterattacks e4 and leaves White almost forced to take with 4.fxe5, after which 4...Nxe4 puts your knight on a strong central square.
4215612887472399|d7d6.principle: When your opponent attacks your centre pawn with a flank pawn, counterattack theirs with a central pawn instead of defending passively.

4215612887472399|f8c5.headline: Against the Vienna Gambit, strike back with 3...d5
4215612887472399|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 lets 4.fxe5 hit the knight on f6, and with no good square it has to go home with 4...Ng8, leaving Black a pawn down and undeveloped. The theory gives 3...d5 as the correct reply: it counterattacks in the centre, and after 4.fxe5 Nxe4 the knight lands on a strong central square instead of retreating.
4215612887472399|f8c5.principle: When White attacks your e-pawn with f4, hit back in the centre so your knight gets e4 instead of being kicked home.

4237788959769826|c1e3.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 10.e5, then develop with 11.Bf4
4237788959769826|c1e3.why: 10.Be3 puts the bishop where 10...Ng4 attacks it, and after 11.Rac1 Nxe3 12.Qxe3 Black has the bishop pair and the better game. 10.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6, which retreats to e8 in the engine line. Then 11.Bf4 develops the last minor piece behind the e5 pawn, and after 11...a6 12.Bb3 b5 13.Rac1 your pieces are all in play while Black's are pushed back.
4237788959769826|c1e3.principle: A knight on f6 in front of your e-pawn is a target: the push gains space and drives it back, and your bishop can then develop behind the pawn.

4245409631012417|d4e5.headline: Bg5 first: hit the queen before opening the d-file
4245409631012417|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 opens the d-file too early: after 5...dxe5 6.Bg5 Qd6 7.Nxe5 Qxd1+ 8.Rxd1 the queens come off, and with them goes Black's main problem, the misplaced queen. You still have a large advantage, but a smaller one. 5.Bg5 first develops the bishop with an attack on the queen on f6; after 5...Qg6 6.dxe5 you win a pawn with the queens still on, and 7.Qd2 and 9.O-O-O follow, keeping a large advantage.
4245409631012417|d4e5.principle: Develop with threats while the opponent's queen is exposed; release the central tension only after it has gained you time, not in a way that lets the queen trade itself off.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

4245409631012417|f1c4.headline: Hit the early queen: 5.Bg5 develops with tempo
4245409631012417|f1c4.why: 5.Bc4 lets Black pin your knight with 5...Bg4, and after 6.Bg5 Bxf3 7.Qd2 Qg6 8.gxf3 exd4 your kingside pawns are split and Black has taken the d4 pawn; your large advantage is cut in half. The theory notes on 2...Qf6 say an early queen gives the opponent chances to develop with tempo. 5.Bg5 does exactly that: it develops the bishop and attacks the queen on f6, and after 5...Qg6 6.dxe5 you win a pawn and keep a large advantage.
4245409631012417|f1c4.principle: When your opponent brings the queen out early, look for developing moves that attack it; each one gains a tempo and often wins material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

4251014388407323|b8c6.headline: Answer 2.Nc3 with 2...d5 to stop e4.
4251014388407323|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 does nothing to control e4, so White plays 3.e4 and gets a big pawn centre, later gaining more space with 6.d5. 2.Nc3 is aimed at e4, and 2...d5 stops it: Black now controls e4 with knight and pawn, so 3.e4 would only be a pawn gambit. That is why 2...d5 is played in 82.9% of master games.
4251014388407323|b8c6.principle: When a knight move prepares e4, put a pawn on d5 so the square is covered twice before White can occupy it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. Nc3/2...d5

425955225904234|g7g6.headline: Answer 5.f3 with 5...e5, kicking the d4 knight
425955225904234|g7g6.why: 5...g6 ignores what 5.f3 is for: White keeps the option of c4 and gets an easy set-up with 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.Be3, and after 7...h5 8.h3 h4 9.Bc4 White is better. Theory gives 5...e5 as the main reply: it claims the centre and attacks the knight on d4, so White spends 6.Nb3, and Black can then contest c4 with ...Be6 and ...Rc8 or prepare ...d5. After 6...Be7 7.c4 a5 8.Be3 O-O you are developed and the game is level; masters play 5...e5 57.5% of the time.
425955225904234|g7g6.principle: A knight in the centre that a pawn can attack is a target: the push gains space and time, and here it also stops White from playing e5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

426883407817076|c5b4.headline: Retreat the attacked bishop to b6, not into the open with 6...Bb4+
426883407817076|c5b4.why: 6...Bb4+ checks, but after 7.Nc3 the bishop stands where White's pieces and pawns can chase it: 9.Nd5, 10.Qa4 and 11.b4 hound it while White develops. 6...Bb6, the La Bourdonnais variation, retreats the attacked bishop to a safe diagonal at once, still pressing on the d4 pawn. Black then develops calmly with 7.Bb5 Bd7 8.Nc3 Nge7.
426883407817076|c5b4.principle: When a pawn attacks your bishop, retreat it to a square where pawns and pieces cannot keep chasing it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. c3

4292473947156740|e4d5.headline: Defend e4 with 4.Nbd2; 4.exd5 frees Black's bishop
4292473947156740|e4d5.why: Black threatens 4...dxe4. 4.exd5 answers it by swapping, but after 4...exd5 the position is symmetrical, Black's c8 bishop has an open diagonal, and your edge almost disappears. 4.Nbd2 defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the tension; after 4...Nf6 5.Bd3 c5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 you have a French structure with extra space and d4 well supported. 4.e5 is also fine.
4292473947156740|e4d5.principle: When a centre pawn is attacked, defend it with a developing piece rather than exchanging it, because the exchange only frees your opponent's pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4

4293527898658762|g1f3.headline: Recapture 4.cxd4: keep the e4-d4 centre instead of gambiting
4293527898658762|g1f3.why: The pawn on d4 is attacked twice, by your c3 pawn and queen, and nothing defends it. 4.Nf3 leaves it there and Black answers 4...dxc3, so after 5.Nxc3 you are playing a Smith-Morra a pawn down, with your edge gone. 4.cxd4, played in 97.3% of master games, takes back and gives you two centre pawns side by side; after 4...d5 5.e5 you reach a French-style structure with more space and a small edge.
4293527898658762|g1f3.principle: When your opponent trades a wing pawn for a centre pawn, recapture toward the centre so your pawns on e4 and d4 stand together.

4304063535539389|g7g6.headline: Take d5 away from the c3 knight: 7...e6
4304063535539389|g7g6.why: 7...g6 leaves d5 uncovered, and 8.Nd5 lands there at once: after 8...Nd7 White builds up freely with 9.Qd2, 10.f3 and 12.h4 and has a clear edge. 7...e6 is the main move (63.7% of master games): the e-pawn takes d5 away from the knight on c3 and opens e7 for the bishop (9...Be7), so Black can castle quickly with 11...O-O. 7...e5, hitting the knight on d4, is also fine.
4304063535539389|g7g6.principle: Ask where your opponent's pieces want to go before you set up your own plan: here White's knight wants d5, so take that square away first.

4324455140961344|d1e2.headline: Block 3...Qe5+ with a developing move: 4.Be2, not the queen.
4324455140961344|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2 offers a queen trade, and after 4...Qxe2+ 5.Bxe2 Black's misplaced queen is gone, so White can no longer gain time against it. 4.Be2 develops another piece while blocking the check, and the queen on e5 is in the way of Black's e-pawn and will probably have to move again, as in 4...c6 5.d4 Qc7.
4324455140961344|d1e2.principle: When checked, block with a piece you wanted to develop anyway, and keep your queen home so the opponent's early queen stays a target.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

4386914372944806|b4b5.headline: In the Pianissimo, gain queenside space with 7.a4, not 7.b5.
4386914372944806|b4b5.why: 7.b5 kicks the knight to a5, where it hits the bishop on c4; after 7...Na5 8.Bb3 d5 Black frees the game in the centre. 7.a4 gains queenside space and threatens to push on and chase the bishop on b6, so Black spends 7...a6 giving it a retreat square. White then castles and brings the knight round with 9.Nbd2 and 11.Nf1, keeping the slow centre intact. Masters play 7.a4 in 70.2% of games.
4386914372944806|b4b5.principle: Push a pawn at a piece only when the piece has nowhere better to go: the bishop on b6 must be given room, while a knight chased from c6 lands on a5 and hits your bishop.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3/4...Nf6

4424038725631884|g1f3.headline: Break the pin on e2 with tempo: 5.d4 hits the queen
4424038725631884|g1f3.why: The bishop on e2 is pinned by the queen on e5, so after 5.Nf3 Bxf3 you can only take back with 6.gxf3, your kingside pawns are broken and the advantage passes to Black. 5.d4 attacks the pinning queen with a central pawn: after 5...Bxe2 6.Ngxe2 you recapture with a developing move, the queen still has to move, and 7.b4 gains more time on it. The theory says ...Qe5+ achieves little for exactly this reason: the queen blocks Black's e-pawn and gets chased again.
4424038725631884|g1f3.principle: An early queen in the centre is a target: attack it with pawns and pieces that also develop or free your position, and each time it must move you gain a tempo.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

4444685778052974|e7e5.headline: 6...e5 hands White the d5 square: play 6...e6
4444685778052974|e7e5.why: 6...e5 kicks the knight, but it goes forward to 7.Nf5, and after 7...Nc6 8.Qf3 Bxf5 9.exf5 Be7 10.Bxf6 Bxf6 11.Bd3 you have given up your light-squared bishop. With your pawns on d6 and e5 and no c-pawn, d5 can never be attacked by a black pawn again, and White is clearly better. 6...e6 (78.2% of masters games) is the main answer to 6.Bg5: it frees the queen and the f8 bishop to cover f6, so your pawns cannot be doubled, and the e6 pawn keeps watch over d5 and f5. 6...Nbd7 is also playable.
4444685778052974|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check which squares it can no longer guard; ...e5 here turns d5 into a permanent outpost for White's pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6/6. Bg5

4444685778052974|h7h6.headline: Against 6.Bg5, prepare to recapture on f6: play 6...e6
4444685778052974|h7h6.why: 6...h6 does nothing about the threat to your pawn structure: 7.Bxf6 gxf6 doubles your f-pawns and opens the kingside, and 8.Qh5 aims straight at it, giving White a clear edge. The theory says Black must react to 6.Bg5 to avoid doubled f-pawns, and 6...e6 is the almost universal answer (78.2% of master games). It opens the queen's line to f6, so a capture there can be met by the queen, and it prepares ...Be7; 6...Nbd7 solves the same problem with the knight.
4444685778052974|h7h6.principle: Spend your pawn moves on pawns that free your pieces: ...e6 opens lines for the queen and bishop, while ...h6 only asks a question that White is happy to answer.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6/6. Bg5

4472366471003602|a2a3.headline: Hit the b5 pawn with 4.a4; 4.a3 is too slow
4472366471003602|a2a3.why: 4.a3 prepares b3 to break up Black's pawns, but it is a move too slow: after 4...a6 5.Nf3 e6 6.b3 cxb3 Black keeps the extra pawn, and by the end of the line is two pawns ahead. 4.a4 attacks the pawn on b5 straight away, and the theory calls it the move that punishes 3...b5: 4...a6 fails because 5.axb5 pins the a-pawn to the rook, so Black has to defend with 4...c6. Masters play 4.a4 in 98% of 492 games.
4472366471003602|a2a3.principle: The b5 pawn is the base that holds up the c4 pawn; strike it with the a-pawn at once, before Black can support it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. e4/3...b5

4491386101925356|c5c4.headline: Capture toward the centre: 3...cxd4 is the point of the Sicilian
4491386101925356|c5c4.why: 3...c4 leaves the pawn with no support, and 4.Bxc4 simply takes it while developing, so you are a pawn down for nothing and White is clearly better. 3...cxd4, played in 99.8% of master games, captures toward the centre with a flank pawn and breaks up White's two-pawn centre. After 4.Nxd4 you have two central pawns to White's one and the half-open c-file, and 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Qc7 leads into a normal Taimanov.
4491386101925356|c5c4.principle: Trade a flank pawn for an enemy centre pawn whenever you can: it leaves you more pawns in the middle and opens a file for your rooks.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4

4491386101925356|d7d5.headline: Trade your c-pawn for White's centre pawn: 3...cxd4
4491386101925356|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the position before you have developed: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 6.O-O Nf6 7.Nc3 Bg4 8.Bg5 all of White's pieces are out, both of your knights are pinned, and White is clearly better. 3...cxd4 (99.8% of masters games) captures toward the centre with a flank pawn and breaks up White's two-pawn centre. After 4.Nxd4 you have two central pawns to White's one and the half-open c-file, and you can choose your ...e6 Sicilian.
4491386101925356|d7d5.principle: Trade a wing pawn for a centre pawn whenever you can: it breaks up your opponent's centre and leaves you with more central pawns for the middlegame.

4499356755733709|d2d3.headline: Black retreated the queen: grab the centre with 4.d4
4499356755733709|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is timid: it lets Black take the centre with 4...Nc6 and 5...e5, after which White has nothing. Black's 3...Qd8 spent a move un-developing the queen, so White has a free hand; 4.d4 takes space in the centre and opens the bishop on c1, and it is the choice in 85% of master games. After 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 White develops smoothly and keeps the edge.
4499356755733709|d2d3.principle: When the opponent spends time un-developing, use it to put a second pawn in the centre, taking the squares Black's pieces need.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

4513314094589663|b1c3.headline: 8.Bxf7+ and queen checks pick up the loose c5 bishop
4513314094589663|b1c3.why: 8.Nxc3 is natural, but after 8...d6 the bishop on c5 is defended and most of your advantage is gone. 7...dxc3 spent another move on a pawn while that bishop stood undefended next to an uncastled king. 8.Bxf7+ Kxf7 9.Qd5+ checks the king and hits the bishop, and after 9...Ke8 10.Qh5+ Kf8 11.Qxc5+ you have the piece back, the f7 pawn is gone and Black can no longer castle; 12.Qxc3 then collects the c3 pawn too.
4513314094589663|b1c3.principle: Look at checks first, especially when an enemy piece is undefended: a check that also attacks the loose piece wins it back with interest.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4552034363865958|d7d5.headline: Behind in development, keep the centre closed: play 4...a6
4552034363865958|d7d5.why: White already has a knight in the centre and is ready to develop the bishops, while you have nothing out. 4...d5 opens lines for White: 5.Bb5+ Bd7 6.exd5 exd5 7.O-O Bc5 8.Re1+ Ne7 9.Nf5 leaves your king stuck on the open e-file, and White is clearly better. 4...a6, the Kan, is the masters' top choice (39.8%): it takes b5 away from White's pieces, so that Bb5+ is gone, and Black develops only after White commits. 4...Nc6 and 4...Nf6 are the other main moves.
4552034363865958|d7d5.principle: When you are behind in development, keep the position closed until your pieces are out; opening the centre helps the side that is already developed.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4
