4559296915298785|f1d3.headline: Bd3 cuts the queen off from d4: develop with 6.Nf3
4559296915298785|f1d3.why: Your d4 pawn is defended only by the queen on d1, and 6.Bd3 blocks that line. 6...Qxd4 takes it, and 7.Bxf5 Qe5+ 8.Be4 Nxe4 leaves you a pawn down, because the queen check also hits the bishop. 6.Nf3 develops toward the centre and defends d4; it also punishes 5...Bf5, which left b7 without its defender, since after 6...e6 7.Qb3 your queen attacks it, with a clear edge.
4559296915298785|f1d3.principle: Develop the king's knight before the bishop: Nf3 has an obvious square that guards d4, while a bishop on d3 can block your own queen's defence.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. d4

4572718139339834|c1a3.headline: Castle first: the e7 queen eyes e4 with check
4572718139339834|c1a3.why: The queen on e7 attacks e4, which nothing defends, and your king is on the same file. 8.Ba3 attacks the queen, but she answers 8...Qxe4+, taking the pawn with check, and after 9.Kd1 you have also lost the right to castle, and Black is much better. 8.O-O (100% of masters games) takes the king off the e-file first; in the main line the bishop still reaches a3 later, with 12.Ba3, once the king is safe; the game is balanced.
4572718139339834|c1a3.principle: Get your king off the open e-file before starting play elsewhere; a central king turns every enemy capture on that file into a check.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

4572718139339834|c1g5.headline: Castle with 8.O-O before attacking; 8.Bg5 allows 8...Qxe4+
4572718139339834|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 hits the queen, but she steps aside with 8...Qxe4+, taking a pawn with check because your king still stands on the e-file; after 9.Kf1 you have lost the right to castle and Black is clearly better. 8.O-O, the only move masters play here, takes the king off the e-file first, and your lead in development pays for the gambit pawn: after 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 Bxd4 you bring out the rest with 11.Nc3 and 12.Ba3, with balanced chances.
4572718139339834|c1g5.principle: In a gambit the e-file opens quickly, so castle before you start attacking; while the king sits on e1, every loose centre pawn can be taken with check.

4572718139339834|f3g5.headline: Castle with 8.O-O; a lone knight raid on f7 just loses e4
4572718139339834|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time and achieves nothing: 8...Nh6 covers f7, the knight has to go back with 10.Nf3, and 10...Qxe4 takes your centre pawn, leaving you two pawns down without compensation. In the Evans you have given a pawn for time, so spend it on 8.O-O, the move every master game in the database chose. After 8...Bb6 9.cxd4 you rebuild the centre, and 11.Nc3 and 12.Ba3 bring out your last minor pieces with full compensation.
4572718139339834|f3g5.principle: In a gambit the centre opens fast and Black's queen already stands on the e-file, so castle before starting an attack with a single piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

4589106906936820|f1c4.headline: After the slow 2...c6, take the centre with 3.d4
4589106906936820|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 points the bishop at the pawn on e6, and 3...d5 hits it at once; after 4.Bd3 dxe4 5.Bxe4 Nf6 Black gains time attacking it again and White's centre is gone. 2...c6 is a slow move that doesn't contest the centre, so 3.d4 takes it with two pawns side by side. After 3...d5 4.Nbd2 the e-pawn stays protected and White can gain space with 6.e5.
4589106906936820|f1c4.principle: When the opponent spends a move on a quiet pawn move, use it to occupy the centre with both pawns.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3

4603395450140279|g1f3.headline: 3...Nc6 declines the gambit: recapture with 4.cxd4
4603395450140279|g1f3.why: The Smith-Morra offers a pawn for development, but 3...Nc6 hasn't taken it. 4.cxd4 recaptures and gives you the classical pawn centre on d4 and e4, which masters choose 96% of the time. 4.Nf3 lets Black take after all with 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3, reaching the regular Smith-Morra a pawn down when you could have had the centre for free.
4603395450140279|g1f3.principle: When your opponent declines a gambit pawn, take it back and build the centre; there is no reason to offer it again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3

4670522513947528|h2h4.headline: 4...e6 lets you take on f5: play 5.Bxf5
4670522513947528|h2h4.why: 5.h4 lets Black trade bishops on their own terms: after 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 c5 Black strikes at the base of your chain, and the game is level. The theory notes call 4...e6 a highly unusual reply, and with ...e6 already played, the only way to recapture after 5.Bxf5 is 5...exf5. That leaves Black with doubled f-pawns for the rest of the game, and you keep a clear edge.
4670522513947528|h2h4.principle: Judge trades by the structure they leave: when a capture forces your opponent to recapture with a pawn and double it, that lasting difference favours you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...Bf5/4. Bd3/4...e6

4675628834516483|f1d3.headline: Don't block the queen's guard of d4: 5.Be2, not 5.Bd3
4675628834516483|f1d3.why: Black's c5 pawn and knight on c6 both attack d4, and 5.Bd3 cuts the queen off from defending it: after 5...cxd4 6.cxd4 Nxd4 the pawn is simply gone, and with it your opening edge. 5.Be2, the most popular master move (45.9%), keeps the d-file open and, as the theory says, waits for Black's light-squared bishop to commit before 6.Nf3. With the bishop on e2, a later ...Bg4 no longer pins the knight on f3 to your queen.
4675628834516483|f1d3.principle: In the Advance structure Black piles up on d4, so before every move count its attackers and defenders, and never cut one of your defenders off.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5/4. c3/4...Nc6

4701892040283773|b8c6.headline: When White plays 2.d4, take the pawn with 2...exd4
4701892040283773|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 defends e5 but lets White gain space with tempo: 3.d5 kicks the knight to e7, where it blocks your pieces, and after 3...Nce7 4.Nf3 d6 5.c4 White has a big space advantage. 2...exd4 removes White's centre pawn and is played in over 95% of master games. If White takes back with the queen, 3...Nc6 develops with tempo; after 3.Nf3 Bb4+ Black develops with check and has an easy game.
4701892040283773|b8c6.principle: When White offers a centre pawn trade, take it so White is left with one centre pawn and has to spend time winning the pawn back.

4701892040283773|d7d5.headline: Against 2.d4, take with 2...exd4 instead of leaving e5 hanging
4701892040283773|d7d5.why: 2...d5 leaves the pawn on e5 hanging: 3.dxe5 takes it, and copying with 3...dxe4 runs into 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8, an endgame where Black's king can no longer castle. 2...exd4 removes White's centre pawn at once and is played in 95% of master games. White then has to spend time getting the pawn back, and 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen.
4701892040283773|d7d5.principle: After 2.d4 your e5 pawn is attacked and loose, so settle the tension by capturing before you start anything new.

4701892040283773|d7d6.headline: Take 2...exd4; 2...d6 lets White trade queens and keep space.
4701892040283773|d7d6.why: 2...d6 is an inferior route into the Philidor: White can take 3.dxe5 and, after 3...dxe5 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8, Black has lost the right to castle, or simply transpose with 3.Nf3. 2...exd4 takes the pawn White offered and is chosen in 95.3% of master games; if White recaptures with the queen, Black develops ...Nc6 with tempo on it.
4701892040283773|d7d6.principle: When White opens the centre with a pawn offer, capture and keep it open on your terms; defending with a pawn just hands over space and time.

4701892040283773|d8h4.headline: Take with 2...exd4; the early 2...Qh4 just gets chased
4701892040283773|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home: after 3.Nf3 Qxe4+ 4.Be2 Qf5 5.dxe5 Nc6 6.Nc3 d6 7.Nb5 White develops with gain of time while the queen keeps moving. 2...exd4 takes the pawn instead and is played in 95% of master games. White has to spend time getting it back, and 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen.
4701892040283773|d8h4.principle: Leave the queen at home and let White's queen be the early target: capture, then develop with tempo against it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4

4701892040283773|f7f5.headline: Answer 2.d4 with 2...exd4, not a lunge with the f-pawn
4701892040283773|f7f5.why: 2...f5 leaves e5 attacked and loosens the pawns in front of your king. After 3.exf5 Black has to spend 3...Qe7 to hold e5, which blocks the bishop on f8, while White develops with 4.Nf3 and 5.Be2 and castles with 6.O-O. 2...exd4 removes White's centre pawn at once and is the master choice in over 95% of games; White then has to spend time getting the pawn back while you develop.
4701892040283773|f7f5.principle: With your king still in the centre and White opening lines, don't loosen the f-pawn; settle the centre with a capture and develop toward castling.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4

4701892040283773|f7f6.headline: Capture on d4; f6 doesn't hold e5
4701892040283773|f7f6.why: 2...f6 doesn't save the e5 pawn: after 3.dxe5 Black recaptures with the f-pawn, and 5.Bc4 then aims at a king whose diagonal you opened yourself. 2...exd4 simply wins the pawn White offered, so White must spend time getting it back, and after 3.Nf3 Bb4+ Black develops with check.
4701892040283773|f7f6.principle: When White strikes at e5 with the d-pawn, capture: trading keeps material level and opens lines for your pieces, while f6 only weakens your king.

4701892040283773|g8f6.headline: Take on d4 first; 2...Nf6 lets 3.dxe5 kick the knight
4701892040283773|g8f6.why: 2...Nf6 leaves e5 to be taken with 3.dxe5, which also hits the knight; it can grab 3...Nxe4, but 4.Qe2 attacks it again, and after 4...Nc5 5.Nc3 the knight has moved three times while White develops. 2...exd4 takes the pawn first and is played in 95% of master games. White has to spend time recovering it, and 3.Qxd4 lets Black develop 3...Nc6 with tempo on the queen.
4701892040283773|g8f6.principle: When a pawn attacks your centre pawn, look at the capture first: it settles the tension on your terms before you develop.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4/2...exd4

4722555415307870|d8g5.headline: Strike the centre with 2...d5; keep the queen home
4722555415307870|d8g5.why: 2...Qg5 brings the queen out with four minor pieces still at home, and White gains time on it: 3.d4 attacks e5 and opens the c1 bishop's diagonal toward g5, so the queen has to retreat with 3...Qe7. After 4.dxe5 Qxe5 5.Ne2 the queen has moved three times while White develops. 2...d5 uses the weakness of 1.f3: it opens lines for your pieces and takes on White's centre before White can develop.
4722555415307870|d8g5.principle: Develop pieces and hit the centre with pawns; an early queen just gives your opponent targets to develop against.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. f3/1...e5

473877128562412|b7b5.headline: Hit the bishop with 4...Na5 instead of hanging a pawn
473877128562412|b7b5.why: 4...b5 simply hangs a pawn: the bishop on c4 takes it with 5.Bxb5, and Black gets nothing for it. 4...Na5 attacks the bishop with a piece it can't capture, and in the line 5.Bd5 c6 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 White ends up giving the bishop for a single pawn.
473877128562412|b7b5.principle: Attack an enemy bishop with a piece it cannot capture; a pawn sent toward it that nothing defends just becomes a free meal.

4756123934331352|d7d6.headline: 5.d3 opened the bishop's line to h6: counterattack with 5...Nd4
4756123934331352|d7d6.why: 5.d3 opened the diagonal of the c1 bishop, so the knight on h6 is hanging, and 5...d6 does nothing about it: 6.Bxh6 wins the knight and even sets up mate on f7. 5...Nd4 answers with a bigger threat, hitting the queen on f3 and the pawn on c2, so White has no time for Bxh6. After 6.Qd1 b5 7.Bd5 c6 8.c3 cxd5 9.cxd4 exd4 Black comes out a pawn up.
4756123934331352|d7d6.principle: Before a quiet move, look at White's forcing moves: 5.d3 uncovered 6.Bxh6, so reply with a forcing move of your own that attacks the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...g6/4. Qf3

4781739738408769|b1c3.headline: Look for checks: 9.Qd5+ forks the king and the e5 knight
4781739738408769|b1c3.why: 8...Nxe5 leaves the knight on e5 undefended while the black king stands exposed on f7. 9.Nbc3 develops but lets Black tidy up with 9...Kg8, and most of your advantage is gone. 9.Qd5+ gives check and attacks the knight at the same time: the king has to go to g6, and 10.Qxe5 wins a whole piece.
4781739738408769|b1c3.principle: Check every check before you develop: a queen check that also hits a loose piece is a fork, and an exposed king makes those checks easy to find.

4842782731159492|a7a6.headline: White's castling left e4 hanging: take it with 4...Nxe4
4842782731159492|a7a6.why: 4...a6 is too slow: 5.Bxc6 dxc6 6.Nxe5 removes the defender of e5 and wins the pawn, and Black has nothing in return. Castling left e4 attacked and undefended, so 4...Nxe4, the Open Berlin, takes it; when White wins back e5 it is only a trade of pawns, as in 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5.
4842782731159492|a7a6.principle: Before a quiet move, check what is loose on both sides: White's e4 pawn hangs now, and your e5 pawn will too once its defender is taken.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6/4. O-O
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6/4. O-O/4...Nxe4

4844296345294265|g4g5.headline: After h3 and g4, stop pushing pawns: develop with 7.Nc3.
4844296345294265|g4g5.why: 7.g5 is another pawn move that develops nothing, and it gives up control of h5: after 7...Na5 8.Bb5+ c6 9.Ba4 b5 10.Bb3 Black's bishop returns with 10...Bh5 and the knight wins the bishop pair with 11...Nxb3. 7.Nc3 brings a new piece toward the centre and keeps the g4 pawn covering h5, so the bishop on g6 stays passive. White follows with 8.Qe2 and 11.Bg5, finishing development first.
4844296345294265|g4g5.principle: Once your kingside pawns have advanced, stop pushing them: each further push leaves squares behind it, so bring out the queenside pieces instead.

4845873281403230|d7d5.headline: Develop with 3...Nc6 before opening the centre with ...d5
4845873281403230|d7d5.why: 3...d5 opens the centre while your kingside pieces are still at home: after 4.exd5 exd5 5.Bb5+ Nc6 White pins the knight, and 8.Bxc6+ comes later to damage your pawns. 3.b3 is slow and does nothing about d4, so 3...Nc6 develops toward the centre first. If 4.Bb5, then 4...Nge7 lets you recapture on c6 with a knight, as in 6.Bxc6 Nxc6, and after 7.d4 cxd4 8.Nxd4 you have a comfortable Sicilian.
4845873281403230|d7d5.principle: Your king is still on e8 with no kingside piece out, so keep the centre closed and develop the knights before a break like ...d5 lets White check on b5.

4846046788305631|c8e6.headline: In the Philidor, control d4 with 3...c5 before developing
4846046788305631|c8e6.why: 3...Be6 puts the bishop where White's knight can hit it: in the line 4.d4 Nd7 5.Ng5 the knight attacks e6, the centre opens with 5...exd4 6.Qxd4, and White later takes the bishop with 8.Nxe6. 3...c5 takes control of d4, so White cannot easily crack open the centre, and Black develops calmly with 4...Be7 and 5...Nf6.
4846046788305631|c8e6.principle: Ask where White wants to break: d4 is the main lever against the Philidor, so cover it before putting a bishop where Ng5 can reach it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6

4846046788305631|f7f5.headline: Keep it closed: 3...c5 stops d4, while 3...f5 opens your king
4846046788305631|f7f5.why: 3...f5 opens lines while Black is behind in development: after 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe4 Nf6 6.Nxf6+ gxf6 Black's kingside pawns are broken and 7.Bc4 aims at the weakened squares around the king. 3...c5 does the opposite: it takes control of d4, so White cannot blow open the centre with d4, the critical plan against 2...d6. Black then develops calmly with 4...Be7 and 5...Nf6.
4846046788305631|f7f5.principle: When behind in development, keep the centre closed: control d4 with a pawn rather than opening the f-file in front of your own king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...d6

4867591183206233|b8c6.headline: Put the knight on f6, where it hits e4 at once
4867591183206233|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 lets White gain space with tempo: after 3.d4 e5 4.d5 the knight is kicked and has to retreat with 4...Nce7, where it gets in the way of Black's other pieces. 2...Nf6, the most common master move (43.5%), develops toward the centre and attacks e4, the knight's job in the Pirc; 1...d6 already covers e5, so White cannot kick the knight with that pawn.
4867591183206233|b8c6.principle: Develop the knights where they pressure the centre: from f6 the knight attacks e4, while on c6 it waits to be chased by d4 and d5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6

4870221886044145|e1h1.headline: 5...e6 made e4 a target: guard it with 6.Bd3 before castling
4870221886044145|e1h1.why: 5...e6 blunts your bishop on c4, and e4 is attacked by the bishop on b7 with nothing defending it, so 6.O-O allows 6...Bxe4, a clean pawn. 6.Bd3 moves the blunted bishop to a square where it guards e4, and you keep a comfortable centre: after 6...d6 7.O-O Ne7 8.Re1 the rook adds a second defender. 6.Qe2 also holds the pawn.
4870221886044145|e1h1.principle: After every opponent move, quiet ones included, ask what it now threatens; here ...e6 shut out your bishop, so e4 needs a defender before you castle.

4876809165764258|c8g4.headline: Answer 5.d4 with 5...exd4; that pawn attacks your bishop on c5
4876809165764258|c8g4.why: 5.d4 attacks the bishop on c5, and 5...Bg4 ignores the threat: 6.dxc5 wins the bishop, and the counterattack 6...Qf6 on the pinned knight runs into 7.Bg5. 5...exd4 removes the attacking pawn before it can take, and it is the only move masters play here, in all 30 games.
4876809165764258|c8g4.principle: Before starting your own plan, check what the opponent's last move threatens: a pawn that attacks a piece has to be answered first.

4879166842565878|c1g5.headline: d4 is attacked three times, defended twice: take it with 8.cxd4
4879166842565878|c1g5.why: 8.Bg5 develops with an attack on the queen but does nothing about d4: 8...f6 blocks and hits the bishop, and after 9.cxd4 Nxd4 10.Nxd4 fxg5 the exchanges favour Black, who keeps the extra pawns. d4 is attacked three times and defended only twice, so 8.cxd4 wins the pawn back at once and gives you the e4 and d4 pawn centre. In the main line 8...Bb6 9.h3 Na5 10.Bd3 keeps your bishop, and 11.Nc3 completes your development with a balanced game.
4879166842565878|c1g5.principle: Count attackers and defenders on the central pawn first: when a capture wins it back outright, take it before making developing moves elsewhere.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4879166842565878|f1e1.headline: Two pawns down in the Evans: recapture 8.cxd4 now
4879166842565878|f1e1.why: You have given two pawns for the centre, and 8.Re1 does nothing to get one back: Black pins your knight with 8...Bg4, and after 9.e5 d5 10.Be2 dxc3 11.Nxc3 you are still two pawns down with no centre to show for it, and Black is clearly better. The pawn on d4 is attacked three times and defended twice, so 8.cxd4 wins it and gives you pawns on e4 and d4, the centre the Evans Gambit is played for.
4879166842565878|f1e1.principle: Count attackers and defenders on the pawn in the middle of the board: three against two means you can take it, and here taking it also rebuilds your centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4879166842565878|f3g5.headline: Rebuild the centre with 8.cxd4; d4 is attacked three times
4879166842565878|f3g5.why: 8.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and 8...Nh6 covers f7 at once; then 9...dxc3 takes another pawn and Black castles in peace, clearly better. d4 is attacked three times and defended only twice, so 8.cxd4 wins the pawn back and gives you pawns on d4 and e4, the centre that is your compensation in the Evans. In the main line the bishop retreats with 8...Bb6, and you keep developing with 10.Bd3 and 11.Nc3.
4879166842565878|f3g5.principle: In a gambit your compensation is the centre: when you can recapture toward it with a pawn, do so before starting an attack with single pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Bc5

4886445385944472|c2c3.headline: Take on e5 and keep c3 for your knight

ideas.title: Settle the d4 tension
ideas.text: Black's pawn and knight both hit d4, so you must push, capture or defend it before 3...Nxd4.

ideas.title: Make the knight pay
ideas.text: Black's knight came out early; the best replies make it move again, as after 3.dxe5 Nxe5 and 5.f4.

ideas.title: Keep c3 for your knight
ideas.text: Your knight belongs on c3, guarding e4 and d5. A pawn there leaves e4 loose.

ideas.title: Black's ...d5 break
ideas.text: Against slow set-ups Black frees the game with ...d5, as after 3.c3 d5.

habit.why: 3.c3 lets Black strike with 3...d5 at your e4 pawn, which no piece defends. After 4.dxe5 Be6 5.exd5 Qxd5 you can't chase the queen with Nc3, and after 6.Nf3 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 O-O-O+ your king is stuck in the middle and the game is level.

strays.text: The pawn takes the knight's square, so nothing guards e4 against 3...d5.

taught.why: 3.dxe5 captures first, and after 3...Nxe5 the knight stands in the centre with nothing defending it. 4.Nc3 develops onto the square 3.c3 would have taken, and after 4...Bc5 5.f4 Nc6 the knight is back on c6 while your pawns on e4 and f4 hold the centre.

enforces.text: Black's knight spends three moves to end up back on c6 while you gain space.

4886445385944472|c2c3.principle: A knight in the centre with no pawn to protect it is a target: 5.f4 gains space and sends it back, while 3.c3 attacks nothing.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 3.d5 gains space and sends the knight on a long trip, 3...Nce7 4.Nf3 Ng6, and 5.h4 threatens to kick it again.
alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 is just as good but keeps the game open: you chase the knight with 4.Nc3 Bc5 5.f4 instead of playing on the wings around a locked centre. Masters prefer it, 43% to 31%.

alternatives.label: inaccuracy
alternatives.before: 3.Nf3 turns the game into a sound Scotch Game, but after 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.Nxc6 bxc6 6.Bd3 d5 your knight has moved three times only to be swapped off, and the position is level.
alternatives.after: 3.dxe5 keeps your e4 pawn alone in the centre and your knight on c3 guards d5, so Black gets no easy ...d5 and your small edge stays.

sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. d4/2...e5

After 4.dxe5 Be6 5.exd5 Qxd5 you can't chase the queen with Nc3, and after 6.Nf3 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 O-O-O+ your king is stuck in the middle and the game is level. 3.dxe5 captures first, and after 3...Nxe5 the knight stands in the centre with nothing defending it. 4.Nc3 develops onto the square 3.c3 would have taken, and after 4...Bc5 5.f4 Nc6 the knight is back on c6 while your pawns on e4 and f4 hold the centre.

4907156095699170|c8f5.headline: Nothing guards f5: 3...Bf5 just hangs the bishop
4907156095699170|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 puts the bishop on a square the bishop on d3 attacks, and no black piece or pawn defends f5, so 4.Bxf5 wins a whole bishop. Offering the bishop trade only works when you can recapture. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and controls e4; the light-squared bishop still gets out later, as in 3...Nf6 4.Nf3 Bg4, and the game is level.
4907156095699170|c8f5.principle: Before putting a piece on a new square, check whether an enemy piece attacks it there and whether you can recapture; an undefended piece facing an attacker is simply lost.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

4920065110243890|c2c3.headline: 2...e5 hangs a pawn: take it with 3.dxe5
4920065110243890|c2c3.why: 3.c3 offers a gambit against a move that already hangs a pawn: after 3...exd4 Black wins the d-pawn anyway, and a winning position turns into a level one. The theory says Black should play 2...cxd4; 2...e5 instead leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and defended by nothing. 3.dxe5 takes it and claims the centre, and since your pawn has left d4, the threat of 3...cxd4 disappears with it.
4920065110243890|c2c3.principle: When both sides have pawns en prise, look at the captures first: taking with your attacked pawn wins material and removes the opponent's threat in one move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

4920065110243890|d4d5.headline: 2...e5 leaves e5 hanging: take it with 3.dxe5
4920065110243890|d4d5.why: Black's 2...e5 is a mistake: the theory notes say Black should take with 2...cxd4, and here the pawn on e5 is attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing. 3.d5 does answer Black's threat of 3...cxd4, but it passes up the free pawn and closes the centre; after 3...Nf6 4.Nd2 Be7 your large edge is cut by more than half. 3.dxe5 removes the threat and wins the pawn at the same time, keeping a large advantage.
4920065110243890|d4d5.principle: After every opponent move, check what it left undefended; a capture that wins a loose pawn and removes a threat beats a move that only parries the threat.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

4947710214196192|b1c3.headline: Defend the extra e5 pawn with 3.Nf3
4947710214196192|b1c3.why: 3.Nc3 doesn't protect e5, so 3...dxe5 wins the pawn back, and after 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 the queens are off with material level. 3.Nf3 develops the knight toward the centre and defends the e5 pawn, so Black's gambit stays a pawn short. As the theory says, if White plays carefully, White stays ahead throughout the game.
4947710214196192|b1c3.principle: Count the attackers on your extra pawn: e5 is hit by the pawn on d6, so defend it with a developing move instead of ignoring it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5/2...d6

494920144507383|c6d4.headline: Develop the last knight with 5...Nf6, don't move one twice
494920144507383|c6d4.why: 5...Nd4 moves the knight again while the g8 knight and c8 bishop are still at home, and it achieves nothing: 6.Na4 hits the bishop on c5, and after 6...Qe7 7.Nxc5 dxc5 8.Nxd4 cxd4 Black has traded off the bishop and handed White the bishop pair. 5...Nf6 is the most common master move (46%), developing toward the centre and getting ready to castle in this slow, manoeuvring Italian.
494920144507383|c6d4.principle: In a quiet opening, bring out a new piece each move; moving one twice only pays when it wins something concrete.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

4965498870244384|c1f4.headline: Take on d5 so Black must recapture with a piece
4965498870244384|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 lets Black grab the pawn with 4...dxc4, and the knight on c6 then backs up a quick 5...e5, so White gets nothing for the time spent. 3...Nf6 left d5 without pawn support, and 4.cxd5 punishes it: Black has to recapture with a piece. After 4...Qxd5 White gains time with 5.Nc3, 6.e4 and 7.d5, chasing the queen and the knight on c6 while building a big centre.
4965498870244384|c1f4.principle: When your opponent must recapture in the centre with the queen, develop with moves that attack it and build your pawn centre at the same time.

497056438217906|b8c6.headline: Challenge d4 with the c-pawn before playing Nc6
497056438217906|b8c6.why: 5...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, Black's natural lever against d4, and lets White take the whole centre with 6.Nc3 and 7.e4. 5...c5 strikes at d4 straight away, the standard freeing move in the Queen's Gambit Accepted; the knight still reaches c6 later, as in 6.O-O a6 7.a4 Nc6.
497056438217906|b8c6.principle: In queen's-pawn openings, challenge d4 with the c-pawn before putting a knight in front of it.

4975913143337329|a2a3.headline: Hit f7 with 5.Ng5; 5.a3 allows the centre fork trick
4975913143337329|a2a3.why: 5.a3 is a slow pawn move that leaves e4 loose: 5...Nxe4 6.Nxe4 d5 is the centre fork trick, hitting the bishop on c4 and the knight on e4 and winning the piece back with a free game for Black. 4...d6 was passive, and 5.Ng5 punishes it by lining up knight and bishop against f7. Black has to block with 5...d5, and 6.exd5 wins a pawn.
4975913143337329|a2a3.principle: With the bishop on c4 aimed at f7, a knight jump to g5 doubles the attack on the square only the king defends.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

4975913143337329|c4d5.headline: Hit f7 with the knight when Black skips Be7
4975913143337329|c4d5.why: 5.Bd5 moves the bishop a second time for no gain, and after 5...Nd4 6.Bc4 it has to go back, so Black has gained time. 4...Nc6 left f7 guarded only by the king, and 5.Ng5 attacks it with knight and bishop; Black has to block with 5...d5, and 6.exd5 wins a pawn.
4975913143337329|c4d5.principle: With a bishop on c4 and f7 defended only by the king, bringing a knight to g5 adds a second attacker and forces concessions.

4975913143337329|d2d3.headline: 4...d6 left f7 weak: hit it with 5.Ng5
4975913143337329|d2d3.why: 5.d3 lets Black hunt the bishop with 5...Na5: in the engine line 6.Bd5 c6 leaves it to give itself up with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, a bishop for a pawn. Black's 4...d6 was passive and left f7 guarded only by the king, while the c4 bishop already aims at it. 5.Ng5 adds the knight to that attack, and after 5...d5 6.exd5 White wins a pawn.
4975913143337329|d2d3.principle: When f7 is defended only by the king and your bishop already aims at it, add a second attacker before making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6/4. Bc4

4981514382355858|b8c6.headline: Accept with 3...dxc3 or decline properly; 3...Nc6 does neither
4981514382355858|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 does not stop 4.cxd4, so White gets the pawn back for free and has the ideal pawns on e4 and d4; after 4...d5 5.exd5 Qxd5 6.Nf3 e5 7.Nc3 White develops with gain of time and is better. 3...dxc3 accepts the gambit (54.5% of masters games and the engines' choice): after 4.Nxc3 you are a pawn up, and White's lead in development is the price, with the game level. If you prefer to decline, 3...Nf6 heads for an Alapin Sicilian.
4981514382355858|b8c6.principle: Facing a gambit, decide: take the pawn if you can consolidate, or decline with a move that stops your opponent's ideal centre; a neutral move gives them the centre without any sacrifice.

4997272018450256|c5b4.headline: Escape the pawn fork with 5...Bd6, guarding the knight
4997272018450256|c5b4.why: 5.d4 forks the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5. 5...Bb4 saves the bishop but leaves the knight hanging, so 6.dxe5 wins a piece. 5...Bd6 saves the bishop and guards the knight at once; after 6.dxe5 Bxe5 Black has the piece back and material is level. Masters play it in 99.3% of games.
4997272018450256|c5b4.principle: When a pawn forks two pieces, find the retreat that moves one and protects the other, so nothing is left loose.

4997272018450256|c5d4.headline: d4 is guarded by the queen: retreat the bishop, don't capture
4997272018450256|c5d4.why: 5...Bxd4 takes the forking pawn, but 6.Qxd4 simply takes the bishop back, so Black gives a bishop for a pawn. 5...Bd6 steps out of the fork while guarding the knight on e5. After 6.dxe5 Bxe5 material is level again, and masters choose it 99.3% of the time.
4997272018450256|c5d4.principle: Before capturing, count: d4 is guarded by White's queen and attacked only by your bishop, so taking there just loses the piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

4997272018450256|d8f6.headline: Against the fork, save the bishop where it still guards the knight
4997272018450256|d8f6.why: 5.d4 is a fork: the pawn hits both the bishop on c5 and the knight on e5. 5...Qf6 defends the knight but not the bishop, so 6.dxc5 wins a piece, and the queen is out with two minor pieces still at home. 5...Bd6 saves the bishop and still guards the knight; after 6.dxe5 Bxe5 material is level, which is why masters play it 99.3% of the time.
4997272018450256|d8f6.principle: When a pawn forks two pieces, look for the one move that saves both: retreat the attacked piece to a square where it protects the other.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

5001203520556314|c8f5.headline: Against the Queen's Gambit, support d5 with 2...c6
5001203520556314|c8f5.why: 2...Bf5 leaves d5 without pawn support, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn, and to get it back Black has to give the bishop for a knight with 3...Bxb1 4.Rxb1 and bring the queen out with 4...Qxd5. 2...c6, the Slav, supports d5 with a pawn, so Black can recapture with a pawn after cxd5 and keep control of e4, while the light-squared bishop stays free to come out later.
5001203520556314|c8f5.principle: Against the Queen's Gambit, keep a pawn on d5 controlling e4: support it with the c- or e-pawn before developing the bishop.

5001203520556314|e7e5.headline: Support d5 with 2...c6, the Slav, instead of gambiting e5
5001203520556314|e7e5.why: 2...e5 gives up a pawn after 3.dxe5; the d4 wedge of the Albin Countergambit gives Black some play, but masters choose it in under 1% of games and White can return the pawn later for a positional edge. 2...c6, the Slav, is the most common master reply (50%): it supports d5 with the c-pawn so that cxd5 can be met by a pawn recapture, and unlike ...e6 it leaves the bishop on c8 free to develop.
5001203520556314|e7e5.principle: When White attacks your d5 pawn, keep a pawn there by supporting it, rather than giving up a centre pawn.

If the knight takes back with 3...Nxd5, 4.e4 chases it away and White gets the whole centre. 2...c6, the Slav, supports d5 with a pawn, so a pawn can recapture and keep control of e4. Unlike ...e6, it does this without locking in the bishop on c8.
5001203520556314|g8f6.principle: Against the Queen's Gambit, defend d5 with a pawn so that a pawn, not a piece, recaptures there.

505062396368968|b1c3.headline: Take the free pawn on e5 before developing
505062396368968|b1c3.why: 2.Nc3 lets Black swap the pawn off: after 2...exd4 3.Qxd4 Nc6 the queen is chased and Black develops with gain of time, so the gambit has cost Black nothing. 2.dxe5 takes the free pawn, since e5 was attacked once and not defended at all. Black must now spend time winning it back, and the theory calls this White's best answer.
505062396368968|b1c3.principle: When your opponent leaves a pawn undefended in front of your own pawn, take it before developing, or it escapes with a trade.

505062396368968|e2e4.headline: Take the Englund pawn with 2.dxe5; don't give your own
505062396368968|e2e4.why: 2.e4 leaves the d4 pawn hanging: 2...exd4 takes it, and White is the one a pawn down. 2.dxe5 simply takes the pawn Black offered, since e5 was attacked and not defended at all. The theory calls this the best answer to the Englund Gambit, and 90.4% of masters play it; Black then has to spend time trying to win the pawn back.
505062396368968|e2e4.principle: Accept an unsound gambit pawn when it is free and you can keep developing, instead of offering a pawn of your own in return.

505062396368968|g1f3.headline: Take the Englund pawn: 2.dxe5.
505062396368968|g1f3.why: 2.Nf3 lets Black push 2...e4 and kick the knight, which has to retreat with 3.Nfd2, and Black gains space. 1...e5 offers a pawn that is attacked once and defended by nothing, and 2.dxe5 simply wins it. The Englund Gambit is unsound, and after 2.dxe5 Black has to work to find compensation.
505062396368968|g1f3.principle: When the opponent offers an unsound gambit, take the pawn and make them prove the compensation.

5083117640380754|b8c6.headline: Answer c3 by hitting e4 at once: 3...Nf6
5083117640380754|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 puts no pressure on e4, so White plays 4.d4 straight away and after 4...cxd4 5.cxd4 has the two-pawn centre that 3.c3 was preparing, with a clear edge. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 first, and with a pawn on c3 White can no longer bring a knight to c3 to defend it. White has to deal with e4 before anything else, and in the main line d4 only arrives with 8.d4, with the game level.
5083117640380754|b8c6.principle: When White plays c3 to prepare d4, contest the centre immediately with a developing move that attacks e4, so the pawn centre never gets built for free.

5083117640380754|e7e6.headline: Hit e4 with 3...Nf6 before White's d4 arrives
5083117640380754|e7e6.why: 3.c3 prepares d4 for a full pawn centre and blunts the long diagonal a later ...Bg7 would use. 3...e6 lets White build it: after 4.d4 Nc6 5.d5 White gains space, your knight retreats with 6...Nce7, and White is comfortably better. 3...Nf6 attacks e4 at once, so White must look after it before pushing d4; masters play it 98.6% of the time and the position stays level.
5083117640380754|e7e6.principle: Develop with a threat against the centre: a knight attacking e4 makes White spend time defending instead of building the d4 centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. c3

5092403403866739|b8c6.headline: Take on d4 first: 4...cxd4, or White takes on c5
5092403403866739|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 allows 5.dxc5, which wins a pawn: recapturing with the d-pawn opens the d-file for a queen trade with check, as in the game line 8...dxc5 9.Qxd8+, and White has a large advantage. 4...cxd4 is played in 99.9% of master games: it trades your c-pawn for White's centre pawn, which is the point of 1...c5. After 5.Nxd4 a6 6.Be3 Nf6 Black develops normally.
5092403403866739|b8c6.principle: When pawns attack each other in the centre, look at the captures first: if you don't take on d4, White takes on c5.

5100201113541958|b2b3.headline: Develop with tempo: 4.Nc3 hits the queen on d5
5100201113541958|b2b3.why: 4.b3 neither develops nor attacks the queen, and Black uses the time: 4...Bg4 pins the knight on f3 to White's queen, and 5...Qe6+ checks down the open e-file, forcing 6.Qe2 and leaving White's pieces tangled. 4.Nc3 develops a knight and attacks the queen on d5 at once, so Black spends a move retreating with 4...Qd8 while White continues with 5.d4. Masters play it 93.1% of the time.
5100201113541958|b2b3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop with a move that attacks her, so you gain a move while she retreats.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...Nc6/2. Nf3

513248652268614|c1e3.headline: 10.Nb5 hits the queen and d6, winning the pawn back
513248652268614|c1e3.why: 9...Qc7 puts the queen where your knight can hit it from b5, and the d6 pawn already faces your rook on d1. 10.Be3 is a natural developing move but lets Black castle with 10...O-O, and Black is slightly better. 10.Nb5 attacks the queen on c7 and adds a second attacker to d6; after 10...Qb8 11.Bf4 e5 12.Bg5 O-O 13.Bxf6 Bxf6 14.Nxd6 you win the gambit pawn back and keep a small edge.
513248652268614|c1e3.principle: Count the attackers on d6: your rook on d1 already hits it, so adding the knight while chasing away the queen, one of its defenders, tips the count your way.

5136765216062701|f1c4.headline: Put the bishop on d3, or go 5.h4, not 5.Bc4
5136765216062701|f1c4.why: With Black's pawn on e6, ...d5 is coming, and 5.Bc4 puts your bishop where that pawn hits it: after 5...d5 6.exd5 exd5 7.Bd3 you have spent two moves to reach d3. 5.Bd3 goes there directly, and the engine's 5.h4 uses the idea theory credits to Fischer against the Modern: push the h-pawn to loosen the fianchetto before Black castles.
5136765216062701|f1c4.principle: Develop a piece straight to the square where it will end up; if a pawn push will chase it, you'll have to move it twice.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

5143411063260921|d8b6.headline: Guard d5 with 7...e6; 7...Qb6 drops it to 8.Nxd5
5143411063260921|d8b6.why: White's queen on b3 eyes b7, and the knight on c3 eyes d5. 7...Qb6 covers b7 but takes your queen off the d-file, so 8.Nxd5 wins the d5 pawn with tempo on the queen and White is clearly better. 7...e6 gives d5 a solid pawn defender and frees your f8 bishop; if White plays 8.e4 Bxe4 9.Qxb7, you have taken the e4 pawn in return and keep developing with 9...Nd7 and 10...Rc8, with a level game.
5143411063260921|d8b6.principle: With two minor pieces still at home, a queen sortie becomes a target; defend the centre with a pawn and develop instead.

5165721780484766|d2d3.headline: Against the French, build the two-pawn centre with 2.d4
5165721780484766|d2d3.why: 2.d3 is a sideline that lets Black take an equal share of the centre: after 2...d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 the queens are gone, your king has lost the right to castle, and the game is level. The theory says White almost always answers 1...e6 with 2.d4 (89.5% of master games): it puts a second pawn in the centre and opens lines for both bishops and the queen. After 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 you gain space, and 5.f4 supports the e5 pawn.
5165721780484766|d2d3.principle: When the opponent lets you, occupy the centre with two pawns; a timid pawn move hands Black the central share 1...e6 was preparing for.

5165721780484766|e4e5.headline: Build the two-pawn centre before advancing
5165721780484766|e4e5.why: 2.e5 advances a pawn with no support, and Black undermines it with 2...c5 and 4...d6, so White ends up trading it off with 5.exd6 without gaining anything. 2.d4 builds the two-pawn centre and opens both bishops; after 2...d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 the pawn advances only once d4 stands behind it.
5165721780484766|e4e5.principle: Occupy the centre with both pawns first; a lone advanced pawn is easy to undermine.

5165721780484766|f1c4.headline: Against the French, build the centre with 2.d4
5165721780484766|f1c4.why: 2.Bc4 lets Black play 2...d5 with gain of time: the pawn hits the bishop, and after 3.exd5 exd5 4.Be2 the bishop has moved twice and Black has a free, open game. 2.d4 is played in 89.5% of master games: White takes the chance to put a second pawn in the centre and opens lines for the queen and the bishop on c1. Black almost always answers 2...d5, and White then chooses how to meet the attack on e4, for example with 3.Nc3.
5165721780484766|f1c4.principle: When the opponent spends a move preparing ...d5 instead of occupying the centre, occupy it yourself with a second pawn.

5165721780484766|f2f4.headline: Against the French, build the two-pawn centre with 2.d4
5165721780484766|f2f4.why: 2.f4 spends the move on a flank pawn and does nothing about the coming 2...d5; after 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nxe4 c5 Black has traded off your e-pawn and strikes at the centre with an easy game. 2.d4 puts a second pawn in the centre and opens lines for the bishop and queen, which is what White plays almost every time here. The f-pawn can still come later, as in 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4, once the centre is fixed and the pawn supports e5.
5165721780484766|f2f4.principle: When Black's first move only prepares ...d5, occupy the centre with a second pawn so you have something to meet it with.

5169185492904926|c8f5.headline: The c8 bishop guards b7: play 3...Nf6 first
5169185492904926|c8f5.why: 3...Bf5 takes away the only defender of b7, and 4.Qb3 attacks it at once. 4...Qc7 holds, but after 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.Nc3 White's queen, knight and the bishop on g2 all aim at d5, Black has to cover it with 6...e6, and White is better. 3...Nf6 (87.1% of masters games) develops toward the centre and adds a defender to d5, and after 4.Nf3 g6 5.b3 Bg7 your kingside is ready to castle.
5169185492904926|c8f5.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it was defending; when White's queen can reach b3, the c8 bishop is b7's only guard.

5184811817876652|e1h1.headline: 6.O-O drops e4: chase the knight with 6.e5 first
5184811817876652|e1h1.why: Black threatens 6...Nxe4, and 6.O-O doesn't stop it: the knight on f6 and the bishop on b7 both hit e4, so after 6.O-O Nxe4 you are a pawn down and Black is better. 5...Nf6 made that threat, but it also put the knight in front of your e-pawn. 6.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight, which in the engine line ends up on the rim after 6...Ng4 7.Na3 Qc8 8.h3 Nh6; you gain space and keep a clear advantage.
5184811817876652|e1h1.principle: Check your opponent's captures before a quiet move like castling, and look for an answer that meets the threat with a threat of your own.

5200406229951823|e1f2.headline: In the Traxler, step aside with 6.Kf1 and keep the fork
5200406229951823|e1f2.why: 6.Kxf2 takes the bishop but walks into 6...Nxe4+, a check that drives the king to 7.Ke3, where 7...Qh4 starts a hunt in the middle of the board and Black's attack levels the game. 6.Kf1, the masters' choice 63% of the time, gets out of check without letting the knight take on e4 with check. It still attacks the bishop on f2 and keeps the knight's fork of queen and rook alive: after 6...Qe7 7.Nxh8 White has won a rook.
5200406229951823|e1f2.principle: When a sacrifice tries to drag your king forward, prefer the quiet square that keeps it sheltered and your own threats intact.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...Bc5/5. Nxf7

5214612586178464|d2d3.headline: Castle before ...d5 opens the d-file
5214612586178464|d2d3.why: 4.d3 allows 4...d5, hitting the bishop on c4, and after 5.Bb3 dxe4 6.dxe4 Qxd1+ 7.Kxd1 the queens come off and White's king has lost the right to castle. 4.O-O castles first, so the ...d5 break holds no such trick: after 4...d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5 the bishop pins the knight on c6 and 7.d4 strikes at Black's centre. Masters play it in 69% of games.
5214612586178464|d2d3.principle: Against an early ...d5 break, castle before the centre opens so a queen trade on the d-file can't cost you the right to castle.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

5215145015608227|c8f5.headline: Develop the knight first; 4...Bf5 lets Qb3 hit b7 and d5
5215145015608227|c8f5.why: 4...Bf5 takes away b7's only defender while d5 is already eyed by the bishop on g2: 5.Qb3 hits both, and in the game line Black ties the queen to b7 with 5...Qc8 and answers 6.Nc3 with 6...e6, a passive setup that gives White the edge. 4...Nc6 develops toward the centre and keeps the bishop guarding b7 a little longer. After 5.d4 the bishop comes out with 5...Bf5 anyway, followed by ...Nf6 and ...e6, with a good game.
5215145015608227|c8f5.principle: In these symmetrical structures bring the knights out before the light-squared bishop: the bishop is guarding b7, and its best square can wait until the queenside is safe.

5231539809808326|e6e5.headline: Recapture 4...Qxd5; 4...e5 just hangs a pawn to the knight
5231539809808326|e6e5.why: 4...e5 puts a pawn on a square the knight on f3 attacks and nothing defends: 5.Nxe5 wins it, and after 5...Qxd5 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Nxd7 you are a pawn down and clearly worse. 4...Qxd5, the most common master move (58.5%), takes back the pawn on d5, which your queen and e6 pawn both attack. With White's pawn on c3, White's knight cannot hit your queen from c3, and in the main line it goes to a3 instead, as in 5.Na3 Nf6 6.d4 Nc6. Recapturing with 4...exd5, as the theory describes for 2...e6, is also good.
5231539809808326|e6e5.principle: Count attackers and defenders before moving a centre pawn: d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, while e5 would be attacked by the knight and defended by nothing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6

5254169560142503|c1d2.headline: Use your gambit lead: 7.Ng5 hits f7 instead of passive 7.Bd2
5254169560142503|c1d2.why: 7.Bd2 answers the pin on c3 passively: Black develops with 7...Nf6 and castles, your gambit compensation runs out and Black is simply a pawn up. In the Smith-Morra you are a pawn down for a lead in development, so use it: 7.Ng5 joins the bishop on c4 against f7, which only the king defends, and in the main line Black has to spend 7...Nh6 guarding it. After 8.O-O O-O 9.Qh5 a third piece aims at f7 and the position stays in your favour.
5254169560142503|c1d2.principle: A gambit's compensation is time, and it disappears if you play passively; use the lead to attack the weak point f7 before Black castles.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

5265791031076490|b5d7.headline: 7.Qe2 guards the b5 bishop and hits e5 at once
5265791031076490|b5d7.why: 6...Bd7 threatens 7...Bxb5, winning a bishop, but 7.Bxd7+ answers it by trading your only developed bishop and bringing Black's queen out with 7...Qxd7; after 8.O-O O-O-O 9.d4 Nxd5 Black is quickly developed and stands better. The point of 5...Na5 was to chase your bishop, so keep it and make Black react instead. 7.Qe2 covers b5 along the diagonal and attacks the pawn on e5, so Black spends 7...Bd6 defending it; only then do you trade with 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nc3, and the game stays balanced.
5265791031076490|b5d7.principle: When a piece is attacked, look first for a defending move that also creates a threat, so your opponent has to answer you instead of developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Na5

5269510306588935|f1c4.headline: Kick the knight with 6.e5 before ...Nc6 covers e5
5269510306588935|f1c4.why: 5...Nf6 puts the knight where your e-pawn can hit it. 6.Bc4 is natural but lets Black cover e5 first with 6...Nc6, so after 7.e5 the knight has 7...Ng4 and the game is level. 6.e5 kicks it at once: in the engine line it goes all the way back with 6...Ng8, and after 7.Bc4 d5 8.exd6 Bxd6 9.O-O you have a big lead in development for the pawn. The theory gives the same idea against an early ...Nf6 in the Morra: e5 is a free tempo that embarrasses Black.
5269510306588935|f1c4.principle: A knight that a pawn can attack is a target: push the pawn while the knight has no good square, before Black adds a defender to the push square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

5284557229021992|d3d4.headline: Castle first; 7.d4 takes away e4's only pawn guard.
5284557229021992|d3d4.why: The pawn on d3 is what protects e4. After 7.d4 exd4 8.exd4 Nxe4 the knight on f6 takes the pawn, and White's king is still in the centre. 7.O-O tucks the king away and puts the rook on the half-open f-file that the earlier recapture opened. White can prepare central play after that.
5284557229021992|d3d4.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check what it was defending, and get your king safe before opening the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d3/4...Bc5

5286148894410756|d3c2.headline: Release the tension with 7.dxc5; don't move the bishop twice
5286148894410756|d3c2.why: Black's c5 pawn, knight on c6 and queen on b6 all hit d4, and your bishop on d3 blocks the queen's defence, so 7...cxd4 is a real threat. 7.Bc2 moves the bishop again without solving it: after 7...cxd4 8.cxd4 Nb4 the knight swaps off that bishop with 9...Nxc2, and Black is slightly better. 7.dxc5, the top master choice (51.3%), removes the target: after 7...Bxc5 8.O-O you are castled, the e5 pawn still cramps Black, and 10.Nbd2 and 11.Nb3 bring the knight to hit the bishop on c5, keeping a small edge.
5286148894410756|d3c2.principle: With the knight on b1 and bishop on c1 still at home, a second move with the same bishop must win something; here it only gives Black time to cash in on d4.

5414391277109696|b1c3.headline: Bishop on g4 is loose: 5.Bxf7+ and 6.Ng5+ win it back
5414391277109696|b1c3.why: 4...Bg4 leaves the bishop undefended on the diagonal of your queen, with only the knight on f3 in between. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves that knight with check, so after 6...Ke8 7.Qxg4 you have your piece back, Black can no longer castle, and after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 your queen and knight on g5 stand next to the stuck king, with a large advantage. 5.Nc3 is normal development but misses it, and after 5...e6 6.Be3 Nc6 7.Qd2 Bxf3 your edge shrinks to a small one.
5414391277109696|b1c3.principle: Early on the king alone guards f7; when a bishop sacrifice there is followed by a knight check that uncovers your queen on a loose piece, play it.

5414391277109696|c2c3.headline: 5.Bxf7+ and 6.Ng5+ win back the loose g4 bishop
5414391277109696|c2c3.why: 4...Bg4 left the bishop undefended and f7 guarded only by the king. 5.c3 is too quiet: Black covers f7 with 5...e6, later swaps with 7...Bxf3, and most of your advantage is gone. 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+ moves the knight off the queen's diagonal with check, so 7.Qxg4 wins the piece back; after 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Black's king is stuck in the centre with your queen and knight next to it, and White is close to winning.
5414391277109696|c2c3.principle: f7 is defended only by the king, so with a bishop on c4 and a knight ready for g5, always check a sacrifice there, especially when a loose piece can be collected afterwards.

5414391277109696|h2h3.headline: Don't ask with 5.h3: 5.Bxf7+ exploits the undefended g4 bishop
5414391277109696|h2h3.why: 5.h3 lets Black solve their problems by swapping: after 5...Bxf3 6.Qxf3 e6 f7 is covered and your big chance has passed. The bishop on g4 has no defender, so strike at once with 5.Bxf7+ Kxf7 6.Ng5+: the knight leaves with check, your queen's diagonal to g4 opens, and 7.Qxg4 takes the bishop back. After 7...Bxd4 8.Qe6 Black can no longer castle, Black's king faces your queen and knight, and White is close to winning.
5414391277109696|h2h3.principle: When an enemy piece is undefended, look for a check that unblocks one of your pieces against it; here the sacrifice on f7 and the knight check do exactly that.

5431389031817647|c6e5.headline: Bring out a new piece that attacks e4
5431389031817647|c6e5.why: 4...Ne5 moves the knight a second time while three minor pieces are still at home, and 5.f4 chases it straight back with 5...Nc6, so White gains two moves for free. 4...Nf6 develops a new piece and attacks the pawn on e4 at once; theory calls this the Schmidt variation, where White usually trades with 5.Nxc6 bxc6.
5431389031817647|c6e5.principle: When the opponent's knight stands in the centre, develop a new piece with a threat rather than moving a knight that is already out.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6

5431389031817647|d7d6.headline: Seize the initiative with 4...Nf6 against e4
5431389031817647|d7d6.why: 4...d6 is passive: it shuts in the bishop on f8 and lets White develop freely with 5.Nc3, 6.Bf4, 7.Qd2 and 8.O-O-O. Wikibooks stresses that Black has a chance to take the initiative here that should not be wasted. 4...Nf6 develops the knight with immediate pressure on the pawn on e4, so White has to spend the next move dealing with it, usually 5.Nxc6 bxc6.
5431389031817647|d7d6.principle: Develop with a threat when you can: a knight that attacks a centre pawn gains time because White must answer it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Nxd4

5459128121989910|g7g5.headline: White's 3.Nf3 left e4 undefended: take it with 3...Nxe4
5459128121989910|g7g5.why: 3...g5 throws a pawn away: 4.fxg5 removes it, and 4...Nxe4 only wins it back, so Black ends up with level material and a loosened kingside. 3.Nf3 left the pawn on e4 attacked by the knight on f6 and defended by nothing, so 3...Nxe4 wins it. After 4.Nc3 Nf6 the knight returns and Black finishes the Pirc setup with 5...g6 and 6...Bg7.
5459128121989910|g7g5.principle: Before any plan, check what is undefended: when White plays f4 without guarding e4, that pawn is often there for the taking.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6

5459128121989910|g7g6.headline: After 2.f4 Nf6 3.Nf3, the e4 pawn is free: take it.
5459128121989910|g7g6.why: 3...g6 lets White use the pawn instead: 4.e5 kicks the knight back to d7, and White gains space and time. 3.Nf3 develops but leaves e4 attacked once and not defended at all, so 3...Nxe4 wins a pawn. The knight drops back with 4.Nc3 Nf6 and Black carries on with 5...g6, a pawn up in the normal fianchetto set-up.
5459128121989910|g7g6.principle: Each time White makes a developing move in the Pirc, check whether e4 is still defended; when nothing guards it, your knight on f6 takes it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6

5465976377681862|d8f6.headline: Take the knight: 4...Nxe5, then meet the fork with 5...Bd6.
5465976377681862|d8f6.why: The knight on e5 is attacked once and defended by nothing, and 4...Qf6 only attacks it. After 5.Ng4 it escapes with gain of time on the queen, and Black is a pawn down. 4...Nxe5 wins the knight. White gets the material back with 5.d4, but after 5...Bd6 6.dxe5 Bxe5 the material is level again.
5465976377681862|d8f6.principle: When a piece is free to take, take it with a minor piece rather than attacking it with the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

5477278678228721|c1f4.headline: Play 4.e3 and win back c4 before anything else
5477278678228721|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 lets Black hold on to the c4 pawn: 4...b5 5.a4 c6 keeps it protected, and White has nothing to show for it. 4.e3 prepares to develop the kingside and win back c4, as the theory puts it. After 4...c5 5.Bxc4 the pawn is regained with the bishop developed and White ready to castle; 79.7% of masters choose it.
5477278678228721|c1f4.principle: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, free the king's bishop to recover the c4 pawn before Black can support it with the b-pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6/4. e3

5482220977229606|g7g6.headline: After 2.Nc3, take the centre with 2...d5 before White plays e4.
5482220977229606|g7g6.why: 2...g6 gives White a free hand in the centre: 3.e4 d6 4.d4 sets up a broad pawn centre, a Pirc where White has the useful moves already in. 2.Nc3 blocks White's c-pawn and aims only at e4, so 2...d5 stops that pawn push and stakes out the centre for Black. Masters reply 2...d5 in 77.1% of games.
5482220977229606|g7g6.principle: When White's knight blocks the c-pawn and eyes e4, put a pawn on d5 and keep White from building a two-pawn centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. Nf3/1...Nf6

5530528877961804|f3d4.headline: Meet 3...e4 with 4.Qe2: pin the pawn, don't retreat
5530528877961804|f3d4.why: 3...e4 kicks your knight and threatens 4...exf3, hoping to seize the initiative. 4.Nd4 saves the knight but moves it a second time and gives back the d5 pawn to 4...Qxd5, and White's advantage is gone. 4.Qe2, the masters' choice in 75.4% of games, attacks the e4 pawn and pins it to the king on e8, so it can't take your knight, and 5.d3 then undermines Black's advanced pawn.
5530528877961804|f3d4.principle: When a pawn attacks your piece, look for a pin on that pawn before retreating; a pinned pawn can't capture.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5/3...e4

5540647116069974|f1c4.headline: Against the Owen, take the big centre with 4.d4.
5540647116069974|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 lets Black hit the bishop with gain of time: after 4...Nf6 5.e5 d5 it has to retreat all the way with 6.Bf1. The theory notes that the Owen allows White to play d4 and control the centre easily, and 4.d4 does exactly that, putting two pawns side by side in the middle. Masters play it in 88% of games, and if Black strikes at the centre with 6...c5 as the Owen plans, 7.dxc5 wins a pawn.
5540647116069974|f1c4.principle: When an offbeat defence leaves the centre to you, occupy it with pawns first; your bishops find their squares once the centre is set.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6

5580466240815728|c8f5.headline: Same Slav rule: knight to f6 before the bishop leaves c8
5580466240815728|c8f5.why: Theory is blunt here too: avoid 3...Bf5, because 4.cxd5 cxd5 5.Qb3 attacks b7 and d5 at once and wins a pawn; after 5...Nf6 6.Qxb7 White later takes on a7 as well. 3...Nf6 is by far the most common reply: the knight controls e4 and adds a defender to d5, keeping the position level.
5580466240815728|c8f5.principle: Knights before bishops: in the Slav the knight on f6 defends d5 and covers e4, while the c8 bishop's best moment comes later.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3

5588080788603958|c7c6.headline: 2...dxe4 takes a pawn White cannot win straight back
5588080788603958|c7c6.why: 2...c6 declines the gambit into a Caro-Kann, and after 3.e5 Bf5 White gets an Advance-style position with extra space, so the small edge you had passes to White. After 2.e4 the e4 pawn is attacked once and not defended at all, and theory rates the Blackmar-Diemer as suspect at professional level: there is no way for White to win the pawn back immediately. After 2...dxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 you develop with the extra pawn, and if White tries 3.f3 instead, 3...e5 is the strong answer.
5588080788603958|c7c6.principle: Accept a gambit when you can develop normally afterwards; here ...Nf6 and ...Bf5 come naturally, so the pawn is a clean gain.

5588080788603958|c8e6.headline: Accept the Blackmar-Diemer pawn with 2...dxe4
5588080788603958|c8e6.why: 2...Be6 blocks Black's e-pawn and walks into 3.exd5 Bxd5 4.c4, which kicks the bishop again, so White gains time and a broad centre. 2.e4 left e4 attacked and undefended; 2...dxe4 accepts the gambit and wins a pawn, and White has no way to win it back at once. Masters choose it in 74.8% of games.
5588080788603958|c8e6.principle: Accept a gambit when the pawn is free and you can develop normally afterwards, as with ...Nf6 and ...Bf5 here.

5588080788603958|e7e5.headline: Accept the Blackmar-Diemer pawn with 2...dxe4; 2...e5 just drops one
5588080788603958|e7e5.why: 2...e5 leaves Black's own e-pawn hanging and reaches the Beyer Gambit by transposition: 3.dxe5 takes it, and 3...dxe4 4.Qxd8+ Kxd8 leaves Black's king stuck in the centre. 2.e4 offered a pawn that nothing defends, and 2...dxe4 takes it; masters accept in 75% of games. White's compensation is development, so Black's job is to develop soundly, as in 3.Nc3 Nf6.
5588080788603958|e7e5.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can develop normally afterwards, rather than offering a pawn of your own back.

5641703819423939|c8f5.headline: 4.f3 leaves c4 undefended: take it with 4...dxc4
5641703819423939|c8f5.why: After 4.f3 the c4 pawn is attacked by your d5 pawn and has no defender. 4...Bf5 walks into 5.g4: after 5...Bc8 6.g5 Nh5 7.e4 White has chased your pieces back and built a big centre with gain of time, and stands better. 4...dxc4 takes the pawn now, and your c6 pawn supports 7...b5 to hold it, so you stay a pawn up with the better game.
5641703819423939|c8f5.principle: Once f3 is played, White's g-pawn can chase a bishop on f5 with tempo, so do not develop it into that pawn storm; grab the loose c4 pawn instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nc3/3...Nf6

5651959838826145|f7f6.headline: In the Scotch Gambit, develop with 4...Nf6 and hit e4.
5651959838826145|f7f6.why: 4...f6 does nothing to hold the pawn on d4: 5.Nxd4 Nxd4 6.Qxd4 wins it back at once. It also takes the f6 square from the knight and weakens the diagonal the bishop on c4 aims along toward f7. 4...Nf6 is the most played move: it develops and attacks the pawn on e4, so White has to spend time before recovering the pawn, as in 5.e5 d5 6.Bb5 Ne4.
5651959838826145|f7f6.principle: When you are a pawn up against a lead in development, develop with threats instead of making pawn moves that loosen your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...exd4/4. Bc4

5687709244296283|e4e5.headline: Defend e4 with 5.Re1 instead of pushing it
5687709244296283|e4e5.why: 5.e5 pushes the attacked pawn forward, but it can't be held there: after 5...Ng4 6.Re1 d6 Black undermines it, and following 7.exd6 Bxd6 White's centre pawn is traded off and Black's pieces come out actively. 5.Re1, played in 80.6% of master games, simply guards e4 with a piece that was waiting for the e-file. If Black grabs anyway with 5...Nxe4 6.Rxe4 d5, then 7.Bxd5 Qxd5 8.Nc3 hits the queen and material is level.
5687709244296283|e4e5.principle: Answer an attack on a centre pawn with a developing move that defends it, not a push that leaves the pawn to be undermined.

57158813525553|f1d3.headline: The c5 pawn is loose: take it with 5.dxc5
57158813525553|f1d3.why: 4...Bf5 develops but leaves the pawn on c5 attacked by your d4 pawn and defended by nothing. 5.Bd3 lets the chance pass: after 5...Bxd3 6.Qxd3 e6 7.Nf3 Nd7 Black has time to cover c5, so when White does take with 9.dxc5 Black recaptures with 9...Nxc5 and the game is level. The theory notes say Black should first add pressure with 4...Nc6; without it, 5.dxc5 wins a clean pawn, and 7.b4 later supports it.
57158813525553|f1d3.principle: After each opponent move, check what it left undefended; a free pawn in the centre is worth taking before you continue developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. e5/3...c5/4. c3

5811727298789441|f6g4.headline: When 9.e5 attacks the knight, take with 9...dxe5.
5811727298789441|f6g4.why: 9...Ng4 moves the knight a second time and puts it where White's h-pawn chases it: 10.h3 Nh6 11.h4 leaves the knight offside, and White's attack on the king rolls on with 13.h5. 9...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacked the knight, and after 10.Nxe5 Qd6 Black develops with gain of time against the knight on e5. The knight on f6 stays home defending the king, and Black comes out a pawn up after 13...Nxh5.
5811727298789441|f6g4.principle: When a pawn attacks one of your pieces, look first for a capture of that pawn; captures decide the position before a retreat does.

5850892143506287|b1c3.headline: Block with 5.Bd2; 5.Nc3 still leaves the bishop on f4 hanging
5850892143506287|b1c3.why: 4...Qb4+ attacks the bishop on f4 as well as the king, and 5.Nc3 blocks the check without defending it. After 5...Qxf4 White can grab the rook with 6.Nd5 Qe4 7.Nxc7+ Kd8 8.Nxa8, but the knight is stuck in the corner, 8...Nxe5 wins back the pawn, and White's advantage is gone. 5.Bd2 blocks with the attacked bishop itself and hits the queen on b4, so Black has to move the queen again, as in 5...Qe7.
5850892143506287|b1c3.principle: Against a queen check, ask what else the queen attacks before blocking; the right block moves or guards that piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5

5850892143506287|b1d2.headline: Block the check with 5.Bd2; 5.Nbd2 drops the bishop on f4
5850892143506287|b1d2.why: 4...Qb4+ checks the king and also attacks the bishop on f4 along the fourth rank. 5.Nbd2 blocks the check but leaves that bishop undefended, and 5...Qxf4 wins a whole piece. 5.Bd2 blocks with the attacked bishop itself and hits the queen on b4, so Black has to move the queen again, as in 5...Qe7.
5850892143506287|b1d2.principle: A queen check often hits a second target; before blocking, see which of your pieces it also attacks and block with that piece or guard it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5

5859332280044982|b8c6.headline: Meet 1.d4 with 1...Nf6, the most flexible reply
5859332280044982|b8c6.why: 1...Nc6 is the rare Mikenas defence: the knight blocks Black's c-pawn and stands in front of White's d-pawn, so 2.d5 kicks it at once and after 2...Ne5 3.Nc3 White gains space and time. 1...Nf6 is the Indian defence: it develops, controls e4 and keeps every pawn setup open, so Black can fight for the centre later on their own terms. Masters choose it in 60.9% of games.
5859332280044982|b8c6.principle: Against 1.d4, stop White's second centre pawn: a knight on f6 controls e4 so White cannot simply play it.

5859332280044982|e7e5.headline: Against 1.d4, develop with 1...Nf6 instead of giving a pawn
5859332280044982|e7e5.why: 1...e5 is the Englund Gambit, which the theory calls unsound: after 2.dxe5 Black is a pawn down and gets too little for it against careful play. 1...Nf6 is the most popular reply among masters (60.9%): it develops a knight and controls e4. White can't simply build a two-pawn centre, because 2.e4 loses a pawn to 2...Nxe4.
5859332280044982|e7e5.principle: Answer 1.d4 with a move that develops a piece and controls e4, not a pawn move that can simply be taken.

5860472034319888|e7e6.headline: 3.Bg5 left e4 undefended: take it with 3...Nxe4
5860472034319888|e7e6.why: 3...e6 blocks the bishop on c8 and gives White time for 4.Nc3, which defends e4, and White then builds a big centre with 5.f4. 3.Bg5 develops a piece but leaves the pawn on e4, attacked since 2...Nf6, without a defender, so 3...Nxe4 wins it. After 4.Be3 g6 the knight drops back with 5...Nf6, and Black finishes the Pirc setup with 6...Bg7.
5860472034319888|e7e6.principle: After every White move, ask whether e4 is still defended: the pawn the Pirc knight attacks from f6 is often left loose.

5864435021787537|d2d3.headline: Open the centre with 4.d4 against Black's misplaced queen
5864435021787537|d2d3.why: 3...c6 spent another pawn move and left Black further behind in development, with the queen exposed on f6. 4.d3 is too quiet: in the engine line Black gets time for 4...d6 and 6...Nf6 and catches up. 4.d4 opens the centre while you lead: after 4...exd4 5.Bg5 your bishop develops by attacking the queen, and 6.Nxd4 regains the pawn with more pieces in play.
5864435021787537|d2d3.principle: When you are ahead in development and your opponent's queen is out, open lines so your pieces can attack it with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

5864435021787537|f1c4.headline: Open the centre with 4.d4 against Black's misplaced queen
5864435021787537|f1c4.why: 4.Bc4 develops, but Black catches up with 4...Bb4 5.O-O d6 6.d4 Bg4, pinning your knight, and half of your advantage is gone. Theory explains that 2...Qf6 takes the f6 square from Black's knight and that an early queen gives the opponent chances to develop with tempo; one plan is to open the centre and gain time on the misplaced queen. 3...c6 spent another move on a pawn, so open it now: after 4.d4 exd4 5.Bg5 the bishop develops with tempo on the queen, and after 5...Qd6 6.Nxd4 h6 7.Bh4 Qc7 she has moved again while you have a big lead in development.
5864435021787537|f1c4.principle: When you are ahead in development and the enemy queen is exposed, open the centre at once so your pieces can hit her with tempo.

5876653910199998|c8e6.headline: When a pawn hits the bishop on c5, move it: 5...Bb6
5876653910199998|c8e6.why: 5.d4 attacks the bishop on c5 with a pawn, and 5...Be6 doesn't deal with it: after 6.Bxe6 fxe6 7.dxc5 White trades bishops and then takes the c5 bishop, a whole piece. 5...Bb6 simply saves the bishop. If White takes 6.dxe5, Black develops with 6...Bg4, pinning the knight on f3, and 7...Nf6; 5...exd4 is also fine.
5876653910199998|c8e6.principle: Look at White's captures first: 6.dxc5 takes a bishop, so any move that ignores it loses a piece.

5887905008267832|c2c4.headline: Give the d5 pawn back with 3.d4 and take the centre
5887905008267832|c2c4.why: 3.c4 tries to hold the extra pawn, but Black chips at it with 3...c6, and after 4.d4 cxd5 the pawn is gone and you are in a Caro-Kann Panov attack, which theory now rates as only even. 3.d4, the masters' main move at 53.2%, gives the pawn back at once but takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the queen's bishop. After 3...Nxd5 4.Nf3 White usually adds c4 to kick the knight, and Black can end up cramped.
5887905008267832|c2c4.principle: A pawn you can't keep isn't worth defending: spend the move building a central pawn front instead.

5887905008267832|f1c4.headline: Give the d5 pawn back with 3.d4 and take the centre
5887905008267832|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 gives up the pawn on d5 for nothing: 3...Nxd5 recaptures, Black develops freely with ...Bf5 and ...e6, and later trades off the bishop with 7...Bxd3. The theory calls 3.d4 White's most robust reply: it returns the pawn too, but takes the centre and opens lines for the queen and the bishop on c1. After 3...Nxd5 White usually follows with Nf3 and c4, and Black can end up cramped.
5887905008267832|f1c4.principle: When you can't keep a gambit pawn safely, give it back on your own terms, in return for the centre.

5915229736017859|c5d4.headline: 4.d4 left e4 hanging: take it with 4...dxe4
5915229736017859|c5d4.why: 4.d4 ignores the attack on e4: the pawn is hit by your d5 pawn and nothing defends it. 4...cxd4 lets White off the hook with 5.e5, closing the centre into a French-style structure where the game is level. 4...dxe4 takes the pawn and hits the knight on f3 at the same time, so White has to retreat with 5.Nfd2, and after 6...cxd4 you are a clean pawn up with a clear advantage.
5915229736017859|c5d4.principle: When your opponent makes a pawn move in the centre, first check what they left undefended: here e4 had no guard, and taking it also attacks a knight.

591532767997359|c6d4.headline: Develop the other knight: 3...Nf6, the Four Knights
591532767997359|c6d4.why: 3...Nd4 moves the same knight twice with three minor pieces still at home, and it takes the defender away from e5: 4.Nxe5 simply wins the pawn. 3...Nf6 develops toward the centre and attacks e4, entering the Four Knights Game; masters choose it 92% of the time. Against 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4, Black develops with 5...Bb4, pinning the knight on c3.
591532767997359|c6d4.principle: With three pieces still undeveloped, a second knight move must win something; here it gives up the e5 pawn instead.

591532767997359|d7d6.headline: Mirror White with 3...Nf6: the Four Knights is the main line
591532767997359|d7d6.why: 3...d6 is passive: it shuts in your f8 bishop and gives White a free hand in the centre. In the engine line 4.d4 Nf6 5.d5 Ne7 White gains space and pushes your knight back, then plays 6.Bg5 to add pressure. 3...Nf6, played in 92% of master games, enters the Four Knights: the theory notes that none of the ways to break the symmetry are appealing, so develop the knight and keep the bishop free to come out in one move later.
591532767997359|d7d6.principle: When both of your knights have obvious squares, develop them before committing pawns that block your bishops.

591532767997359|f7f5.headline: Answer 3.Nc3 with 3...Nf6; 3...f5 opens lines to your king.
591532767997359|f7f5.why: 3...f5 loosens Black's king while White is ready to strike in the centre: the line 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 Bb4 6.Qh5+ shows how the open diagonal toward e8 is exploited. 3...Nf6 puts the knight on its best square and enters the quiet but sound Four Knights Game, chosen in 92.2% of master games.
591532767997359|f7f5.principle: Don't open lines toward your own uncastled king: an early f-pawn push loosens the diagonal from h5 to e8.

5925543013863182|e7e5.headline: e5 is covered by the f3 knight: develop with 2...Nf6
5925543013863182|e7e5.why: 2...e5 puts a pawn where the knight on f3 already attacks it and nothing defends it, so 3.Nxe5 simply wins it. 2...Nf6 is the most common master move (44.8%): it develops toward the centre, and Black follows with ...g6, ...Bg7 and castles (5...O-O in the main line) with a level game.
5925543013863182|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into the centre, count: a square attacked by an enemy knight and defended by none of your pieces is not available yet.

5945701382218233|d4c5.headline: Push past the c-pawn with 2.d5; don't trade your centre pawn
5945701382218233|d4c5.why: 2.dxc5 trades White's centre pawn for a flank pawn that Black wins back easily: after 2...e6 3.e4 Bxc5 material is level and Black's bishop is developed. The theory warns against taking for this reason. 2.d5 keeps the pawn in the centre, gains space and cramps Black, and 76.3% of masters choose it.
5945701382218233|d4c5.principle: When a flank pawn challenges your centre pawn, advance past it rather than trading your centre pawn for it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...c5

5965252915693730|b8c6.headline: Take the King's Gambit pawn while ...Qh4+ still works
5965252915693730|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 develops, but after 3.Nf3 White covers h4, so the ...Qh4+ reply disappears and fxe5 becomes a real threat; in the line 3...exf4 4.d4 g5 5.d5 White gains time on the knight. 2...exf4 takes the undefended pawn at once, while ...Qh4+ is still a threat, so White must deal with it before building the centre. Masters accept in 67.3% of games.
5965252915693730|b8c6.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when it is free and your reply comes with a threat; waiting lets White cover the weakness first.

5965252915693730|d7d6.headline: The King's Gambit pawn is free: take it with 2...exf4
5965252915693730|d7d6.why: 2...d6 declines passively and lets White develop and choose when to take on e5, as in 3.d3 Nc6 4.Nf3 g6 5.fxe5 Nxe5. 2.f4 offers a pawn that is attacked and not defended at all; 2...exf4 takes it, and now ...Qh4+ is a real threat that White has to spend time on. Masters accept in 67.3% of games.
5965252915693730|d7d6.principle: Take a gambit pawn when it costs you nothing and your position stays sound; then White must prove the compensation.

5965252915693730|f7f5.headline: Take the f4 pawn instead of offering your own
5965252915693730|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is the old Panteldakis Countergambit and simply loses a pawn to 3.exf5, which also opens the diagonal to Black's king and gives White the threat of Qh5+. 2...exf4 takes the undefended pawn instead, and the threat of ...Qh4+ makes White spend time on the king rather than on attack. Masters accept in 67.3% of games.
5965252915693730|f7f5.principle: Answer a gambit by taking the free pawn, not by opening lines toward your own king.
