5981569862362187|b1c3.headline: 4...d6 left f7 weak: hit it with 5.Ng5
5981569862362187|b1c3.why: 5.Nc3 lets Black go after your bishop with 5...Na5: in the engine line it ends with 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, and White only wins the knight back with 8.b4 and 9.bxa5. Black's 4...d6 was a slip that left f7 defended only by the king, with the c4 bishop already aiming at it. 5.Ng5 adds a second attacker, and after 5...d5 6.exd5 White wins a pawn.
5981569862362187|b1c3.principle: When f7 is defended only by the king and your bishop already aims at it, add a second attacker before making quiet moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. d3

6004567141016616|c1f4.headline: 1...b6 ignores the centre, so take it with 2.e4
6004567141016616|c1f4.why: 2.Bf4 lets Black stop e4 with 2...Nf6, and with the bishop coming to b7 Black keeps White from ever getting two central pawns. 1...b6 does nothing for the centre, so 2.e4 takes it at once: White gets two pawns side by side, reaching an Owen's Defence. 56.1% of masters choose it.
6004567141016616|c1f4.principle: When your opponent's first move ignores the centre, put a second pawn there before they can contest it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...b6

6047686001480310|e4e5.headline: Against 3...e6, develop and keep it open; don't play 4.e5
6047686001480310|e4e5.why: 4.e5 closes the centre and gives Black a French-style game where ...c5 strikes at the base of White's pawn chain; after 4...c5 5.dxc5 Bxc5 Black's bishop develops actively. 3...e6 shuts in Black's light-squared bishop and wastes the move ...c6 that a French player would use for ...c5, so White should keep the position open: 4.Bd3 develops and offers the d4-pawn, and after 4...dxe4 5.Nxe4 Qxd4 6.Nf3 White gains time on the queen and castles with a clear lead in development.
6047686001480310|e4e5.principle: When your opponent's setup locks in a bishop and spends moves on pawns, keep lines open and develop quickly rather than closing the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3

6065829209254937|f1c4.headline: 3...Bb7 hits e4: develop with 4.Bd3, which guards it
6065829209254937|f1c4.why: The bishop on b7 attacks e4, which nothing defends. 4.Bc4 develops but leaves the pawn hanging, so 4...Bxe4 wins it and Black is better. 4.Bd3, played in 94.9% of master games, develops and guards e4 with the same move; after 4...c5 5.c3 Nf6 6.Qe2 d5 7.e5 you gain space with a firm centre and a clear edge. The theory describes the e6b6 setup as aimed at the d5 and e4 squares, so e4 is always the point to check.
6065829209254937|f1c4.principle: Ask what your opponent's last move threatens: the bishop on b7 targets e4, so pick the developing move that also defends it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...b6/3. Nf3/3...Bb7

6104332673881535|d7d6.headline: Against 2.c3, hit e4 with 2...Nf6 while White can't play Nc3

ideas.title: White wants two centre pawns
ideas.text: 2.c3 prepares 3.d4, so White can retake with the c-pawn and keep pawns on d4 and e4.

ideas.title: No Nc3 for White
ideas.text: The c3 pawn takes the knight's square: White can't guard e4 with Nc3 or chase your pieces from d5.

ideas.title: Strike the centre at once
ideas.text: Black's best replies, 2...Nf6 and 2...d5, both hit e4 straight away; slow moves hand White the full centre.

ideas.title: Chip at the e5 pawn
ideas.text: After 3.e5 Nd5 the advanced pawn becomes a target for ...cxd4 and ...d6.

habit.why: 2...d6 attacks nothing, so White plays 3.d4 and gets the full centre for free. After 3...Nf6 4.Bd3 cxd4 5.cxd4 White has pawns on d4 and e4 and a lasting space edge.

strays.text: 2...d6 makes no threat, so 2.c3 gets exactly what it was played for.

taught.why: 2...Nf6 attacks e4, and with no Nc3 available White usually pushes 3.e5. After 3...Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 you hit the e5 pawn and the chances are equal.

enforces.text: The knight hits e4 and then sits safely on d5, since no white knight can reach c3.

6104332673881535|d7d6.principle: Contest the centre your opponent is building: 2.c3 prepares 3.d4, so attack e4 with 2...Nf6 now instead of letting White set up pawns on d4 and e4.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 2...Nc6 develops but lets White play 3.d4, and after 3...cxd4 4.cxd4 White has the two-pawn centre. It's the most common club move here, but rare among masters.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 gives White no free 3.d4: after 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 you are already attacking the centre.

alternatives.label: slightly worse
alternatives.before: 2...e6 is solid, but after 3.d4 d5 4.e5 you're in an Advance French, with your light-squared bishop shut in behind the e6 pawn.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 keeps it a Sicilian: after 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4 cxd4 5.cxd4 d6 the e5 pawn is under attack and your c8-bishop's diagonal stays open.

alternatives.label: sound
alternatives.before: 2...d5 hits back in the centre: after 3.exd5 Qxd5 your queen stands well because no white knight can hit it from c3. It's the old main line, played in a third of master games.
alternatives.after: 2...Nf6 is more popular with masters (45% to 33%) and fully level, while 2...d5 opens the centre and often leads to isolated-pawn middlegames or an early queen trade.

612982152772711|d1b3.headline: Castle first with 7.O-O; 7.Qb3 walks into ...Na5
612982152772711|d1b3.why: 7.Qb3 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home, and after 7...Qe7 8.O-O Na5 the knight attacks your queen and bishop together; following 9.Qb5 Nxc4 10.Qxc4 your strong bishop is gone and the game is level. 7.O-O tucks the king away first while the centre is open. After 7...d3 8.e5 Be7 the pawn has pushed Black's bishop back, and only now 9.Qb3 hits f7: after 9...Kf8 10.Bxf7 you win a pawn and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
612982152772711|d1b3.principle: In an open centre, castle before starting queen operations; once your king is safe, the same queen move comes with real threats.

612982152772711|f3g5.headline: Castle first, then hit the d6 bishop with e5
612982152772711|f3g5.why: 7.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home: 7...Ne5 hits your bishop, and after 8.Bb3 h6 9.Nf3 Nxf3+ the knight has walked back and been traded off, and Black is better. 7.O-O gets your king safe and keeps the central play. The bishop on d6 blocks Black's d-pawn, as the theory notes, and stands where your e-pawn can hit it: in the main line 8.e5 drives it to e7, 9.Qb3 lines up with the bishop on c4 against f7, and 10.Bxf7 wins a pawn.
612982152772711|f3g5.principle: A second knight move must win something concrete; when ...Ne5 and ...h6 can simply push it back, castle and use your pawns and pieces in the centre instead.

6180716488927123|d7d6.headline: Hit the loose e4 pawn with 3...d5 against the Ponziani
6180716488927123|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends e5, which was not really threatened, hems in the bishop on f8, and lets White play 4.d4 for a big two-pawn centre; Wikibooks calls it passive. 3.c3 took the c3 square from White's knight, so the pawn on e4 is loose, and 3...d5 strikes at it at once. If White takes on d5, Black's queen recaptures without Nc3 to chase it.
6180716488927123|d7d6.principle: Strike at the centre pawn your opponent can no longer defend easily: with c3 played, e4 has lost its natural knight defender.

6180716488927123|f7f5.headline: Against the Ponziani, hit e4 with 3...d5.
6180716488927123|f7f5.why: 3...f5, the Ponziani Countergambit, gives up a pawn after 4.exf5 and loosens Black's own king. It is thought to give White an advantage when White knows the theory. 3.c3 left e4 loose and took c3 away from White's knight. 3...d5 attacks e4, and if 4.exd5 Qxd5 the queen is safe because White cannot chase it with Nc3.
6180716488927123|f7f5.principle: When the opponent's opening leaves a centre pawn loose, attack it with a centre pawn, not with a flank pawn that weakens your king.

6180716488927123|f8c5.headline: Against the Ponziani, hit e4 at once with 3...d5.
6180716488927123|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 ignores what 3.c3 is for: White plays 4.d4, gaining time on the bishop, and after 4...exd4 5.cxd4 Bb6 owns a two-pawn centre. 3...d5 attacks the pawn on e4, which is loose because c3 has taken the knight's natural square. If 4.exd5 Qxd5, White has no Nc3 to chase the queen away, so Black gets a free hand in the centre.
6180716488927123|f8c5.principle: When White spends a move on c3 to prepare d4, strike at the centre before d4 arrives, aiming at the pawn that c3 left without a knight's support.

6186919355194995|f1c4.headline: Against ...d6 and ...e6, play 3.d4, not the bishop
6186919355194995|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 runs into 3...d5, which attacks the bishop and the e4 pawn at once: after 4.exd5 exd5 the bishop must retreat with 5.Be2, and the time White had is gone. 2...e6 is passive, so 3.d4 takes the centre with both pawns and keeps the bishop for later. In the engine line White adds 5.c4 and 6.Nc3 and gains space with 7.d5.
6186919355194995|f1c4.principle: Don't develop a bishop to a square an enemy pawn can hit with a useful central move; here ...d5 both attacks c4 and challenges e4.

6196978325404138|b8c6.headline: Challenge the London with 3...c5 before ...Nc6.
6196978325404138|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so Black gives up the ...c5 break and lets White build the London setup in peace. After 4.Nf3 Bg4 5.c4 White even takes over the initiative. 3...c5 is the most common reply: it strikes at d4 and challenges the bishop's setup. The knight still comes to c6 afterwards, as in 3...c5 4.Nf3 Nc6.
6196978325404138|b8c6.principle: Against a solid pawn centre, put your c-pawn to work before your queen's knight blocks it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Bf4/2...Nf6/3. e3

6230854239967859|c2c3.headline: Break the pin with 5.Be2 before ...Bxf3 costs you d4
6230854239967859|c2c3.why: 4...Bg4 pins your knight and threatens 5...Bxf3, removing the piece that guards d4. 5.c3 adds a pawn defender but leaves the pin in place: in the game line Black plays 5...e5, castles queenside, piles up on d4 and wins it with 8...exd4 9.cxd4 Nxd4. 5.Be2, played in 88.1% of master games, develops and breaks the pin, so a capture on f3 can be answered by a piece instead of ruining your pawns, and 6.Be3 adds another guard to d4.
6230854239967859|c2c3.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen and that knight guards a centre pawn, break the pin by developing a piece in between before the pinner captures.

6239823014560158|e2e4.headline: Develop with 3.Bf4; 3.e4 gives away a pawn
6239823014560158|e2e4.why: 3.e4 pushes a pawn that nothing defends: after 3...dxe4 the knight on f3 is attacked, and 4.d5 Nb4 5.Nfd2 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nfxd5 leaves Black a clean pawn up. 3.Bf4 is the most common master move (34%): it develops the bishop to an active square before 4.e3 closes its diagonal, as in 3...Bg4 4.e3 e6 5.c4.
6239823014560158|e2e4.principle: Before pushing a pawn into contact, count who defends it: e4 is hit by Black's d5 pawn and covered by nothing of yours.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nc6

6251023477722752|c1e3.headline: Bishop to c4 and castle: the book plan against ...Bf5
6251023477722752|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 is not a mistake, but it is off the main path: it develops the queen's bishop before the king's bishop and delays castling, and in the game line your king's bishop then goes to d3 only to be traded off with 7...Bxd3. 6.Bc4 is the most common master move (37%) and the setup the theory gives against ...Bf5 and ...e6, with White standing better: the bishop takes an active diagonal and you castle next with 7.O-O. Then 8.Nh4 goes after the f5 bishop, and after 8...Bg6 9.Nxg6 hxg6 you have the bishop pair.
6251023477722752|c1e3.principle: Develop the kingside pieces first so you can castle: the king's bishop has an obvious active square, while the queen's bishop can wait to see where it is needed.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

6277794409955082|b7c6.headline: Recapture 4...dxc6 to open lines for queen and bishop
6277794409955082|b7c6.why: After 4...bxc6 the d-pawn still blocks Black's queen and bishop, and the e5 pawn has no tactical cover, so 5.d4 exd4 6.Qxd4 lets White's queen take over the centre; Wikibooks gives White a small advantage. 4...dxc6 is the main move: it opens lines for the queen and the bishop on c8, and the pawn on e5 is defended by a trick, since Nxe5 runs into ...Qd4, forking the knight and the pawn on e4.
6277794409955082|b7c6.principle: Recapture in the way that opens lines for your undeveloped pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...a6/4. Bxc6/4...dxc6

6280706797964752|c2c3.headline: e4 is attacked twice: add a defender with 4.Qe2
6280706797964752|c2c3.why: After 3...Nf6 the pawn on e4 is attacked by the knight on f6 and the bishop on b7 and defended only by the bishop on d3. 4.c3 adds nothing there: 4...Nxe4 wins it, the knight on e4 is then protected by the bishop on b7, and Black is better. The theory notes say White adds a defender, most often 4.Qe2 (69.3% of masters games), which keeps your pawn and your edge. 4.Nd2 and 4.Nc3 also defend it.
6280706797964752|c2c3.principle: Count attackers and defenders on every pawn your opponent is aiming at; two attackers against one defender means you need a second defender now.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3/3...Nf6

6280706797964752|g1f3.headline: e4 is attacked twice: add a defender with 4.Qe2
6280706797964752|g1f3.why: The bishop on b7 and the knight on f6 both hit e4, and only the bishop on d3 defends it, so 4.Nf3 simply loses the pawn to 4...Nxe4 and Black is better. Theory says White adds a defender here, most often 4.Qe2, 4.Nd2 or 4.f3. 4.Qe2 holds e4 with a second guard, and after 4...e6 5.Nf3 d5 6.e5 you gain space with tempo on the knight and keep a clear edge.
6280706797964752|g1f3.principle: Before a natural developing move, count the attackers and defenders of your centre pawns; if a pawn is attacked twice and defended once, add a defender first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3/3...Nf6

6285819280081780|d2d3.headline: Castle first, then open the centre against the early queen
6285819280081780|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is safe but passive: it spends a move on a one-square pawn push, and after 4...Nc6 5.Nc3 Nge7 Black has caught up in development and the chance to punish the early queen is gone. 4.O-O gets the king safe and keeps the d-pawn free to go two squares. After 4...d6 5.Nc3 Ne7 6.d4 White strikes in the centre while Black's king is still uncastled and the queen on f6 is exposed; after 6...Bxd4 7.Nxd4 exd4 8.Nb5 the knight jumps in.
6285819280081780|d2d3.principle: White is ahead in development and Black's queen came out early, so castle and open the centre quickly before Black catches up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6/3. Bc4

6309463160940467|e1h1.headline: 6...d6 left f7 weak: hit it twice with 7.Qb3
6309463160940467|e1h1.why: 6...d6 does nothing for f7, which is defended only by the king and already eyed by your bishop on c4. 7.O-O lets Black untangle: 7...Nc6 8.Ng5 Ne5 9.Qb3 Nxc4 swaps off that bishop, and your initiative fades. 7.Qb3 doubles on f7 at once: after 7...Nh6 8.Bxh6 Bxh6 9.Bxf7+ Kf8 you remove the knight that guarded it, take the f7 pawn and leave Black's king stuck on f8, keeping the advantage.
6309463160940467|e1h1.principle: With your bishop already on c4, adding the queen against f7 forces Black to defend it at once, before Black can trade off the bishop or castle.

6359291933074994|d7d5.headline: In the Vienna, prepare ...d5 with 2...Nf6 first
6359291933074994|d7d5.why: 2...d5 comes too early: the knight on c3 and the e4 pawn both attack d5, so 3.Nxd5 simply wins a pawn, and after 3...Nf6 4.Nxf6+ Qxf6 your queen is out early as well. 2...Nf6 develops, attacks e4 and adds a guard to d5, so ...d5 becomes possible later, for instance as the answer to f4. Masters choose it in 72% of games.
6359291933074994|d7d5.principle: Before pushing ...d5, count: Nc3 and the e4 pawn attack it twice and only the queen defends it, so add a defender with the knight first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3

6359291933074994|f7f5.headline: Don't open your own kingside; develop the knight to f6
6359291933074994|f7f5.why: 2...f5 is a King's Gambit reversed with White's queen knight already out: after 3.exf5 Black is a pawn down with a loosened kingside and less development. 2...Nf6 develops a knight, attacks e4 and contests d5, and prepares to meet White's f4 with a counter-strike in the centre.
6359291933074994|f7f5.principle: Opening lines near your own king only pays when you lead in development; here White is ahead, so Black develops first.

6363157341111651|d1e2.headline: Block the queen check with a bishop, not your queen
6363157341111651|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2 blocks the check with the queen, so Black trades with 5...Qxe2+ and the early queen trip costs Black nothing. 3...Qe6+ is a common amateur try that achieves little: 4.Be2 blocks with a developing piece, and the queen on e6 blocks Black's e-pawn and will have to move again, as in 4...Nf6 5.Nf3 Qd6. White gains time for 6.d4 and castling.
6363157341111651|d1e2.principle: When an early queen checks you, block with a developing piece so the queen, not you, has to spend another move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

6375481783376729|g1f3.headline: Punish 2...d6 with 3.dxc5 and chase the recapturing queen
6375481783376729|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 lets Black play 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 and reach a normal Open Sicilian, and theory notes that trading the c-pawn for your d-pawn was the whole point of 1...c5; most of your edge disappears. By playing 2...d6 instead of 2...cxd4, Black left you the choice, so take first: in the engine line Black regains the pawn with the queen, 3.dxc5 Qa5+ 4.Nc3 Qxc5, and 5.Be3 develops with tempo on her. After 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 Qxd5 7.Nxd5 Kd8 the queens are off and Black's king has lost the right to castle.
6375481783376729|g1f3.principle: When your opponent has to win a pawn back with the queen, develop your pieces with attacks on her and bank the time you gain.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4

6379793223839|c7c6.headline: Take back with 2...Qxd5; the 2...c6 gambit gives too little
6379793223839|c7c6.why: 2...c6 offers a pawn: after 3.dxc6 Nxc6 4.Nf3 e5 5.Nc3 you have some development for it, but the theory calls the gambit inferior, and White keeps a clear edge. 2...Qxd5, the main line (70.4% of master games), takes back the pawn, which nothing defends. White gains a tempo with 3.Nc3, but your queen steps to a safe square such as d6 (3...Qd6) and you develop normally with ...Nf6 and ...c6. 2...Nf6, the Modern Scandinavian, delays recovering the pawn and is also good.
6379793223839|c7c6.principle: A pawn sacrifice needs concrete compensation; when the pawn you gave can simply be taken back, recover it and develop instead of gambiting a second one.

6423991710179470|e1h1.headline: Before castling, strike f7 with 6.Ne5 after 5...Bg4.
6423991710179470|e1h1.why: 6.O-O is a natural developing move but misses the moment: after 6...e6 Black shuts the bishop on c4 out of f7, and 7.h3 Bxf3 8.Qxf3 leaves White only a small edge. 5...Bg4 left f7 guarded only by the king, and 6.Ne5 attacks it at once, threatening a bishop mate on f7 while opening the queen's line to the bishop on g4. Black has to give up the bishop with 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6, and is left with doubled e-pawns and a weakened king.
6423991710179470|e1h1.principle: Before a quiet move like castling, check for a forcing move; a knight jump that threatens mate on f7 comes first, because castling can wait.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

6423991710179470|h2h3.headline: With your bishop on c4, answer 5...Bg4 with 6.Ne5.
6423991710179470|h2h3.why: 6.h3 is the book move when White has a pawn on d4, but here it lets Black swap with 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 and White keeps only a small edge. With the bishop on c4, 5...Bg4 left f7 guarded only by the king, and 6.Ne5 hits it at once: it threatens a bishop mate on f7 and also opens the queen's line to the bishop on g4. Black has to give up the bishop with 6...Be6 7.Bxe6 fxe6, and is left with doubled e-pawns and a weakened king.
6423991710179470|h2h3.principle: With your bishop aimed at f7, check whether f7 is defended by anything but the king; a knight jump that adds a second attacker often wins on the spot.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

6438780653454793|g7g6.headline: White's 3.d4 left e4 hanging: take it with 3...Nxe4
6438780653454793|g7g6.why: 3...g6 declines the Roscher gambit, and after 4.Nc3 White has defended e4 and reaches a comfortable Classical Pirc with extra space, as in 4.Nc3 Bg7 5.Be3 O-O 6.Qd2. 3.d4 left the pawn on e4 attacked by the knight and defended by nothing, so 3...Nxe4 wins it. After 4.Bd3 Nf6 5.c4 White hopes for a development lead, but the theory holds that the gambit gives no real compensation, and Black finishes development with 5...g6 and 6...Bg7.
6438780653454793|g7g6.principle: Take an offered pawn when you can consolidate: here the knight drops back to f6, the bishop goes to g7, and Black is simply a pawn up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6

6457800965205690|d8f6.headline: Block the bishop's line to f7 with 4...d5, not the queen
6457800965205690|d8f6.why: 4...Qf6 brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home, and it becomes a target: after 5.Nf3 Be7 6.d4 Qf5 7.d5 White develops and gains space while the queen keeps moving. 4...d5 attacks the bishop on c4 and cuts it off from f7, supports the knight on e4 and frees the c8 bishop. After 5.Be2 Bd6 6.Nf3 O-O Black is comfortably developed.
6457800965205690|d8f6.principle: Meet pressure on f7 with a pawn move that blocks and attacks, not by bringing the queen out where White develops against it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

6457800965205690|e4g5.headline: Strike back with 4...d5; 4...Ng5 loses time and a pawn.
6457800965205690|e4g5.why: 4...Ng5 moves the knight again with three minor pieces still at home, and after 5.d4 d5 6.Bxg5 Qxg5 7.Bxd5 White has won a pawn and leads in development. 4...d5 claims the centre and attacks the bishop on c4, so Black catches up with gain of time; after 5.Be2 Bd6 6.Nf3 O-O Black's pieces come out freely.
6457800965205690|e4g5.principle: Answer with a pawn move that attacks a piece and opens lines for your own, instead of moving the same knight yet again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

6457800965205690|f7f6.headline: Hit the c4 bishop with 4...d5; 4...f6 opens your king
6457800965205690|f7f6.why: 4...f6 kicks the e5 knight but opens the diagonal from h5 to your king: after 5.Qh5+ g6 6.Nxg6 Qe7 the knight goes on to take your rook with 7.Nxh8+. 4...d5 is the theory's answer to 4.Nxe5: it gives Black a strong grip on the centre with the e4 knight already there, and attacks the c4 bishop so White has to move it to a worse square.
6457800965205690|f7f6.principle: Answer an attack with a central move that hits something, so your opponent has to respond instead of attacking you.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Bc4/3...Nxe4

6474108653422325|g2g4.headline: In the Modern, castle with 4.O-O instead of lunging with 4.g4.
6474108653422325|g2g4.why: 4.g4 does nothing for development and leaves e4 short of defenders: after 4...Nf6 5.h3 Nxe4 Black has won a pawn, and White's kingside is loosened for good. 4.O-O tucks the king away, and 5.Re1 guards the pawn on e4 before White builds a solid centre with 7.d3. Masters castle here in 53.8% of games.
6474108653422325|g2g4.principle: A flank pawn push needs a concrete reason; when it neither develops nor defends the centre, it only leaves your own pawns loose.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

6499681702415085|d8h4.headline: Against 2.Qh5, defend e5 with 2...Nc6, never offer queens
6499681702415085|d8h4.why: 2...Qh4 puts the queen where nothing defends it, so 3.Qxh4 simply wins it. 2.Qh5 attacks e5 and eyes f7; 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing, and Black can later gain time by attacking the exposed queen. Masters choose it in 89.6% of games.
6499681702415085|d8h4.principle: Before putting your queen next to the enemy queen, check what defends the square: nothing covers h4.

Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

6499681702415085|g7g6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6 before you chase the queen
6499681702415085|g7g6.why: 2...g6 attacks the queen but leaves e5 hanging: 3.Qxe5+ checks the king and hits the rook on h8 at the same time, so Black loses the rook in the corner. 2...Nc6 defends e5 while developing the knight to its most active square. If White follows with 3.Bc4, Black answers 3...g6 and 4...Nf6, blocking the queen's view of f7 and gaining time on it.
6499681702415085|g7g6.principle: The queen on h5 already attacks the e5 pawn, so cover that loose pawn first; only then gain time by attacking the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5

6499681702415085|g8h6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...Nh6 drops it with check.
6499681702415085|g8h6.why: White's queen attacks e5 as well as f7, and 2...Nh6 guards neither: 3.Qxe5+ wins the pawn with check, and after 3...Qe7 4.Qxe7+ Bxe7 Black is simply a pawn down. 2...Nc6 defends e5 and develops the knight to its best square. Against 3.Bc4, Black then gains time on the queen with ...g6 and ...Nf6.
6499681702415085|g8h6.principle: Against an early queen, first make sure everything it attacks is defended, then develop with gain of time against it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6

6508411408913645|f8c5.headline: Defend e5 with 3...Nc6; the bishop move leaves it hanging
6508411408913645|f8c5.why: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 undefended, and 4.Nxe5 takes it. Black can regain the pawn with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4, but that costs the dark-squared bishop and White develops quickly with 7.Bd3. 3...Nc6 protects e5 with a developing move and reaches the Four Knights Game, Black's most common answer here.
6508411408913645|f8c5.principle: Once White's knight is on f3, check whether e5 is defended before anything else, and protect it with a piece that also develops.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nc3/2...Nf6/3. Nf3

6510830178396203|b2b4.headline: 7.Qb3 hits d5 and wins the e5 pawn through a pin
6510830178396203|b2b4.why: 7.b4 is slow and loosens the queenside: in the engine line the pawn falls to 10...Ndxb4 a few moves later. 7.Qb3 lines up the queen behind the bishop on c4 against the knight on d5, with f7 behind it. After 7...Na5 8.Qa4+ Nc6 the knight on c6 is pinned against the king, so 9.Nxe5 wins the e5 pawn.
6510830178396203|b2b4.principle: Make your queen move attack something, so it gains time; then look for the checks that follow, like the one that pins a defender to the king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

6511980734057505|h2h3.headline: Release the tension with 5.cxd5; 5.h3 lets Black win a pawn
6511980734057505|h2h3.why: 5.h3 spends a move on the edge while the pawns in the centre attack each other, and Black takes first: after 5...cxd4 6.a3 Qa5+ 7.Qd2 Nc6 8.Qxa5 Nxa5 9.Nxd4 Nxc4 the pawn on c4 falls. 5.cxd5 resolves the tension on White's terms: after 5...Nxd5 6.Bg5 Be7 7.Bxe7 Qxe7 8.dxc5 Qxc5 pieces are traded and the material stays level.
6511980734057505|h2h3.principle: With pawns tense in the centre, spend your moves on the centre or on development; a rook-pawn move gives the opponent time to capture first.

6545901527067225|d4e5.headline: Develop against the early queen with 4.Nc3; don't trade on e5
6545901527067225|d4e5.why: 4.dxe5 dxe5 releases the central tension for nothing: Black's position frees up, the bishop gets d6 (5...Bd6), and more than half of your advantage is gone. 3...Qf6 brought the queen out early and took the f6 square from Black's knight, so keep developing with 4.Nc3. The queen then becomes a target: 5.Bg5 hits it, and after 5...Qg6 the h-pawn chases it again with 6.h4 and 7.h5.
6545901527067225|d4e5.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, keep the position tense and develop pieces that attack it, gaining a tempo each time it must move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

6574951213252263|e7e5.headline: Fianchetto and castle; 4...e5 just drops a pawn
6574951213252263|e7e5.why: 4...e5 loses a pawn: after 5.dxe5 the pawn on e5 also attacks the knight on f6, and 5...Nh5 leaves Black a pawn down with the knight on the rim. 4...Bg7 follows the Pirc plan: the bishop puts pressure on the centre from the long diagonal, and 5...O-O gets the king safe. Masters choose it in almost every game.
6574951213252263|e7e5.principle: Facing three white pawns in the centre with your king still on e8, finish the fianchetto and castle before striking with a central pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6

6589282572039958|b8c6.headline: Develop to f6 and attack e4; c6 gets kicked by d5
6589282572039958|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 puts the knight where 3.d5 kicks it straight back to b8, so White gains space and time. 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre and attacks the pawn on e4; the e-pawn cannot safely advance to e5, so White must spend a move defending it, usually with 3.Nc3. Then Black continues with ...g6 and ...Bg7, the main line of the Pirc.
6589282572039958|b8c6.principle: A knight in front of an unopposed central pawn gets chased; put it where a pawn can't hit it and where it attacks something.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6

6593387168284860|b1c3.headline: Kick the knight with 4.e5, then take back c4 with 5.Bxc4
6593387168284860|b1c3.why: 4.Nc3 defends e4 but gives Black time to strike with 4...e5; after 5.Nf3 exd4 6.Qxd4 Qxd4 7.Nxd4 Bc5 the queens are off and Black still has the extra pawn on c4. 4.e5 attacks the knight on f6 and gains space, the Alekhine-like play the theory describes for 3...Nf6, and after 4...Nd5 5.Bxc4 White has won the gambit pawn back with a broad centre. Masters choose 4.e5 in about 93% of 1679 games.
6593387168284860|b1c3.principle: A knight that attacks your centre pawn can often be chased by pushing it: the pawn gains space and the time you win pays for recovering material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. e4

6601544122617741|c2c4.headline: Accept the Blackburne gambit with 3.dxc6
6601544122617741|c2c4.why: 3.c4 tries to keep the d5 pawn, but 3...Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd5 wins it back anyway, and Black has a comfortable game. 3.dxc6, played in 68.8% of master games, takes a second pawn: Black recaptures with 3...Nxc6 and is a pawn down, with only a little development in return. White develops with 4.Nf3 and 5.Nc3, pins with 6.Bb5, and stays a pawn up.
6601544122617741|c2c4.principle: Accept a gambit when your pieces can still come out naturally; then the extra pawn stays and the opponent's lead in development fades.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...c6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

6601544122617741|d2d4.headline: Take the gambit pawn with 3.dxc6; 3.d4 just gives it back
6601544122617741|d2d4.why: After 2...c6 Black threatens 3...cxd5, and 3.d4 does nothing about it: 3...cxd5 restores material and your edge almost disappears. 3.dxc6 accepts the Blackburne gambit, and after 3...Nxc6 you are a clear pawn up. Black's compensation is the faster development the theory describes, so keep developing with 4.Nf3, 5.Nc3 and 6.Bb5 and hold on to the extra pawn.
6601544122617741|d2d4.principle: When a gambit pawn is on offer and you can finish your development afterwards, take it; a half-measure that lets the opponent recapture for free wastes the chance.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...c6

6606016440769341|g5f7.headline: Black has castled: f7 is defended twice, so don't sacrifice
6606016440769341|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 gives two minor pieces for a rook and pawn after 6...Rxf7 7.Bxf7+ Kxf7, and Black's king is perfectly safe, so White ends up clearly worse. With Black castled, the rook guards f7 as well as the king and there is no attack. 6.a3 is a quiet useful move instead; after 6...Nc6 7.Nf3 the knight comes back and White carries on with 9.h3 and castling.
6606016440769341|g5f7.principle: f7 is attacked twice and defended twice by rook and king, so the captures only swap two minor pieces for a rook and pawn; count before sacrificing there.

6613050291850908|f6g4.headline: Answer e5 with 5...dxe5 instead of moving the knight again
6613050291850908|f6g4.why: 5.e5 attacks the knight on f6, but 5...Ng4 moves it a second time and 6.h3 Nh6 sends it to the edge, where 7.Bf4 leaves White with more space and smoother development. 5...dxe5 removes the attacking pawn at once. After 6.Nxe5 O-O 7.Be3 c5 Black hits d4, and the bishop on g7 bears down the long diagonal, which is the pressure on White's centre the Pirc is built for.
6613050291850908|f6g4.principle: In the Pirc, trade off a pawn that reaches e5 so the bishop on g7 can press on d4 along the long diagonal.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

6621416387177535|d7d6.headline: Question the Spanish bishop with 3...a6 instead of pinning yourself
6621416387177535|d7d6.why: 3...d6 defends a pawn that was not really at risk and pins Black's own knight on c6 against the king, so after 4.d4 Black must either give up the centre with 4...exd4 or defend passively with ...Bd7. 3...a6, the Morphy defence, puts the question to the bishop at once: after 4.Ba4 Nf6 Black develops normally and can end the pressure on the knight with ...b5 when needed.
6621416387177535|d7d6.principle: When a bishop on b5 eyes your knight on c6, keep it from turning into a real pin: question the bishop with the a-pawn rather than locking the pin with d6.

6621416387177535|f7f6.headline: Question the bishop with 3...a6; e5 doesn't need ...f6
6621416387177535|f7f6.why: 3...f6 defends a pawn that wasn't hanging, takes the f6 square from Black's knight and weakens the kingside, and White just opens the centre with 4.d4. 3...a6, the Morphy defence, makes the bishop take or retreat, and 71.4% of masters play it. After 4.Ba4 Nf6 Black develops normally and can end the pressure on the knight on c6 with ...b5 whenever needed.
6621416387177535|f7f6.principle: A pawn move in the opening should free a piece or gain time; one that takes your knight's best square only creates a weakness.

6658785597570768|f7f6.headline: Block the mate with a knight: 3...Nf6, not ...f6.
6658785597570768|f7f6.why: White threatens 4.Qxf7#. 3...f6 stops it but takes the knight's best square and leaves the king stuck: after 4.Ne2 Bc5 5.Qg3 Black plays 5...Kf8 and gives up castling. 3...Nf6 blocks the queen's path to f7 with a developing move. Black stays ready to castle.
6658785597570768|f7f6.principle: When the queen and the bishop on c4 aim at f7, defend by developing a piece into the queen's path, not by moving the f-pawn.

6658785597570768|g8h6.headline: Block the mate threat with 3...Nf6, the knight's central square
6658785597570768|g8h6.why: White threatens 4.Qxf7#, and both knight moves stop it, but 3...Nh6 puts the knight on the edge, where it guards f7 and little else. 3...Nf6 blocks the queen's line to f7, develops toward the centre and attacks e4. The queen on f3 also takes that square from White's own knight, so after 4.Ne2 Black is comfortable.
6658785597570768|g8h6.principle: When you have to parry a threat, pick the defence that also develops toward the centre: a knight on f6 blocks the queen and fights for e4 and d5.

666558173554|g5f7.headline: Kick the d4 knight with 6.c3 before any sacrifice on f7
666558173554|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 is the Fried Liver idea at the wrong moment: after 6...Kxf7 you are simply a knight for a pawn down, and the knight on d4 covers f3, so your queen has no quick check to follow up. 6.c3, played in 93.8% of master games, hits that knight, which has few squares to retreat to. In the main line 6.c3 b5 7.Bf1 Nxd5 the sacrifice 8.Nxf7 Kxf7 does work, because 9.cxd4 removes the knight and 10.Qf3+ follows with check, and White keeps a small edge.
666558173554|g5f7.principle: A knight in the centre that a pawn can attack is a target: hit it with c3 first, and only sacrifice on f7 once that knight no longer guards f3.

6673250859790786|e7e6.headline: Against 4.Bc4, take the second pawn: 4...cxb2
6673250859790786|e7e6.why: 4.Bc4 leaves your pawn on c3 alive, and 4...e6 lets White take it back with 5.Nxc3, reaching a normal Smith-Morra where White has development for one pawn and you only have a small edge. 4...cxb2 takes a second pawn, and after 5.Bxb2 you are two pawns up with a clear advantage. The theory calls this Danish-style offer too much material for the compensation; follow up with 5...e6, which also blunts the bishop on c4.
6673250859790786|e7e6.principle: Accept a gambit when you can consolidate: here the extra pawns are worth more than White's lead, as long as you blunt the attacking bishop and keep developing.

6730545248551000|c4f7.headline: No sacrifice on f7: prepare d4 with 4.c3
6730545248551000|c4f7.why: 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 5.Nxe5+ Nxe5 gives a bishop and a knight for two pawns, and the fork 6.d4 does not save it: after 6...Bxd4 7.Qxd4 d6 you are a piece for a pawn down. The real plan in the Giuoco Piano is in the centre: Black controls d4 three times and White only twice. 4.c3, the classical variation (54.9% of masters games), adds a third guard so that White can follow with d4 and build a two-pawn centre.
6730545248551000|c4f7.principle: Before striking in the centre, count who controls the square you want to occupy, and add a pawn to it first; c3 prepares d4 rather than forcing anything early.

6730545248551000|d2d4.headline: Prepare d4 with 4.c3 before pushing it
6730545248551000|d2d4.why: Black controls d4 three times and White only twice, so 4.d4 just loses the pawn: after 4...Nxd4 5.Be3 Qf6 6.Bxd4 exd4 Black is a pawn up. 4.c3 adds a third guard to d4, so White can follow with d4 and build a two-pawn centre. It is the classical plan in the Giuoco Piano and the master choice in 55% of games.
6730545248551000|d2d4.principle: Before pushing to a contested square, count: d4 is covered by the knight on c6, the bishop on c5 and the e5 pawn, so add a supporter with c3 first.

6730545248551000|f3e5.headline: The c6 knight guards e5: prepare d4 with 4.c3
6730545248551000|f3e5.why: The pawn on e5 is defended by the knight on c6, so 4.Nxe5 Nxe5 just gives a knight for a pawn, and the knight on e5 then hits your bishop on c4 too. The Giuoco Piano plan is in the centre: Black controls d4 three times and White twice, so 4.c3 (54.9% of masters games) adds a guard on d4 and prepares the d-pawn advance. 4.O-O and 4.d3 are fine alternatives.
6730545248551000|f3e5.principle: Before capturing a pawn, count its defenders: one attacker against one defender means you lose the capturing piece for a pawn.

6730545248551000|f3g5.headline: With no knight on f6, the d8 queen covers g5: play 4.c3
6730545248551000|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight a second time and simply drops it: the queen on d8 sees g5 along the open diagonal, so 4...Qxg5 wins a whole piece. The Giuoco Piano move order, ...Bc5 before ...Nf6, exists precisely to keep that control of g5. 4.c3 is the classical plan instead: it adds control of d4 so your d-pawn can go there, and after 4...Nf6 the quiet 5.d3 holds e4 with a normal game.
6730545248551000|f3g5.principle: A second move with an already developed knight needs a concrete gain; when it wins nothing, bring out a new piece or prepare d4.

6739498744433180|c1g5.headline: Push 4.e5 at once; the knight on f6 is driven back
6739498744433180|c1g5.why: 4.Bg5 lets Black strike first with 4...d5: after 5.Bxf6 exf6 6.exd5 O-O 7.g3 Re8+ White has a pawn more, but has given up the bishop and faces a rook check on the open e-file with the king still in the centre. Black played 3...Bg7 instead of 3...d6, the Pirc move the theory gives here, so nothing stops 4.e5, which attacks the knight on f6 and sends it back to g8 after 4...Ng8. White then develops with 5.Bf4 and 6.Qd2 while Black's knight starts over.
6739498744433180|c1g5.principle: When nothing stops your e-pawn from advancing, a knight on f6 is a target: push the pawn with tempo before Black can play ...d5.

6739498744433180|g1f3.headline: Push 4.e5 now, before 4...d5 gives the knight a good square
6739498744433180|g1f3.why: 4.Nf3 is natural but gives Black time for 4...d5. Then 5.e5 no longer chases the knight home: it jumps to e4 with 5...Ne4, supported by the pawn on d5, and after 7.Bd3 Nxc3 8.bxc3 c5 Black has doubled White's pawns and hits the centre. Played right away, 4.e5 attacks the knight on f6 before Black's centre is ready, and after 4...Ng8 the knight is back on its starting square while White gains space and develops with 5.Bf4.
6739498744433180|g1f3.principle: When nothing stops your e-pawn from advancing, a knight on f6 is a target: push the pawn with tempo before Black can play ...d5.

6748390364152037|d2d3.headline: The g5 knight is attacked: retreat it with 9.Nf3
6748390364152037|d2d3.why: 8...h6 attacks the knight on g5, and 9.d3 ignores it: 9...hxg5 10.Bxg5 leaves you a knight for a pawn, which is a lost position. Retreat with 9.Nf3, which also attacks the e5 pawn; Black usually gains space with 9...e4, and 10.Ne5 puts the knight on a central square with a balanced game. Masters split almost evenly between 9.Nf3 and 9.Nh3, and both keep the balance.
6748390364152037|d2d3.principle: Before each developing move, check which of your pieces are attacked and undefended; a knight hit by a pawn has to move first.

6756346848148721|d7d5.headline: No early ...d5 in the Sicilian: play 2...d6 and develop
6756346848148721|d7d5.why: 2...d5 opens the centre before you have developed anything, and after 3.exd5 you either leave the pawn or bring your queen out. Leaving it, as in 3...Nf6 4.Bb5+ Bd7 5.Bxd7+ Qxd7 6.c4, White keeps the extra pawn; taking back with 3...Qxd5 lets 4.Nc3 gain time on the queen, and because the c5 pawn blocks the way to a5, she has to go back with 4...Qd8. 2...d6 is the main line (46.1% of masters games): it frees the c8 bishop, defends c5 and controls e5 so ...Nf6 is safe, and after 3.d4 Nf6 4.Nc3 cxd4 5.Nxd4 a6 you have a Najdorf.
6756346848148721|d7d5.principle: Don't open the centre in a way that forces your queen to recapture early; she gets chased and you lose the time you needed for development.

6773809115680684|d1d5.headline: d5 belongs to your knight: put the queen on b3
6773809115680684|d1d5.why: 7.Qd5 hits f7, but 7...Qe7 defends it and your queen has to retreat with 8.Qd3; after 8...Qd8 9.O-O Nf6 you have spent two queen moves for nothing and most of your advantage is gone. 6...h6 spent another move on a pawn, and with Black's pawn on e5 and no c-pawn, d5 is a square no black pawn can ever attack. 7.Qb3 aims at f7 from behind the bishop, Black spends 7...Qe7 defending, and after 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 the knight takes that square with tempo on the queen, keeping a big advantage.
6773809115680684|d1d5.principle: A central square that enemy pawns can no longer attack is best used by a knight; keep your queen behind the lines and plant the knight there.

6773809115680684|d1e2.headline: Aim queen and bishop at f7 with 7.Qb3
6773809115680684|d1e2.why: 7.Qe2 is too slow: after 7...Nf6 8.O-O Be7 9.Be3 O-O Black has castled, the gambit pawn is just a pawn, and Black is slightly better. 6...h6 spent a move on a pawn while f7 is defended only by the king, and theory stresses how dangerous your c4 bishop is against f7 in the Smith-Morra. 7.Qb3 adds the queen to that pressure, so Black spends 7...Qe7 defending; after 8.O-O d6 9.Nd5 your knight jumps into the hole left by ...e5 with tempo on the queen, and you keep a big advantage.
6773809115680684|d1e2.principle: With your bishop on c4 and the king on e8, add the queen to the pressure on f7: every move Black spends defending it is a move not spent developing.

6773809115680684|e1h1.headline: Punish 6...h6 with 7.Qb3, hitting f7 twice
6773809115680684|e1h1.why: 6...h6 spends a tempo on a pawn move while f7 is still defended only by the king. 7.O-O is natural but lets Black catch up with 7...d6 and 8...Bg4, and most of your advantage slips away. 7.Qb3 lines up the queen with the bishop on c4 against f7, so Black must defend it, and the engine's 7...Qe7 shuts in the bishop on f8; after 9.Nd5 the queen is hit again and you keep a clear advantage.
6773809115680684|e1h1.principle: With the bishop already on c4, adding the queen against f7 forces Black to defend instead of developing, which is how you cash in Black's lost tempo.

6790604267482997|e2f3.headline: Let the queen take g2: develop with 5.Nf3
6790604267482997|e2f3.why: Black threatens 5...Qxg2, but 5.Bf3 defends it by moving the bishop a second time while two minor pieces are still at home, and after 5...e5 Black catches up in development and most of your advantage is gone. Theory says chasing the g2 pawn is folly and White should be happy to give it up. After 5.Nf3 Qxg2 6.Rg1 Qh3 you have four pieces developed, d4 is coming and the rook on the open g-file can kick the queen again with Rg3, while Black has only the queen out.
6790604267482997|e2f3.principle: When your opponent's queen comes out early, keep developing and let her grab a pawn: every piece you add gains time on her.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

6819507096459648|f7f6.headline: Develop with 4...Be7 and castle; no more pawn moves
6819507096459648|f7f6.why: 4...f6 is another pawn move with Black's kingside pieces still at home: it takes f6 from the knight and loosens the king, while White just keeps building with 5.d4. 4...Be7 develops the bishop that 3...d6 shut in and prepares ...Nf6 and castling, as in 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Nc3 O-O.
6819507096459648|f7f6.principle: With White already castled and your centre under pressure, bring out the kingside pieces and castle before making more pawn moves near your king.

6819507096459648|g8f6.headline: Play 4...Be7 first so 5.Ng5 doesn't hit f7
6819507096459648|g8f6.why: 4...Nf6 lets White's knight jump to g5 and attack f7 together with the c4 bishop: after 5.Ng5 d5 6.exd5 White wins a pawn. 4...Be7 develops the bishop that 3...d6 shut in and covers g5 for now. In the engine line the knight comes to f6 only after White's f3 knight has left for d4, and Black castles next.
6819507096459648|g8f6.principle: With an enemy bishop on c4 aiming at f7, don't let a knight land on g5 until f7 has extra cover.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

6820108232337383|f1c4.headline: Against the Petrov, take e5 with 3.Nxe5; 3.Bc4 hangs e4
6820108232337383|f1c4.why: Theory calls 3.Bc4 a beginner's move here: it copies the Italian setup but leaves e4 hanging, and after 3...Nxe4 4.Nxe5 d5 Black has the pawn back and the easier game. 3.Nxe5 is the main line. Black can't recapture at once, since 3...Nxe4 4.Qe2 runs into pins on the e-file (4...Nf6?? 5.Nc6+ wins the queen), so Black first plays 3...d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 and White keeps a small edge.
6820108232337383|f1c4.principle: When both e-pawns are under attack, capture first or defend e4; developing instead lets the opponent take with tempo.

6833062692676193|b1c3.headline: Against the Alekhine, kick the knight with 2.e5.
6833062692676193|b1c3.why: 2.Nc3 is solid but less testing: after 2...e5 it becomes a Vienna Game, and Black has avoided the Alekhine's main problems. 1...Nf6 attacks e4 to provoke White's pawns forward, and 2.e5 accepts the offer, kicking the knight with gain of time and taking space. After 2...Nd5 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 White has a broad centre, and masters choose 2.e5 in 84.9% of games.
6833062692676193|b1c3.principle: A knight on f6 that a pawn can attack is a target: kick it and gain space and time.

6833062692676193|d1f3.headline: Against Alekhine's, chase the knight with 2.e5
6833062692676193|d1f3.why: 2.Qf3 guards e4 with the queen, but it takes f3 from White's knight and becomes a target: in the line 2...Nc6 3.Nc3 e5 4.Bd3 Nd4 Black hits it, and 5.Qg3 has to move it again. 2.e5 is played in 84.9% of master games: it attacks the knight on f6, gains space and makes it move, usually with 2...Nd5, where 3.c4 kicks it once more.
6833062692676193|d1f3.principle: A knight that attacks your centre pawn from f6 can be chased with e5, gaining space and time instead of defending passively.

6833062692676193|d2d3.headline: Kick the knight with 2.e5 and take space.
6833062692676193|d2d3.why: 2.d3 saves the pawn on e4 but shuts in the bishop on f1, and after 2...e5 Black has an easy, equal game. 1...Nf6 put a knight where White's e-pawn can attack it. 2.e5 gains space with tempo: the knight has to move, usually to d5, and after 3.c4 Nb6 4.d4 White builds a big centre. Masters play it 85% of the time.
6833062692676193|d2d3.principle: When an enemy knight stands in front of your centre pawns, push a pawn to gain space and time by chasing it.

6833062692676193|f2f3.principle: When an enemy knight sits in front of your centre pawns, kick it with a pawn rather than defending with a pawn move that weakens your king.

6833062692676193|f2f4.headline: Against the Alekhine, 2.e5 gains space and kicks the knight

6833062692676193|f2f4.principle: When a knight on f6 attacks your e-pawn, the pawn advance that hits the knight defends nothing and attacks something, so it gains time.

6849990694088956|b2b4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5, not 4.b4
6849990694088956|b2b4.why: 4.b4 hands Black a pawn: after 4...Bxb4 5.Nxe5 O-O 6.Nc4 Re8 Black is castled with a rook bearing down on e4 while your king is still on e1, and Black is clearly better. 4.Nxe5 takes the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, while the knight on c3 still covers e4. Black has to spend moves to regain it, as in 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 7.Bd3 d5 8.Bxe4 dxe4, and White stays clearly better.
6849990694088956|b2b4.principle: Before reaching for a wing gambit, check what is loose in the centre: an undefended e5 pawn is the simplest gain on the board.

6849990694088956|d2d4.headline: 3...Bc5 left e5 undefended: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|d2d4.why: 4.d4 exd4 5.Nxd4 trades off the pawn you could have taken for free, and after 5...O-O Black develops easily and the game is level. 3...Bc5 left e5 attacked once and defended by nothing, so 4.Nxe5 wins it. In the engine line Black hits back with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4 to regain the pawn, but after 7.Bd3 d5 8.Bxe4 dxe4 White keeps a clear edge.
6849990694088956|d2d4.principle: After every opponent move check what has become loose: when a developing move leaves a centre pawn undefended, take it before following your own plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

6849990694088956|f1c4.headline: 3...Bc5 leaves e5 loose: take it with 4.Nxe5
6849990694088956|f1c4.why: The usual replies to 3.Nc3 are 3...Nc6, reaching the Four Knights, or 3...Bb4; 3...Bc5 develops but leaves the e5 pawn undefended. 4.Nxe5 takes it, and in the main line Black gives up the dark-squared bishop to win material back with 4...Bd4 5.Nf3 Bxc3 6.dxc3 Nxe4. 4.Bc4 lets Black cover e5 with 4...d6 5.d3, and the position is level.
6849990694088956|f1c4.principle: Check every developing move by the opponent for what it stopped defending; an undefended centre pawn in front of your knight is often simply free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3

6850591830216347|g8h6.headline: Develop the knight to f6, toward the centre.
6850591830216347|g8h6.why: From h6 the knight controls none of the central squares, so 6.Nd5 lands on d5 with no knight to challenge it. 5...Nf6 develops toward the centre: it attacks e4, covers d5 and lets Black castle. After 6.Na4 a6 7.Nxc5 dxc5 Black has a comfortable game.
6850591830216347|g8h6.principle: Put your knights where they control the centre, normally f6 and c6; a knight on the edge leaves central squares to the opponent.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6

6863144374799225|f3d4.headline: Hit the early queen first: 5.Bg5, then take on d4
6863144374799225|f3d4.why: 5.Nxd4 recaptures at once and lets Black develop calmly with 5...Bb4, so a large part of your advantage disappears. 5.Bg5 develops the bishop with an attack on the queen on f6, so Black has to spend the move on the queen (5...Qd6) instead of playing 5...dxc3, and only then 6.Nxd4 takes the pawn back with your bishop already developed and a big edge. This is the theory's point against 2...Qf6: the queen blocks the knight's best square and hands you developing moves with tempo.
6863144374799225|f3d4.principle: When the opponent's queen sits on an exposed square, look for a developing move that attacks it before you recapture material.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Qf6

6886380190448217|f3d5.headline: Take on d5 with the bishop, with check: 8.Bxd5+
6886380190448217|f3d5.why: d5 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, and 8.Qxd5+ does take the knight, but it brings your queen to the centre with two minor pieces still at home: after 8...Ke8 Black develops with 9...Bd7 and 10...Rd8, and most of your advantage is gone. 8.Bxd5+ wins the same knight with a minor piece and keeps your queen on f3. After 8...Be6 9.Bxc6 bxc6 10.Qxc6 you have won a pawn as well and keep a big advantage.
6886380190448217|f3d5.principle: Capture with a minor piece when you can; taking with the queen puts it in the middle of the board, where Black develops with gain of time.

6931592131044425|c6d4.headline: Develop the bishop instead of moving the knight again
6931592131044425|c6d4.why: 3...Nd4 moves the knight a second time while three minor pieces are still at home; after 4.Nxd4 exd4 5.O-O and 6.Re1 White is ahead in development, and the pawn on d4 falls to 7.c3 and 8.cxd4. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to its best diagonal and keeps control of d4 and g5, ready for ...Nf6 and castling.
6931592131044425|c6d4.principle: With three minor pieces still at home, each move should bring a new one out; a second knight move needs a concrete gain.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6/3. Nf3

6931592131044425|f7f5.headline: Develop before touching the f-pawn in the Italian
6931592131044425|f7f5.why: 3...f5 opens the diagonal from c4 toward your king while you are undeveloped, and after 4.d4 exd4 5.Ng5 Ne5 6.Qxd4 Qe7 7.Bxg8 White wins a knight. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to its best diagonal, keeps control of g5 until Black is ready to castle and adds a third guard to d4, so White's central break needs preparation.
6931592131044425|f7f5.principle: Against a bishop on c4, bring out a minor piece before moving the f-pawn; pawn moves near the king only weaken f7 and the diagonal toward g8.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6931592131044425|f7f6.headline: Develop a piece against the Italian; don't spend a move on ...f6
6931592131044425|f7f6.why: 3...f6 guards e5, which the knight on c6 already defends, and in exchange it takes the f6 square from Black's own knight and loosens the king. White opens the centre with 4.d4 exd4 5.O-O and develops quickly while Black's kingside is still at home. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, develops the bishop to an active diagonal, adds control of d4 and gets Black ready to castle.
6931592131044425|f7f6.principle: When a pawn is already protected by a piece, defending it again with a pawn only costs time and a good square for your knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6931592131044425|g8h6.headline: Develop toward the centre with 3...Bc5, not a knight on the rim
6931592131044425|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 puts the knight on the edge, where it neither pressures e4 nor helps fight for the centre. In the engine line White plays 5.d4 and the knight has to move again with 6...Ng4, and after 7.Bb3 Nxd4 8.Qxd4 White's queen dominates the centre. 3...Bc5, the Giuoco Piano, puts the bishop on its most active diagonal and keeps the queen's control of g5, so 4...Nf6 and castling follow safely.
6931592131044425|g8h6.principle: Bring each piece to a square that fights for the centre; a knight on the rim controls half as much and usually has to move again.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|c8e6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 wins the pawn back.
6936096123661830|c8e6.why: 5...Be6 develops but lets White keep the extra pawn: 6.Nf3 retreats the knight, and Black has nothing for it. 5.Nxe5 left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 attacks both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5, so after 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black regains the pawn with check.
6936096123661830|c8e6.principle: When you are a pawn down after a trade, look for a forcing queen move that hits two loose targets before you develop quietly.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|d8e7.headline: Punish 5.Nxe5 with 5...Qd4, hitting knight, pawn and f2
6936096123661830|d8e7.why: 5...Qe7 gives White time: 6.d4 defends the knight and takes the centre, and after 6...Bb4+ 7.c3 Black has nothing to show for the lost pawn. 5...Qd4 is a multiple attack: it hits the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 and, with the bishop on c5, threatens mate on f2. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black has the pawn back, and after 7.Qe2 Qxe2+ 8.Kxe2 White's king is stuck in the centre.
6936096123661830|d8e7.principle: With your bishop on c5 already aiming at f2, a queen move to d4 can add a mating threat to attacks on loose pieces in the centre.

6936096123661830|d8f6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 hits the knight, e4 and f2 at once.
6936096123661830|d8f6.why: 5...Qf6 lets White keep the extra pawn: 6.d4 gains time on the bishop, and Black has nothing to show for the pawn. 5...Qd4 exploits what the knight on e5 left behind: it attacks the knight and the e4 pawn and threatens mate on f2. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black has the pawn back.
6936096123661830|d8f6.principle: After a knight grabs a pawn on e5, check what it left loose: e4 and f2 are unguarded, and one queen move can hit them together with the knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|f7f6.headline: Answer 5.Nxe5 with 5...Qd4, forking the knight and e4.
6936096123661830|f7f6.why: 5...f6 opens the e8-h5 diagonal: 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Nxg6 hxg6 8.Qxh8 and Black loses a rook and a pawn for a knight. 5.Nxe5 took a pawn but left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 attacks both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5, so after 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black wins the pawn back with check.
6936096123661830|f7f6.principle: When the opponent grabs a pawn with a piece, look for a queen move that attacks the piece, a loose pawn and f2 together.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

6936096123661830|g8f6.headline: Fork with 5...Qd4 before White can protect e4.
6936096123661830|g8f6.why: 5...Nf6 attacks e4 only once, and 6.Qe2 defends it, so White keeps the extra pawn. 5.Nxe5 left the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 loose. 5...Qd4 hits both and threatens mate on f2 with the bishop on c5. After 6.Nd3 Qxe4+ Black wins the pawn back with check.
6936096123661830|g8f6.principle: When you can attack two loose targets and threaten mate in one move, do that before a single attack the opponent can parry.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Bc5

695832176392433|g7g6.headline: Kick the pinning bishop with h6
695832176392433|g7g6.why: The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 to your queen, and 6...g6 does nothing about it: 7.Nd5 adds a second attacker, and after 7...Nxd5 8.Bxd8 Black has given the queen for a knight. 6...h6 puts the question to the bishop at once; after 7.Bxf6 Qxf6 the pin is gone, and 8.Nd5 is met by 8...Qd8.
695832176392433|g7g6.principle: When a bishop pins your f6-knight to the queen, challenge it with the h-pawn before White can bring another attacker to d5.

6967288124345715|g1f3.headline: Defend e4 with 3.d3; 3.Nf3 leaves it hanging
6967288124345715|g1f3.why: 3.Nf3 leaves e4 undefended, and 3...Nxe4 takes it; after 4.Nxe5 d5 the pawn hits the bishop and Black has the easier game. 3.d3 defends e4 with a pawn and opens the diagonal for the queen's bishop. It is the main line, played in 86.4% of master games.
6967288124345715|g1f3.principle: When the knight on f6 attacks your e4-pawn, defend it before developing elsewhere, ideally with a move that also frees a piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. Nf3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nf6/3. d3

6980672627372882|d7d5.headline: Develop with 4...Nf6; ...d5 here just drops a pawn
6980672627372882|d7d5.why: 4...d5 opens the centre before Black is ready, and 5.exd5 wins a pawn, since d5 is hit by the pawn on e4, the knight on c3 and the bishop on c4. 4...Nf6 develops toward the centre, attacks e4 and prepares castling; masters choose it in 82.9% of games.
6980672627372882|d7d5.principle: Before pushing ...d5 here, count: White's pawn, knight and bishop all hit d5, so develop the knight first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6980672627372882|f7f6.headline: In the Giuoco Piano, bring out 4...Nf6, not the f-pawn
6980672627372882|f7f6.why: 4...f6 develops nothing, takes the f6 square from Black's own knight and weakens the light squares near Black's king, which White's bishop on c4 already aims at. 4...Nf6 develops the last kingside piece, adds pressure on e4 and gets Black ready to castle; masters choose it in 82.9% of games.
6980672627372882|f7f6.principle: With White's pieces out and aimed at your king, finish developing so you can castle; a pawn move like f6 has no concrete reason.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5

6994580878022218|b7b6.headline: Settle the centre with 5...cxd4 instead of a slow pawn move
6994580878022218|b7b6.why: 5...b6 develops nothing: White brings out pieces with 6.Nc3 and 7.Be3 while your queenside pawns run forward with 7...c4 and 8...b5, and 9.Ne5 plants a knight on a square both the d4 and f4 pawns support, leaving White better. 5...cxd4 trades your c-pawn for White's d-pawn and opens lines for your pieces: after 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Bb5+ Bd7 8.Bxd7+ Qxd7 9.Nc3 Nc6 you are developed with no time lost and slightly better. 5...Nf6 is also fine.
6994580878022218|b7b6.principle: Only make the pawn moves that free your pieces or fight for the centre; here the capture on d4 does both, while ...b6 just costs a tempo.

7050462614834999|c1b2.headline: Step out of the pin with a threat: 9.Qb3 hits b7
7050462614834999|c1b2.why: 9.Bb2 is too slow: Black develops with 9...Nf6, and after 10.h3 Bh5 11.d5 Bxf3 12.Qxf3 Ne5 the knight takes a strong central square and Black has fully equalised. 8...Bg4 pinned your knight to the queen and left b7 without the bishop's protection. 9.Qb3 leaves the pin with a threat on b7, and also lines up with the bishop on c4 against f7. In the main line Black gives up the bishop with 9...Bxf3 10.Qxf3, and you keep the bishop pair and the big centre.
7050462614834999|c1b2.principle: When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, move the queen off the line with a threat, so the pin stops mattering and the opponent has to react.

7062831770535036|c1e3.headline: Push 7.d5 first and keep the b8 knight off c6
7062831770535036|c1e3.why: 7.Be3 lets Black develop with 7...Nc6, and after 8.d5 O-O-O 9.Nf4 Qxd1+ 10.Rxd1 Ne5 the queens are off and Black's knight sits comfortably in the centre, leaving you only a small edge. 7.d5 claims the centre before Black's queenside gets going and takes c6 away from the b8 knight, so it has to go to d7 instead. After 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 Nbd7 9.Be3 O-O-O 10.O-O-O you keep the queens on, more space and a clear advantage.
7062831770535036|c1e3.principle: Before developing, ask where your opponent's next piece wants to go; a pawn move that takes that square away gains space and time at once.

7062831770535036|e1h1.headline: Grab space with 7.d5 before Black sets up ...e6 and ...c6
7062831770535036|e1h1.why: 7.O-O is safe but lets Black build a solid shell with 7...e6 and 9...c6, and your edge shrinks. 7.d5 gains central space at once while Black's queen sits out of play on h5 and Black's light-squared bishop is already gone: the pawn takes c6 away from Black's knight, which has to go to d7. After 7...Nf6 8.Qd3 Nbd7 9.Be3 both sides castle queenside and you keep a clear edge.
7062831770535036|e1h1.principle: Judge the differences: Black's queen is offside and their light-squared bishop has been traded, so use the moment to take central space they cannot challenge.

7121051583391236|f3c3.headline: Put the queen where it attacks: 6.Qb3 hits b7 and f7.
7121051583391236|f3c3.why: 6.Qc3 hits nothing Black needs to worry about, so Black catches up in development with 6...Nd7 and 7...Ne7. The theory calls 3...Bg4 dubious because it delays development, and after giving up that bishop b7 is left loose: 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7, and the queen also lines up behind the bishop on c4 against f7. Black has to spend 6...b6 on defence, and White develops with 7.Nc3 and 9.Nd5, when the knight hits the queen on f6.
7121051583391236|f3c3.principle: When your queen must move anyway, put it where it attacks something, so the opponent answers your threat instead of developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

7121051583391236|f3d3.headline: The b7 pawn is loose: hit it with 6.Qb3
7121051583391236|f3d3.why: 6.Qd3 puts the queen on a passive square and gives Black time: after 6...Nc6 Black develops and castles long with 7...O-O-O. The bishop that guarded b7 was traded on f3, so 5...Qf6 left that pawn with no defender, and 6.Qb3 attacks it. Black has to weaken the queenside with 6...b6, while White keeps developing with 7.Nc3 and 8.O-O.
7121051583391236|f3d3.principle: After every exchange, check which pawns lost their defender; a loose pawn gives your queen a move with a threat.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4/3...Bg4

7127830528967939|e7e6.headline: Grab space with 3...d4 against the Grob's wing pawns
7127830528967939|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is solid but passive: it shuts in your c8 bishop, and after 4.d4 White's odd first move hardly matters any more and the game is level. 3...d4 takes space instead: in the engine line your pawns follow up with ...e5 and ...e4, driving White's knight back home with 7.Ng1, while 4...h5 makes the advanced g-pawn commit with 5.g5, and Black has a clear advantage. 3...dxc4 is also fine; the theory notes White then has to spend a move on Qa4 to win the pawn back.
7127830528967939|e7e6.principle: When White spends their first moves on wing pawns like g4 and c4, claim the centre with your pawns and use the space to push White's pieces back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...d5/2. Bg2/2...c6

7139051363978185|e7e5.headline: Prepare ...e5 with 3...d6; pushed at once, it just drops a pawn
7139051363978185|e7e5.why: 3...e5 puts a pawn on a square hit twice, by the d4 pawn and the knight on f3, and defended only by the bishop on g7, so 4.dxe5 simply wins it. 3...d6 is the normal move in the Modern, played in 81% of master games: it covers e5 so that ...e5 can follow with support, as in 4.h3 Nf6 5.Bd3 Nc6 6.c3 e5.
7139051363978185|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a contested square, count its attackers and defenders, and add a defender first if it comes up short.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

7139051363978185|g8f6.headline: In the Modern, play 3...d6 first so e5 can't kick the knight.
7139051363978185|g8f6.why: After 3...Nf6, White pushes 4.e5 and the knight has to move again. On e4 it is attacked by 5.Bd3, and Black has to spend 5...d5 propping it up. 3...d6, played 81% of the time, controls e5 first. After 4.h3 the knight can come to f6 safely.
7139051363978185|g8f6.principle: Against a pawn centre on e4 and d4, control e5 before putting a knight on f6 where the e-pawn can chase it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4/2...Bg7

7152453611816462|c1f4.headline: Win back c4 first: 4.e3 frees the bishop on f1
7152453611816462|c1f4.why: 4.Bf4 develops but does nothing about the pawn on c4, and Black gets time to keep it: after 4...a6 5.Nc3 Bb4 6.a4 Nc6 7.e3 Na5 the knight guards c4. 4.e3 opens the diagonal for the bishop on f1, and 5.Bxc4 wins back the gambit pawn while developing. That is why 74.4% of masters play it.
7152453611816462|c1f4.principle: In the Queen's Gambit Accepted, recover the c4 pawn first by freeing the king's bishop; develop the rest afterwards.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3

7172083930230506|d2d3.headline: Punish 3...h6 with 4.d4 in the centre
7172083930230506|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too quiet: Black gets 4...Nf6 in and reaches a normal Italian position where the h-pawn move has cost nothing. 3...h6 spends a tempo, and 4.d4 strikes in the centre at once to exploit it; if Black plays ...Nf6 anyway, the pawn on e5 falls. After 4...exd4 5.O-O Nf6 6.e5 White gains space and keeps the lead in development.
7172083930230506|d2d3.principle: When the opponent spends a move on a flank pawn, open the centre with a pawn break while you are ahead in development.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

7232835087865144|d2d3.headline: Develop and attack e5 with 2.Nf3, not the passive 2.d3
7232835087865144|d2d3.why: 2.d3 defends e4, which was not attacked, shuts in the bishop on f1 and brings out no piece; Wikibooks calls it insipid and notes it gives Black easy equality with 2...Nc6 or 2...Nf6 followed by 3...d5. 2.Nf3 develops the knight, controls d4 and attacks the undefended pawn on e5, so Black has to spend the next move defending it. Masters choose it in 92% of games.
7232835087865144|d2d3.principle: When nothing of yours is attacked, bring out a piece that makes a threat rather than a pawn move that guards what is already safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d3
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7232835087865144|d2d4.headline: Develop first with 2.Nf3; 2.d4 opens the centre too early
7232835087865144|d2d4.why: 2.d4 opens the centre before any piece is out: after 2...exd4 White must either spend a queen move on Qxd4, which ...Nc6 then attacks with tempo, or play a gambit to get the pawn back. Masters play it in under 1% of games. 2.Nf3 develops the knight, controls d4 and attacks the undefended pawn on e5, keeping White's first-move initiative without giving anything away.
7232835087865144|d2d4.principle: Open the centre only once your pieces are ready to use the open lines; until then develop with a threat.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3

7232835087865144|f2f3.headline: Develop with 2.Nf3, attacking e5; 2.f3 only weakens your king
7232835087865144|f2f3.why: The theory calls 2.f3 one of the worst second moves: it defends e4 but takes the f3 square from your knight and weakens your king, and in the line 2...Bc5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Na4 Be7 5.d4 exd4 you end up a pawn down. 2.Nf3, played in 92.2% of master games, develops a piece and attacks the undefended e5 pawn, so Black has to react. It also controls d4 and makes room to castle.
7232835087865144|f2f3.principle: Every opening move should develop a piece or fight for the centre; a pawn move that does neither, and blocks a knight's best square, just hands your opponent time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5

7232835087865144|f2f4.headline: Develop the knight and hit e5; the King's Gambit drops a pawn.
7232835087865144|f2f4.why: 2.f4 gives up a pawn after 2...exf4, and it weakens White's own king: in the line 3.Nf3 g5 4.d4 g4 5.Ne5 Qh4+ 6.g3 fxg3 Black keeps the extra pawn and uses the e1-h4 diagonal for a queen check. 2.Nf3 attacks the undefended pawn on e5 while developing a piece, controls d4 for a later d4, and starts to clear the way to castle. That is why masters choose it 92% of the time.
7232835087865144|f2f4.principle: When the opponent's centre pawn is undefended, attack it with a developing move instead of a pawn move that loosens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5

7232835087865144|g2g3.headline: Develop with a threat: the knight attacks e5
7232835087865144|g2g3.why: 2.g3 spends a move preparing a fianchetto although the bishop could already come out, and 2...d5 hits e4 at once; after 3.exd5 Qxd5 the queen attacks the rook on h1 along the diagonal that g3 opened. 2.Nf3 develops a piece, controls d4 and attacks the pawn on e5, so Black has to spend the next move defending it.
7232835087865144|g2g3.principle: A developing move that attacks something forces a reply; a quiet pawn move gives Black a free hand to strike in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5
