7273207378554101|d7d5.headline: Trade off the attacked pawn with 2...exd4
7273207378554101|d7d5.why: 2...d5 leaves the pawn on e5 attacked by the d4 pawn and undefended, so 3.dxe5 wins it. 2...exd4 removes the attacker first and is the most common master reply. After 3.exd4 d5 Black has an equal share of the centre and open lines for both bishops.
7273207378554101|d7d5.principle: When your pawn is attacked and undefended, deal with it before making a new move; capturing the attacker is the simplest way.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5/2. d4

7273207378554101|e5e4.headline: Trade with 2...exd4, then claim the centre with 3...d5
7273207378554101|e5e4.why: 2...e4 pushes the pawn past the centre, where it gives up d4 and becomes a target: in the engine line White takes space with 3.c4 and 5.d5 and Black is cramped. 2...exd4, played in 79% of master games, trades off the attacked pawn; after 3.exd4 d5 Black has an equal share of the centre and open lines for both bishops.
7273207378554101|e5e4.principle: When your centre pawn is attacked, trade it if pushing it would hand your opponent the squares it was controlling.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5/2. d4

7276016824343167|c8e6.headline: Take on d4 before the pawn forks knight and bishop
7276016824343167|c8e6.why: 4...Be6 puts the bishop next to the knight on c6, both in reach of White's d-pawn, so 5.d5 attacks them at once; after 5...Bc8 6.dxc6 bxc6 Black has lost a knight for a pawn. 4...exd4 removes the d-pawn before it can advance, and after 5.Nxd4 Nf6 Black develops normally.
7276016824343167|c8e6.principle: Don't line up pieces where an enemy pawn can attack two at once; with White's d-pawn able to advance, trade it off first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Nc6

7292743344203540|f1c4.headline: Open the Sicilian with 3.d4; 3.Bc4 hits a wall
7292743344203540|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 aims at f7, but Black blunts it with ...e6 and then hits it with ...d5, as in 3...e6 4.O-O d5 5.exd5 exd5 6.Bb5, and the bishop has spent two moves for little. 3.d4 is the Open Sicilian, played in 58% of master games: it takes space in the centre, and after 3...cxd4 4.Nxd4 White has open lines for all the pieces to develop.
7292743344203540|f1c4.principle: Fight for the centre with your pawns first; a bishop aimed at a square the opponent can easily close loses time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4

7319360163413787|f3g5.headline: Ng5 hits nothing here; castle and keep developing
7319360163413787|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 moves the knight again for a one-move attack on f7, which 6...e6 shuts down by blocking the bishop on c4. The knight then has nothing to do and returns with 10.Nf3, while Black catches up in development. 6.O-O keeps the time Black spent on ...Qd8: White castles and follows with 8.d4, taking space in the centre.
7319360163413787|f3g5.principle: Black's queen went back to d8, so White is ahead in development; keep adding pieces and castle rather than spending moves on one knight.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qd8

7372822453560713|d1b3.headline: Castle now; the e-file is about to open
7372822453560713|d1b3.why: 9.Qb3 leaves the king in the centre: after 9...d5 10.exd5 Ng6 11.Nf3 Re8+ the e-file opens with check, 12.Kf1 gives up castling, and Black wins back the pawn on b5 with 13...axb5. 9.O-O gets the king safe before the centre opens; after 9...d6 10.Nf3 Re8 11.Re1 White meets Black's rook on the e-file with one of its own.
7372822453560713|d1b3.principle: With Black castled and ready to open the e-file with ...d5 and ...Re8, castle before sending the queen after pawns.

7372822453560713|d1f3.headline: Castle before the e-file opens; 9.Qf3 walks into ...d6
7372822453560713|d1f3.why: 9.Qf3 aims at f7, but 9...d6 kicks the knight on e5, and the sacrifice 10.Nxf7 Rxf7 11.Bxf7+ Kxf7 hands Black two pieces for a rook and pawn while White's king is still in the centre. 9.O-O gets the king safe first; after 9...d6 the knight simply drops back with 10.Nf3, and White is ready when the centre opens with 11.Re1 d5 12.exd5.
7372822453560713|d1f3.principle: Black has castled and the e-pawns are off, so lines toward White's king on e1 are about to open; castle before starting an attack.

7413259852066043|h7h6.headline: Meet the knight on g5 by blocking the bishop with 4...d5
7413259852066043|h7h6.why: 4...h6 is too slow: 5.Nxf7 takes the pawn and forks the queen on d8 and the rook on h8, and after 5...d5 6.Nxd8 Black ends up giving the queen for a bishop and a knight. 4...d5 shuts the bishop on c4 off from f7 and attacks it at the same time. After 5.exd5 h6 6.Nf3 the knight has to go back, and Black gains more time with 6...e4.
7413259852066043|h7h6.principle: Your f7 pawn is guarded only by the king, and the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4 both aim at it, so break that attack at once instead of preparing to.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

741393967202585|e4f5.headline: Castle and let Black release the tension: 5.O-O, not 5.exf5
741393967202585|e4f5.why: 5.exf5 trades your centre pawn for Black's f-pawn: 5...d5 then builds a big centre with tempo on your bishop, and after 6.Bb3 Bxf5 Black has the pawn back with a developed bishop and a slightly better game. The theory calls 4.d3 the best answer to the Rousseau Gambit, leaving Black a difficult position, so keep it that way with 5.O-O: your king is safe and the tension stays. If 5...Bb4 6.c3 fxe4 7.dxe4, you recapture toward the centre, and 8.b4 and 9.a4 gain queenside space with tempo on the bishop, keeping a clear edge.
741393967202585|e4f5.principle: When the opponent's f-pawn is about to open lines, castle first and let them make the exchange, so your king is safe and you recapture toward the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...f5/4. d3

741414726801315|c1f4.headline: Black took on c4, so take the whole centre with 5.e4
741414726801315|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 develops but leaves the c4 pawn in Black's hands: after 5...c6 6.a4 Bb4 Black keeps the pawn for now and pins the knight on c3. 5.e4 claims the centre with both pawns while Black's pawn sits on c4, and 6.Bxc4 then regains it with the bishop developed. If Black takes on e4 with 6...Nxe4, White castles with 7.O-O and has active pieces; 54.8% of masters choose 5.e4.
741414726801315|c1f4.principle: When Black has given up the centre to take on c4, occupy it with both pawns, then win the c4 pawn back with a developing move.

7422621539281278|c1g5.headline: Strike at d6 with 7.Nb5 before ...a6 covers b5
7422621539281278|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 hits the queen, but 7...Ne7 simply blocks, and after 8.O-O Nbc6 9.Qd2 a6 Black has covered b5 and is ready to castle, so most of your advantage is gone. 6...e6 on top of ...g6 left d6 with no pawn able to cover it and the bishop gone to g7. 7.Nb5 goes straight for that square: after 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 Black's king is stuck in the centre, and 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 11.exf6+ Bxf6 rips its cover open.
7422621539281278|c1g5.principle: When you are ahead in development and the opponent's position has a hole, attack it at once; one quiet move lets them cover it and castle.

7422621539281278|e1h1.headline: ...g6 plus ...e6 leaves d6 bare: jump in with 7.Nb5
7422621539281278|e1h1.why: 7.O-O gives Black time for 7...a6, which takes b5 away from your knight, and most of your advantage disappears. 6...e6 on top of ...g6 leaves d6 with no pawn able to cover it, and the bishop that should guard it has gone to g7. 7.Nb5 heads straight there: after 7...Nf6 8.Nd6+ Ke7 Black's king is stuck in the centre, and 9.e5 Ne8 10.Bg5+ f6 11.exf6+ Bxf6 tears its cover open.
7422621539281278|e1h1.principle: A square that no enemy pawn can attack is a home for your knight; when Black's pawns leave d6 uncovered, put a knight there with check.

744743001475587|b1c3.headline: Play the Queen's Gambit 2.c4 to challenge d5
744743001475587|b1c3.why: 2.Nc3 is sound but blocks your c-pawn, so it can no longer challenge Black's d5 pawn, and in the engine line Black develops freely with 2...Nf6 and 3...e6. That's why masters play it in only 1% of games. 2.c4, the Queen's Gambit, is the main line at 77%: it attacks d5 from the flank, and if Black takes, their pawn is pulled away from the centre and White takes a bigger share of it.
744743001475587|b1c3.principle: Use a flank pawn to attack your opponent's central pawn before your pieces block that pawn's path.

744743001475587|e2e3.headline: After 1.d4 d5, challenge the centre with 2.c4
744743001475587|e2e3.why: 2.e3 is solid but passive: it shuts in White's dark-squared bishop and puts no pressure on d5, so Black develops freely with 2...Nf6. 2.c4, the Queen's Gambit, is played in 76.9% of master games: White offers a pawn to challenge d5 at once, and if 2...dxc4 White can take a bigger share of the centre with 3.e4.
744743001475587|e2e3.principle: With 1.d4 d5, attack Black's centre pawn with the c-pawn: trading a flank pawn for a centre pawn wins you central control.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4

7494602145104629|d2d3.headline: The Elephant Gambit is unsound: take the pawn with 3.exd5
7494602145104629|d2d3.why: 3.d3 turns down the gambit and lets Black open the centre on equal terms: after 3...dxe4 4.Nxe5 Nf6 5.Be2 exd3 6.Nxd3 the material is level and so is the game. The theory notes call 2...d5 unsound and say that taking either pawn wins for White; 3.exd5 is the main move. Black's best try is 3...e4, and 4.Qe2 defends the knight by pinning the pawn, keeping your extra pawn and a clear edge. 3.Nxe5 and 3.d4 are also good.
7494602145104629|d2d3.principle: Take a gambit pawn when you can consolidate; here 4.Qe2 shows you can, so declining with a passive pawn move just hands Black the open game they wanted.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5

7494602145104629|f1d3.headline: Against the Elephant Gambit, take on d5.
7494602145104629|f1d3.why: 3.Bd3 doesn't stop 3...dxe4, and it blocks the d-pawn. After 3...dxe4 4.Bxe4 f5 5.Bd3 e4 the bishop is chased and the pawn forks the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3. 2...d5 is an unsound gambit, and 3.exd5 accepts it. If 3...Qxd5, 4.Nc3 gains time on the queen, and against 3...e4 White has 4.Qe2, pinning the pawn.
7494602145104629|f1d3.principle: When the opponent offers an unsound gambit, take the pawn that removes the threat and develop with tempo against whatever recaptures.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d5/3. exd5

7498080805028408|f3b3.headline: Trade with check, 9.Bxc6+, before Black's knight joins in
7498080805028408|f3b3.why: 9.Qb3 moves the queen a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and Black gains time on it: 9...Nd4 hits the queen, and after 10.Qd3 Bg4 11.h3 Bh5 12.c3 Rd8 Black's rook bears down on your bishop on d5. Your advantage is gone. 9.Bxc6+ removes the knight on c6 with check before it can jump in, breaks Black's pawns with 9...bxc6, and 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the king, which can no longer castle, stuck in the centre, and White keeps a large advantage.
7498080805028408|f3b3.principle: When the enemy king is exposed, look at checks and captures first; a forcing trade keeps the initiative, while a quiet queen move hands your opponent time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nxd5/6. Nxf7/6...Kxf7

7498080805028408|f3f6.headline: Keep the queens on: Black's king is your target
7498080805028408|f3f6.why: Black's king can no longer castle, and your queen is the main piece attacking it. 9.Qxf6 trades it off: after 9...gxf6 10.Bxc6+ bxc6 Black's king is far easier to defend, and your large advantage shrinks to a modest one. 9.Bxc6+ bxc6 10.Qh5+ g6 11.Qe2 keeps the queens on, the king stays in the centre and Black's pawns are split, so your large advantage stays.
7498080805028408|f3f6.principle: Judge the position by its differences: your trump is Black's exposed king, so avoid the queen trade that takes it away and keep the pieces that attack it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nxd5/6. Nxf7/6...Kxf7

7498176079464762|g1f3.headline: Against the misplaced queen on e6, push 5.d4 and gain time.
7498176079464762|g1f3.why: The theory notes that 3...Qe6+ achieves little: the queen blocks Black's e-pawn and will have to move again. 5.Nf3 is natural but gives Black time to regroup with 5...Qd7 before White's centre arrives. 5.d4 claims the centre at once and threatens to push on and hit the queen on e6 and the knight on c6 together; after 5...Qd6 6.d5 Ne5 7.Qd4 White keeps chasing Black's pieces and gains more time.
7498176079464762|g1f3.principle: When your opponent's queen and knight sit in front of your centre pawns, advance the pawns at them: every push gains space and costs Black another move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

7521748049854142|b8c6.headline: Against 2.e3, put the knight on f6 and keep the c-pawn free
7521748049854142|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so Black loses the natural ways to challenge d4 or support d5 with it, and the knight becomes a target, as in 3.Nf3 Bf5 4.Bb5 where it gets pinned. 2...Nf6 is the natural developing move, played in three quarters of master games: it controls e4 so White can't push there freely, and prepares ...e6 and castling, as in 3.Nf3 e6 4.Bd3 Be7 5.O-O O-O.
7521748049854142|b8c6.principle: In closed d-pawn openings, develop the king's knight to f6 to guard e4 and leave the c-pawn free for the fight against d4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

7521748049854142|e7e5.headline: Develop with 2...Nf6; 2...e5 just drops a pawn
7521748049854142|e7e5.why: 2...e5 puts a pawn where the d4 pawn attacks it and nothing defends it, so 3.dxe5 wins it. 2...Nf6 is the most common master reply: it develops the knight toward the centre, and Black's d5 pawn is already defended by the queen.
7521748049854142|e7e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn into contact, count attackers and defenders: e5 would be attacked once and defended zero times.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

7528031277512488|c1e3.headline: Against 3...Qa5, develop with 6.Bc4 and keep d2 for the bishop
7528031277512488|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 puts the bishop where it can be hit and leaves your c3 knight pinned by the queen on a5; after 6...Bf5 7.Nh4 Nbd7 8.Nxf5 Qxf5 9.Bd3 Qg4 10.Qxg4 Nxg4 the queens are off and the knight attacks your bishop, so you keep little of your edge. Theory describes White's usual set-up as Nf3 and Bc4, with the d2 square freed for the bishop so the c3 knight can later move with tempo on the queen. 6.Bc4, played by masters 65.5% of the time, follows that plan: after 6...Bf5 7.Bd2 the pin is gone and you castle long with 9.O-O-O in the engine line.
7528031277512488|c1e3.principle: Develop each piece to the square the opening's plan gives it, here Bc4 and then Bd2, instead of a square that gives your opponent targets.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

7560471072032627|b1c3.headline: Take on d5 with 2.exd5, then develop with tempo
7560471072032627|b1c3.why: 1...d5 attacks e4, and 2.Nc3 lets Black kick the knight with 2...d4, so it has to go back with 3.Nb1 and Black has gained space for free. 2.exd5 is played in 97% of master games: it trades off Black's central pawn, and after 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 your knight develops with gain of time on the queen, which has to move again.
7560471072032627|b1c3.principle: Trading on d5 draws Black's queen into the centre, where your pieces can develop by attacking it.

7560471072032627|d2d3.headline: Meet 1...d5 with 2.exd5, not the timid 2.d3
7560471072032627|d2d3.why: 2.d3 looks like it defends e4, but after 2...dxe4 3.dxe4 Qxd1+ 4.Kxd1 the queens come off and White's king has lost the right to castle; Wikibooks calls the move timid. 2.exd5 is played in 97% of master games: it removes Black's central pawn, and if Black takes back with 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 develops with gain of time on the queen.
7560471072032627|d2d3.principle: When a pawn challenges your centre pawn, capture it so that your opponent's recapture brings a piece out where you can attack it.

7560471072032627|d2d4.headline: Take on d5: 2.d4 just hands Black the e4 pawn.
7560471072032627|d2d4.why: After 1...d5 the pawn on e4 is attacked, and 2.d4 does nothing about it: 2...dxe4 wins a pawn and you are in the Blackmar-Diemer gambit, a line considered suspect at a high level. 2.exd5 trades the attacked pawn, and if Black recaptures with 2...Qxd5 the queen stands exposed in the centre, so 3.Nc3 develops with tempo against it. That is why 2.exd5 is played in 96.9% of master games.
7560471072032627|d2d4.principle: Answer the opponent's threat first: when a pawn attacks your centre pawn, capture rather than add a pawn that doesn't defend it.

7560471072032627|f1d3.headline: Against the Scandinavian, trade with 2.exd5 and chase the queen
7560471072032627|f1d3.why: 2.Bd3 blocks White's d-pawn, and after 2...dxe4 3.Bxe4 e5 4.Nc3 Nf6 the bishop is hit and must move again with 5.Bf3, while Black has a free hand in the centre. 2.exd5 is played in 96.9% of master games: White trades the attacked pawn, and after 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 White develops with tempo against the queen.
7560471072032627|f1d3.principle: When your centre pawn is attacked, the trade that brings the opponent's queen out lets you develop with threats, Nc3 hitting the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5

7560471072032627|f2f3.headline: Trade on d5 and gain time on the queen
7560471072032627|f2f3.why: 2.f3 defends e4 at the cost of the g1-knight's best square and a weaker king, and Black simply adds 2...e5 for a fine centre. 2.exd5 trades the pawn, and when Black recaptures with 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 develops with an attack on the queen, which has to move again.
7560471072032627|f2f3.principle: When the opponent can only recapture with the queen, trade: a queen in the centre lets you develop with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

7560471072032627|f2f4.headline: Against 1...d5, take the pawn: 2.exd5.
7560471072032627|f2f4.why: Black is threatening 2...dxe4, and 2.f4 does nothing about it, so the e-pawn is simply lost: 2.f4 dxe4. 2.exd5 trades the attacked pawn off at once and keeps the centre balance. If Black takes back with 2...Qxd5, 3.Nc3 develops a knight while chasing the queen, which is the main drawback of the Scandinavian.
7560471072032627|f2f4.principle: When a centre pawn is attacked by a pawn, deal with the threat first, and prefer the capture that leaves the opponent's queen exposed to your developing moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5

7560471072032627|g1f3.headline: Trade on d5 with 2.exd5 and gain time on the queen
7560471072032627|g1f3.why: Black threatens 2...dxe4, and 2.Nf3 doesn't stop it: the pawn falls with tempo on your knight, and after 3.Ng5 e5 4.h4 h6 5.Nxe4 Be6 Black has a strong centre and the better game. Theory says 2.exd5 is almost always played because trading pawns is in White's interest. When Black recaptures with the queen, 2...Qxd5 3.Nc3 develops with tempo on her, and after 3...Qd8 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 you have the freer development; masters choose 2.exd5 96.9% of the time.
7560471072032627|g1f3.principle: When an exchange forces the enemy queen to recapture in the centre, make it: your pieces then develop with gain of time on her.

7590461919375344|b8c6.headline: Against the London, play 2...Nf6 and keep the c-pawn free.
7590461919375344|b8c6.why: 2...Nc6 puts the knight in front of the c-pawn, so Black can no longer play the ...c5 break, one of the two main ways of fighting the London. 2...Nf6 is Black's most common reply: it develops, controls e4, and keeps both plans open, ...c5 with pressure on b2 or ...e6 with ...Bd6, as in 2...Nf6 3.e3 c5.
7590461919375344|b8c6.principle: In queen's pawn openings, don't block the c-pawn with a knight before you've decided whether you need the ...c5 break.

7590461919375344|f7f6.headline: Against the London, develop with 2...Nf6; leave the f-pawn home
7590461919375344|f7f6.why: 2...f6 takes the best square from Black's own king's knight and loosens the squares around the black king, all to stop a knight that hasn't reached e5 yet. 2...Nf6 develops toward the centre, controls e4 and keeps the f-pawn home; Black then counters the London with ...c5 or ...e6, as in 3.e3 c5.
7590461919375344|f7f6.principle: Develop the king's knight to f6 before touching the f-pawn; a pawn move here fixes nothing and takes the knight's square.

7617223119001726|f3g5.headline: Castle first; 4.Ng5 attacks nothing and walks back to f3
7617223119001726|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight again with two minor pieces still at home, and the attack on f7 ends after 4...e6, which blocks the bishop on c4. White ends up playing 8.Nf3 anyway, and Black develops comfortably with ...Bg7 and ...Nge7. 4.O-O is the master choice (50.5%): White castles in the manner of the Italian Game and keeps the knight on f3, where it supports the centre and ideas such as 5.e5.
7617223119001726|f3g5.principle: A knight that jumps to g5 must win something at once; if a single pawn move like ...e6 parries it, the trip only costs time.

7623551723116652|f3g5.headline: g5 belongs to Black's queen; play 6.d4 instead
7623551723116652|f3g5.why: 6.Ng5 loses a knight: the queen on d8 sees g5 along the open diagonal and nothing of White's defends the square, so 6...Qxg5 wins a piece. Black is also threatening 6...Bxe4, since the bishop on g6 is aimed at the pawn on e4. 6.d4 claims the centre and challenges e5, and 7.Nc3 follows to cover e4.
7623551723116652|f3g5.principle: Before landing a piece on a square, count who covers it: g5 is attacked by the queen on d8 and defended by nothing.

7652733641084001|b8c6.headline: Against the Colle, play 3...e6 and keep the c-pawn free
7652733641084001|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks Black's c-pawn, so the natural ...c5 break against White's centre is off, and after 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 White fights for d5 with the c-pawn while Black cannot. 3...e6 is the most common reply: it opens the dark-squared bishop and prepares 4...c5, with the queen's knight coming out later.
7652733641084001|b8c6.principle: In queen's pawn games keep the c-pawn free: ...c5 is Black's main way to challenge d4, so develop the queen's knight after it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. e3

7701337958463963|d7d6.headline: Follow 1...e6 with 2...d5 and challenge e4
7701337958463963|d7d6.why: 2...d6 leaves both of White's centre pawns unchallenged: after 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bd3 White develops freely and later gains more space with 7.d5. 2...d5 is the point of 1...e6: it claims the centre and attacks the pawn on e4 at once. 98.8% of masters play it, and however White answers, Black has a share of the centre.
7701337958463963|d7d6.principle: Use the support that 1...e6 gives to put the d-pawn on d5 and challenge e4, instead of settling for a small, passive centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. d4/2...d5

7701337958463963|f8b4.headline: In the French, strike at e4 with 2...d5.
7701337958463963|f8b4.why: 2...Bb4+ achieves nothing: 3.c3 blocks with a useful move that supports d4, and the bishop has to retreat with 3...Be7. Meanwhile White keeps two pawns in the centre. 2...d5, played 99% of the time, challenges e4 at once and threatens ...dxe4. That is the point of 1...e6.
7701337958463963|f8b4.principle: When the opponent builds a two-pawn centre, challenge it with a pawn right away instead of giving a check that can be blocked with gain of time.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e6/2. e4

7739923539884250|b7b6.headline: Answer 5.d4 with 5...c4, not the slow 5...b6
7739923539884250|b7b6.why: 5.d4 attacks your c5 pawn and threatens 6.dxc5. 5...b6 spends a move holding it while your king is still on the open e-file: 6.Bb5+ Bd7 7.Qe2+ Be7 8.Nxd5 wins the d5 pawn, because the bishop on d7 cuts your queen off from d5, and White is close to winning. 5...c4 steps out of the attack and keeps everything protected; play continues 6.g3 h6 7.Bg2 Nf6.
7739923539884250|b7b6.principle: With your king still in the centre and the e-file open, don't spend moves on side pawns; every check costs you time or material.

7739923539884250|g8f6.headline: Settle the c5 pawn with 5...c4, then develop
7739923539884250|g8f6.why: 5.d4 threatens 6.dxc5, and with the e-file open your king is short of time. 5...Nf6 is common even among masters, but it lets White develop with pins and checks: 6.Bb5+ Nc6 7.O-O Bg4 8.Bg5, then 10.Re1+, and White gets a clear edge. 5...c4 removes the target first and keeps the balance; the knight still reaches f6 a move later, as in 6.g3 h6 7.Bg2 Nf6.
7739923539884250|g8f6.principle: Before developing, look at your opponent's forcing moves; with the e-file open, every check and pin they get costs you a tempo.

7780638886141553|c2c4.headline: Castle first: 6.O-O guards g2, while 6.c4 drops a pawn
7780638886141553|c2c4.why: The queen on d5 already threatens 6...Qxg2. 6.c4 attacks her, but with your light-squared bishop traded off nothing defends c4, so 6...Qxc4 wins a pawn and Black is clearly better. 6.O-O, played in 96.6% of master games, guards g2 with the king and gets it out of the centre; c4 still comes, as 8.c4 in the main line once 7.Nd2 covers that square.
7780638886141553|c2c4.principle: Black has the lead in development and a queen aimed at your king's side, so castle before starting pawn moves; the theory warns that White easily succumbs here if the centre opens before castling.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6/3. d4/3...Bg4

7782133965544018|f1c4.headline: Against 2...c6, take the free pawn with 3.Nxe5.
7782133965544018|f1c4.why: 2...c6 leaves the e5 pawn attacked once and not defended at all, and 3.Bc4 lets Black play 3...d5, hitting the bishop and taking the centre at no cost. 3.Nxe5 wins the pawn, and 2...c6 has also taken the c6 square from Black's queen's knight, so there is little compensation. After 3...Nf6 4.Bc4 d5 5.exd5 White keeps developing; the theory warns only that 4.d3 loses to 4...Qa5+, forking king and knight.
7782133965544018|f1c4.principle: After each opponent move, check what was left undefended; an unprotected centre pawn next to your knight is usually a free pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...c6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...c6/3. Nxe5

7803977633029211|c8e6.headline: With Ng5 and Bc4 aiming at f7, guard it with 6...Nh6
7803977633029211|c8e6.why: 6...Be6 lets White trade on e6: after 7.Bxe6 fxe6 8.Nxe6 the knight takes a pawn and attacks the queen and the bishop on c5, and Black's kingside falls apart, as 11.Nxg7+ shows. 6...Nh6 develops the last minor piece and adds a second defender to f7 against the knight on g5 and the bishop on c4. If White adds the queen with 7.Qh5, Black castles and the rook defends f7 too.
7803977633029211|c8e6.principle: When White's knight and bishop both aim at f7, add a defender to f7 before doing anything else.

7827708463373629|c2c3.headline: Block with 5.Nc3; 5.c3 hands the b2 pawn to the queen
7827708463373629|c2c3.why: 4...Qb4+ checks the king and eyes the pawn on b2. 5.c3 blocks the check but lets 5...Qxb2 take that pawn, and after 6.Nbd2 Qxc3 the queen grabs a second one, so White ends up a pawn down instead of a pawn up. 5.Nc3 blocks with a developing move and keeps the extra pawn: after 5...Qa5 6.Qd5 White offers the queen trade, and after 7.Qxa5 Bxa5 Black's queen can no longer go pawn hunting.
7827708463373629|c2c3.principle: Block a check with a piece you want to develop anyway, not with a pawn move that leaves new targets for the queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...e5/2. dxe5

7832135918552384|d2d3.headline: Black gives you the centre: take it with 2.d4
7832135918552384|d2d3.why: 1...g6 is a hypermodern opening: Black allows White a big centre and hopes to undermine it later. 2.d3 declines the offer, and after 2...c5 3.g3 Nc6 4.Bg2 Bg7 Black has an easy, equal game. 2.d4 (95.1% of masters games) puts a second pawn in the centre while Black has not contested it, gains space and opens the way for your pieces; you keep a small edge.
7832135918552384|d2d3.principle: When the opponent lets you build a two-pawn centre, build it: pawns on e4 and d4 take space and give your pieces room before Black can challenge them.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4

7832135918552384|f2f4.headline: Take the full centre with 2.d4 when Black allows it
7832135918552384|f2f4.why: 2.f4 doesn't develop anything and leaves d4 unsupported: Black strikes with 2...d5, and after 3.e5 c5 4.d4 cxd4 White has lost a pawn. 1...g6 is a hypermodern move that lets White build a classical centre and hopes to undermine it later. 2.d4, played in 95% of master games, accepts the invitation: two pawns in the centre, more space, and lines open for both bishops.
7832135918552384|f2f4.principle: When your opponent doesn't contest the centre, occupy it with both centre pawns before anything else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6/2. d4

7839204652261332|f1c4.headline: Against the Caro-Kann, put a second pawn in the centre
7839204652261332|f1c4.why: 1...c6 prepares 2...d5, and 2.Bc4 puts the bishop right where that pawn hits it: after 2...d5 3.exd5 cxd5 it has to move again with 4.Bb3, and Black has swapped the c-pawn for White's central e-pawn. 2.d4, played in 80.5% of master games, takes the two-pawn centre that Black's quiet first move allowed. After 2...d5 3.e5 White gains space and keeps the pawn out of harm's way.
7839204652261332|f1c4.principle: If your opponent's first move doesn't stop d4, claim the centre with pawns first; bishops go out once you know which squares the enemy pawns will hit.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6

7839204652261332|f2f4.headline: Against the Caro-Kann, put the second pawn on d4
7839204652261332|f2f4.why: 2.f4 doesn't defend e4 against 2...d5, and after 3.d3 dxe4 4.dxe4 Qxd1+ 5.Kxd1 the queens are gone and your king has lost the right to castle. 1...c6 neither makes a threat nor controls d4, so 2.d4 builds a two-pawn centre; it is the choice in over 80% of master games. After 2...d5 3.e5 White gains space and Black has to find a home for the bishop with 3...Bf5.
7839204652261332|f2f4.principle: When the opponent's first move doesn't contest d4, occupy it: two centre pawns give your pieces room and take squares from Black's.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4

7896021651424943|f1e2.headline: Against 3...Bg4, open the centre at once with 4.d4.
7896021651424943|f1e2.why: 4.Be2 is too slow: Black answers 4...Nc6 and sets up comfortably with no pressure on e5. The Philidor is a passive defence whose pawn on d6 blocks Black's own bishop, and the main plan against it is the d4 break. 4.d4 strikes at e5 at once; after 4...Nc6 5.Bb5 exd4 6.Qxd4 White's queen is centralised and Black has given up the centre.
7896021651424943|f1e2.principle: When the opponent's setup is passive, open the centre with d4 while your pieces are the more active ones.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6

7902974846795865|b4b5.headline: 8.b5 chases the knight to a5, where it trades your bishop
7902974846795865|b4b5.why: 8.b5 kicks the knight on c6, but 8...Na5 attacks the bishop on c4. White can grab a pawn with 9.Nxe5, yet after 9...Qe8 10.Ng4 Nxg4 11.Qxg4 Nxc4 12.dxc4 Black has traded off White's Italian bishop and left White with doubled c-pawns, and Black is better despite the pawn. 8.a4 gains queenside space with the idea a5 against the bishop on b6, so Black spends 8...a6 making room for it, and White completes development with 9.Nbd2 and 10.Re1.
7902974846795865|b4b5.principle: Chase a piece with a pawn only when its new square is worse: from a5 Black's knight attacks the bishop on c4.

7908463020324267|b8c6.headline: Hit e4 with 4...Nf6 first so White has no time for c4
7908463020324267|b8c6.why: 4...Nc6 attacks nothing, so White has time for 5.c4, putting pawns on c4 and e4 that clamp the d5 square; after 6.Nc3 g6 7.f3 Black is cramped. 4...Nf6, chosen in 99.5% of master games, hits the e4 pawn first, and White defends it with 5.Nc3, which blocks the c-pawn and rules out an early c4. Then you pick your system, for example 5...a6 as in the taught line.
7908463020324267|b8c6.principle: Develop with a threat: a knight move that attacks e4 makes White spend their move on Nc3 instead of building a pawn clamp on c4 and e4.

7908463020324267|g7g6.headline: Gain time on e4 with 4...Nf6 before anything else
7908463020324267|g7g6.why: 4...g6 is not a blunder, but it puts no pressure on White, who gets to choose a set-up freely: the theory notes say White would love to play 5.c4, the Maróczy bind that makes ...d5 very hard, and in the line 5.Be3 Nf6 6.Nc3 Nc6 7.f3 Bg7 8.Qd2 O-O 9.Bc4 White develops exactly as they like and keeps a small edge. 4...Nf6 (99.5% of masters games) develops and attacks the pawn on e4, so White has no time for 5.c4, which would drop the pawn to 5...Nxe4, and usually defends with 5.Nc3, blocking the c-pawn.
7908463020324267|g7g6.principle: Develop with a threat when you can: a knight move that attacks a pawn forces your opponent to respond and keeps them from setting up the structure they want.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4

7917889477711464|c6d4.headline: Develop the other knight; 4...Nd4 leaves e5 hanging.
7917889477711464|c6d4.why: 4...Nd4 moves the same knight again and stops guarding e5, so 5.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and after 5...Qf6 6.Bxf7+ Kd8 7.Bxg8 White's bishop on c4 also strikes at f7. 4...Nf6 develops a new piece to a good square where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares to castle. That calm setup is what the slow Giuoco Pianissimo calls for.
7917889477711464|c6d4.principle: In a quiet opening, bring out the pieces still at home rather than moving a developed piece again and abandoning what it guards.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

7917889477711464|f7f6.headline: Knight to f6: develop and castle, don't play f6
7917889477711464|f7f6.why: 4...f6 takes the king knight's best square and weakens the diagonal from c4 toward g8; after 5.Nh4 g6 6.O-O Black ends up moving the king with ...Kf8 instead of castling. 4...Nf6 develops the knight to a good square where it pressures e4, controls d5 and prepares to castle kingside, and masters choose it in 91.7% of games.
7917889477711464|f7f6.principle: In the quiet Italian, finish developing and castle; a pawn move that blocks a knight and loosens the king costs more than it supports e5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. d3

7920350690808360|f8c5.headline: Develop with 3...Nf6; 3...Bc5 runs into 4.d4
7920350690808360|f8c5.why: White wants 4.d4 anyway, and 3...Bc5 makes it stronger: the theory notes the pawn takes the centre, gains time on the bishop and opens the c1 bishop to win back the f4 pawn. After 4.d4 Be7 5.Bxf4 the gambit pawn is gone. 3...Nf6, the Schallopp defence, develops and attacks e4; if White pushes 4.e5, the theory recommends 4...Nh5 to keep defending f4.
7920350690808360|f8c5.principle: Don't put a piece where a pawn can attack it with gain of time; develop to squares where your piece attacks something instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. f4/2...exf4/3. Nf3

7994400733701852|d7d5.headline: Knight before ...d5: 3...Nc6, then ...Ne5 hits queen and bishop
7994400733701852|d7d5.why: 3...d5 comes too early: after 4.exd5 exd5 the d5 pawn is attacked by the bishop on c4 and the queen on f3 and defended only by your queen, so 5.Qxd5 wins it and threatens mate on f7. The theory says Black should play ...Nc6 before ...d5. 3...Nc6 develops and punishes the early queen: after 4.Ne2 Ne5 the knight hits the queen and the bishop at once, and 5.Qc3 Nxc4 6.Qxc4 gets rid of White's light-squared bishop, leaving Black better.
7994400733701852|d7d5.principle: When White's queen comes out early, develop with threats against it; your pieces gain time while the queen keeps moving.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

8013895061699550|d5d6.headline: Keep the extra pawn: develop with 7.Qe2 hitting e5
8013895061699550|d5d6.why: You are a pawn up, and 7.d6 hands it straight back: the pawn on d6 is attacked by the knight on f5, the queen and the c7 pawn and defended by nothing, so 7...Nxd6 wins it, and after 8.Be2 h6 9.Nf3 e4 Black is better. 7.Qe2 develops with a threat against the pawn on e5 and keeps the d5 pawn and a small edge. 7.d4 and 7.O-O are also fine.
8013895061699550|d5d6.principle: When you are ahead in material, prefer a developing move that creates a threat over a pawn push that runs into more attackers than defenders.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nd4/6. c3

8021519334015813|d2d3.headline: Take the free e5 pawn: 4.Nxe5 is the main line
8021519334015813|d2d3.why: 4.d3 leaves e5 alone and lets the bishop on b4 pin your knight on c3 to the king, which is what the theory says 3...Bb4 was hoping for; after 4...d5 Black takes over the centre and is slightly better. 4.Nxe5, played in 67% of master games, takes the pawn nothing defends, and e4 is safe for now: if 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4, then 6.Qg4 forks the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. Black usually gets the pawn back later, as in 5.Be2 Re8 6.Nd3 Bxc3 7.dxc3 Nxe4 8.O-O, but you keep the bishop pair and a small edge.
8021519334015813|d2d3.principle: Count before you capture: e5 has no defender and the knight on c3 covers e4, so the pawn is free unless Black can remove that defender safely.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4

8021519334015813|d2d4.headline: Take 4.Nxe5 first; 4.d4 pins your own knight and drops e4
8021519334015813|d2d4.why: As the theory says, 3...Bb4 threatens to pin your knight as soon as the d-pawn moves. 4.d4 does exactly that, so the knight on c3 can no longer take back on e4: 4...Nxe4 grabs the pawn, and after 5.Qd3 d5 6.dxe5 O-O 7.a3 Bxc3+ 8.bxc3 Re8 Black is better. 4.Nxe5, the main move (67% of master games), takes the free pawn while e4 is still covered; if 4...Bxc3 5.dxc3 Nxe4, then 6.Qg4 forks the knight on e4 and the g7 pawn. Black usually regains the pawn with 4...O-O and 7...Nxe4, but White keeps a small edge.
8021519334015813|d2d4.principle: Before moving the d-pawn, look at the bishop on b4: once d2 is empty your knight on c3 is pinned to the king and stops defending e4.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4

8041898991527130|d1e2.headline: In the exchange French, play 4.d4, not an early queen check
8041898991527130|d1e2.why: 4.Qe2+ brings the queen out with three minor pieces still at home: 4...Be7 blocks the check while developing, the queen shuts in the bishop on f1, and after 5.d4 Nf6 she has to go back with 6.Qd1. 4.d4, chosen in 97.4% of master games, claims the centre and opens the bishop on c1, reaching the exchange French with a free hand for development such as 5.Bd3.
8041898991527130|d1e2.principle: A queen check that the opponent blocks with a developing move only helps the opponent; develop the minor pieces first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e6/2. Nf3/2...d5

8076559324931644|b1c3.headline: Punish 2...f6 with 3.Nxe5: the pawn on f6 can't defend e5
8076559324931644|b1c3.why: 2...f6 only seems to defend e5, and 3.Nc3 lets Black get away with it and develop normally. 3.Nxe5 takes the pawn, because 3...fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxe5+ forks the king and the rook on h8. Black's best try is 3...Qe7, and after 4.Nf3 White keeps a big lead in development; don't play 4.Qh5+ there, since 4...g6 leaves the queen with nowhere to go.
8076559324931644|b1c3.principle: Look at captures first and check what forcing reply follows: here the weakened diagonal to Black's king makes the capture safe.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6/3. Nxe5

8144277447096351|f1c4.headline: Black gave up the c8 bishop: hit b7 with 6.Qb3
8144277447096351|f1c4.why: 6.Bc4 lets Black answer 6...Qf6, and after 7.Qb3 Nd7 8.Qxb7 Rb8 9.Qa6 Qxa6 10.Bxa6 the queens come off and Black's pieces get active, so you keep less of your edge. Theory calls 3...Bg4 dubious, and after 4...Bxf3 Black no longer has the light-squared bishop that guards b7. 6.Qb3 attacks the pawn on b7 at once, before Black's queen can help, and after 6...Nd7 7.Be3 Bc5 8.Bxc5 Nxc5 9.Qb5+ Nd7 10.Qxb7 you win the pawn with queens still on.
8144277447096351|f1c4.principle: When your opponent trades off a bishop, the squares it guarded become weak; aim your pieces at them, here the light squares b7 and f7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...Bg4

8151329472450239|d2d3.headline: Punish the slow 3...g6 by striking at once with 4.d4
8151329472450239|d2d3.why: 3...g6 is slow, with Black's kingside undeveloped and e5 held only by the d6 pawn. 4.d3 lets Black complete the fianchetto with 4...Bg7, and after 5.Ng5 Nh6 f7 is covered and most of White's edge is gone. 4.d4 strikes at e5 before the bishop reaches g7, so Black has to hold it with the queen, 4...Qe7, while White develops with 5.Nc3.
8151329472450239|d2d3.principle: With more pieces out, open the centre right away, before the opponent's slow setup catches up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

8153210382746448|f6g4.headline: When 4.e5 attacks your knight, capture with 4...dxe5 instead of retreating.
8153210382746448|f6g4.why: 4...Ng4 saves the knight but sends it toward the edge: 5.h3 Nh6 leaves it badly placed while White develops with 6.Bf4 and 7.Nf3. 4...dxe5 removes the pawn that attacked the knight, and after 5.dxe5 Qxd1+ 6.Nxd1 the knight lands on a central square with 6...Nd5. The queens are off and Black develops smoothly with 7...Bg7 to follow.
8153210382746448|f6g4.principle: When a pawn attacks your developed piece, look first for a capture that removes the attacker rather than spending a move retreating to a worse square.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. d4/2...Nf6/3. Nc3/3...g6

8186436489067117|b5e2.headline: Keep the bishop on b5 and free the other with 8.d3
8186436489067117|b5e2.why: 8.Be2 retreats the bishop a second time with two minor pieces still at home, and Black gains time on your knight: after 8...h6 9.Nh3 Bxh3 10.gxh3 Qc8 11.d3 Qxh3 your kingside pawns are wrecked, the extra pawn is gone and Black is clearly better. 8.d3 leaves the bishop on b5 pinning the c6 knight and opens the diagonal for your c1 bishop. After 8...Qd5 9.Bxc6+ Qxc6 10.O-O Bd6 11.Qf3 you have castled and kept the extra pawn.
8186436489067117|b5e2.principle: Instead of retreating a piece that is doing a job, make the move that brings a new piece into play.

8211444126196396|c1f4.headline: 5.e3 props up d4 and opens the f1 bishop toward c4
8211444126196396|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 does nothing for the pawn on d4 or against the pawn on c4. After 5...a6, White's try to win back c4 with 6.Nd2 takes a defender away from d4 and blocks the queen's guard of it, so 6...Qxd4 picks up a second pawn. 5.e3, the most common master move (36% of 124 games), supports d4 and opens the way for the bishop on f1 to recapture on c4. After 5...b5 6.a4 White attacks Black's queenside at once, the theory's plan for disrupting Black's hold on the c-pawn.
8211444126196396|c1f4.principle: Pick the pawn move that does two jobs: e3 supports the centre pawn and frees the bishop that targets the gambit pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nc3

8224292196866816|b8c6.headline: Support d5 with 3...e6; 3...Nc6 lets White take the centre
8224292196866816|b8c6.why: 3...Nc6 blocks the c-pawn, so after 4.cxd5 Nxd5 Black has no pawn left on d5: 5.Bb5 pins the knight, and 7.Bxc6+ Qxc6 8.e4 lets White take the centre with gain of time on the queen. 3...e6 supports d5 with a pawn, so cxd5 can be answered by a pawn recapture, and it opens the bishop on f8 for development, as in 4.Nc3 Be7.
8224292196866816|b8c6.principle: When White attacks your d5 pawn with c4, support it with a pawn so you keep a foothold in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5

826798325202564|c2c3.headline: Take back with 4.Nxd4: that is why 3.Nf3 came first
826798325202564|c2c3.why: 3.Nf3 is the Morphy gambit, and 3...e6 does nothing to keep the pawn: d4 is attacked twice and defended by nothing. 4.c3 offers a second pawn instead of collecting the first, and after 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 you are a pawn down with Black slightly better. 3.Nf3 was played to recapture with the knight rather than the queen, which Black would hit with ...Nc6, so 4.Nxd4 (99.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and reaches a normal Open Sicilian with a small edge for White.
826798325202564|c2c3.principle: 3.Nf3 offered d4 as a gambit; once Black declines to secure the pawn, take it back with the piece you prepared and keep your share of the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. Nf3

8290697107627463|f6d5.headline: Trade queens with check, then win the loose e5 pawn
8290697107627463|f6d5.why: 4...Nd5 saves the knight but spends a second move on it, and 5.Bc4 hits it at once, so Black has to prop it up with 5...c6 and 6...e6 while White develops freely. 4...Qxd1+ trades queens with check, so 5.Kxd1 costs White the right to castle. Then 5...Ng4 attacks the e5 pawn, which nothing defends, and after 6.Ke1 Nxe5 Black is a pawn ahead.
8290697107627463|f6d5.principle: Look at checks and captures first: a capture with check removes the threat to your knight and gives you time to attack what is loose.

8290697107627463|f6g4.headline: Trade queens with check first, then take e5 with the knight
8290697107627463|f6g4.why: 4...Ng4 leaves the queens facing each other, so White trades first with 5.Qxd8+ Kxd8 and it is Black's king that loses the right to castle, while the knight has moved twice and 6.Nf3 keeps e5 protected. 4...Qxd1+ captures first with check: after 5.Kxd1 White can no longer castle, and 5...Ng4 6.Ke1 Nxe5 wins the pawn on e5.
8290697107627463|f6g4.principle: When queens face each other on an open file, capture first with check so the opponent's king is the one dragged out of its corner.

8292354532353769|d2d3.headline: Trade on d4 and win the overextended pawn
8292354532353769|d2d3.why: 4.d3 lets Black trade with 4...Nxf3+ 5.Qxf3, so the double knight move becomes a harmless exchange and White's edge is gone. 4.Nxd4 removes the knight instead: after 4...exd4 the pawn on d4 is cut off, and 5.O-O, 6.Re1 and 7.c3 win it with 8.cxd4. Avoid the bait 4.Nxe5, which runs into 4...Qg5.
8292354532353769|d2d3.principle: The opponent's knight trip cost time; trade it off, castle and open the centre while you lead in development.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

8292354532353769|f3e5.headline: The e5 pawn is poisoned: trade knights with 4.Nxd4
8292354532353769|f3e5.why: 4.Nxe5 falls into the trap: 4...Qg5 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2 at once, and after 5.O-O Qxe5 you have lost a knight for a pawn. Theory calls 3...Nd4 a one-trick pony: Black moved the knight a second time to tempt you into taking e5, and as long as you avoid that you are comfortably ahead. 4.Nxd4 exd4 trades the knights and dislodges Black's pawn from e5, and after 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 d6 7.c3 Be7 8.cxd4 you win a pawn with a lead in development.
8292354532353769|f3e5.principle: When your opponent moves the same knight twice to bait you, don't take the bait: trade the knight off and the time they spent on it is simply lost.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4

8292354532353769|f3g5.headline: Against 3...Nd4, trade knights with 4.Nxd4; 4.Ng5 drops a piece.
8292354532353769|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 puts the knight where the queen on d8 can simply take it: 4...Qxg5, and the knight that moved twice is gone. 3...Nd4 is the Blackburne Shilling gambit, a trap that only works if White grabs e5 with 4.Nxe5, and its knight is misplaced. 4.Nxd4 exd4 trades it off and drags Black's pawn away from e5, and after 5.O-O Nf6 6.Re1 White ends up a pawn ahead with 8.cxd4.
8292354532353769|f3g5.principle: Before moving a piece, check whether it lands on a square an enemy piece already covers; g5 is on the diagonal of Black's queen.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nd4/4. Nxd4

8297553024226585|f3g5.headline: Castle with 5.O-O; Ng5 only gives Black time
8297553024226585|f3g5.why: 5.Ng5 moves the knight again for an attack on f7 that 5...O-O shuts down at once. After 6.O-O Na5 7.Nc3 Nxc4 8.dxc4 Black has won the bishop pair and doubled White's c-pawns, and 9.Nf3 admits the knight trip was wasted. 5.O-O, the masters' choice 78.7% of the time, tucks the king away and keeps the quiet buildup that suits this solid Hungarian setup.
8297553024226585|f3g5.principle: A second knight move needs a concrete gain; once castling covers f7, the jump wins nothing and costs a tempo.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Be7

8308599203837326|e4f5.headline: Meet the Rousseau Gambit with 4.d4, not 4.exf5
8308599203837326|e4f5.why: Black threatens 4...fxe4, but 4.exf5 lets Black kick your knight with 4...e4, and after 5.Nd4 Nf6 most of your advantage is gone; theory calls the capture a common beginners' mistake. 3...f5 loosens Black's centre, so hit it: after 4.d4 fxe4 5.Nxe5 you are in an improved version of the Latvian Gambit main line, and after 4...exd4 5.e5 the centre opens and you castle quickly with a big initiative.
8308599203837326|e4f5.principle: When your opponent loosens their centre with an early flank pawn move, strike in the centre with your own pawn instead of grabbing the flank pawn they offer.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...f5
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...f5/4. exf5

8341087684859850|g5f7.headline: After 5...Nxd5, 6.Qh5 keeps the attack without giving a piece
8341087684859850|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 gives a knight for a pawn: after 6...Kxf7 7.Qf3+ Ke6 Black's king holds in the centre, and White has to keep attacking a piece down with much less of an edge. 5...Nxd5 took the knight away from f6, where it guarded h5, so 6.Qh5 comes in with a mate threat on f7, hit by both the queen and the knight on g5. Black has to weaken with 6...g6, and White keeps the pressure with 7.Qf3 while keeping all the material.
8341087684859850|g5f7.principle: f7 is guarded only by the king; when Black's knight leaves f6 it stops covering h5, so bring the queen there as a second attacker on f7.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

8342193165505706|d7d6.headline: Save the d-pawn for ...d5: play 4...a6, not 4...d6
8342193165505706|d7d6.why: The theory's answer to 2.Bc4 is ...e6 followed by ...d5, which hits the bishop and gives Black a free centre, as in 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.O-O d5. 4...d6 parks the d-pawn one square short, and after 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Nf6 7.Be3 White has a comfortable Open Sicilian and a small edge. 4...a6, the most common master move (49.3%), keeps the d-pawn free to go to d5 and takes b5 away from White's knight and bishop; after 5.d4 cxd4 6.Nxd4 Qc7 the game is close to level. 4...Nf6 is also good.
8342193165505706|d7d6.principle: Make each pawn move count: the d-pawn belongs on d5, where it hits the bishop on c4 and frees your pieces, so don't spend a tempo putting it on d6.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

8358083107211199|g7g6.headline: Hit the knight on e5 while you develop
8358083107211199|g7g6.why: 4...g6 is too slow with a white knight already on e5: after 5.Bc4 White threatens mate on f7, and Black has to answer 5...e6, shutting in the c8 bishop. 4...Nbd7 develops a piece and challenges the knight on e5 at once, so White must spend another move on it; after 5.Nc4 e5 6.Be2 Bc5 Black has a central pawn and active pieces.
8358083107211199|g7g6.principle: When an enemy knight sits in your half of the board, develop a piece that attacks it, so your development gains time instead of losing it.

8378513320650736|e1h1.headline: e4 is hit twice: add a defender with 5.Qe2
8378513320650736|e1h1.why: After 4...Nf6, e4 is attacked twice, by the bishop on b7 and the knight on f6, and defended only by the bishop on d3. 5.O-O ignores this and 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn. 5.Qe2, the most common master move (62.6%), adds a second defender; after 5...d5 6.e5 Nfd7 7.c3 you have a French-style space advantage and a clear edge. 5.Nbd2 also defends, and 5.e5 kicks the knight away.
8378513320650736|e1h1.principle: Each time your opponent adds an attacker to a pawn, count again: two attackers against one defender means you must add a defender or move the pawn before doing anything else.

8399621132422899|b1c3.headline: Start with a centre pawn to free your pieces
8399621132422899|b1c3.why: 1.Nc3 is sensible but blocks the c-pawn, and it doesn't stop 1...d5, which threatens 2...d4 to kick the knight and gain space. 1.e4 claims the centre and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop at once, and with a pawn on e4 Black can't push a pawn there to chase a knight from f3.
8399621132422899|b1c3.principle: Begin by putting a pawn in the centre: it controls key squares and frees your pieces, while an early knight in front of the c-pawn can be chased.

8399621132422899|e2e3.headline: Start with a centre pawn: 1.e4 claims the centre
8399621132422899|e2e3.why: 1.e3 is not a mistake, but the theory calls it passive: it lets Black take over the centre with ...e5 and ...d5, and the pawn on e3 shuts in your queenside bishop, so White's first-move edge is gone. 1.e4 puts a pawn in the centre, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and keeps a black pawn off e4, so your knight can go to f3 without being kicked. It is the most popular first move at every level (45.5% of master games); 1.d4, 1.Nf3 and 1.c4 are good too.
8399621132422899|e2e3.principle: The opening is a race for development and control of the centre, so the first move should put a pawn on a central square and open lines for your pieces.

8399621132422899|g2g3.headline: Start with 1.e4: put a pawn in the centre at once
8399621132422899|g2g3.why: 1.g3 doesn't touch the centre; it only prepares to fianchetto the bishop, so Black takes central space for free with 1...e5 and gets an easy game. 1.e4 occupies the centre, controls d5 and f5, and opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop at the same time. It is the most popular first move among masters, played in 45.5% of their games.
8399621132422899|g2g3.principle: On move one, a central pawn move both claims space and frees your pieces, so it does two jobs where a flank pawn move does neither.

8399621132422899|g2g4.headline: Start with 1.e4: take the centre, not the flank
8399621132422899|g2g4.why: 1.g4, Grob's Attack, is considered one of the worst first moves: it does nothing for the centre and loosens White's kingside, and after 1...d5 Black takes the centre while the g4-pawn becomes a target. 1.e4 controls d5 and f5, opens lines for the queen and the king's bishop, and is the most popular first move at every level, played in 45.5% of master games.
8399621132422899|g2g4.principle: The first moves should fight for the central squares and free your pieces; a flank pawn move does neither.

8425508266792292|f6g4.headline: Take back the bishop on c6 first.
8425508266792292|f6g4.why: The bishop on c6 is attacked twice and defended by nothing, yet 4...Ng4 leaves it there. After 5.Ba4 it escapes and White keeps the knight it captured, and 6.exf5 even adds a pawn. 4...dxc6 wins the bishop back and opens the c8 bishop's diagonal, and Black is fine in the reference line.
8425508266792292|f6g4.principle: After every capture, look first at recapturing: count what attacks the capturing piece before making any other plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8425508266792292|f8d6.headline: Recapture on c6 before anything else.
8425508266792292|f8d6.why: 4...Bd6 develops but ignores the bishop on c6, which is attacked twice and defended by nothing. After 5.Ba4 the bishop retreats and White stays a whole piece up, and 5...Nxe4 only wins back a pawn. 4...dxc6 takes back the bishop and frees the c8 bishop, so the position is level again.
8425508266792292|f8d6.principle: When the opponent has just captured, recapture before developing; a developing move cannot make up for a missing piece.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8432999302569785|c2c3.headline: Recapture 4.Nxd4: open lines are what you get for the pawn
8432999302569785|c2c3.why: The pawn on d4 is attacked twice and defended only by the knight on c6. The theory notes call 4.c3 a playable gambit that turns into a Smith-Morra, but after 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 e6 6.Be2 d6 you are a pawn down and Black is already slightly better. 4.Nxd4 (99.8% of masters games) wins the pawn back and gives you open lines for your bishops in return for Black's extra centre pawn.
8432999302569785|c2c3.principle: In the Open Sicilian, White trades a centre pawn for open lines and fast development; recapture on d4 so that trade happens on equal material instead of a pawn down.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4

8432999302569785|f1c4.headline: You played 3.Nf3 to recapture: do it now with 4.Nxd4
8432999302569785|f1c4.why: The point of 3.Nf3 is to take back on d4 with the knight and reach a normal Open Sicilian. 4.Nxd4 does exactly that, and masters choose it 99.8% of the time. 4.Bc4 leaves Black the extra pawn and time to hit back in the centre with 4...Nf6 5.Qe2 d5, and Black is the one who ends up better.
8432999302569785|f1c4.principle: Recapturing in the centre with a piece keeps your central presence; leaving the pawn hands the opponent both material and central play.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. Nf3

843339252523142|d2d4.headline: Kick the b4 knight before opening the centre: 10.a3
843339252523142|d2d4.why: 10.d4 gives Black time to untangle: 10...Qf6 offers a queen trade, and after 11.Qe2 Kd7 the king walks to safety on c7, your attack is gone and Black is the one with the edge. 10.a3 attacks the knight on b4 first, and after 10...Na6 it no longer protects d5. Then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens the centre while Black's king is still on e6, and 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ wins a pawn with check.
843339252523142|d2d4.principle: In the Fried Liver your compensation is the exposed king, and it fades if you give it time; remove its defenders first, then open lines while the king is still in the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Nxd5/6. Nxf7/6...Kxf7

843339252523142|e1h1.headline: Keep the initiative: 10.a3 kicks the b4 knight before castling
843339252523142|e1h1.why: You are a piece for a pawn down, so every move must keep the pressure on the king on e6. 10.O-O lets Black regroup: 10...Qf6 offers a queen trade, 11.Qd1 avoids it, and after 11...Kd7 the king heads for safety and the extra piece starts to tell. 10.a3 hits the knight on b4, which retreats to a6, out of play; then 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.d4 opens lines against the king, and after 12...e4 13.Qxe4+ you have won a pawn back with check, the king is still exposed, and White keeps an edge.
843339252523142|e1h1.principle: After a sacrifice you have to keep attacking: make moves that create threats against the king or its defenders, or the extra piece decides the game.

8455496353401048|c1g5.headline: 6...Nf6 leaves f7 weak: 7.Ng5 hits it with knight and bishop
8455496353401048|c1g5.why: 7.Bg5 is natural development, but it lets Black play 7...Be7 and 8...O-O, and your gambit compensation is gone: Black is slightly better. After 6...Nf6 the f7 square is defended only by the king, and 7.Ng5 lines up the knight with the bishop on c4 against it. Black has to block the bishop with 7...d5, and 8.Nxd5 wins that pawn with a large advantage.
8455496353401048|c1g5.principle: While the opponent's king is still on e8, f7 is guarded only by the king; when a knight can join your c4 bishop against it, look at that first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3/3...dxc3/4. Nxc3

8465086871106005|f1d3.headline: Against the Philidor, strike with 3.d4 before developing the bishop
8465086871106005|f1d3.why: 3.Bd3 blocks White's own d-pawn, so White gives up the d4 break and Black develops at leisure, as in 3...Nf6 4.O-O Be7 5.Re1 O-O. 3.d4 is the main line, played in 88.8% of master games: it attacks e5 again and threatens to crack the centre open, and since the d6-pawn is pinned to the queen, Black can't comfortably recapture after dxe5 and must trade or defend at once.
8465086871106005|f1d3.principle: When Black defends e5 with a pawn, attack it again with your d-pawn before developing pieces that would block it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4

8471347538789945|c2c3.headline: 3.c3 doesn't defend e4: develop the bishop to d3
8471347538789945|c2c3.why: 2...Bb7 attacks e4, and 3.c3 is a pawn move that neither develops nor defends it: 3...Bxe4 wins the pawn, and after 4.c4 e6 5.Nc3 Bb7 you have spent two moves on the c-pawn and Black is better. 3.Bd3, the main move (68.7% of masters games), defends e4 and develops a piece at the same time, keeping your edge. 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 also defend the pawn.
8471347538789945|c2c3.principle: In the opening, make the pawn moves that free your pieces or hold the centre; a support move like c3 is pointless when a developing move can defend the pawn under attack.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3

8471347538789945|g1f3.headline: 2...Bb7 attacks e4: defend it with 3.Bd3 before anything else
8471347538789945|g1f3.why: The bishop on b7 hits e4 and nothing defends that pawn, so 3.Nf3 simply drops it to 3...Bxe4 and your clear edge turns into a worse position. 3.Bd3 is the main move (68.7% of masters games): it develops a piece and defends e4 at the same time, so you keep the two-pawn centre and your edge. 3.Nc3 and 3.Nd2 also defend the pawn.
8471347538789945|g1f3.principle: When the opponent's last move creates a threat, stop it first, ideally with a developing move, and only then continue your own plan.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...b6/2. d4/2...Bb7/3. Bd3

848566465308848|c8e6.headline: After 5.Nxe5, 5...Qd4 forks the knight and the e4 pawn.
848566465308848|c8e6.why: 5...Be6 leaves White simply a pawn up: after 6.d3 the e4 pawn is defended and the chance is gone. 5...Qd4 attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on e4 at once, and after 6.Nf3 Qxe4+ 7.Qe2 Black has the pawn back. This ...Qd4 fork is the standard answer when White takes on c6 and grabs e5 without first defending e4.
848566465308848|c8e6.principle: After White trades on c6 and takes on e5, check what is undefended: the knight and the e4 pawn can both be hit by one queen move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bb5/3...Nf6

8493377761529667|g8f6.headline: Challenge the g4 pawn with 2...h5 before putting a knight on f6
8493377761529667|g8f6.why: 2...Nf6 walks into White's plan: the theory notes that 2.Bg2 keeps the g-pawn ready to kick a knight on f6, and after 3.g5 Nh5 the knight sits on the rim and is later taken by 6.Bxh5. 2...h5 attacks the g4 pawn at once. After 3.gxh5 d5 Black takes the centre and White's kingside is left without its g-pawn.
8493377761529667|g8f6.principle: Don't develop a knight where an advancing pawn can kick it; first deal with the pawn that would chase it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. g4/1...e5

853185718049302|d4e5.headline: Keep the tension and develop: 5.Be3, not 5.dxe5
853185718049302|d4e5.why: 5.dxe5 dxe5 releases the tension on Black's terms: the e5 pawn is solid again, Black's bishop gets d6 (6...Bd6), and most of your advantage is gone. Black has made only pawn moves and a queen move, so keep adding pieces with 5.Be3. In the main line 5...Nc6 6.Nc3 Bg4 7.d5 drives the knight back with 7...Nb8, and 8.Nb5 followed by 9.Nxa7 wins a pawn.
853185718049302|d4e5.principle: When the opponent has spent the opening on pawn moves and an early queen, keep developing and let the central tension work for you instead of trading it off.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. Bc4

8545457925751746|d2d3.headline: Develop with 4.Nc3; Black's pawn moves have given you time
8545457925751746|d2d3.why: 4.d3 is too slow: 4...d5 hits the bishop on c4, and after 5.exd5 cxd5 6.Bb3 Black has a full pawn centre and the time lost on ...f6 and ...c6 no longer matters. 4.Nc3 develops a piece and adds a guard to d5, so the same break costs Black more: in the line Black needs 5...b5 and 6...b4 to dislodge the knight, more pawn moves, while White strikes in the centre with 8.d4.
8545457925751746|d2d3.principle: Black's ...f6 and ...c6 cost time, so answer with pieces and central breaks while you lead in development, not with quiet pawn moves.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...f6

8567362508613525|d2d4.headline: Push 6.a4 to chase the b6 bishop; 6.d4 drops a pawn
8567362508613525|d2d4.why: 6.d4 opens the centre too early: after 6...exd4 White does not get the pawn back, the refutation goes 7.Qb3 Qe7 8.O-O, and Black ends up better. 6.a4 uses the pawns you have already pushed: it threatens a5 to trap the bishop on b6, the plan the theory gives against this decline, so Black spends time on 6...a6 and 8...Ba7 while you castle and play 8.d3, keeping a slight edge.
8567362508613525|d2d4.principle: Your pawns on b4 and c3 already give you queenside space, so play on that wing with a4-a5 against the bishop on b6 instead of opening the centre for Black's pieces.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bb6

8573734277279845|g8f6.headline: Defend e5 with 2...Nc6; 2...Nf6 hits the queen but drops e5.
8573734277279845|g8f6.why: White threatens 3.Qxe5+, and 2...Nf6 attacks the queen without stopping it: 3.Qxe5+ Be7 wins the pawn with check. 2...Nc6 develops the knight and guards e5, and the queen on h5 remains a target that Black later gains time on, as in 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.Qd1.
8573734277279845|g8f6.principle: Before attacking the queen, check White's own forcing moves: a capture with check on e5 comes first.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e3/1...e5

8583587100088489|c6d4.headline: Defend e5 with 5...d6; 5...Nd4 lets 6.Nxe5 take a pawn.
8583587100088489|c6d4.why: 5...Nd4 removes e5's only defender, so 6.Nxe5 takes the pawn, and White's knight and bishop then combine against f7, as in 8.Nxf7 Rxf7 9.Bxf7+. 5...d6 defends e5 with a pawn and opens Black's light-squared bishop, keeping the solid Giuoco structure.
8583587100088489|c6d4.principle: Before moving a piece, check what it was defending: the knight on c6 is the only guard of the e5 pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. O-O

8640031168129389|f3g5.headline: Don't raid with Ng5; castle and prepare c3 and d4
8640031168129389|f3g5.why: 4.Ng5 moves the knight a second time with two minor pieces still at home. Black answers 4...e6, shutting the bishop on c4 off from f7, then 5...h6 drives the knight back to f3 and 6...d5 gains time on the bishop, which is exactly the ...e6 and ...d5 plan the theory gives Black against the Bowdler Attack. 4.O-O, the top master move (35.7%), keeps the knight in the centre and prepares 5.Re1, 6.c3 and 7.d4 to build a pawn centre.
8640031168129389|f3g5.principle: Every knight trip to g5 and back hands Black two free moves; spend them on castling and on c3 and d4 instead.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Bc4

8645343577179290|g7g6.headline: Shut the c4 bishop's diagonal with 7...e6 before e5 opens lines
8645343577179290|g7g6.why: 7...g6 leaves the bishop on c4 aiming straight at f7, and after 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.e5 Ng4 10.Re1 d5 11.Nxd5 cxd5 12.Bxd5 the centre blows open around your uncastled king and White is clearly better. Theory notes that against the Sozin bishop Black almost always answers with ...e6, closing its diagonal toward f7. With 7...e6 the bishop bites on a pawn, and after 8.Nxc6 bxc6 9.Re1 e5 White has to retreat it with 10.Bf1, and the game stays roughly level.
8645343577179290|g7g6.principle: With your king still in the centre and a bishop aimed at f7, block that diagonal before you spend time on a kingside fianchetto.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nf6/5. Nc3/5...a6/6. Bc4

8671130214522057|b1a3.headline: After 5...Na5, save the bishop with check: 6.Bb5+.
8671130214522057|b1a3.why: 5...Na5 attacks the bishop on c4, and 6.Na3 does nothing about it while dropping a knight to 6...Bxa3; after 7.Bb5+ c6 8.dxc6 bxc6 White is simply a piece down. 6.Bb5+ moves the attacked bishop away with check, so Black must answer it first, and after 6...c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Bd3 the bishop is safe and White keeps the pawn won on move five. Masters choose 6.Bb5+ in 97.6% of games.
8671130214522057|b1a3.principle: When a piece is attacked, look first for a move that saves it with check, so your opponent has to react instead of grabbing something else.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Na5

8671130214522057|d1e2.headline: Save the bishop with check: 6.Bb5+
8671130214522057|d1e2.why: 5...Na5 attacks the bishop on c4, and 6.Qe2 doesn't save it: after 6...Nxc4 7.Qxc4 Qxd5 Black wins back the pawn, and after 8.Qxd5 Nxd5 it is Black who has the easier game. 6.Bb5+ moves the attacked bishop with check, so Black must block with 6...c6, and after 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Bd3 White stays a pawn up. Masters play it in almost every game.
8671130214522057|d1e2.principle: When a piece is attacked, move it with a check if you can, so the opponent must answer you instead of following up.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Na5

8671130214522057|g5f7.headline: Save the attacked bishop with check: 6.Bb5+
8671130214522057|g5f7.why: 6.Nxf7 is a Fried Liver idea that fails here: after 6...Kxf7 White is a knight for a pawn down, and the bishop on c4 is still attacked by the knight on a5, so it must retreat with 7.Be2 and Black takes back 7...Qxd5. 6.Bb5+, played in 97.6% of master games, moves the bishop out of danger with check, so Black has no time for 6...Nxc4. After 6...c6 7.dxc6 bxc6 8.Bd3 White is still a pawn up and Black plays for development in return.
8671130214522057|g5f7.principle: When a piece is attacked, look for a check that moves it to safety, so you keep the tempo instead of losing it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Nf6/4. Ng5/4...d5/5. exd5/5...Na5

8673706909167185|c1a3.headline: Castle and open lines: 8.O-O, then e5 and Rd1
8673706909167185|c1a3.why: 8.Ba3 does nothing about the d4 pawn: 8...dxc3 opens the position for Black, and after 9.O-O Nge7 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 your bishop has been traded off and Black is clearly better. 8.O-O, the only move in the 63 master games, gets the king safe and brings the rook toward the centre. In the main line 8...d3 9.e5 drives the queen away with tempo, and after 10.Rd1 Nge7 11.Bxd3 you win back a pawn, with 12.Ba3 still to come.
8673706909167185|c1a3.principle: In the Evans your pawns buy a lead in development: castle and open lines with e5 and the rook on the d-file before Black can untangle.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...Bc5/4. b4/4...Bxb4/5. c3/5...Ba5/6. d4

8692601699406729|d7d5.headline: Don't open the centre behind in development: play 5...Qc7
8692601699406729|d7d5.why: 5...d5 opens the position while White has more pieces out: after 6.exd5 exd5 the d5 pawn is attacked by the c3 knight, 7.Bb5 pins the knight on c6, and once 7...Bd7 blocks the queen's defence of d5, 8.Nxd5 wins the pawn. 5...Qc7 is the main move (65.6% of master games): the queen takes a safe square with good scope, and Black develops the queenside first with ...a6, ...b5 and ...Bb7, keeping a normal Sicilian.
8692601699406729|d7d5.principle: When the opponent has more pieces developed, keep the centre closed and finish developing before you play the freeing pawn break.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6
Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6/5. Nc3/5...Qc7

8692601699406729|g8e7.headline: Keep d6 covered: 5...Qc7, not a knight that blocks your bishop
8692601699406729|g8e7.why: 5...Nge7 shuts in the f8 bishop, the only piece guarding the hole on d6 that 2...e6 left, so 6.Ndb5 threatens mate on d6. After 6...Ng6 7.Nd6+ Bxd6 8.Qxd6 Qe7 9.Qxe7+ Kxe7 you have lost the bishop pair and the right to castle, and White is clearly better. 5...Qc7, the Bastrikov, puts the queen on a safe square with good scope where it also watches d6, and Black continues with queenside development, ...a6 and ...b5, as in 6.Be3 a6 7.Qf3 b5; masters choose it 65.6% of the time.
8692601699406729|g8e7.principle: In the ...e6 Sicilians, know that d6 is the square White's knights want, and develop so that it stays covered rather than blocking the bishop that guards it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...e6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Nxd4/4...Nc6
