8698679373330427|c8f5.headline: 3.Bf4 leaves c4 hanging: take it with 3...dxc4
8698679373330427|c8f5.why: After 3...Bf5 4.Nc3 Qb6 5.Qd2 Nf6 6.f3 h6 7.e3 e6 8.g4 White gains kingside space and chases your bishop, and the edge passes to White. 3.Bf4 develops a piece but leaves c4 behind: the c4 pawn is attacked once and not defended at all, with the f1 bishop still shut in by the e2 pawn. 3...dxc4 wins it, and after 4.g3 Nf6 5.Nf3 Nd5 6.Bd2 b5 your queenside pawns hold the extra pawn; masters take on c4 45.2% of the time.
8698679373330427|c8f5.principle: When your opponent leaves a pawn en prise and you can support it afterwards, take it: in the Slav the c6 pawn already backs up ...b5.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6

8700918547269120|e2e3.headline: Kick the early bishop with 4.Ne5 instead of the quiet 4.e3
8700918547269120|e2e3.why: 4.e3 lets Black finish the setup in peace: after 4...e6 5.h3 Bh5 6.Qb3 Qb6 the pawn on b7 is covered and the bishop sits comfortably outside Black's pawn chain. 3...Bg4 put the bishop where the knight on f3 can hit it from e5, a square the theory says 3.Nf3 was aimed at. 4.Ne5 attacks it at once, and in the line it goes all the way back with 4...Bc8, so Black has spent two moves on the bishop for nothing. White uses the time to open the centre with 5.cxd5 cxd5 6.e4, even giving a pawn to get ahead in development.
8700918547269120|e2e3.principle: When the opponent develops a piece where you can attack it, hit it at once: every retreat is a move you get to spend on the centre.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...c6/3. Nf3

8706009982340637|b2b3.headline: Black's queen eyes e5: never open the long diagonal to a1
8706009982340637|b2b3.why: 5.b3 opens the long diagonal to the rook on a1, and 5...Qe5+ checks the king and attacks the rook at once; after 6.Be2 Qxa1 White is a rook down. In this Modern Scandinavian Black's queen reached d5 without losing time, so White should claim the centre with 5.d4 and open the bishop on c1 instead of handing her targets. It is the most popular master move here (38.2%).
8706009982340637|b2b3.principle: With Black's queen in the centre, look at her checks before any quiet move: ...Qe5+ is always available, so keep the rook on a1 off her lines.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Nf6

8716466597702343|b1c3.headline: Take the gambit pawn: 3.dxe6 keeps you a pawn up
8716466597702343|b1c3.why: 2...e6 hits your d5 pawn, and 3.Nc3 lets Black recapture with 3...exd5: material is level again and so is the game. 3.dxe6 removes the attacker and takes a second pawn; after 3...Bxe6 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 you are a clean pawn up with normal development. The theory rates 2...e6 an inferior gambit that does not give enough for the pawn.
8716466597702343|b1c3.principle: Accept a gambit when you can develop normally afterwards: here Nf3 and d4 come easily, so take on e6 and keep the extra pawn.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

8716466597702343|c2c4.headline: Take the second pawn with 3.dxe6; 3.c4 doesn't hold d5
8716466597702343|c2c4.why: 3.c4 doesn't stop Black from winning the pawn back: after 3...exd5 4.cxd5 Nf6 the d5 pawn stands alone and Black has easy development. 3.dxe6 simply takes: after 3...Bxe6 White is a clean pawn up, and 4.Nf3 and 5.d4 build a solid centre. Theory rates the 2...e6 gambit as not giving enough for the pawn.
8716466597702343|c2c4.principle: Accept a gambit pawn when you can consolidate; capturing the attacker leaves no weak pawn for Black to win back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

8716466597702343|d2d4.headline: Take the gambit pawn with 3.dxe6: 2...e6 gives too little
8716466597702343|d2d4.why: Black threatens 3...exd5 to win the pawn back, and 3.d4 does nothing about it: after 3.d4 exd5 you reach a symmetrical, quiet position where queens can come off with 6.Qe2+ Qe7 7.Qxe7+ Kxe7, and most of your advantage is gone. Theory lists 2...e6 among the Scandinavian gambits that are inferior and don't give enough for the pawn. 3.dxe6 Bxe6 simply keeps the extra pawn, and after 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.d4 you are developed and a clean pawn up.
8716466597702343|d2d4.principle: When an unsound gambit offers you a pawn that you can keep without danger, take it and develop; giving it back only hands your opponent the equality they gambled for.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5

8733953429179306|c6e5.headline: Don't move the knight twice; develop with 4...Nf6
8733953429179306|c6e5.why: 4...Ne5 moves the knight a second time with three minor pieces still at home, and after 5.Qg3 it has to go back with 5...Nc6, so Black has spent two moves for nothing; 6.Bd2 d5 7.exd5 then leaves Black a pawn down. 4...Nf6 develops the other knight toward the centre and pressures e4, and Black continues with ...Bc5 and castling.
8733953429179306|c6e5.principle: Attacking a queen that can simply step aside with tempo is not worth a second knight move; bring out a new piece instead.

8751595729469873|c1a3.headline: Hit the queen first: 9.e5 gains time before 10.Nxc3
8751595729469873|c1a3.why: 9.Ba3 aims at e7 to keep Black's king in the centre, but 9...Nge7 blocks the diagonal, and after 10.Bxe7 Qxe7 11.Nxc3 O-O Black has castled and keeps their extra pawns with the better game. 9.e5 attacks the queen on f6 first, so after 9...Qg6 you recapture with 10.Nxc3 having gained a tempo, and your e5 pawn takes f6 away from Black's knight, which has to develop with 10...Nge7; White keeps a small edge.
8751595729469873|c1a3.principle: Develop with threats: a pawn move that hits the queen lets you win back material with gain of time, while a quiet bishop move gives Black the time to block and castle.

877042167833906|c1f4.headline: Grab the centre with 5.e4 while Black spends time on 4...a6
877042167833906|c1f4.why: 5.Bf4 doesn't touch the c4 pawn, and Black uses the time for 5...b5; after 6.a4 b4 the knight is driven to the rim with 7.Na2 and Black keeps the extra pawn. 5.e4, the masters' main move (67% of 1038 games), builds the pawn centre that 3...Nf6 was meant to prevent, and after 5...b5 6.e5 Nd5 7.a4 e6 8.axb5 White wins the pawn back.
877042167833906|c1f4.principle: When the opponent spends moves holding on to a gambit pawn on the wing, take the centre: the space and time let you win the pawn back later.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...d5/2. c4/2...dxc4/3. Nf3/3...Nf6

8832130732345993|f1d3.headline: Kick the knight with 4.e5 instead of leaving d4 to fall
8832130732345993|f1d3.why: 4.Bd3 blocks your queen's defence of d4: after 4...dxe4 5.Nxe4 Qxd4 Black simply takes the d-pawn. 3...Nf6 put the knight where your e-pawn can reach it, and 4.e5 punishes that: the pawn gains space and sends the knight back to g8, so Black's last move was wasted. The game turns into an Advance Caro-Kann with a closed centre, which Black was probably hoping to avoid.
8832130732345993|f1d3.principle: A knight on f6 in front of your e-pawn is a target: push the pawn to gain space and send the knight back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4/2...d5/3. Nc3

8832130732345993|f2f3.headline: Gain space with 4.e5; 4.f3 doesn't hold e4.
8832130732345993|f2f3.why: Black threatens 4...dxe4, winning a pawn, and 4.f3 doesn't stop it: after 4...dxe4 5.fxe4 e5 Black hits the centre, and once the queens come off with 6.dxe5 Qxd1+ 7.Nxd1 Nxe4 Black's knight on e4 is active and White's kingside is loosened by the f-pawn. 4.e5 claims the centre and attacks the knight on f6, which has to go back with 4...Ng8, and White develops comfortably with 5.Bd3.
8832130732345993|f2f3.principle: When an enemy knight on f6 sits in front of your e-pawn, advance the pawn to gain space and drive the knight back.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c6/2. d4

8849788781204745|g7g6.headline: Don't open the long diagonal: 7...g6 loses the h8 rook
8849788781204745|g7g6.why: Your g7 pawn is the only thing between the queen on d4 and the rook on h8. 7...g6 opens that diagonal and 8.Qxh8 wins the rook, which decides the game. 7...Nf6, the usual move (82.2% of master games), develops and keeps the diagonal shut; after 8.Bg5 e6 you follow with ...Be7 and castle, with a normal, roughly level game.
8849788781204745|g7g6.principle: Before each pawn move, look at the captures it allows: moving the g-pawn here opens the d4-h8 diagonal straight to an undefended rook.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. Nf3/2...d6/3. d4/3...cxd4/4. Qxd4

8865411260070790|g8f6.headline: Avoid 3...Nf6 4.e5: hit the centre with 3...c5 first
8865411260070790|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 lets White kick the knight straight back home with 4.e5 Ng8, and in the engine line White plays 5.d4 and keeps building with extra space. The theory explains why: in this setup Black needs ...d6 first to prevent e5. 3...c5 fights for d4 instead, and after 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 Nc6 Black develops with a half-open c-file, and 6...Nf6 comes safely.
8865411260070790|g8f6.principle: Don't put a knight on f6 while White can push e5 and chase it; control the centre first so the knight can't be kicked.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

8877803564094104|d2d3.headline: Stop ...Ng4 with 6.h3: the Stafford aims at f2
8877803564094104|d2d3.why: In the Stafford, Black gives up a pawn to open lines for the bishop on c5 and a knight jump to g4, both aimed at f2. 6.d3 develops but doesn't stop it: 6...Ng4 7.Be3 Nxe3 8.fxe3 Bxe3 wins the pawn back and plants the bishop deep in your camp, leaving Black better. 6.h3 takes g4 away first, and after 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 Qe5 8.d3 you keep the extra pawn in a sound position.
8877803564094104|d2d3.principle: Ask what your opponent's gambit is aiming at and take that square away first, as h3 does against ...Ng4, then develop.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nf6/3. Nxe5

8877803564094104|d2d4.headline: 6.h3 stops ...Ng4 and keeps your extra pawn
8877803564094104|d2d4.why: Black's bishop on c5 already aims at f2, and 6...Ng4 would add the knight and win a pawn. 6.d4 hits the bishop, but it simply takes, 6...Bxd4, and Black has the pawn back with a level game. 6.h3 takes g4 away from the knight and you stay a pawn up; Black's queen comes out with 6...Qd4 7.Qf3 Qe5, but after 8.d3 Bd4 9.Nd1 the queens come off with 10...Qxg3 and you keep the extra pawn.
8877803564094104|d2d4.principle: Ask what your opponent wants: here everything Black has aims at ...Ng4 and f2, so one small pawn move that takes g4 away keeps the pawn you won.

8979060161382028|e4e5.headline: Defend e4 with 3.Nc3; pushing 3.e5 just gets the pawn traded.
8979060161382028|e4e5.why: 3.e5 gains nothing here, because the pawn on d6 simply takes it: after 3...dxe5 4.Nxe5 Nbd7 White's knight is chased again by 5.Nc4 b5, and Black develops with gain of time. 3.Nc3 defends the pawn on e4 against 3...Nxe4 while developing a knight toward the centre. After 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4 White gets an open game with quick development, and masters play 3.Nc3 in 82.6% of games.
8979060161382028|e4e5.principle: Defend an attacked centre pawn with a developing piece, so the defence also brings a new piece into play.

8979060161382028|f1c4.headline: Defend e4 while developing: 3.Nc3, not 3.Bc4
8979060161382028|f1c4.why: 3.Bc4 develops but leaves the pawn on e4 attacked by the knight on f6 and defended by nothing, so 3...Nxe4 wins it, and after 4.d4 Nf6 Black is simply a pawn up. 3.Nc3, the master choice in 82.6% of games, develops the knight and defends e4 in one move. Black can then transpose into an Open Sicilian with 3...c5 4.d4 cxd4 5.Nxd4, as the theory notes.
8979060161382028|f1c4.principle: Before each developing move, check what is loose: with Black's knight on f6 attacking e4, choose the developing move that also guards it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d6/2. Nf3

8999636484543636|g8f6.headline: Guard e5 with 4...Nc6; 4...Nf6 blocks the g7 bishop
8999636484543636|g8f6.why: The g7 bishop is the only thing guarding e5, and 4...Nf6 cuts it off, so 5.Nxe5 wins the pawn. 4...Nc6 develops the knight toward the centre and defends e5 directly, so your pawn holds and the bishop keeps watching the long diagonal.
8999636484543636|g8f6.principle: Count the defenders of a pawn before every move: a move that blocks the only defender's line leaves the pawn hanging.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...g6

922389477039223|d2d3.headline: Cover d4 with 4.Ne2 before Black's knight jumps in.
922389477039223|d2d3.why: Black threatens 4...Nd4, winning a pawn, and 4.d3 doesn't stop it: the knight hits the queen on f3, and after 5.Qd1 White has lost time while Black gains space with ...d5. 4.Ne2 develops the knight and covers d4, so White continues calmly with d3 and Nbc3, as in 4...Na5 5.d3 d6 6.Nbc3.
922389477039223|d2d3.principle: Ask which square the opponent's knight wants next to attack your early queen, and develop a piece that covers it.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Bc4/2...Nc6

950795499557785|f7f6.headline: Release the tension with 4...exd4, then develop the knight
950795499557785|f7f6.why: White threatens 5.dxe5, and 4...f6 holds e5 at a cost: it takes f6 from the g8 knight and opens the diagonal from c4 toward your king. In the engine line White castles, plays 7.dxe5 dxe5 anyway and lands a knight on d5 with 8.Nd5. 4...exd4 trades the attacked pawn off; after 5.Nxd4 Nf6 your knight develops to its natural square and the f8 bishop comes out next.
950795499557785|f7f6.principle: Defend a centre pawn with pieces or trade it off; a defending pawn move like ...f6 blocks your own development and weakens your king.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...d6

953559814433764|g8f6.headline: Cover f7 before you chase the queen
953559814433764|g8f6.why: 3...Nf6 attacks the queen but leaves f7 guarded only by the king, and 4.Qxf7# is Scholar's Mate on the spot. 3...g6 blocks the queen's path to f7 and attacks it at the same time, so White has to spend another move on the queen; after 4.Qf3 Nf6 Black develops with ...Bg7 and castles.
953559814433764|g8f6.principle: When a queen and a bishop both aim at f7, the king is its only defender, so first check that f7 is still covered before making any attacking move.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Qh5/2...Nc6/3. Bc4

953559814433764|g8h6.headline: Block the mate and attack the queen with g6
953559814433764|g8h6.why: 3...Nh6 does stop 4.Qxf7#, but it puts the knight on the rim, where it neither controls the centre nor gains time, and White keeps a comfortable game with 4.Nc3. 3...g6 blocks the mate and attacks the queen at the same time; White has to move it again with 4.Qf3, and Black develops with 4...Nf6 and ...Bg7.
953559814433764|g8h6.principle: Meet an early queen attack with a move that both defends and hits the queen, so the defence also wins time.

956431266193433|d2d3.headline: Hit the e5 queen with 5.Nf3 instead of a pawn move
956431266193433|d2d3.why: 5.d3 is a quiet pawn move that lets Black catch up: 5...Bg4 6.Be3 Bxe2 7.Qxe2 Nf6 and your edge is gone. As the theory notes say, the early queen check achieves little and the queen will have to move again. 5.Nf3 develops the knight toward the centre and attacks the queen on e5; after 5...Qd6 6.d4 e6 7.Nb5 Qd8 she has been driven all the way home while you developed, and you keep a clear edge.
956431266193433|d2d3.principle: When the opponent's queen comes out early, develop with moves that attack it; every tempo she spends running is a developing move you gain.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3

961430540554751|c1e3.headline: Ask the g4 bishop at once: 6.h3 before Black develops
961430540554751|c1e3.why: 6.Be3 gives Black time for 6...Nf6, and when h3 comes a move later the bishop escapes with 7...Bh5 8.g4 Bg6, exactly the retreat route the theory describes, and White's edge shrinks. 6.h3, played in 84.2% of master games, hits the bishop on g4 while it still has to decide: 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 gives you the bishop pair and an active queen, then 8.Bd2 unpins the knight on c3 and 9.O-O-O follows.
961430540554751|c1e3.principle: A bishop that pawns can attack is a target: kick it with the h-pawn right away, before Black's development lets it retreat to a safe square for free.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

961430540554751|f1e2.headline: Question the g4 bishop with 6.h3 and take the bishop pair
961430540554751|f1e2.why: 6.Be2 is passive: Black continues 6...Nd7 and trades off the light-squared bishop with 7...Bxe2, and half of your advantage is gone. 6.h3, the choice in 84.2% of master games, puts the question to the bishop at once. After 6...Bxf3 7.Qxf3 you have the bishop pair and an active queen, and 8.Bd2 and 9.O-O-O follow; if the bishop retreats instead, the theory notes it gets chased to g6.
961430540554751|f1e2.principle: Create imbalances that favour you: forcing the bishop to take on f3 gives you the bishop pair in an open position, while a passive bishop move lets Black swap off a piece cheaply.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...d5/2. exd5/2...Qxd5/3. Nc3/3...Qa5

962560137426404|a7a6.headline: Use the centre fork trick: 4...Nxe4 beats slow moves like ...a6
962560137426404|a7a6.why: 4...a6 spends a move on the edge while White's pieces are ready: 5.Ng5 threatens to win a pawn on f7, and in the game line 5.d4 exd4 6.Nxd4 White opens the centre with Black a step behind. 4...Nxe4 is the centre fork trick: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and Black regains the piece with 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4, having removed White's centre pawn and equalised.
962560137426404|a7a6.principle: Check forcing moves before quiet ones: with White's bishop on c4 and knight on c3 both within reach of a pawn push, a capture on e4 sets up a fork.

962560137426404|d7d6.headline: Use the centre fork trick: 4...Nxe4 and 5...d5
962560137426404|d7d6.why: 4...d6 is too slow: White answers 5.Ng5, hitting f7 with knight and bishop, and after 5...d5 6.exd5 Black is simply a pawn down. 4...Nxe4 is the centre fork trick: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and Black wins the piece back with 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4. Black has removed White's central e-pawn and equalised, which is why masters avoid 4.Bc4 here.
962560137426404|d7d6.principle: When an enemy bishop on c4 and knight on c3 can both be hit by one pawn push, look at the capture that sets it up before any quiet move.

962560137426404|d8e7.headline: Use the fork trick 4...Nxe4 to take White's centre pawn
962560137426404|d8e7.why: 4...Qe7 brings the queen out with two minor pieces still at home and shuts in the f8 bishop. In the engine line White develops around it and hits the queen with 9.Nd5. 4...Nxe4 is only a temporary sacrifice: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 leaves Black with the piece back and a good foothold in the centre.
962560137426404|d8e7.principle: Look at captures before quiet moves: a capture on e4 is safe when a pawn fork wins the piece back.

962560137426404|h7h6.headline: Use the fork trick 4...Nxe4 instead of the slow 4...h6
962560137426404|h7h6.why: 4...h6 stops 5.Ng5 but spends a move on a pawn that neither develops nor fights for the centre. White uses the time to open the centre with 5.d4, and in the engine line 8.e5 hits your f6 knight. 4...Nxe4 is only a temporary sacrifice: after 5.Nxe4 d5 the pawn forks knight and bishop, and 6.Bd3 dxe4 7.Bxe4 leaves Black with the piece back and a good foothold in the centre.
962560137426404|h7h6.principle: Prefer a forcing move that fights for the centre over a pawn move that only prevents something.

966581453995947|c8g4.headline: Win the pawn back with 6...Bxf2+ and 7...Qd4+
966581453995947|c8g4.why: 6...Bg4 puts the bishop on a square the e5 knight covers, and 7.Nxg4 simply takes it. 6...Bxf2+ uses forcing moves instead: after 7.Kxf2 Qd4+ the queen checks the king and hits the e5 knight, and 8.Kf1 Qxe5 regains the pawn. White's king has also lost the right to castle.
966581453995947|c8g4.principle: When your opponent's pieces are loose, look at checks first: a check that also attacks an undefended piece often wins material back.

966581453995947|d8d4.headline: Check first with 6...Bxf2+, then fork with 7...Qd4.
966581453995947|d8d4.why: Here the knight on c3 guards e4, so 6...Qd4 only threatens the knight, and 7.Nd3 covers f2 and attacks the bishop on c5, leaving Black a pawn down. 6...Bxf2+ drags the king out first: after 7.Kxf2 Qd4+ the queen checks the king and hits the knight on e5 at once, and 8...Qxe5 wins a pawn. White's king also loses the right to castle.
966581453995947|d8d4.principle: When a quiet attack can be parried, look for a check that sets up the same attack with tempo.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Nc3/3...Bc5

972282943199495|g1f3.headline: 3...d6 declines the gambit: take back with 4.cxd4
972282943199495|g1f3.why: With 3...d6 Black declines the Smith-Morra, and the pawn on d4 is attacked twice and defended by nothing. 4.Nf3 lets Black accept after all: after 4...dxc3 5.Nxc3 you are a pawn down in a gambit with no edge left. 4.cxd4 (98.7% of masters games) wins the pawn back and gives you the ideal two-pawn centre with pawns on e4 and d4, and a clear edge.
972282943199495|g1f3.principle: When your opponent declines your gambit, recover the pawn and take the centre; do not keep offering material you no longer need to give.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...c5/2. d4/2...cxd4/3. c3

977859217629606|e4e5.headline: Guard e4 with 11.Re1; 11.e5 runs into ...d6
977859217629606|e4e5.why: 10...Nf6 hits your e4 pawn, but 11.e5 overreaches: 11...d6 attacks your queen on c5 and the e5 pawn together, and after 12.Qb5 a6 13.Qb3 dxe5 Black has won the pawn and most of your advantage is gone. 11.Re1 defends e4 by bringing the rook to the e-file, where Black's king still stands on e8. After 11...d6 12.Qb5 Bd7 13.Qb3 Qe7 14.Nxc3 you pick up the c3 pawn while developing and keep a clear advantage.
977859217629606|e4e5.principle: Before pushing a pawn, check whether a counter-push can hit it and a loose piece of yours at once; here your queen on c5 makes ...d6 a double attack.

983258444083142|b1c3.headline: Kick the f6 knight with 7.e5 and gain time
983258444083142|b1c3.why: 7.Nc3 is a natural developing move, but it gives Black time for 7...d6 and ...Be7, and more than half of your advantage slips away. 6...Nf6 put the knight where your e-pawn can hit it: 7.e5 gains space with tempo, and in the main line the knight retreats with 7...Nh7, the poor square that ...h6 made available. Then 8.Nc3 and 9.Ne4 bring your knight to 10.Nd6+, and after 10...Bxd6 11.Qxd6 your queen sits deep in Black's camp while the king is still in the centre.
983258444083142|b1c3.principle: When an enemy piece can be attacked by a pawn or piece that also improves your position, do that first, so the opponent spends the move retreating instead of developing.
sources: Chess Opening Theory/1. e4/1...e5/2. Nf3/2...Nc6/3. Bc4/3...h6

987839445230107|e7e6.headline: Hit White's two-pawn centre at once with 3...e5
987839445230107|e7e6.why: 3...e6 is too slow: White takes back the pawn with 4.Bxc4 and keeps a broad pawn centre without having lost any time. 3...e5 attacks White's centre at once and opens the dark-squared bishop's diagonal. White has to answer 4.Nf3, because 4.Bxc4 is met by 4...Qxd4 and 4.dxe5 by 4...Qxd1, both forcing queen trades that suit Black.
987839445230107|e7e6.principle: When White builds a two-pawn centre, strike at it with your own centre pawn at once instead of preparing slowly.

987839445230107|f7f6.headline: Strike back at White's centre with e5
987839445230107|f7f6.why: 3...f6 does nothing for the c4 pawn, which falls to 4.Bxc4, and it weakens the diagonal toward your king that 8.Qh5+ exploits later in that line. 3...e5 attacks White's centre and opens the dark-squared bishop, and White can't grab the pawn back at once: 4.Bxc4 runs into 4...Qxd4, and 4.dxe5 into 4...Qxd1.
987839445230107|f7f6.principle: When White builds a big centre with two pawns, strike at it with a central pawn rather than making flank pawn moves.

991686180194659|e2e4.headline: Cover e4 with 4.Nc3 before pushing the pawn there
991686180194659|e2e4.why: 4.e4 puts a pawn on a square the knight on f6 attacks and nothing defends, so 4...Nxe4 wins it. 4.Nc3 develops the knight and covers e4 first; after 4...Bg7 White plays 5.e4 and builds the big centre the King's Indian allows. 77.2% of masters play it.
991686180194659|e2e4.principle: Before pushing a pawn to a square, count: e4 is attacked by the knight on f6, so it needs a defender first.
